Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 36 Filed 08/27/26 Page 1 of 6 Pagellb#s7s
8/27/2026

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD

The Honorable Judge
Ivan D. Davis

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

PLAINTIFE’S REPLY IN SUPPORT OF HIS MOTION FOR LEAVE
TO SERVE LIMITED DISCOVERY UNDER RULE 26(d)(1)

INTRODUCTION

NCMEC moves to dismiss on the ground that its statements are true. It then opposes the
three interrogatories that would test that ground. NCMEC cannot both assert the truth of the records
it holds and forbid Plaintiff from learning what those records say. Three questions decide the

Motion.

ARGUMENT
I. Why Do These Three Answers Matter?

Because NCMEC moves to dismiss on the ground that “[t]he Statements are True, and Thus
Not Actionable,” and because NCMEC’s own Motion does not say what the underlying reports

identify. That omission controls this dispute.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 36 Filed 08/27/26 Page 2 of 6 PagelD# 380

NCMEC states that the CyberTipline linkage could concern Plaintiff, could concern “a
person with the same name,” or could concern an email address. Those are three different facts.
The April 22 letters join Plaintiff’s legal name, the name Plaintiff uses, and Plaintiff’s email
identifier with the connector “and/or.” The letters do not say which identifier appeared in either
report as NCMEC originally received it.

The three interrogatories ask that one question.

The question is not speculative. Plaintiff has declared, under penalty of perjury, that he
never used “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to identify or operate a Meta account. Plaintiff declared that he
used “Jay Ballentine.” Plaintiff declared that his full legal name appeared in the April 9 materials
because it was his legal and litigation name. Interrogatory No. 1 asks whether “Marvelle J.
Ballentine” appeared in either CyberTipline report as NCMEC originally received it, or whether
that name entered only through Plaintiff’s later litigation materials.

Plaintiff does not seek discovery to learn whether he has a claim. Plaintiff seeks three
source-level facts. Those facts test a truth defense NCMEC has already asked the Court to decide.

II. Why Are the Answers Needed Now?

Because NCMEC asks the Court to decide the truth of its statements now, and truth cannot
be decided against Plaintiff without the records these answers identify.

Truth is an affirmative defense. It supports dismissal at the pleading stage only when it
appears on the face of the Complaint. It does not appear here. It depends on the contents of two
CyberTipline reports that exist nowhere in the record and that only NCMEC holds. NCMEC
confirms this. NCMEC states that Plaintiff “simply cannot possibly know” what those reports
contain, and asks the Court to dismiss on that basis. NCMEC’s own Motion supplies three different

possibilities in answer to that question. It states the linkage could concern Plaintiff, a person of the

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 36 Filed 08/27/26 Page 3 of 6 PagelD# 381

same name, or an email address. A truth defense cannot be granted while the defendant’s own
submission leaves the identifying fact in three versions, only one of which makes the
representation true as to Plaintiff. The three answers resolve which version the source records
contain.

That produces two paths, and both require these answers before any ruling.

If the Court decides truth on the pleadings, the defense fails now. The defense does not
appear on the face of the Complaint. The discovery is not premature.

If the Court instead weighs the reports NCMEC invokes, Rule 12(d) converts the Motion to
one for summary judgment, and Rule 56(d) entitles Plaintiff to the limited discovery needed to
respond. These three answers are that discovery, and no more.

The prejudice is definite. Without these answers, a dispositive ruling would decide the truth
of NCMEC’s statements against Plaintiff before Plaintiff could obtain the records on which truth
depends. That is the unusual circumstance Rule 26(d)(1) addresses. The answers are needed now
because the ruling NCMEC seeks comes now.

III. Why Is This Particular Discovery Appropriate?

Because the discovery is limited to the information NCMEC has made material.

The Motion seeks three interrogatories about two identified records. Each interrogatory
permits one of three answers: “Yes,” “No,” or “Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry.” The
interrogatories seek no reports. They seek no narratives, no provider identities, no victim
information, no dates, no report numbers, and no metadata. They seek no general discovery. They
exclude Plaintiff-supplied information, court filings, and public sources. They exclude information

obtained or added after NCMEC originally received the reports.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 36 Filed 08/27/26 Page 4 of 6 PagelD# 382

NCMEC identifies no burden. NCMEC identifies no expense. NCMEC identifies no
disclosure of protected report content that the three answers would cause. NCMEC’s objection is
categorical instead: no discovery before Rule 26(f), “regardless of how limited” the request.

Rule 26(d)(1) permits the Court to authorize discovery before the conference. The
discovery here is three closed answers about two records. NCMEC made those records material to
a defense it asks the Court to decide now.

The Motion should be granted.

Date: August 27, 2026 Respectfully submitted,

>

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847
Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503
jayballentine@protonmail.com

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD                  Document 39           Filed 08/31/26         Page 1 of 9 PageID# 389




                              IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
                             FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
                                         Alexandria Division


  MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE.,                                       )
                                                                 )
                    Plaintiff,                                   )
                                                                 ) Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
                             v.                                  )
                                                                 )
  KATIE HALL, NATIONAL                                           )
  CENTER FOR MISSING &                                           )
  EXPLOITED CHILDREN;                                            )
  META PLATFORMS, INC. and                                       )
  JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,                                            )
                                                                 )
                    Defendants.                                  )


         REPLY MEMORANDUM OF LAW IN SUPPORT OF DEFENDANT META
       PLATFORMS, INC.’S MOTION TO DISMISS PLAINTIFF’S FIRST AMENDED
                                COMPLAINT

      I.       INTRODUCTION

           Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc.’s (“Meta”) Motion to Dismiss (“Motion” or “Mot.”)

  established that Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) should be dismissed because it fails

  to plausibly allege either his 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) (“Section 1985(2)”) or his common law

  conspiracy claims. Plaintiff’s “Protective Opposition1” (“Opposition” or “Opp.”) fails to

  meaningfully contest any of the grounds for dismissal, instead largely re-iterating the vague and

  confusing allegations of a conspiracy from the FAC.

           First, the Opposition fails to identify any specific allegations in the FAC showing that Meta

  and co-Defendants National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) and Katie Hall

  (together the “NCMEC Defendants”) reached an agreement to deter Plaintiff from pursuing his


  1
   Plaintiff styled his Opposition as a “Protective Opposition” because he has also filed a Motion to File a
  Supplemental Complaint. See Dkt. No. 26.

                                                            1

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 39       Filed 08/31/26       Page 2 of 9 PageID# 390




  claims in two other actions brought by Plaintiff against Meta and others. Instead, the Opposition

  confirms that Plaintiff’s conspiracy claims rely solely on the allegations that:

           •   Meta (along with other co-defendants) filed motions to stay discovery in the two other

               actions (Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc. et al., No. 6:26-cv-376 (“Ballentine 2” or

               the “376 Action”) and Ballentine v. Accenture, LLP et al., No.5:26-cv-472 (“Ballentine

               3” or the “286 Action”)); and

           •   One day later, the NCMEC Defendants responded to proposed subpoenas Plaintiff sent

               NCMEC in connection with the 376 and 286 Actions, providing information Plaintiff

               had been seeking from Meta in the underlying actions.

  Nothing in the Opposition explains how these two actions constitute evidence of a conspiracy,

  merely because they coincidentally occurred within a day of each other.

           Second, the Opposition fails to counter Meta’s arguments that the FAC fails to allege the

  “force, intimidation, or threat” or “injury” necessary to state a claim under Section 1985(2).

           Third, the Opposition confirms that the FAC fails to allege an underlying tort to support

  Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy claim. Indeed, the FAC fails to allege any underlying tort, for

  the reasons stated in the NCMEC Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss.

     The FAC should be dismissed with prejudice.

     II.       ARGUMENT

               a. The FAC Fails to State a Claim Under Section 1985(2)

           Meta’s Motion to Dismiss established that the FAC failed to sufficiently allege any of the

  three elements required to state a claim under 42. U.S.C. § 1985(2). See Motion at 8-12. Nothing

  in Plaintiff’s Opposition changes that conclusion.




                                                    2

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD           Document 39        Filed 08/31/26     Page 3 of 9 PageID# 391




                     i. The FAC Fails to Plausibly Allege Any Agreement Between Meta and
                        NCMEC

         Meta’s Motion to Dismiss established that Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim fails because

  Plaintiff fails to allege any facts plausibly suggesting an agreement between Meta and the NCMEC

  Defendants. See Mot. at 8-11. In response, Plaintiff admits that he has not pled any facts showing

  “direct evidence of an express meeting of the minds” but contends he alleged “circumstantial facts”

  sufficient to state a claim. Opp. at 12. But as explained in Meta’s Motion and further refuted

  below—none of the FAC’s alleged “circumstantial facts” plausibly suggest an agreement of any

  kind, much less a conspiracy.

         As set forth in Meta’s Motion to Dismiss, the FAC fails to plausibly allege an agreement

  because the factual allegations relied on by the FAC constitute contradictory conduct by Meta and

  the NCMEC Defendants, inherently inconsistent with an agreement to pursue a common objective.

  See Mot. at 9-10. Plaintiff’s response to this argument is confusing, but the Opposition appears to

  argue that Meta’s and NCMEC’s alleged conduct was not, in fact, contradictory because NCMEC’s

  letters were meant to “displace[]” the discovery Plaintiff sought, arguing that the letters somehow

  constituted “an unsworn and source-free substitution for the subject of imminent examination.”

  Opp. at 8. It is not clear what that means and, in any event, Plaintiff fails to explain how NCMEC’s

  letters (which were never filed or raised in either the 376 Action or the 286 Action) “displaced”

  the discovery he sought from the parties in those actions or somehow constituted a “substitution”

  for the then-upcoming depositions. Indeed, the Motions to Stay Discovery in the 376 and 286

  Actions did not assert that discovery was inappropriate because Plaintiff already had (or would be

  receiving) the information sought. Instead, the Motions to Stay Discovery argued that discovery

  was premature in light of the defendants’ motions to dismiss. See Ballentine 2, Dkt. No. 92;

  Ballentine 3, Dkt. No 49. And, to the extent any of Plaintiff’s claims in Ballentine 2 survive

                                                   3

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD                  Document 39            Filed 08/31/26          Page 4 of 9 PageID# 392




  defendants’ motion to dismiss,2 Plaintiff can again seek the discovery he claims was “displaced”

  or “substituted” by the letters. Accordingly, nothing in the Opposition changes the fact that the

  alleged acts underlying the asserted conspiracy are fundamentally contradictory and do not

  plausibly suggest an agreement. See Mot. at 8-11.3

           Aside from the contradictory nature of the purported conspiracy, the Opposition confirms

  that the FAC relies only on the coincidental timing of Meta’s Motions to Stay Discovery and

  NCMEC’s letters to support his purported conspiracy. Plaintiff attempts to frame his allegations as

  something more substantial by purporting to separate his allegations into “nine numbered

  circumstances.” But, at bottom, all of the “supporting circumstances” amount to nothing more than

  (1) Meta moved to stay discovery prior to imminently noticed depositions and, (2) one day later,

  NCMEC responded to Plaintiff’s proposed subpoenas, despite not yet being required to respond.

  See Opp. at 7-8. Plaintiff’s conclusory assertion that these allegations constitute “factual matter

  that plausibly suggests agreement” is unsupported by the actual factual allegations. Opp. at 8. As

  Meta’s Motion to Dismiss established, the FAC’s conclusory allegations of coincidentally timed

  conduct between two defendants are insufficient to plausibly suggest agreement. See Mot. at 10.

                         ii. The FAC Fails to Allege the Use of Force, Intimidation, or Threats

           Meta’s Motion to Dismiss also established that the FAC fails to allege the use of force,

  intimidation, or threats by Meta or the NCMEC Defendants, which is necessary to state a claim.



  2
    Ballentine 3 has been dismissed. See Mot. at 4-5.
  3
   Although the Opposition takes issue with Meta’s description of the burden to plead agreement for Section 1985
  conspiracy claims (Opp. at 12), courts routinely dismiss such claims at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, recognizing the high
  burden for alleging conspiracy claims under Section 1985. See Caldwell v. Green, 451 F. Supp. 2d 811, 821 (W.D. Va.
  2006) (granting motion to dismiss and recognizing that the “Fourth Circuit noted in Simmons that plaintiffs ‘rarely, if
  ever ... set forth sufficient facts to establish a 1985 conspiracy’ and [] courts frequently grant motions to dismiss for
  these claims.”) (quoting Simmons v. Poe, 47 F.3d 1370, 1377 (4th Cir. 1995)); Davis v. Hudgins, 896 F. Supp. 561,
  571 (E.D. Va. 1995) (“Because of the high threshold that a Plaintiff must meet to establish a prima facie case under
  section 1985, courts often grant motions of dismissal.”).


                                                             4

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 39        Filed 08/31/26      Page 5 of 9 PageID# 393




  Mot at 11-12. In response, Plaintiff concedes that the FAC fails to allege any threats or use of force

  but summarily claims that he has sufficiently pled intimidation. Opp. at 14-15. But as Plaintiff

  admits in his Opposition, his intimidation theory rests solely on the NCMEC Defendants’ allegedly

  premature response to an “Advance Notice of Intended Subpoena” that Plaintiff himself sent. Mot.

  at 11; Opp. at 16. Those alleged facts do not plausibly suggest that anyone was attempting to

  intimidate Plaintiff in any manner, and Plaintiff does not point to any authority suggesting that

  such conduct is sufficient to state claim for intimidation.

         The Opposition’s attempts to distinguish authority cited or referred to in Meta’s Motion are

  unavailing. First, Plaintiff’s attempt to distinguish Scott v. Mountain Mission Sch., Inc. 809 F. 2d

  786, 1987 WL 36169, at *2 (4th Cir. 1987) by asserting that Scott involved “an accusation

  communicated to a third party” while the letters from NCMEC were not shared with anyone else

  is nonsensical. See Opp. at 16. The fact that the letters here were entirely private cuts against any

  intimidation, because absent any intentional publication of the letters, there is no indication that

  the letters were meant to pressure Plaintiff into dropping his claims. Similarly, Plaintiff also

  attempts to distinguish Glynn v. Impact Science & Tech. by asserting that the conduct at issue in

  Glynn (counterclaims raised by defendant) were “litigation conduct,” and Plaintiff contends the

  responses to the proposed subpoenas in the 376 and 286 Actions are somehow not “litigation

  conduct.” Opp. at 17. But Glynn held that the Section 1985(2) claim failed because the defendant

  had “a reasonable basis in fact and law to pursue [the] counterclaims,” precluding a finding of

  improper motive. 807 F. Supp. 2d 391, 422 (D. Md. 2011). Here, the NCMEC Defendants similarly

  had a reasonable basis for sending the letters, because they were responding to proposed subpoenas




                                                    5

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD                 Document 39           Filed 08/31/26         Page 6 of 9 PageID# 394




  from Plaintiff requesting the provided information.4 Plaintiff’s Opposition thus confirms that the

  FAC fails to allege force, intimidation, or threats intended to deter his claims.

                       iii. The FAC Fails to Plead Injury

           Meta’s Motion to Dismiss established that Plaintiff also failed to plead any facts showing

  that the discovery NCMEC provided impacted his ability to testify or pursue his claim, particularly

  because Plaintiff has continued to aggressively litigate both actions. The Opposition merely recites

  the conclusory allegations in the FAC that Plaintiff was “impact[ed]” by his receipt of the letters,

  without identifying any non-conclusory basis for his assertion that this impact “materially

  diminished” his ability to continue pursuing his claims. See Opp. at 18-19. As established in Meta’s

  Motion, such conclusory allegations do not suffice to plead injury. Mot. at 12.

           Neither Haddle v. Garrison, 525 U.S. 121 (1998) nor King v. Rubenstein, 825 F.3d 206 (4th

  Cir. 2016)—Plaintiff’s sole authority for establishing injury—support the sufficiency of Plaintiff’s

  allegations here. In Haddle, the Supreme Court found that plaintiff’s allegations that defendants

  conspired to have him fired (and that he was fired), was sufficient to establish injury. Haddle, 525

  U.S. at 125-26. In King, the plaintiff alleged that he was forced to have surgery on his genitals that,

  among other things, left painful scarring in addition to mental anguish. King, 825 F.3d at 218.

  Neither set of allegations are remotely similar to the allegations here, which consist solely of

  conclusory allegations of emotional distress from receiving information that Plaintiff himself

  requested. Mot. at 12


  4
    In his Opposition, Plaintiff takes issue with the fact that Meta’s Motion to Dismiss sometimes refers to the
  proposed subpoenas simply as “subpoenas,” which Plaintiff asserts improperly treats the proposed subpoenas as an
  “operative request.” Opp. at 5. Whether the proposed subpoenas are treated as operative requests for information or
  merely a notice that Plaintiff intended to make the request operative at a later date is immaterial. The fact remains
  that Plaintiff sent to NCMEC two documents containing a request for information (in the format of a subpoenas) and
  NCMEC responded to those requests. The only logical inference from the receipt of such requests is that Plaintiff is
  interested in receiving the requested information. There was simply no reason for NCMEC to believe, based on the
  face of the proposed subpoenas, that Plaintiff did not want the requested information unless and until Plaintiff
  followed up with formal service.

                                                           6

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD             Document 39       Filed 08/31/26       Page 7 of 9 PageID# 395




         Finally, the Opposition appears to concede that Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim does not

  rely on the “attending court” prong of Section 1985(2), instead relying solely on “Plaintiff’s

  prospective-witness status,” alleging only “a purpose to deter testimony,” not to deter the pursuit

  of his claims. Opp. at 20-21. But Plaintiff has not identified any non-speculative opportunity for

  him to provide testimony in any action. Indeed, in light of the pending motion to dismiss in the

  376 Action (which, if granted, will entirely dispose of Plaintiff’s claims before discovery

  commences), and the fact that Plaintiff’s complaint has already been dismissed in the 286 Action,

  it is likely that no such potential testimony will ever come to fruition. The FAC’s failure to identify

  any actual testimony in federal court that Plaintiff has or likely will offer independently dooms

  Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim.

         B. The FAC Fails to Allege a Common Law Conspiracy Claim

         As explained in Meta’s Motion to Dismiss, Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy claim fails

  for the same reasons as his Section 1985(2) claim: because he fails to allege any non-conclusory

  facts showing an agreement. See Mot. at 13; Opp. at 21.

         Meta’s Motion to Dismiss also established that Plaintiff’s common law conspiracy claim

  fails because the FAC fails to establish the commission of any underlying tort. Mot. at 13-14.

  Plaintiff’s Opposition does not substantively respond to Meta’s argument and instead merely refers

  to his opposition to the NCMEC Defendants’ motion to dismiss. But Plaintiff’s Opposition to

  NCMEC’s motion to dismiss fails to refute the multiple, independent reasons that Plaintiff has

  failed to sufficiently plead a predicate tort as thoroughly explained in NCMEC’s briefing in support

  of its Motion to Dismiss. See Dkt. Nos. 10-11 (the NCMEC Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss).

  Accordingly, Plaintiff does not refute that his failure to plead an underlying tort is independently

  fatal to his conspiracy claim against Meta.

     III.      CONCLUSION

            For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court dismiss the FAC with

  prejudice.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA

ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
V. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

EXHIBIT A

PLAINTIFEF’S SUR-REPLY TO DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S
REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO DISMISS

Meta’s Reply largely reiterates its opening arguments. One argument appears for the first
time at page 7. Meta now contends that Plaintiff “has not identified any non-speculative
opportunity for him to provide testimony in any action” and that the FAC fails to identify “any
actual testimony in federal court that Plaintiff has or likely will offer.” ECF No. 39 at 7. The First

Amended Complaint alleges precisely what Meta says is absent.

I. META’S NEW ARGUMENT IS CONTRADICTED BY THE FIRST AMENDED
COMPLAINT

Start with the pleading. Paragraph 31 of the FAC alleges:

Plaintiff was a prospective witness in both actions concerning his account history,
the July 4, 2022 enforcement event, the absence of any law-enforcement contact
with Plaintiff, and his damages. Plaintiff expected to testify under oath at deposition
and at trial concerning those subjects.

ECF No. 5 ¥ 31. That paragraph identifies the witness, the actions, the subjects of the
testimony, and the settings in which it was expected to be given.

The FAC then pleads what Defendants sought to do about that testimony and what they
knew. The purpose of the alleged understanding was “to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from
continuing to attend the 376 Action and the 286 Action as a party, and from testifying freely, fully,
and truthfully as a prospective witness in those pending federal proceedings, including concerning
the CyberTipline-reporting question.” Id. ¥ 158. The intimidation “was directed both at Plaintiff’s
continued attendance as a party in the two pending federal actions and at Plaintiff’s own
prospective sworn testimony concerning his account, the July 4, 2022 enforcement event, the
absence of any law-enforcement contact with Plaintiff, and his damages.” Id. § 159. And
Defendants “knew that Plaintiff was pro se; that the noticed depositions depended on Plaintiff’s
personal preparation and examination; that the CyberTipline issue was central to the noticed
examinations; and that Plaintiff was a prospective witness concerning his account, the enforcement
event, and his damages.” Id. § 160. Count IV incorporates those allegations, id. { 234, and
separately repeats the alleged purpose and injury, id. {J 237, 239.

Meta’s argument therefore does not identify an omitted allegation. It asks the Court to
disregard an allegation that is already there.

Rule 12(b)(6) does not permit that. The Court “must accept as true all of the factual
allegations contained in the complaint,” and must draw “all reasonable inferences” in Plaintiff’s
favor. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co. v. Kolon Indus., Inc., 637 F.3d 435, 440 (4th Cir. 2011); King

v. Rubenstein, 825 F.3d 206, 212 (4th Cir. 2016). Meta cites no authority imposing an additional

requirement that a § 1985(2) plaintiff identify a future testimony event certain or likely to occur.
Meta’s argument instead asks the Court to find that Plaintiff’s expected testimony was unlikely to
happen. But a plaintiff “need not demonstrate that her right to relief is probable or that alternative
explanations are less likely.” Houck v. Substitute Tr. Servs., Inc., 791 F.3d 473, 484 (4th Cir. 2015).
The question “is not whether there are more likely explanations” for the facts alleged. Woods v.
City of Greensboro, 855 F.3d 639, 649-50 (4th Cir. 2017).

The point can be stated simply. Whether Plaintiff ultimately would have testified is a
factual question concerning what later occurred. The Rule 12 question presented by Meta’s new
argument is whether the FAC plausibly alleges that Plaintiff was a prospective witness and that
the alleged object was to deter his testimony. Paragraphs 31 and 158 through 160 expressly plead

those facts.

Il. META USES LATER PROCEDURAL EVENTS TO NEGATE THE
CIRCUMSTANCES ALLEGED TO EXIST WHEN THE CONDUCT OCCURRED

Meta’s argument depends on two events. The first is the dismissal of the 286 Action. The
second is a motion to dismiss now pending in the 376 Action, which Meta says, “if granted, will
entirely dispose of Plaintiff’s claims before discovery commences.” ECF No. 39 at 7. From those
two events Meta concludes that “it is likely that no such potential testimony will ever come to
fruition.” Id.

Both events postdate the conduct alleged. The FAC pleads the circumstances that existed
on April 22, 2026, when the letters issued. Both federal actions were pending. ECF No. 5 { 27.
Plaintiff was a prospective witness in both. Id. ¥ 31. Plaintiff had noticed Accenture’s Rule 30(b)
(6) deposition for April 29 and 30, 2026, with CyberTipline reporting as a matter for examination.

Id. §§ 51-52. Plaintiff had noticed Anderson’s deposition for April 28, 2026. Id. 4 53. Plaintiff had

retained a court reporter and a videographer. Id. 4] 54. The alleged purpose of the understanding
was to deter that prospective sworn testimony. Id. {{ 158-164.

A later procedural development does not erase the circumstances the FAC alleges existed
when Defendants acted. Both actions were then pending. Plaintiff was then a prospective witness
in both. Depositions were then noticed and imminent. Plaintiff then expected to testify under oath
at deposition and trial. The alleged agreement was then directed at deterring that prospective
testimony. The FAC alleges the circumstances that existed when the challenged conduct occurred.
Later procedural developments do not negate those pleaded historical facts on a Rule 12(b)(6)
motion.

Nor can the possibility that a pending Rule 12 motion may later terminate another action
be converted, on this Rule 12 motion, into a factual determination that Plaintiff’s pleaded
prospective testimony was speculative. The 376 Action has not been dismissed. Meta’s prediction
that Plaintiff’s anticipated testimony is unlikely ever to occur remains a prediction about the future
posture of another case. A prediction about the future of another case is not a ground for dismissing
a well-pleaded allegation about the past in this one.

Ill, META’S REPLY ITSELF DEMONSTRATES WHY ITS NEW CERTAINTY
THEORY FAILS

Meta’s Reply addresses the 376 Action twice. Read together, the two passages establish
one thing: the future posture of that action is unresolved.

At pages 3 and 4, answering Plaintiff’s point that the letters displaced the discovery he had
noticed, Meta says that “to the extent any of Plaintiff’s claims in Ballentine 2 survive defendants’
motion to dismiss, Plaintiff can again seek the discovery he claims was ‘displaced’ or ‘substituted’

by the letters.” ECF No. 39 at 3-4. At page 7, answering Plaintiff’s prospective-witness allegation,

Meta says that because the same motion to dismiss is pending, “it is likely that no such potential
testimony will ever come to fruition.” Id. at 7.

Put those statements side by side. On pages 3 and 4, Meta acknowledges that the 376
Action may survive and that discovery may resume. On page 7, Meta relies on the same unresolved
motion to argue that Plaintiff’s potential testimony is unlikely ever to occur. Meta itself recognizes
that the posture of the 376 Action remains unresolved. A pending motion to dismiss therefore
supplies no factual basis at Rule 12 to declare the FAC’s expressly pleaded prospective testimony
nonexistent or insufficiently concrete.

The statute confirms the point. Section 1985(2) addresses a conspiracy to “deter, by force,
intimidation, or threat, any party or witness in any court of the United States from attending such
court, or from testifying to any matter pending therein, freely, fully, and truthfully.” 42 U.S.C. §
1985(2). The statute expressly protects a party or witness from being deterred from testifying to a
matter pending in federal court. The FAC alleges that both matters were pending, ECF No. 5 { 27;
that Plaintiff was a prospective witness who expected to testify under oath at deposition and trial,
id. 431; the subjects of that testimony, id. J 31, 159; and an alleged purpose to deter it, id. {4 158,
237. Meta cites no authority imposing an additional requirement that the FAC identify a future

testimony event certain or likely to occur.

CONCLUSION

Meta’s new argument supplies no basis for dismissal. The FAC expressly pleads Plaintiff’s
prospective-witness status, the subjects of his anticipated sworn testimony, Defendants’
knowledge of that status, and the alleged purpose of deterring that testimony while both federal
actions were pending. The Court should reject the argument first advanced at page 7 of Meta’s

Reply and deny Meta’s Motion to Dismiss.

Date: September 1, 2026 Respectfully submitted,

YD

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se
1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847

Alexandria, Virginia 22307

PLAINTIFE’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SUR-REPLY
TO DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S REPLY
IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO DISMISS

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves the Court, under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1), for leave
to file the Proposed Sur-Reply attached as Exhibit A. The Proposed Sur-Reply answers one
argument that Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) raised for the first time in its Reply
Memorandum filed August 31, 2026 (ECF No. 39). In support, Plaintiff states as follows.

1. Meta moved to dismiss the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) on August 21,
2026 (ECF Nos. 21, 22). Plaintiff filed his opposition on August 24, 2026 (ECF No. 30). Meta
filed its Reply on August 31, 2026 (ECF No. 39).

2. Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) provides for an opening memorandum, an opposition,
and a reply. After that, “[nJo further briefs or written communications may be filed without first

obtaining leave of Court.”

9/1/2026

3. Meta’s Reply largely reiterates or develops arguments advanced in its opening

round of briefing on those matters.

4. One argument is different. At page 7, Meta argues for the first time that Count IV
fails because Plaintiff “has not identified any non-speculative opportunity for him to provide
testimony in any action,” and that “[t]he FAC’s failure to identify any actual testimony in federal
court that Plaintiff has or likely will offer independently dooms Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim.”
ECF No. 39 at 7. Meta rests that argument on later procedural developments: the dismissal of the
286 Action and the pending motion to dismiss in the 376 Action. Id.

3. Meta’s opening memorandum did not advance that argument. It argued that
Plaintiff had not pleaded injury because he continued to litigate. ECF No. 22 at 12. It suggested in
a footnote that “attending court” might require physical presence at a proceeding. Id. at 12 n.1. It
did not argue that a prospective witness must plead a presently identifiable and sufficiently certain
future occasion to testify. It did not argue that the FAC fails for want of allegations identifying

underlying actions as a test of Plaintiff’s witness status. Plaintiff therefore has had no opportunity
to respond.

6. The Proposed Sur-Reply is confined to that one argument. It introduces no new
evidence. It relies only on the existing Rule 12 record, principally the First Amended Complaint
and Meta’s Reply.

7. Plaintiff does not request a hearing on this Motion and waives oral argument. The
Motion is procedural and confined to a single question, and the written submissions present it in

full. Plaintiff therefore submits the Motion for decision on the papers pursuant to Federal Rule of

9/1/2026

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA

ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
V. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION
FOR LEAVE TO FILE SUR-REPLY

I. INTRODUCTION

Plaintiff does not seek another round of argument on Meta’s Motion to Dismiss. Meta’s
Reply (ECF No. 39) largely reiterates or develops arguments advanced in its opening
memorandum (ECF No. 22), or responds to arguments in Plaintiff’s opposition (ECF No. 30).
Plaintiff seeks no additional briefing on those matters.

One argument is different. Meta argues for the first time in reply that Count IV fails because
Plaintiff “has not identified any non-speculative opportunity for him to provide testimony in any
action” and because the FAC supposedly fails to identify “any actual testimony in federal court
that Plaintiff has or likely will offer.” ECF No. 39 at 7. Meta’s opening memorandum did not
advance that proposed pleading requirement. Plaintiff therefore has had no opportunity to address

it. The Proposed Sur-Reply is confined to that issue.

The Proposed Sur-Reply requires no new evidence. The new argument is answered by the

First Amended Complaint itself.

Il. STANDARD

Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) permits an opening memorandum, an opposition, and a reply.
Beyond those three, “[nJo further briefs or written communications may be filed without first
obtaining leave of Court.” E.D. Va. Loc. Civ. R. 7(F)(1).

This Court has stated the governing principles. “[A]llowing a surreply is within the court’s
discretion.” Taylor v. Revature LLC, No. 1:22-cv-1153 (RDA/WBP), Dkt. 81, at 8-9 (E.D. Va.
Mar. 5, 2025) (quoting Adams v. Applied Bus. Servs., 2019 WL 7817080, at *1 (E.D. Va. Aug. 30,
2019)). In deciding whether to exercise that discretion, the Court “consider[s] whether prejudice
will result from the court considering a new argument without the opposing party’s having an
opportunity to respond.” Id. at 9. “To cure any such prejudice, a surreply is appropriate where ‘a
party brings forth new material or deploys new arguments in a reply brief.’” Id. (quoting Clawson
v. FedEx Ground Package Sys., Inc., 451 F. Supp. 2d 731, 734 (D. Md. 2006)). A sur-reply is not
appropriate where the reply merely “further support[s] an argument made in [the] opening brief”
or responds to arguments first raised in the opposition. Id. Sur-replies “are generally disfavored”
and are reserved for “rare instances.” Id. (quoting Steele v. Johns Hopkins Health Sys. Corp., 2020
WL 4471710, at *2 (D. Md. Aug. 4, 2020)).

The Court applied those principles this year in SkyBell Technologies, Inc. v. Alarm.com,
Inc., No. 1:25-cv-01105 (RDA/WBP), Dkt. 32 (E.D. Va. Mar. 4, 2026). There, whether the reply
raised new arguments was “a closer call.” Id. at 8. The Court granted leave anyway, reasoning that
considering the sur-reply would “accomplish dispositional efficiency and . . . avoid prejudice to
either party.” Id. Plaintiff’s application identifies the new proposition, the page on which it first

appears, and the confined response he seeks to make.

Ill, META FIRST ADVANCED THE PROSPECTIVE-TESTIMONY REQUIREMENT
IN REPLY

The briefing progressed in three steps.

First, Meta’s opening memorandum attacked injury. It argued that Plaintiff had not pleaded
facts showing that the letters actually impaired his ability to testify or pursue his claims, because
he continued to litigate both actions. ECF No. 22 at 12. In a footnote, Meta suggested that
“attending court” might require physical presence at a proceeding. Id. at 12 n.1. Meta did not argue
that a prospective witness must plead a presently identifiable, sufficiently certain, “non-
speculative” future occasion to testify. It did not argue that Count IV fails for want of allegations
identifying testimony Plaintiff “has or likely will offer.” It did not use the later dismissal of one
underlying action, or the pendency of a motion to dismiss in the other, as a test of Plaintiff’s
witness status when the alleged conduct occurred.

Second, Plaintiff’s opposition answered the injury argument by pointing to the FAC’s
allegations of functional impairment despite continued prosecution. ECF No. 30 at 18—19. Plaintiff
also explained that the conditional physical-presence footnote did not reach the statute’s separate
protection against deterring testimony, because the FAC pleads Plaintiff’s prospective-witness
status and a purpose to deter that testimony. Id. at 20—21.

Third, Meta’s Reply introduced a new proposition. Meta now contends that “Plaintiff has
not identified any non-speculative opportunity for him to provide testimony in any action,” and
that “[t]he FAC’s failure to identify any actual testimony in federal court that Plaintiff has or likely
will offer independently dooms Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim.” ECF No. 39 at 7. Meta supports
that proposition with procedural developments occurring after the alleged April 22, 2026 conduct:
the dismissal of the 286 Action and the pending motion to dismiss in the 376 Action, from which

Meta concludes that “it is likely that no such potential testimony will ever come to fruition.” Id.

The distinction is narrow but consequential. An argument that Plaintiff failed to plead
injury from alleged intimidation is different from an argument that Plaintiff was insufficiently a
prospective witness because future testimony was not certain enough to occur. The opening
argument concerned whether the alleged intimidation caused the required injury. The Reply adds
a different proposition: that the prospective-testimony theory independently fails because the FAC
identifies no sufficiently certain future testimony. Meta itself calls that proposition independently
dispositive. ECF No. 39 at 7.

Plaintiff acknowledges that Meta’s page-7 discussion begins by responding to the
opposition’s reliance on the testimony branch. But the subject was already joined; the new
independent ground for dismissal was not. The FAC pleaded Plaintiff’s prospective-witness status
from the outset. ECF No. 5 4 31, 158-160. Meta had that pleading when it filed its opening
memorandum and chose to attack injury. The opposition did not introduce a new theory; it
identified an existing allegation. What is new is Meta’s contention that Count IV independently
fails unless the FAC identifies testimony sufficiently certain or likely to occur. Plaintiff has had

no prior opportunity to address that contention.

IV. ‘THE PROPOSED SUR-REPLY IS CONFINED TO THE NEW ISSUE

Exhibit A answers the new proposition from the four comers of the FAC. It quotes the
paragraphs that plead Plaintiff’s prospective-witness status, the subjects of his expected swom
testimony, Defendants’ knowledge of that status, and the alleged purpose of deterring that
testimony. ECF No. 5 § 27, 31, 51-54, 158-160. It applies the Rule 12(b)(6) standard to those
allegations. It does not revisit Meta’s previously briefed arguments concerning agreement,
intimidation, or Plaintiffs continued litigation as evidence of injury. It attaches no declaration,
introduces no new evidence, and relies only on the existing Rule 12 record, principally the FAC

and Meta’s Reply.

Meta’s argument does not identify an omitted allegation. It asks the Court to disregard an
allegation that is already there. A short response confined to that point does not delay the Motion
to Dismiss. It permits the Court to decide the newly raised issue on a complete adversarial
presentation, which is the purpose the Court identified in SkyBell.

V. CONCLUSION
The Court should grant leave under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) to file the Proposed Sur-Reply

attached to the Motion as Exhibit A, and should deem it filed as of the date of the Court’s Order.

Date: September 1, 2026 Respectfully submitted,

“rp

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847
Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503
jayballentine@protonmail.com

CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE

Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File Sur-Reply to the Clerk of Court through the Court’s Electronic

Document Submission System for docketing on CM/ECF. Upon docketing, counsel for all parties

Marvelle J. Ballentine

will receive notice through the Court’s CM/ECF system.

     TO PLAINTIFF’S MOTION TO VACATE HEARING SET FOR SEPTEMBER 30, 2026

        Defendant the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children [“NCMEC”], by and

through undersigned counsel and pursuant to the Rules and Orders of this Honorable Court,

hereby respectfully opposes Plaintiff’s “Motion to Vacate the September 30, 2026 Hearing and to

Decide the Motion to Dismiss on the Papers.” [Doc. 42] The Motion filed by the Pro Se

Plaintiff fails to state any good cause for the relief requested.

        Plaintiff appears to base his motion on two grounds, neither of which merit the relief

requested. First, Plaintiff asserts that he “does not require oral argument…” Doc. 42 at ¶ 2.

Second, Plaintiff asserts that because he is pro se, and resides in Florida, “attendance at the

hearing would require interstate travel and its attendant expense to argue a motion…” Id. at ¶ 3.

Taking these arguments in order, the hearing was not set for Plaintiff’s benefit or to ensure he

had a full opportunity to be heard. However, given Plaintiff’s pro se status, NCMEC believes

that a hearing would be a useful opportunity for the parties to be heard.

Second, Plaintiff has intentionally availed himself of this Court, and cannot credibly

complain that litigating a matter in this Court is inconvenient or carries undue expense. This

matter is the second lawsuit filed by Plaintiff against NCMEC and its employee, co-defendant

Katie Hall, Esq., and these lawsuits have carried significant inconvenience and expense to

NCMEC, and have served as an unnecessary distraction of resources from NCMEC’s core

missions.1 As a matter of common sense, when one files suit in a given District Court, one must

expect that he or she will be required to travel to the Court for court appearances. Neither of the

grounds set forth by Plaintiff constitute good cause; they simply constitute what Plaintiff feels

would be more convenient.

        In light of the foregoing, Defendant NCMEC respectfully requests that this Honorable

Court deny Plaintiff’s Motion, and that the hearing set for September 30, 2026 remain as

scheduled.




1
 Mr. Ballentine filed a complaint in Ballentine v. NCMEC, et al, Case No. 1:26-cv-01341-MSN-WBP on
May 19, 2026. On June 16, 2026, NCMEC filed a motion to dismiss. Plaintiff filed a motion for leave to
amend his complaint, which was opposed. In lieu of awaiting the Court’s ruling on either the motion to
dismiss or Plaintiff’s motion to amend, Plaintiff voluntarily dismissed that claim on July 29, 2026. The
following day, Plaintiff filed the above-captioned matter, then filed an amended complaint on August 6,
2026, and since that time has filed: a motion for partial summary judgment [Doc. 6], a motion for leave to
conduct early discovery [Doc. 15], a motion to continue the hearing on NCMEC’s motion to dismiss
[Doc. 29], a motion for leave to file a supplemental pleading [Doc. 26], a motion to appear remotely at the
hearing set for September 25 (as to Plaintiff’s own motions) [Doc. 41], the motion at issue [Doc. 42], and
has advised defense counsel of Plaintiff’s intention to file a motion for leave to file a second amended
complaint.

Respectfully submitted,

PLAINTIFF’S PROTECTIVE OPPOSITION TO
DEFENDANT KATIE HALL’S MOTION TO DISMISS

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine files this opposition protectively: it demonstrates that the
First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) states its claims on the facts already pleaded, without awaiting,
and without prejudice to, Plaintiff’s pending motion for leave to file a supplemental pleading under
Rule 15(d). ECF No. 26.

I. HALL’S MOTION PRESENTS THE SAME GROUNDS ALREADY

BRIEFED

Hall’s motion adopts ECF Nos. 10 and 11 and seeks dismissal on the same grounds asserted

by NCMEC: litigation privilege, federal statutory immunity, truth and falsity, defamation by

implication, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and conspiracy.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document51_ Filed 09/03/26 Page 2 of 5 PagelD# 447

ECF No. 30 responds to the corresponding arguments contained in ECF No. 11. Hall’s
adoption therefore places before the Court the same Rule 12 issues Plaintiff has already
substantively answered.

II. PLAINTIFF RELIES UPON HIS EXISTING RESPONSES TO THE

ARGUMENTS HALL HAS ADOPTED

Plaintiff relies upon the arguments set forth in ECF No. 30, to the extent applicable to Hall,
as his opposition to the corresponding arguments Hall has adopted from ECF No. 11.

Plaintiff maintains against Hall each response made in ECF No. 30 concerning litigation
privilege, statutory immunity, truth and falsity, defamation by implication, intentional infliction of
emotional distress, and conspiracy.

Plaintiff opposes ECF No. 45 in its entirety. Each argument asserted in ECF No. 30 against
a corresponding ground in ECF No. 11 is asserted here against Hall’s adoption of that ground. The
abbreviated form of this filing reflects that those substantive issues have already been briefed.

I. HALL’S ADOPTION DOES NOT ALTER THE ISSUES ALREADY

PRESENTED

Hall’s adoption changes the movant asserting the arguments; it does not change the
arguments themselves. By adopting ECF No. 11, Hall invokes the same contentions concerning
litigation privilege, statutory immunity, truth, defamation by implication, intentional infliction of
emotional distress, and conspiracy that Plaintiff has already answered.

Plaintiff’s existing responses therefore apply to Hall’s motion with equal force. ECF No.
45 supplies no separate substantive ground for dismissal beyond those already addressed in ECF

No. 30.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document51_ Filed 09/03/26 Page 3 of 5 PagelD# 448

This opposition is directed to ECF No. 45 as presently framed against the First Amended
Complaint. Plaintiff separately seeks leave to File Supplemental Complaint pursuant to Federal
Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d). Plaintiff preserves his Rule 15 motion and the supplemental
pleading.

Iv. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons and for the reasons stated in Plaintiff’s existing opposition to the
arguments Hall has adopted, ECF No. 30, Defendant Katie Hall’s Motion to Dismiss should be
denied. Plaintiff’s request is made protectively and without prejudice to his pending Motion for

Leave under Rule 15(d) and the resulting pleading posture if that motion is granted.

                          IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
                         FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
                                     Alexandria Division


  MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE.,                            )
                                                      )
                 Plaintiff,                           )
                                                      ) Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
                         v.                           )
                                                      )
  KATIE HALL, NATIONAL                                )
  CENTER FOR MISSING &                                )
  EXPLOITED CHILDREN;                                 )
  META PLATFORMS, INC. and                            )
  JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,                                 )
                                                      )
                 Defendants.                          )

       DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO
      PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SUPPLEMENTAL COMPLAINT

          Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc., (“Meta”) by and through its undersigned counsel, hereby

  respectfully opposes Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine’s Motion for Leave to File a Supplemental

  Complaint pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d), Dkt. No. 26. Meta hereby joins,

  adopts and incorporates all applicable arguments and requested relief contained in Defendant

  National Center for Missing & Exploited Children’s (“NCMEC”) Opposition to Plaintiff’s Motion

  for Leave to File a Supplemental Complaint (Dkt. No. 28). In further support, Meta states as

  follows:

     I.      Procedural History

          As described in Meta’s Motion to Dismiss the First Amended Complaint (“FAC”), Plaintiff

  has filed a series of actions against Meta across several different courts, all stemming from the

  alleged disablement of his Facebook account. See Dkt. No. 22 at 3-5. Across all of these actions,

  Plaintiff has routinely filed amended complaints (or sought leave to do so), consistently delaying



                                                  1

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 53        Filed 09/03/26     Page 2 of 5 PageID# 456




  decision on motions to dismiss across those actions. Indeed, since September 9, 2025 (when

  Plaintiff filed his first complaint against Meta in the United States District Court for the Northern

  District of California), Plaintiff has filed 12 distinct complaints against Meta across four distinct

  courts (not counting his proposed supplemental complaints in the instant action).

           Plaintiff’s present request for leave to supplement continues his strategy of seeking

  repeated amendment to delay decision on motions to dismiss. Indeed, in this court alone, Plaintiff

  has:

              •    Filed a complaint based on the allegations raised in the FAC against NCMEC and
                   Defendant Katie Hall (together, the “NCMEC Defendants) in a distinct action
                   (Ballentine v. Nat’l Ctr. for Missing & Exploited Children, No. 1:26-cv-1341 (E.D.
                   Va.);
              •    Filed a motion for leave to amend that complaint to add claims against Meta;
              •    Voluntarily dismissed that action after the NCMEC Defendants opposed his request
                   for leave to amend;
              •    Filed the complaint and FAC against the NCMEC Defendants and Meta in the
                   instant action; and
              •    Following motions to dismiss, filed the present motion for leave to supplement, and
                   has indicated a future intention to file a second such motion.

  See Dkt. No. 22 at 5.

     II.      Plaintiff’s Supplemental Allegations are Futile.

           “[T]he standards used by a district court in ruling on a motion to amend or on a motion to

  supplement [a complaint] are nearly identical.” Franks v. Ross, 313 F.3d 184, 198, n. 15 (4th Cir.

  2002). In either case, “leave to amend a pleading should be denied. . . when the amendment would

  be futile.” Brannen v. Selene Finance, LP, No. 2:18-cv-602, 2019 WL 13251099, at *2, 5 (E.D.

  Va. Nov. 14, 2019) (denying leave to file supplemental complaint where “it would be futile to

  permit” Plaintiff’s “supplemental pleading” where his “right to relief” remained “a matter of pure

  speculation”).




                                                    2

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD                 Document 53           Filed 09/03/26          Page 3 of 5 PageID# 457




           As to Plaintiff’s supplemental allegations regarding the NCMEC Defendants, Meta fully

  adopts the arguments in NCMEC’s Opposition, which explain why the supplemental allegations

  are “frivolous and futile,” unnecessary, and “a further attempt to prolong” the litigation. Dkt. No.

  32 at 4-5.

           As to Plaintiff’s supplemental allegations regarding Meta, Plaintiff’s proposed supplement

  alleges only that in a motion to dismiss in a separate action brought by Plaintiff (Ballentine v. Meta

  Platforms, Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL (N.D. Cal.)), Meta described Plaintiff’s litigation against

  the NCMEC as one of several actions Plaintiff has brought arising from the alleged disablement

  of his Facebook account. See Dkt. No. 26-2 at ¶ 22-24. Plaintiff asserts that Meta’s “citation of the

  present action . . . demonstrates that, by August 13, 2026, Meta had actual knowledge of the

  existence of the present action” and “of the relationship between the present action and the

  Northern District of California proceeding.” Id. ¶¶ 25, 32.

           But Meta’s knowledge, as of August 13, 2026, that Plaintiff sued NCMEC has no relevance

  whatsoever to Plaintiff’s claims against Meta, which are both premised on Plaintiff’s assertion that

  Meta somehow conspired with NCMEC in connection with letters that NCMEC sent to Plaintiff

  on April 22, 2026. Because Plaintiff’s supplemental allegations against Meta are plainly irrelevant

  to his claims or the issues raised in Meta’s motion to dismiss, amendment would be futile and

  Plaintiff’s motion should be denied. See Dacha v. Moody, No. 3:24-cv-713, 2026 WL 625494, at

  *15 (E.D. Va. Mar. 5, 2026) (denying motion to supplement under Rule 15(d) because

  “[p]ermitting [plaintiff] to supplement the records with the facts” identified in the motion to

  supplement “would be futile” where the facts could not plausibly serve “as a factual basis for any

  claim” against defendants).1


  1
   Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to Supplement should also be denied because Plaintiff failed to attach a copy of the
  proposed amended pleading in its entirety, instead attaching only his supplemental allegations, “incorporating by

                                                            3

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD                Document 53          Filed 09/03/26         Page 4 of 5 PageID# 458




      III.      Conclusion

             For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court deny Plaintiff’s Motion

  for Leave to File a Supplemental Complaint.

26(d)(1) FOR LEAVE TO SERVE FOUR LIMITED INTERROGATORIES ON
META PLATFORMS, INC. BEFORE THE RULE 26(f) CONFERENCE

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine, pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(d)(1),
moves for leave to serve four interrogatories on Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) before
the conference required by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(f). The four interrogatories are set
forth in Exhibit A and are reproduced verbatim here:

INTERROGATORY NO. 1: Between July 1, 2022 and April 22, 2026, did Meta

submit to NCMEC a CyberTipline report in connection with the Facebook account
associated with Plaintiff and terminated on or about July 4, 2022?

INTERROGATORY NO. 2: Did any such report, as submitted by Meta, contain or
otherwise identify “Marvelle J. Ballentine”?

INTERROGATORY NO. 3: Did any such report, as submitted by Meta, contain or
otherwise identify “Jay Ballentine”?

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document54_ Filed 09/03/26 Page 2 of 5 PagelD# 461

INTERROGATORY NO. 4: Did any such report, as submitted by Meta, contain or

otherwise identify jaychizza@icloud.com?

Meta may answer each interrogatory with one of three responses: “Yes,” “No,” or “Unable
to determine after reasonable inquiry.” The interrogatories seek no explanation and no report
content.

Meta has moved to dismiss. ECF No. 21. Its Memorandum in Support (ECF No. 22)
describes the discovery Plaintiff previously sought from Meta as “whether Meta filed a
CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff's [Facebook] account.” ECF No. 22 at 6. The
Memorandum characterizes NCMEC’s April 22, 2026 letters as “the exact discovery that Hall and
NCMEC provided,” id. at 9, and states that NCMEC “provided him with exactly what he asked
for,” id. at 11. The same Memorandum recites that the letters “did not state that Meta... submitted
either report, that either report concerned Plaintiffs Facebook account, or that either report”
concerned the disablement of that account. Id. at 7 (quoting FAC 4 92). The Memorandum nowhere
states that Meta submitted either report. The four interrogatories ask Meta whether its own records
establish those propositions.

This Motion seeks no other relief. The requested relief consists exclusively of four answers
under Rule 33. The Motion seeks no production of any report or any portion of any report; no
report content, narrative, report number, communication, or metadata; no document request,
deposition, or third-party discovery; no follow-up discovery; no discovery from any Defendant
other than Meta; and no commencement of general discovery. General discovery remains closed.
The grounds for this Motion are set forth in the accompanying Memorandum in Support. A

proposed order and Exhibit A are submitted herewith.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document54_ Filed 09/03/26 Page 3 of 5 PagelD# 462

Pursuant to Local Civil Rule 37(E), Plaintiff and counsel for Meta conferred by telephone
on September 3, 2026 regarding the four interrogatories set forth in Exhibit A. Meta did not agree
to answer the interrogatories. The parties were unable to resolve the discovery matter.

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court grant leave under Rule 26(d)
(1) to serve the four interrogatories set forth in Exhibit A on Meta before the Rule 26(f) conference;
require Meta to answer them under oath, pursuant to Rule 33, within seven calendar days after
service, or within such other short period as the Court directs; and grant such other relief as it

deems just.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD          Document 55        Filed 09/03/26     Page 1 of 8 PageID# 467




                            UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                                09/03/2026
                         FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
                                 ALEXANDRIA DIVISION


  MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

                 Plaintiff,

                 V.                                            Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
                                                               The Honorable Judge
                                                               Rossie D. Alston Jr.

  KATIE HALL, individually;
  NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
  META PLATFORMS, INC.;
  and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

                 Defendants.


              MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF'S MOTION UNDER
        FEDERAL RULE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE 26(d)(l) FOR LEAVE TO SERVE
          FOUR LIMITED INTERROGATORIES ON META PLATFORMS, INC.
                              BEFORE THE RULE 26(f) CONFERENCE


         I.      INTRODUCTION

         Meta has moved to dismiss. ECF No. 21. Its Memorandum tells the Court that NCMEC

  "provided him with exactly what he asked for." ECF No. 22 at 11. NCMEC said the same thing

  first. Before Meta appeared, NCMEC told the Court that it had responded "precisely as requested"

  and that "there would be no claim asserted as to ... Meta Platforms, Inc." Ballentine v. NCMEC,

  No. 1:26-cv-01341, ECF No. 20 at 1, 7. Two weeks before that, NCMEC told the Court that what

  discovery revealed "could give rise to further litigation from Mr. Ballentine." Id., ECF No. 11 at

  4. Then Plaintiff's Declaration made concrete what NCMEC said discovery might reveal. ECF No.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 55       Filed 09/03/26     Page 2 of 8 PageID# 468




  31 ,r,r 3-7. Meta's Memorandum does not say that Meta submitted either report. That is the fact

  every one of those statements depends on. The four interrogatories ask Meta to state it under oath.

         Plaintiff asks for four interrogatories, directed to one Defendant, concerning one identified

  Facebook-account enforcement event and one finite period, July 1, 2022 through April 22, 2026.

  Interrogatory No. 1 asks whether Meta submitted a CyberTipline report in connection with that

  account. Interrogatories Nos. 2 through 4 ask whether any such report contained one of three

  identifying terms. Each permits three answers: "Yes," "No," or "Unable to determine after

  reasonable inquiry." Plaintiff does not seek any report.

         Plaintiff does not ask the Court to open discovery. He asks the Court to authorize four

  answers about records Meta itself maintains, concerning a factual equivalence Meta itself has

  placed into its Rule 12 argument.

         II.     BACKGROUND

         A.      The CyberTipline Question Was Directed to Meta Before the April 22

                 Letters.

         Before April 22, 2026, Plaintiff sought to learn whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report

  concerning the Facebook account terminated on or about July 4, 2022. Meta's Memorandum

  describes that history in Meta's own words. It states that Plaintiff "sought early discovery

  regarding 'whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff's [Facebook] account."'

  ECF No. 22 at 6 (quoting FAC ,r 35). It describes Plaintiff's earlier request for admission as

  directed to "whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff." Id. at 4. It describes

  Plaintiff's later notice to NCMEC as concerning "whether a CyberTipline report ... was filed in

  connection with the Facebook account associated with Plaintiff and terminated on or about July 4,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 55        Filed 09/03/26       Page 3 of 8 PageID# 469




  2022." Id. (quoting the notice filed in the 376 Action, Dkt. No. 82, at 1). The question was directed

  to Meta first.

          B.       The April 22 Letters Did Not Identify Meta or the Account.

          The April 22 letters stated that NCMEC had received two CyberTipline reports

  "concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier

  jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present." The letters did not state that Meta

  submitted either report. They did not state that either report concerned Plaintiff's Facebook

  account. They did not state that either report concerned the July 2022 enforcement. Meta's

  Memorandum recites each of those three omissions. ECF No. 22 at 7 (quoting FAC ,r 92). Meta

  does not dispute any of them.

          C.       Meta Now Equates the Letters With the Discovery Sought From Meta.

          Meta's Memorandum characterizes the April 22 letters as "the exact discovery that Hall

  and NCMEC provided on April 22, 2026," which Meta's April 21 motion practice sought "to

  prevent." ECF No. 22 at 9. It states that the NCMEC Defendants "provided him with exactly what

  he asked for." Id. at 11. Those two statements equate the April 22 letters with the discovery

  Plaintiff sought from Meta. That equivalence holds only if a report Meta submitted concerning the

  account at issue is one of the two reports the letters describe. The letters do not say so. The

  equivalence Meta asserts rests on facts the letters never supplied.

          D.       Plaintiff's Existing Sworn Declaration Narrows the Identifier Question.

          Plaintiff's declaration at ECF No. 31 states three facts material here. Before April 22, 2026,

  Plaintiff never used the name "Marvelle J. Ballentine" to create, register, identify, maintain, access,

  or operate any Meta account that he used. ECF No. 31 ,r 3. In connection with his online identity,

  including his use of Meta products, Plaintiff used the name "Jay Ballentine." Id. ,r 6. The name

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD           Document 55        Filed 09/03/26      Page 4 of 8 PageID# 470




  "Marvelle J. Ballentine" appeared in the April 9, 2026 litigation materials because it is Plaintiff's

  legal name and the name under which the underlying litigation was pending, not because Plaintiff

  had used it to identify or operate any Meta account. Id. ,r 7. Those facts make Interrogatories Nos.

  2 through 4 concrete questions about identified terms rather than abstract ones.

         III.    LEGAL STANDARD

         Rule 26(d)(l) bars discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference "except ... when authorized

  by these rules, by stipulation, or by court order." Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(l). The Court may therefore

  authorize discovery now. Discovery must be relevant to a claim or defense and proportional to the

  needs of the case. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(l). District courts have broad discretion over the scope and

  timing of discovery.

         This District has exercised that authority to permit limited discovery before the Rule 26(f)

  conference. See Shenzhenshibairihongmaoyiyouxiangongsi v. Novoluto GmbH, No. 3:25-

  cv-00844-RCY, ECF No. 44 (E.D. Va. Mar. 9, 2026). That decision arose in the preliminary-

  injunction setting and applied a demanding expedited-discovery framework. It nevertheless

  authorized circumscribed discovery where adjudication was imminent, material information was

  held by one side, and the authorized discovery was narrowed to what that adjudication required.

  Plaintiff does not contend that the preliminary-injunction framework governs this Rule 12 posture.

  This four-question request warrants relief even under that demanding approach.

         IV.     ARGUMENT

         A.      Meta Made the Missing Source-Side Facts Material to Its Own Motion.

         Meta could have argued only that the FAC fails to plead an agreement. Meta did more.

  Meta told the Court that the April 22 letters were "the exact discovery" its April 21 motion practice

  sought to prevent, and that NCMEC "provided him with exactly what he asked for." ECF No. 22

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 55        Filed 09/03/26      Page 5 of 8 PageID# 471




  at 9, 11. Those are factual characterizations. They assert that the letters answered the question

  Plaintiff had directed to Meta. That assertion holds only if Meta submitted a report concerning the

  account and enforcement event at issue. Whether Meta did so is therefore relevant to Meta's own

  defense. Rule 26(b)(l) reaches "any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party's claim or

  defense." Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(l). Meta placed the equivalence in its defense. The four

  interrogatories test it.

          B.       Meta Seeks Dispositive Adjudication Now, So the Need Exists Now.

          The ordinary answer to a request for pre-conference discovery is: wait for ordinary

  discovery. Meta is not waiting. Its motion asks the Court to dismiss the claims against it with

  prejudice now. ECF No. 22 at 14. In support, Meta uses the April 22 letters as part of its explanation

  for why Plaintiff's intimidation theory fails: the letters, Meta says, gave Plaintiff exactly what he

  asked for. Id. at 11. The need for the four answers exists now because Meta chose to make the

  asserted equivalence relevant now.

          C.       The Present Request Differs From the Earlier Requests Described in Meta's

                   Memorandum.

          Meta's Memorandum recounts Plaintiff's earlier efforts to learn whether Meta filed a

  CyberTipline report. ECF No. 22 at 3-4, 6. Each of those requests preceded Meta's Rule 12 filing

  in this action. The present four interrogatories arise after Meta represented to this Court that

  NCMEC's April 22 letters furnished the discovery Plaintiff had sought from Meta. This Motion

  tests a factual premise in Meta's current defense. It does not renew an earlier request in its earlier

  posture.

          D.       Interrogatory No. 1 Asks the Question the April 22 Letters Never Answered.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 55        Filed 09/03/26      Page 6 of 8 PageID# 472




         The April 22 letters state that two CyberTipline reports exist. They identify no submitting

  provider. They identify no account. Meta says those letters supplied the discovery Plaintiff sought

  from Meta. Interrogatory No. 1 asks whether Meta submitted a CyberTipline report, between July

  1, 2022 and April 22, 2026, in connection with the Facebook account associated with Plaintiff and

  terminated on or about July 4, 2022. That question is the missing link between the letters as written

  and the equivalence Meta asserts. The letters do not answer it. Meta's records do.

         E.      Interrogatories Nos. 2 Through 4 Identify What Meta Itself Submitted.

         Interrogatories Nos. 2 through 4 mirror the pending motion directed to NCMEC from the

  other side of the transmission. ECF No. 15 asks what NCMEC originally received. This Motion

  asks what Meta submitted. Each of the three interrogatories asks whether any report Meta

  submitted within the defined parameters contained or otherwise identified one specified term:

  "Marvelle J. Ballentine," "Jay Ballentine," or jaychizza@icloud.com. The three terms are the three

  identifiers stated in the April 22 letters. The questions concern nothing else.

         F.      The Request Is Narrow and the Burden Is Minimal.

         Plaintiff seeks four interrogatories, directed only to Meta, concerning one Facebook

  account and one enforcement event, within one bounded period, addressing three identifiers, and

  permitting only three responses. Plaintiff does not seek production of any report or any portion of

  any report. He does not seek any additional interrogatory, document request, deposition, third-

  party discovery, communication, metadata, report number, narrative, or follow-up discovery.

  Review is confined to Meta's own CyberTipline-reporting records sufficient to answer the four

  questions. Answering four closed questions about the answering party's own records imposes a

  burden that is minimal and bounded. The request is proportional to the needs of the case. Fed. R.

  Civ. P. 26(b)(l).

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD           Document 55       Filed 09/03/26     Page 7 of 8 PageID# 473




         G.       Each Possible Answer Narrows the Dispute Without Determining Liability.

         A "Yes" to Interrogatory No. 1 establishes only that Meta submitted at least one

  CyberTipline report within the defined parameters. A "No" establishes only that Meta did not. An

  "Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry" establishes only that Meta cannot presently make

  that determination. Interrogatories Nos. 2 through 4 likewise establish only whether the specified

  identifier appeared in such a Meta-submitted report. No answer adjudicates conspiracy,

  intimidation, defamation, or liability. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to treat any answer as

  adjudicating liability. Every permitted answer reduces uncertainty on a question Meta made

  material. None decides the case.

         H.       Coordinating This Motion With ECF No. 15 Preserves the Court's Existing

                  Discovery Schedule.

         ECF No. 15 seeks three closed source-record answers from NCMEC. The docket sets ECF

  No. 15 and ECF No. 26 for hearing on September 25, 2026, at 10:00 a.m., in Alexandria Courtroom

  301, before Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis. This Motion addresses the submitting-party side of

  the same narrow factual question. ECF No. 15 asks what NCMEC received. This Motion asks

  what Meta sent. Hearing the two motions together permits the Court to resolve the related requests

  on one existing motions docket. It requires no new hearing date. The proposed order leaves general

  discovery closed and authorizes only the four interrogatories identified in the Motion. General

  discovery remains governed by Rule 26(f), the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, and further orders

  of the Court.

         V.       CONCLUSION

         Meta says NCMEC furnished the exact discovery Plaintiff sought from Meta. Meta's own

  Memorandum recites that the letters never identify Meta as the reporting provider and never

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD          Document 55        Filed 09/03/26   Page 8 of 8 PageID# 474




  connect either report to the account and enforcement event at issue. Meta's records answer that

  question. Plaintiff seeks four sworn answers from those records and nothing else. Rule 26(d)(l)

  permits that limited relief. The Motion should be granted.

  Date: September 3, 2026                                                 Respectfully submitted,




                                                                            Marvelle J. Ballentine
                                                                                 Plaintiff, prose
                                                                1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847
                                                                      Alexandria, Virginia 22307
                                                                                  (407) 794-6503
                                                                   jayballentine@protonmail.com
