UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA

ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
v. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

SECOND AMENDED AND SUPPLEMENTAL COMPLAINT
DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

1. On July 4, 2022, Meta Platforms, Inc. invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy
against my Facebook account and cut off the contracts I performed through it. I sued them in
September 2025. Meta filed a motion to dismiss. Meta did not staple a CyberTipline report to the
motion.

2. When Meta’s co-defendants’ lawyers asserted that a “legitimate violation by
Ballentine is consistent with the facts” while repeatedly putting my name beside the words “child
sexual exploitation” in their papers, I sued them in February 2026. Defendants filed motions to
dismiss. Defendants did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

3. I sent Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas to NCMEC in April concerning

those two cases, and their attorney, Ms. Hall, sent me two letters associating my full legal name,

“Marvelle J. Ballentine,” with two CyberTipline reports. I sued them in May 2026 because I have
never even used my full legal name to operate any social media account. NCMEC and Hall filed
motions to dismiss. NCMEC and Hall did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

4. I served Meta on July 31, 2026 concerning its role in the drafting, transmission, and
delivery of the letters. It filed a motion to dismiss. Once again, it did not staple a CyberTipline
report to the motion. Meta substituted the CyberTipline report with a chronicle of my prior
lawsuits, their captions, and their procedural history.

5. I have sworn that I never used my full legal name to create, register, identify,
maintain, access, or operate any account on any Meta product or service that I used. The defense
may move to dismiss this complaint. Whether or not they staple a CyberTipline report to the
motions is to be determined.

6. That matters because the two letters signed by Hall on behalf of NCMEC stated:

“In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National

Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its
written responses as detailed below.

NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1)
Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-
level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the
present.”

7. So, that leaves the remaining questions up for determination: Where did my legal
name come from? How and why did it arrive on those letters? Did either of the two asserted
CyberTipline reports, as originally received by NCMEC, actually identify “Marvelle J.
Ballentine”? Did Meta submit either report? Why did NCMEC and Hall act before formal service?
Why did they not wait the five days until April 27, when one court temporarily stayed discovery,
or the nine days until May 1, when discovery in the other action was temporarily stayed? Where

did the urgency come from?

8. I bring six counts: conspiracy under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and Virginia law against
all Defendants, for letters sent to frighten me out of my own lawsuits; defamation, intentional
infliction of emotional distress, and insulting words against Hall and NCMEC, for what the letters
said and to whom.

JURISDICTION AND VENUE

9. This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(1).
Count IV arises under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2).

10. This Court has supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) over the claims
for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, common-law conspiracy, and insulting
words. Those claims arise from the same nucleus of operative fact as Count IV: the preparation,
approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of the April 22, 2026 letters. They form part of
the same case or controversy.

11. This Court has independent subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)
(1) over Counts I,  II, III, and VI, which are asserted only against Hall and NCMEC. Plaintiff is a
citizen of the State of Florida. On information and belief, Hall is domiciled in a State other than
Florida and is a citizen of that State. NCMEC is a Virginia non-profit corporation with its principal

P. The Objective and the Means of Intimidation
174. The purpose of the understanding was to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from

continuing to attend the 376 Action and the 286 Action as a party, and from testifying freely, fully,

and truthfully as a prospective witness in those pending federal proceedings, including on the
CyberTipline-reporting question.

175. The intimidation targeted Plaintiff’s continued attendance as a party in the two
pending federal actions and his prospective sworn testimony concerning his account, the July 4,
2022 enforcement event, the absence of any law-enforcement contact with him, and his damages.

176. Defendants knew that Plaintiff was pro se. They knew the noticed depositions
depended on his personal preparation and examination. They knew the CyberTipline issue was
central to the noticed examinations. They knew Plaintiff was a prospective witness concerning his
account, the enforcement event, and his damages.

177. They bore the letterhead of the federally designated clearinghouse for CyberTipline
reporting. They carried the signature of its Corporate Counsel. They called themselves responses
to subpoenas before formal service. They associated Plaintiff’s full legal name, alternate name,
and email identifier with CyberTipline reports. They omitted the reporting provider, report dates,
report numbers, matched identifier, platform, account connection, and disposition. They were
keyed to the two federal actions by caption and case number. They issued while the depositions
remained imminent and the protective motions remained pending. They were addressed to
Plaintiff alone.

178. A reasonable reader would take the letters to communicate this: NCMEC possessed
reports generated in connection with apparent violations of federal child-exploitation statutes;
those reports associated one or more of Plaintiff’s identifiers with the reported matter; and those

reports could be available to law enforcement.

179. Plaintiff understood the letters to mean that federal reporting records connected his
identity to suspected child-exploitation conduct and that law enforcement could treat him as a
subject of investigation.

180. Defendants intended that fear of investigation, arrest, or prosecution would cause
Plaintiff to dismiss or withdraw from the two federal actions. That would deter Plaintiff, as a party,
from continuing to attend those proceedings. It would deter Plaintiff, as a prospective witness,
from testifying freely, fully, and truthfully. Abandonment of the contemplated CyberTipline
discovery and impairment of Plaintiff’s preparation were intended and foreseeable consequences
of that deterrence. Defendants’ intent is alleged generally and rests on the facts pleaded in this
Complaint.

R. Injury

185. Plaintiff’s injury began on April 28, 2026, when he read the two letters. He vomited.
He wept.

186. Plaintiff understood the letters to mean that federal reporting records connected his
identity to suspected child-exploitation conduct and that law enforcement could treat him as a
subject of investigation. Plaintiff has engaged in no conduct constituting or appearing to constitute
a violation of any statute enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A. He nonetheless lived in acute fear of
imminent governmental investigation, arrest, search, and prosecution. He believed that continuing
the two actions and pressing the CyberTipline issue could expose him to those consequences. That
fear persisted in acute form in the days after April 28, 2026.

187. Plaintiff feared that Hall and NCMEC had sent copies of the letters to counsel for
the defendants in the two actions. He feared that the letters, each bearing a federal caption and case
number, would be filed on the public dockets of those actions, placing on a public federal docket a
statement from the federally designated clearinghouse for CyberTipline reporting that associated
his legal name with two CyberTipline reports. He feared that family members following those
dockets, including family members with children, would distance themselves from him if the
letters were filed.

188. Each letter was created for one pending action. Each bore that action’s caption and
case number. Each purported to answer discovery directed at the CyberTipline issue. Plaintiff
therefore understood the asserted reports as consequences connected to his continued pursuit of
that issue in the two actions. He believed that dismissing the actions and abandoning the
contemplated discovery would end the proceedings through which the asserted reports had

surfaced and would reduce the perceived risk of further governmental attention.

189. The fear caused Plaintiff an acute psychological and functional injury beginning
April 28, 2026. His sleep was disrupted. His eating was disrupted. He suffered intrusive fear of
contact by law enforcement. He suffered recurrent involuntary recollections of his own childhood
sexual abuse. He could not sustain attention on litigation materials. He lost productive and
income-producing time.

190. During the acute period, Plaintiff distanced himself from his own children. He
expected to be taken into custody.

191. On reading the letters, Plaintiff immediately considered dismissing both federal
actions. He believed that continuing to litigate the CyberTipline issue exposed him to criminal
investigation or prosecution. On multiple occasions in the days after April 28, 2026, Plaintiff
refrained from dismissing the two actions only by deliberate effort.

192. During the acute period, the letters’ assertion that two CyberTipline reports existed
dominated Plaintiff’s attention. He did not examine the letters’ stated procedural predicate. Days
later, on reviewing the letters again, he recognized that no subpoena had been served. He
understood then that the letters were voluntary correspondence, not responses compelled or
authenticated through judicial process. From that realization, the letters’ perceived official and
compulsory force diminished, and Plaintiff’s acute fear of imminent arrest began to subside.

193. The letters’ assertion stands unretracted and uncorrected. The digital reproductions
persist in the agency’s mail-management system, outside Plaintiff’s possession and control.
Apprehension concerning the asserted reports recurred while the two actions remained pending.

194. Plaintiff continued to prosecute the two actions despite the acute impairment. He
did so by deliberate effort and at materially diminished capacity. That diminished capacity

affected his responses to the then-pending stay and protective-order motions, his evaluation and

pursuit of the contemplated NCMEC discovery, and his administration of the canceled deposition
sittings, including his communications with the court reporter and videographer he had retained.

195. Plaintiff ultimately refused to dismiss the two actions. That refusal did not eliminate
the deterrent effect of the intimidation. It did not eliminate the injuries the intimidation caused.

The injuries alleged in this Section, including the impairment of Plaintiff’s litigation preparation,
are consequences of that deterrence.

256. The digital reproduction of the letter persists in the agency’s mail-management
system, outside Plaintiff’s possession and control.

257. That system associates the reproduction with Plaintiff’s verified identity, Plaintiff’s
full legal name, Plaintiff’s mailbox account, and Plaintiff’s photographic identification.

258. Plaintiff does not control that system’s access permissions, administrative access,
audit logs, retention practices, or internal dissemination of scanned mail images associated with
his mailbox account.

259. Hall acted willfully, wantonly, and in conscious disregard of Plaintiff’s rights. She
issued the letter knowing its pre-service process characterization and knowing, or recklessly

disregarding, its defamatory implication. She has refused to correct it. She has defended it as

accurate and proper. NCMEC approved the letter’s issuance and has not withdrawn, corrected, or
retracted it. NCMEC’s filings in the 1341 Action are alleged only as evidence that, after notice of
Plaintiff’s claims, NCMEC continued to maintain that the letter was accurate and proper. Plaintiff
is entitled to punitive damages against Hall and NCMEC to the extent permitted by law, subject to
Va. Code § 8.01-38.1.

COUNT III

INTENTIONAL INFLICTION OF EMOTIONAL DISTRESS
(Against Defendants Katie Hall and NCMEC)

260. Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement,
Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections, and Sections A, B, C, G, H, I,
J, M, O, R, and S of the Facts, as if fully set forth herein.

261. On April 22, 2026, Hall directed two letters at Plaintiff. Each was keyed by caption
and case number to a pending federal action. Each associated Plaintiff’s legal name, alternate
name, and account identifier with two CyberTipline reports. Each called itself a response to a
subpoena before formal service. No subpoena had been served. Plaintiff had not requested or
authorized an early response. No court order required a response. A motion to stay discovery had
been filed in each referenced action the day before. Hall issued the letters when no rule, order, or
obligation required it, before the ruling dates the movants had requested and before the noticed
depositions. Hall directed the case-keyed letters to Plaintiff alone. This Count rests on Hall’s
direct transmission of that targeted correspondence to Plaintiff. It does not depend on third-party
publication or reputational injury.

262. Hall knew, before she issued the letters, that Plaintiff is a disclosed survivor of
childhood sexual abuse. Section C alleges the disclosures. Hall understood the criminal and law-
enforcement significance of associating a named individual with CyberTipline reports. She

understood that invoking subpoena process before formal service would lend the assertion added

official force. Hall directed at Plaintiff a communication associating his legal name with reporting
concerning child sexual exploitation, the subject of the abuse he had disclosed. Hall knew, or
recklessly disregarded, that directing that combination at a disclosed survivor of childhood sexual
abuse created a high probability of acute emotional distress. Hall knew that the association, so
directed, was substantially certain to cause Plaintiff acute emotional distress. She acted with intent
to cause that distress, or in reckless disregard of the substantial certainty that it would result.

263. Directing at a disclosed survivor of childhood sexual abuse a false and
unauthenticated association between that person and child-exploitation reporting offends the
generally accepted standards of decency and morality and exceeds the bounds of what a civilized
community tolerates.

264. Hall performed every act alleged in this Count within the scope of her employment
as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel and in performance of her responsibility for legal
correspondence NCMEC issues in response to claimed legal process. NCMEC, acting through
Hall and one or more additional personnel, approved the wording of the letters and authorized
their issuance and transmission. NCMEC is liable for the conduct alleged in this Count.

265. Hall’s conduct directly and proximately caused Plaintiff severe emotional distress.
Upon reading the letters on April 28, 2026, Plaintiff vomited. He suffered recurrent involuntary
recollections of his own childhood sexual abuse. He lived in acute fear of imminent arrest and
prosecution. Expecting to be taken into custody, he distanced himself from his own children. His
sleep and eating were disrupted. He could not sustain attention on his work. That distress persisted
in acute form until, days later, he recognized that no subpoena had been served. The distress was

severe. It was beyond what a reasonable person could be expected to endure.

266. The severe emotional distress on which this Count rests arises from Hall’s direct
transmission of the letters to Plaintiff and from their content. It does not arise from any
apprehension that the letters would be published to, or read by, any other person.

267. As a direct and proximate result of the conduct alleged in this Count, Plaintiff
sustained compensatory damages for mental anguish, severe emotional distress, physical
manifestation, functional impairment, lost productive capacity, and loss of capacity for the
enjoyment of life. Count III seeks no recovery for reputational injury.

268. The severe emotional distress alleged in this Count continued after the filing of the
First Amended Complaint. The subsequent events alleged in Section O occurred while Plaintiff’s
uncertainty concerning the two reports remained unresolved.

COUNT IV
CONSPIRACY TO DETER A PARTY AND WITNESS, BY INTIMIDATION,
FROM ATTENDING AND TESTIFYING IN COURTS OF THE

UNITED STATES — 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2)
(Against All Defendants)

269. Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement,
Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections, and Sections A through J,
Sections M through O, and Sections P through S of the Facts, as if fully set forth herein.

270. Meta, Hall, and NCMEC are separate and legally distinct persons. Meta is a
corporation. Hall is an individual. NCMEC is a non-profit corporation. Hall is not an officer,
employee, agent, or authorized representative of Meta. NCMEC is not an affiliate, agent, or
representative of Meta. The agreement alleged in Section N was reached between Meta, acting
through one or more of its own officers, employees, agents, or authorized representatives, on one
side, and Hall and NCMEC on the other. The combination alleged in this Count comprises at least

two separate and legally distinct persons.

271. Defendants reached the agreement alleged in Section N of the Facts. Section N
pleads the nine facts on which that allegation rests, including the identical materials received by
NCMEC and by counsel for Meta and Accenture, the April 21, 2026 motions directed at the same
discovery, and the two letters, each keyed to a separate federal action, issued the next day before
formal service and before any court ruled.

272. The purpose of the agreement was to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from
continuing to attend the 376 Action and the 286 Action as a party, and from testifying freely, fully,
and truthfully as a prospective witness in those pending federal proceedings, as alleged in Section
P of the Facts. The letters, on NCMEC letterhead and over the signature of its Corporate Counsel,
associated Plaintiff’s full legal name with two CyberTipline reports, and they issued while the
noticed depositions were imminent and the protective motions were pending.

273. One or more Defendants committed acts in furtherance of the agreement, as alleged
in Section Q of the Facts. Hall signed and transmitted the letters. NCMEC approved their issuance
and authorized the use of its name, letterhead, and institutional identity.

274. The acts in furtherance of the agreement injured Plaintiff in his person and
materially impaired his attendance and testimony as a party and prospective witness, as alleged in
Section R of the Facts. He became physically ill. He feared arrest and prosecution. He distanced
himself from his children. He could not sustain attention on litigation materials.

275. Meta knowingly joined the agreement through one or more authorized
representatives or intermediaries. Hall knowingly joined and implemented the agreement by
preparing or approving the letters, signing them, and authorizing their transmission. NCMEC

knowingly joined and implemented the agreement, acting through Hall and one or more additional

personnel who approved the issuance of the letters. Each Doe Defendant is liable only to the extent
the evidence establishes that the Doe knowingly joined or implemented the common plan.

276. Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the 376 Action, alleged in Section O, is pleaded as
a subsequent fact bearing on Meta’s knowledge, Meta’s state of mind, Meta’s awareness of the
relationship between this action and the 376 Action, and the circumstantial allegations supporting
this Count. It is not an independent basis for liability. Liability under this Count rests on the
conduct alleged in Sections N, P, and Q of the Facts.

277. Defendants’ conduct directly and proximately caused the injuries alleged in this
Complaint.

278. Defendants acted intentionally and with conscious disregard for Plaintiff’s
federally protected status as a party and prospective witness, warranting punitive damages.

COUNT V

COMMON-LAW CONSPIRACY
(Against All Defendants)

279. Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement,
Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections, and Sections A through N and
Sections P through S of the Facts, as if fully set forth herein.

280. This Count arises under the common law of Virginia.

281. Hall, NCMEC, Meta, and one or more Doe Defendants combined through the
understanding alleged in Section N of the Facts. Meta is separate and legally distinct from Hall and
from NCMEC, as this Complaint alleges. The combination comprised at least two separate and
legally distinct persons.

282. The combination was carried out through the preparation, approval, issuance,
transmission, and publication of the two April 22, 2026 letters. The publication of each letter

constituted the defamation alleged in Counts I and II.

283. The participants understood and intended that the letters would travel through the
selected commercial mail channel. They understood and intended that the third-party publication
alleged in Counts I and II would occur in carrying out the understanding.

284. The participants committed the overt acts alleged in Section Q of the Facts. The
publications alleged in Counts I and II occurred.

285. The participants acted intentionally, purposefully, and without lawful justification.

286. As a direct and proximate result of the combination and the acts in furtherance of it,
Plaintiff sustained the damages alleged in Section R of the Facts and in Counts I and II: presumed
damages, humiliation, embarrassment, mental suffering, and injury to reputation. Each participant
is jointly and severally liable for those damages.

287. The participants acted willfully, wantonly, and in conscious disregard of Plaintiff’s
rights, warranting punitive damages subject to Va. Code § 8.01-38.1.

COUNT VI

INSULTING WORDS — VA. CODE § 8.01-45
(Against Defendants Katie Hall and NCMEC)

288. Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement,
Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections, and Sections A, B, C, G, H, I,
J, K, M, O, R, and S of the Facts, as if fully set forth herein.

289. This Count is pleaded in the alternative under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(d)
(2). It does not depend on publication of either letter to any third party. It incorporates no
allegation from Section L of the Facts.

290. Hall directed each of the two April 22, 2026 letters to Plaintiff personally, at
Plaintiff’s mailing address.

291. The words of each letter associated Plaintiff’s full legal name, alternate name, and

email identifier with two CyberTipline reports, on NCMEC letterhead, over the signature of

NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel, and framed as a response to subpoena process before formal
service. Those words, in their usual construction and common acceptation, are insults that tend to
violence and breach of the peace. In the context alleged in Section K of the Facts, the words
convey the imputation described in that Section.

292. The imputation each letter conveys is false. Plaintiff has not engaged in conduct
constituting, or reasonably appearing to constitute, a violation of any statute enumerated in 18
U.S.C. § 2258A.

293. On information and belief, neither report referenced in the letters concerned
Plaintiff personally. On information and belief, neither report, as originally received by NCMEC,
contained or otherwise identified Plaintiff as “Marvelle J. Ballentine.”

294. Hall selected the words of each letter. She knowingly selected language stating that
each letter responded to a subpoena before formal service, when Plaintiff had not waived service
or requested an early response. She acted with knowledge or reckless disregard of the falsity of the
imputation each letter conveyed.

295. Hall performed every act alleged in this Count within the scope of her employment
as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel. NCMEC, acting through Hall and one or more additional
personnel, approved the wording of the letters and authorized their issuance and transmission.
NCMEC is liable for the conduct alleged in this Count.

296. As a direct and proximate result of the conduct alleged in this Count, Plaintiff
sustained the damages alleged in Section R of the Facts: humiliation, embarrassment, mental
suffering, and severe emotional distress.

297. Hall and NCMEC acted willfully, wantonly, and in conscious disregard of

Plaintiff’s rights, warranting punitive damages subject to Va. Code § 8.01-38.1.

PRAYER FOR RELIEF
WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court enter judgment in his favor and

against Defendants and grant the following relief:
A. On Counts I and II, against Defendants Hall and NCMEC, jointly and severally: (1)
compensatory damages in the amount of $42,820,260, including presumed damages and
actual damages; and (2) punitive damages to the extent supported by actual malice findings,
subject to the cap established by Va. Code § 8.01-38.1.
B. On Count III, against Defendants Hall and NCMEC, jointly and severally:
compensatory damages.
C. On Count IV, against all Defendants, jointly and severally: compensatory damages
in an amount to be determined by the jury; and punitive damages.
D. On Count V, against all Defendants, jointly and severally: compensatory damages
in an amount to be determined by the jury; and punitive damages subject to Va. Code §
8.01-38.1.
E. On Count VI, against Defendants Hall and NCMEC, jointly and severally:

compensatory damages; and punitive damages subject to Va. Code § 8.01-38.1.

F. Costs of suit.
G. Pre-judgment and post-judgment interest at the legal rate.
H. Such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper.

DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL
Pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 38(b), Plaintiff demands a trial by jury on all

issues so triable.¹

Date: September 7, 2026 Respectfully submitted,



Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847
Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503
jayballentine@protonmail.com

United States: Hearings Before the S. Comm. on the Judiciary, 102d Cong. (1991) (statement of
Judge Clarence Thomas, Oct. 11, 1991):

“...It’s a national disgrace. And from my standpoint as a black American, as far as
I’m concerned, it is a high-tech lynching...”

“I would have preferred an assassin’s bullet to this kind of living hell that they have

IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED
AND SUPPLEMENTAL COMPLAINT

I, Marvelle J. Ballentine, declare as follows:

1. I am the Plaintiff in this action. I make this Declaration based upon my personal
knowledge. I am competent to testify to the matters stated herein.

2. My legal name is Marvelle J. Ballentine.

3. On July 4, 2022, Meta Platforms, Inc. invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy
against the Facebook account that I operated.

4. The Facebook account against which Meta invoked that policy was operated by me

under the name “Jay Ballentine.”

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document59-2 Filed 09/08/26 Page 3 of 4 PagelD#
561

5. Meta’s July 4, 2022 enforcement action was not issued against an account operated
by me under the name “Marvelle J. Ballentine.”

6. Before April 22, 2026, I never used the name “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to create,
register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any account on any product or service owned or
operated by Meta Platforms, Inc. that I used.

7. I never used “Marvelle J. Ballentine” as a username, profile name, display name,
account name, or other identity by which I identified myself on Facebook, Instagram, Threads,
WhatsApp, Oculus, Meta Quest, or any other Meta product or service that I used.

8. I did not provide “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to Meta Platforms, Inc. as the name
identifying me or any Meta account that I created, maintained, or operated.

9. In connection with my online identity, including my use of Meta products and
services, I used the name “Jay Ballentine,” rather than “Marvelle J. Ballentine.”

10. To the extent “Marvelle J. Ballentine” appeared in the April 9, 2026
correspondence, subpoena materials, or other litigation materials that I transmitted to the National
Center for Missing & Exploited Children, I included that name because it is my legal name and the
name under which the underlying federal litigation was pending. I did not include that name

because I had used it to identify or operate any Meta account.

KATIE HALL, individually;

META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

ORDER

This matter comes before the Court on Plaintiff's Motion for Leave to File Second
Amended and Supplemental Complaint Pursuant to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a)(2) and
15(d), and Request for Expedited Determination on the Papers (the “Motion”). Having considered
the Motion, the Memorandum in Support, the proposed Second Amended and Supplemental
Complaint attached to the Motion as Exhibit A, the Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine attached
as Exhibit B, and the briefing, and finding that leave should be freely given under Rule 15(a)(2) and
that supplementation is appropriate under Rule 15(d), it is hereby

ORDERED that the Motion is GRANTED; and it is further

ORDERED that the Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint attached to the Motion
as Exhibit A is DEEMED FILED as of the date of this Order and is the operative complaint in this

action; and it is further

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document59-3 Filed 09/08/26 Page 2 of 2 PagelD#
564

ORDERED that the Clerk may, to the extent administratively necessary, docket the Second
Amended and Supplemental Complaint separately as the operative pleading; and it is further

ORDERED that Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File Supplemental Complaint Pursuant to
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d) (ECF No. 26) is DENIED AS MOOT, the supplemental
matter proposed therein having been incorporated into the Second Amended and Supplemental
Complaint; and it is further

ORDERED that Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File Sur-Reply (ECF No. 43) is DENIED
AS MOOT, the Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint having replaced the First Amended
Complaint to which the briefing underlying that request was directed; and it is further

ORDERED that Defendants shall respond to the Second Amended and Supplemental
Complaint within the time prescribed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure or such other time as
the Court directs.

It is SO ORDERED.

Alexandria, Virginia

Date: , 2026

Ivan D. Davis
United States Magistrate Judge

                            UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                                  09/08/2026
                         FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
                                 ALEXANDRIA DIVISION


  MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

                 Plaintiff,

                 v.                                           Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
                                                              The Honorable Judge
                                                              Rossie D. Alston Jr.


  KATIE HALL, individually;
  NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
  META PLATFORMS, INC.;
  and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

                 Defendants.


              PLAINTIFF'S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED
         AND SUPPLEMENTAL COMPLAINT PURSUANT TO FEDERAL RULES
                 OF CIVIL PROCEDURE 15(a)(2) AND 15(d), AND REQUEST
                      FOR EXPEDITED DETERMINATION ON THE PAPERS


         Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a)(2) and

  lS(d) for leave to file the complete Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint attached as

  Exhibit A. Plaintiff requests expedited determination of this Motion on the papers. The

  accompanying Memorandum in Support develops the grounds stated below, and Plaintiff

  incorporates it by reference.

         I.      THE COMPLETE PROPOSED PLEADING ELIMINATES THE FORM

                 OBJECTION RAISED IN ECF NO. 53

         1.      On September 3, 2026, Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. ("Meta") filed its

  opposition to Plaintiff's pending Motion for Leave to File Supplemental Complaint Pursuant to

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD           Document 59        Filed 09/08/26      Page 2 of 10 PageID# 498




  Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d) (ECF No. 26). ECF No. 53. Meta raises a form objection to

  ECF No. 26. Meta states that ECF No. 26 attached "only his supplemental allegations,

  'incorporating by reference' the remainder of his FAC," rather than "a copy of the proposed

  amended pleading in its entirety." ECF No. 53 at 3 n.1. Plaintiff does not concede that the objection

  was well taken. Plaintiff has instead elected to eliminate that procedural dispute rather than require

  the Court to adjudicate it. Exhibit A is one complete proposed Second Amended and Supplemental

  Complaint. It incorporates no prior pleading by reference. This Motion therefore places the entire

  proposed operative pleading before the Court in one document.

         II.     RELIEF REQUESTED

         2.      Plaintiff requests leave to file the proposed Second Amended and Supplemental

  Complaint ("SAC") attached as Exhibit A. Plaintiff further requests that the Court deem Exhibit A

  filed, and deem it the operative pleading in this action, upon entry of the order granting leave.

  Plaintiff further requests that, upon granting leave, the Court deny ECF No. 26 as moot and deny

  Plaintiff's Motion for Leave to File Sur-Reply (ECF No. 43) as moot.

         III.    THE PROPOSED PLEADING

         3.      The First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) is the operative pleading. The proposed

  SAC replaces the First Amended Complaint with one integrated pleading.

         4.      The proposed SAC adds no defendant. The proposed SAC adds no cause of action.

  The proposed SAC adds no category of relief. The proposed SAC retains the six-count structure of

  the First Amended Complaint. Count I and Count II plead defamation per se and defamation by

  implication against Defendants Katie Hall and the National Center for Missing & Exploited

  Children ("NCMEC"). Count III pleads intentional infliction of emotional distress against Hall and

  NCMEC. Count IV pleads conspiracy under the first clause of 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) against all

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD           Document 59        Filed 09/08/26      Page 3 of 10 PageID# 499




  Defendants. Count V pleads Virginia common-law conspiracy against all Defendants. Count VI

  pleads insulting words under Va. Code§ 8.01-45 against Hall and NCMEC.

         5.      The proposed SAC pleads additional facts in four categories. First, the proposed

  SAC pleads facts concerning the source-level falsity of the asserted association between the two

  CyberTipline reports and "Marvelle J. Ballentine." The proposed SAC pleads facts concerning the

  person-level falsity of the implication that the reports concerned Plaintiff personally. The proposed

  SAC pleads facts concerning the defamatory implication arising from the letters' wording and

  omitted limitations. Ex. A§§ J, K, S. Second, the proposed SAC pleads facts concerning Plaintiff's

  legal name and Plaintiff's Meta account. Those facts include that Plaintiff never used "Marvelle J.

  Ballentine" to create, identify, or operate any Meta account. Ex. A § S; Ex. B ,, 2-10. Third, the

  proposed SAC pleads events occurring after the First Amended Complaint. Those events bear on

  Defendants' knowledge, on Defendants' state of mind, on the unresolved referent of the April 22,

  2026 letters, and on Plaintiff's continuing injury. Ex. A§ O; Ex. A, Count III. Fourth, the proposed

  SAC incorporates the post-filing allegations presently proposed through ECF No. 26. Those

  allegations include NCMEC's August 12, 2026 memorandum, the August 13, 2026

  communications with counsel for NCMEC and Hall, and Meta's August 13, 2026 filing in the

  Northern District of California. The SAC also pleads Hall's September 2, 2026 filings expressly

  adopting NCMEC's litigation positions. Ex. A§ O; Ex. A, Counts III, IV.

         6.      The    proposed    SAC     combines    amendment      under   Rule    15(a)(2)   with

  supplementation under Rule 15(d) in one pleading. The amended matter and the supplemental

  matter concern the same two April 22, 2026 letters, the same Defendants, and the same six claims.

         IV.     RELATIONSHIP TO ECF NOS. 26 AND 43

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD          Document 59        Filed 09/08/26       Page 4 of 10 PageID# 500




         7.     ECF No. 26 remains pending unless and until the Court grants this Motion. Upon

  grant of this Motion, the supplemental allegations proposed through ECF No. 26 become part of

  the operative pleading through the complete SAC, and ECF No. 26 becomes moot. If the Court

  denies this Motion, ECF No. 26 remains for decision on its own terms.

         8.     ECF No. 43 is Plaintiff's Motion for Leave to File Sur-Reply. ECF Nos. 43, 44.

  That motion is directed to Meta's Rule 12 briefing addressed to the First Amended Complaint. ECF

  Nos. 22, 39. Upon grant of this Motion, the SAC replaces the First Amended Complaint. Plaintiff

  then no longer requires the separate sur-reply vehicle, and ECF No. 43 becomes moot.

         9.     This Motion therefore permits one complete operative pleading to replace two

  separate pending procedural requests.

         V.     PROCEDURAL POSTURE

         10.    This action is at the pleading stage. Plaintiff filed the original Complaint on July 30,

  2026 (ECF No. 1). Plaintiff filed the First Amended Complaint on August 6, 2026 (ECF No. 5).

  NCMEC moved to dismiss the First Amended Complaint on August 12, 2026 (ECF Nos. 10, 11).

  Meta moved to dismiss the First Amended Complaint on August 21, 2026 (ECF Nos. 21, 22). Meta

  filed its reply on August 31, 2026 (ECF No. 39). On September 2, 2026, Hall moved to dismiss the

  First Amended Complaint and expressly adopted and joined NCMEC's Motion to Dismiss and

  Memorandum in Support (ECF No. 45). On September 2, 2026, the Court vacated the hearing on

  NCMEC's motion to dismiss and directed that the motion be decided on the papers (ECF No. 50).

         11.    Plaintiff filed ECF No. 26 on August 21, 2026 (ECF Nos. 26, 27, 28). NCMEC

           12.    On September 1, 2026, Plaintiff filed ECF No. 43, Plaintiff's Motion for Leave to

           13.    As of the filing of this Motion, no Defendant has answered. No scheduling order has

           VI.    BRIEFING AND DETERMINATION ON THE PAPERS

           14.    This Motion is submitted under the ordinary briefing schedule of Local Civil Rule

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 2 of 52 PagelD#

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA

ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
v. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

SECOND AMENDED AND SUPPLEMENTAL COMPLAINT
DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

1. On July 4, 2022, Meta Platforms, Inc. invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy
against my Facebook account and cut off the contracts I performed through it. I sued them in
September 2025. Meta filed a motion to dismiss. Meta did not staple a CyberTipline report to the
motion.

2. When Meta’s co-defendants’ lawyers asserted that a “legitimate violation by
Ballentine is consistent with the facts” while repeatedly putting my name beside the words “child
sexual exploitation” in their papers, I sued them in February 2026. Defendants filed motions to
dismiss. Defendants did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

3. I sent Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas to NCMEC in April concerning

those two cases, and their attorney, Ms. Hall, sent me two letters associating my full legal name,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 3 of 52 PagelD#
587

“Marvelle J. Ballentine,” with two CyberTipline reports. I sued them in May 2026 because I have
never even used my full legal name to operate any social media account. NCMEC and Hall filed
motions to dismiss. NCMEC and Hall did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

4. I served Meta on July 31, 2026 concerning its role in the drafting, transmission, and
delivery of the letters. It filed a motion to dismiss. Once again, it did not staple a CyberTipline
report to the motion. Meta substituted the CyberTipline report with a chronicle of my prior
lawsuits, their captions, and their procedural history.

5. I have sworn that I never used my full legal name to create, register, identify,
maintain, access, or operate any account on any Meta product or service that I used. The defense
may move to dismiss this complaint. Whether or not they staple a CyberTipline report to the
motions is to be determined.

6. That matters because the two letters signed by Hall on behalf of NCMEC stated:

“In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National

Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its
written responses as detailed below.

NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1)
Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-
level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the
present.”

7. So, that leaves the remaining questions up for determination: Where did my legal
name come from? How and why did it arrive on those letters? Did either of the two asserted
CyberTipline reports, as originally received by NCMEC, actually identify “Marvelle J.
Ballentine”? Did Meta submit either report? Why did NCMEC and Hall act before formal service?
Why did they not wait the five days until April 27, when one court temporarily stayed discovery,
or the nine days until May 1, when discovery in the other action was temporarily stayed? Where

did the urgency come from?

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 4 of 52 PagelD#
588

8. I bring six counts: conspiracy under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and Virginia law against
all Defendants, for letters sent to frighten me out of my own lawsuits; defamation, intentional
infliction of emotional distress, and insulting words against Hall and NCMEC, for what the letters
said and to whom.

JURISDICTION AND VENUE

9. This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(1).
Count IV arises under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2).

10. This Court has supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) over the claims
for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, common-law conspiracy, and insulting
words. Those claims arise from the same nucleus of operative fact as Count IV: the preparation,
approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of the April 22, 2026 letters. They form part of
the same case or controversy.

11. This Court has independent subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)
(1) over Counts I, H, II, and VI, which are asserted only against Hall and NCMEC. Plaintiff is a
citizen of the State of Florida. On information and belief, Hall is domiciled in a State other than
Florida and is a citizen of that State. NCMEC is a Virginia non-profit corporation with its principal
place of business in Alexandria, Virginia, and is a citizen of Virginia. Complete diversity exists
between Plaintiff and each Defendant against whom those Counts are asserted. The amount in
controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.

12. Venue is proper in this district under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2). A substantial part of
the events giving rise to the claims occurred here. Hall prepared or approved, signed, and issued

the April 22, 2026 letters from NCMEC’s office in Alexandria, Virginia, within the Alexandria

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 5 of 52 PagelD#
589

Division of this district. The letters were transmitted to Plaintiffs commercial mail-receiving
address in Alexandria, Virginia, where they were opened and processed.

13. This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Hall under Virginia Code § 8.01-
328.1(A)(3). Hall performed the challenged acts in Virginia. She prepared or approved, signed,
issued, and caused the transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters from NCMEC’s Alexandria
headquarters. The first third-party publication alleged in this Complaint occurred in Alexandria,
when the commercial mail-receiving agency opened, reviewed, and scanned the letters. Each
claim against Hall arises from her Virginia conduct.

14. This Court has general personal jurisdiction over NCMEG, a Virginia corporation
with its principal place of business in Alexandria, Virginia. This Court also has specific personal
jurisdiction over NCMEC under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). The April 22, 2026 letters
were prepared or approved, signed, and issued from NCMEC’s Alexandria headquarters, and each
claim against NCMEC arises from that Virginia conduct.

15. This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Meta Platforms, Inc. under
Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3) and the conspiracy-based attribution of forum contacts.
Sections N through Q allege the conspiracy. Meta knowingly participated through one or more
authorized representatives or intermediaries. NCMEC and Hall committed the Virginia acts
alleged in this Complaint in furtherance of that conspiracy. Meta received the April 9, 2026
materials directed to NCMEC’s Legal Department in Alexandria, Virginia. The understanding
alleged in Section N contemplated that Hall would issue the case-specific correspondence from
that Virginia office. Plaintiff’s claim against Meta arises from those Virginia acts.

16. The exercise of personal jurisdiction over each Defendant comports with the Due

Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 6 of 52 PagelD#
590

PARTIES

17. Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine, also known as Jay Ballentine, is an adult citizen of
the State of Florida. At all relevant times Plaintiff maintained a mailing address at 1520 Belle
View Blvd, Ste. #5847, Alexandria, Virginia 22307. A commercial mail-receiving agency
operates that address and is authorized to receive and process mail on Plaintiff’s behalf.

18. Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) is a
Virginia non-profit corporation. Its principal place of business is 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite
125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. NCMEC operates the CyberTipline under federal authorization
in connection with 18 U.S.C. § 2258A. At all relevant times NCMEC employed Defendant Katie
Hall as its Corporate Counsel. Hall was responsible for legal correspondence NCMEC issued in
response to claimed legal process. NCMEC is sued for its own conduct, undertaken through Hall
and one or more additional personnel. NCMEC is also sued vicariously for Hall’s conduct within
the scope of her employment.

19. Defendant Katie Hall is an individual. At all relevant times she served as Corporate
Counsel of NCMEC at 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. On
information and belief, Hall is domiciled in a State other than Florida and is a citizen of that State.
Hall prepared or approved, signed, issued, and caused the transmission of the April 22, 2026
letters. Hall is sued individually for her own tortious conduct.

20. Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) is a Delaware corporation with its
principal place of business in Menlo Park, California. Meta was a defendant in the 376 Action and
in the 286 Action at all relevant times. Meta is an electronic service provider subject to the
reporting duties of 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.

21. Meta owns and operates Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 7 of 52 PagelD#
591

22. Defendants John/Jane Does 1-6 are persons not yet identified who participated in
the communications, authorization, approval, preparation, or transmission alleged in this
Complaint. Their roles include: the Meta representative or representatives who communicated
with NCMEC concerning Plaintiff, the identifiers, the intended subpoenas, or the two federal
actions; any Accenture representative who knowingly joined or implemented the understanding
alleged in this Complaint; the NCMEC personnel who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026
letters; and any intermediary, including counsel or other agents acting for Meta, Accenture, or
NCMEG, through whom the alleged communications occurred. Meta, Accenture, NCMEC, and
their representatives hold the records that identify the Doe Defendants. Plaintiff will seek leave to
amend when those identities are ascertained.

SCOPE OF ALLEGATIONS

23. This Complaint predicates no liability on the filing of any motion, brief, or other
paper in any court. Court filings identified here are alleged solely as facts establishing timing,
notice, knowledge, coordination, and admissions. The claims do not challenge NCMEC’s receipt,
maintenance, or lawful referral of CyberTipline reports. The claims challenge the extra-judicial
agreement alleged below and the preparation, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of
external legal correspondence that falsely invoked compulsory process and served the litigation-
directed purposes alleged below. No claim against Meta seeks liability for the July 4, 2022
account-level enforcement, for any content-related decision, for any failure to restore Plaintiff’s
account, or for any treatment of third-party content. Those matters are alleged only to establish the
subject matter of the pending federal actions, Defendants’ knowledge, Meta’s interest in whether
a CyberTipline report exists, and the testimony Defendants sought to deter. The same is true of the

memorandum, motion to stay, and opposition filed in the 1341 Action and the August 13, 2026

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 8 of 52 PagelD#
592

filing in the 376 Action, each identified in Section O. Each is alleged as an admission and as a fact
establishing timing, coordination, and knowledge. None is conduct on which any claim rests.

FACTS
A. The Federal Proceedings and Plaintiff’s Role as Party and Prospective

Witness

24. Plaintiff filed the 286 Action on February 9, 2026. Plaintiff filed the 376 Action on
February 17, 2026. Each action was pending in a court of the United States at all relevant times.

25. The defendants in the 376 Action included Meta, Accenture, TaskUs, Inc., and
Genpact Limited. Accenture is a limited liability partnership that provides platform policy
enforcement services to Meta. The defendants in the 286 Action included Meta, Devin S.
Anderson, and Christopher W. Keegan. Kirkland & Ellis LLP (“Kirkland”) represented Anderson
and Keegan. Accenture, Anderson, Keegan, TaskUs, Inc., Genpact Limited, Kirkland, Orrick,
Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP (“Orrick”), Diana M. Fassbender, and Mariana Chapleau are not
defendants here. Their conduct is alleged only to establish chronology, notice, knowledge, or the
conduct of the Defendants, including the Doe Defendants.

26. Both actions arise from one event. On July 4, 2022, Meta issued an account-level
enforcement notice against Plaintiff’s Facebook account. That notice interrupted Plaintiff’s ability
to perform third-party contracts through the account.

27. Plaintiff proceeded pro se in both actions. Every act of prosecution depended on
Plaintiff’s personal capacity and participation: discovery, deposition examination, briefing, and
appearance.

28. Plaintiff was a prospective witness in both actions. He expected to testify under
oath, at deposition and at trial, concerning his account history, the July 4, 2022 enforcement event,

the absence of any law-enforcement contact with him, and his damages.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 9 of 52 PagelD#
593

29. The dockets of the 376 Action and the 286 Action were publicly accessible through

the federal Public Access to Court Electronic Records system.
B. The Contested CyberTipline Question

30. One question has been contested since October 2025: whether Meta, or any person
acting in connection with the July 4, 2022 account-enforcement event, transmitted a CyberTipline
report under 18 U.S.C. § 2258A concerning Plaintiff or his account identifiers.

31. Before April 22, 2026, no CyberTipline report concerning Plaintiff had been
identified, produced, or attributed to any provider in any forum.

32.  Plaintiff’s first substantive act in the 376 Action was a motion for leave to serve a
single early request for admission. The request asked whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report
regarding Plaintiff’s account. The court denied the motion.

33. From that denial forward, the defendants in the 376 Action knew what Plaintiff’s
discovery would target: the existence or non-existence of a CyberTipline report.

34. The operative complaint in the 376 Action alleged that Meta filed no CyberTipline
report. Its prayer sought a declaration that no CyberTipline report was filed regarding the July 4,
2022 enforcement event.

35. On April 9, 2026, Meta moved to dismiss the 376 Action (ECF No. 85). Meta
described Plaintiff’s allegation that a CyberTipline report had been submitted and disseminated as
“hypothetical (and elsewhere contradicted).” Meta identified the contradiction as Plaintiff’s
allegation that “Meta filed no CyberTipline report.”

36. In the 286 Action, the existence or non-existence of a CyberTipline report bore on
the claims then pending, including the falsity and factual basis of the statements challenged in that

action.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 10 of 52 PagelD#
594

C. Plaintiff’s Disclosed Survivor Status

37. On September 9, 2025, Plaintiff filed a complaint in Ballentine v. Meta Platforms,
Inc., et al., Case No. 3:25-cv-07671-CRB (N.D. Cal.) (the “California Action”).

38. That complaint contained a single footnote. The footnote states: “As a CSA
survivor, Plaintiff gratefully acknowledges the unwavering support of his wife, whose steady
presence made the psychological recovery, and subsequent preparation of this Complaint
possible. He further acknowledges his children, especially his eldest, who endured his distance
during the preparation of this filing after once celebrating his NRVTA graduation with pride. This
work now returns to them, just as their father and husband does.”

39. The footnote disclosed that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse and had
undergone a psychological recovery that made preparation of the complaint possible.

40. Before April 22, 2026, then, Plaintiff had disclosed that he is a survivor of
childhood sexual abuse. He had described undergoing psychological recovery. He retained the
functional capacity to prepare and prosecute his pending actions.

41. The publicly filed pleadings in the 286 Action disclosed on their face that Plaintiff
is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse. Those pleadings alleged that placing Plaintiff’s name near
child-sexual-exploitation terminology had already caused Plaintiff emotional injury.

42. Meta, Anderson, and Keegan, through their respective counsel, received and
litigated against the 286 Action pleadings containing those disclosures before April 21, 2026.

43. The Kirkland attorneys who appeared for Accenture in the 376 Action also
represented Anderson and Keegan in the 286 Action. They therefore possessed the 286 Action
pleadings before April 21, 2026. Accenture’s authorized representatives knew of the disclosures

before April 21, 2026.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 11 of 52 PagelD#
595

D. CyberTipline Reporting by Meta-Operated Services
44. NCMEC receives CyberTipline reports from Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.
E. Counsel Operating Across Both Actions

45.  Fassbender, an attorney at Orrick, was counsel of record for Meta in the 286 Action
and for Meta and Genpact Limited in the 376 Action.

46. Chapleau and Anderson, attorneys at Kirkland, were counsel of record for
Accenture in the 376 Action. Kirkland, through Chapleau, also represented Anderson and Keegan
in the 286 Action.

47. Anderson held two roles at once. In the 286 Action he was an individual defendant
and a noticed deposition witness. In the 376 Action he was counsel of record for Accenture.

F. The Deposition Program

48. OnApril 7, 2026, Plaintiff served a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition notice on Accenture in
the 376 Action. The notice set a two-day examination for April 29 and April 30, 2026. Plaintiff
served the notice on Chapleau and Anderson.

49. Matter for Examination No. 5 of that notice is captioned “CyberTipline Reporting
and Reportability Status.” It encompasses “whether any CyberTipline Report was Transmitted to
NCMEC in connection with the Account-Level Enforcement Event.”

50. On April 7, 2026, Plaintiff noticed Anderson’s deposition in the 286 Action for
April 28, 2026. On April 10, 2026, Plaintiff re-served the notice with logistical details.

51. Plaintiff retained a court reporter and a videographer for the noticed depositions.

G. The April 9, 2026 Transmissions
52. On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff transmitted to NCMEC’s Legal Department a letter

captioned “Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas — Two Separate Matters.” The letter

10

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 12 of 52 PagelD#
596

identified the 376 Action and the 286 Action by caption and case number. It enclosed copies of the
signed subpoenas Plaintiff intended to serve formally on NCMEC after the notice period had run.
It stated that formal service would occur after the notice period had run.

53. Schedule A to each subpoena commanded one item: a document sufficient to show
whether NCMEC received or maintains any CyberTipline report concerning (1) Marvelle J.
Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com.
Schedule A expressly excluded the contents of any report.

54. The April 9, 2026 transmission gave NCMEC advance notice of the subpoenas and
included copies of the signed subpoenas. Neither subpoena had been formally served on NCMEC.
Plaintiff did not request or authorize a response before formal service. Plaintiff did not waive
service. Plaintiff did not authorize NCMEC or Hall to treat receipt of the advance-notice package
as formal service.

55. On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff served the same materials under Federal Rule of Civil
Procedure 45(a)(4) on counsel for the parties in both actions, including Orrick for Meta and
Kirkland for Accenture.

56. As of April 9, 2026, NCMEC had received the advance notice and its enclosures.
Counsel for Meta and counsel for Accenture had received identical materials for their clients. The
materials identified the same two federal actions, the same three identifiers, and the same
discovery objective. Each recipient knew from the face of the materials that formal service on
NCMEC was announced to occur only after the notice period had run.

57. Hall possessed or reviewed the case-specific materials no later than the moment she

approved, signed, and authorized transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters.

11

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 13 of 52 PagelD#
597

58. Before preparing the two case-keyed letters, Hall either reviewed the publicly filed
pleadings in the 286 Action or received from one or more participants in the two actions case-
specific materials reproducing or describing those pleadings. Those materials disclosed that
Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse and described the psychological recovery that
made preparation of the California Action possible. The source, transmission, and contents of the
materials Hall reviewed or received are maintained in Defendants’ records. Plaintiff cannot reach
them without discovery.

59. Hall was Corporate Counsel of the federally designated clearinghouse for
CyberTipline reporting. She knew what it ordinarily means, in criminal and law-enforcement
terms, to associate a named individual with CyberTipline reports.

60. On the same day, April 9, 2026, Meta filed a motion to dismiss and a motion to
transfer in the 376 Action.

H. The April 21, 2026 Filings

61. On April 21, 2026, Meta, Anderson, and Keegan filed a Joint Motion to Stay
Discovery and Hold Rule 26(f) Requirements in Abeyance in the 286 Action (ECF No. 49).
Chapleau signed for Anderson and Keegan. Fassbender signed for Meta.

62. On April 21, 2026, Anderson and Keegan filed a Time-Sensitive Motion for
Protective Order in the 286 Action (ECF No. 50). The motion sought to prevent Anderson’s April
28, 2026 deposition and requested a ruling by April 24, 2026. It stated: “This motion must be
decided by April 24 because Plaintiff noticed Anderson’s deposition on April 28, 2026.”

63. On April 21, 2026, Meta, Accenture, TaskUs, Inc., and Genpact Limited filed a
Joint Motion to Stay Discovery in the 376 Action (ECF No. 92). Fassbender signed and filed the

motion for Meta and Genpact Limited. Chapleau signed with permission for Accenture. The

12

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 60-1 Filed 09/08/26 Page 14 of 52 PagelD#
598

motion recited that Plaintiff had sought leave to serve a Request for Admission relating to
“whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff’s account.” It stated that Plaintiff
had served “‘advance notices’ and actual notices of specific discovery that Plaintiff intends to seek
such as Rule 30(b)(6) depositions and third-party subpoenas.”

64. On April 21, 2026, Accenture filed a Time-Sensitive Motion for Protective Order in
the 376 Action (ECF No. 93). The motion sought to prevent the April 29-30, 2026 Rule 30(b)(6)
deposition and requested a ruling by April 27, 2026. Accenture attached the deposition notice,
including Matter for Examination No. 5, as Exhibit 1. The motion stated: “This time-sensitive
motion must be decided by April 27 because Plaintiff noticed Accenture’s deposition for April 29-
30.”

65. The April 21, 2026 motions sought relief reaching the Anderson deposition, the
Accenture Rule 30(b)(6) deposition, and Plaintiff’s contemplated third-party discovery. Neither
court had ruled on any of them.

66. Neither April 21, 2026 joint motion—in the 376 Action or the 286 Action—
identified any forthcoming response from NCMEC.

L The April 22, 2026 Letters: Issuance Before Formal Service

67. On April 22, 2026, Hall issued two letters on NCMEC letterhead. That was one day
after the filings described in Section H. It was thirteen days after NCMEC received the advance-
notice package. It was before formal service of either subpoena. Each letter was keyed by caption
and case number to one of the two federal actions. One letter bears on its face Case No. 6:26-cv-
00376-AGM-DCI. The other bears on its face Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI. Two letters,
each keyed to a separate action, reflect the processing of two separate matters under two specific

as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel. NCMEC, acting through Hall and one or more additional

NCMEC is liable for the conduct alleged in this Count.
