9/13/2026
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
09/14/2026
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;

NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;

and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF'S RULE 72(a)
OBJECTIONS TO ECF NOS. 63-65 AND MOTION TO SET ASIDE
ECF NO. 64, SUSPEND ENFORCEMENT AND DISCOVERY
BRIEFING, AND RESTORE ORAL ARGUMENT FOLLOWING
DETERMINATION OF ECF NO. 59

I. PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

Meta objected that Plaintiff's proposed supplemental pleading did not include the proposed
complaint in its entirety. ECF No. 53 at 3 n.1. Plaintiff responded with one complete proposed
Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint. ECF Nos. 59, 59-1. Plaintiff submitted a
declaration addressing his legal name and Meta-account usage. ECF No. 59-2. Plaintiff submitted
a memorandum identifying and locating the material amendments by category and section and

explaining their relationship to the existing claims. ECF No. 60. The motion identifies ECF No. 5

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 _ Filed 09/14/26 Page 2 of 26 PagelD# 698

as the pleading the proposed complaint would replace. ECF No. 59 4 3. Plaintiff did not concede
Meta's objection. ECF No. 59 4 1; ECF No. 60 at 4. Plaintiff removed it from the case.

ECF No. 64 states that the Court lacks sufficient information to decide the amendment
motion. ECF No. 64 requires an additional comparison against ECF No. 1 by September 11, 2026,
two calendar days after entry. Plaintiff receives court notices by mail. Plaintiff does not receive
electronic court notifications. Plaintiff obtained actual notice of the requirement at about 9:09 p.m.
on September 11, 2026. Ex. A 44 3-9.

The orders also changed the disposition of the pending discovery motions. ECF No. 62
withdrew ECF No. 26, vacated its hearing, and expressly preserved the other scheduled hearings.
ECF No. 63 terminated the hearing on ECF No. 15. ECF No. 65 terminated the hearing on ECF No.
94 and set opposition and reply deadlines while the amendment request remained unresolved.

Plaintiff challenges the additional condition on the record presented: the information
already supplied, the cumulative comparison selected, and the notice-and-performance interval
imposed. Plaintiff requests that ECF No. 64 be set aside and that ECF No. 59 proceed to
determination on the existing submissions and permitted briefing. Plaintiff requests briefing on the
discovery motions addressed to the resulting operative pleading, and oral argument on those
motions after that briefing.

Il. GOVERNING REVIEW AND TIMELINESS

A district judge "must consider timely objections and modify or set aside any part of the
order that is clearly erroneous or is contrary to law." Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a); see 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)
(1)(A). A finding is clearly erroneous when the record leaves the reviewing court with a definite
and firm conviction that a mistake has been committed. An order is contrary to law when it applies

an incorrect legal standard or misapplies the governing rules. Local Civil Rule 72 provides that an

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 3 of 26 PagelD# 699

objection under Rule 72(a) "shall be considered a motion and is subject to the briefing and notice
requirements" of Local Civil Rule 7.

These objections address the stated premise of each order and the procedure each order
imposes. Part IV addresses the finding in ECF No. 64 that the Court lacked sufficient information.
Parts III and V address the deadline and the comparison baseline. Part VI addresses the sequence
ECF Nos. 63 and 65 set for the discovery motions. Part VII states the grounds for interim and
continuing case-management relief. Part VIII addresses oral argument. Part IX addresses the
Magistrate Judge's authority to impose the case-wide generative-artificial-intelligence provision
and, alternatively, its specification. Part X states the determinations sought.

The Court entered ECF Nos. 63 and 64 on September 9, 2026. The Court entered ECF No.
65 on September 10, 2026. The Court serves orders on Plaintiff by mail. Ex. A 4 3. Plaintiff
obtained actual notice of ECF Nos. 62 through 65 at about 9:09 p.m. on September 11, 2026. Ex. A
4 8. Plaintiff submitted these objections on September 13, 2026. Fourteen days from September 9 is
September 23. The objections are timely under Rule 72(a) without resort to Rule 6(d). The deadline
for objecting is distinct from the September 11 production date fixed by ECF No. 64. The first
governs this filing. Part II] addresses the second.

Rule 46 requires a party to state the action the party wants the court to take and the grounds
for the objection. Fed. R. Civ. P. 46. Each Part below identifies the ruling, the ground, and the
correction requested.

Il. THE SEPTEMBER 11 DEADLINE DID NOT AFFORD THE NOTICE-
AND-PERFORMANCE INTERVAL REQUIRED IN THESE
CIRCUMSTANCES

A. The chronology established by the declaration

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 4 of 26 PagelD# 700

Plaintiff proceeds pro se. Plaintiff is not a registered CM/ECF user and has not consented to
electronic service. Ex. A 43. Plaintiff receives no Notices of Electronic Filing. Ex. A 43. The Court
serves orders on Plaintiff by mail at his address of record, which is a commercial mail-receiving
agency. Ex. A ¥ 3.

Plaintiff supplements mail service with periodic docket review. At Plaintiff's direction, a
person acting on his behalf accesses PACER and uploads documents to the RECAP archive on
CourtListener. Ex. A q 4. Plaintiff maintains a CourtListener docket alert for this action. Ex. A ¥ 4.
In Plaintiff's experience, a CourtListener alert issues only when a document is added to the RECAP
archive for the docket. Ex. A 4 4. Plaintiff receives no other electronic notification of docket
activity. Ex. A ¥ 4.

Plaintiff's last submission before the orders at issue was the September 7, 2026 EDSS
submission docketed September 8 as ECF Nos. 57 through 61. Ex. A 95. From about September 7
through the afternoon of September 11, 2026, Plaintiff was unwell and did not work on this action.
Ex. A 46. At Plaintiff's direction, no docket review occurred during that period. Ex. A § 6. On the
evening of September 11, Plaintiff resumed work. Ex. A § 7. He understood the September 25,
2026 hearing to remain scheduled as to ECF Nos. 15 and 54. Ex. A 4 7. He intended to prepare for
that hearing and to decide whether to arrange travel pending a ruling on ECF No. 41. Ex. A 4 7.
Plaintiff requested that the docket be reviewed and any new documents uploaded. Ex. A 4 7.

At about 9:09 p.m. Eastern Time on September 11, Plaintiff received a CourtListener alert
for this action. Ex. A 4 8. Plaintiff then opened the CourtListener docket page for this action. That

was the first time Plaintiff learned of ECF Nos. 62, 63, 64, or 65. Ex. A JJ 8-9.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 5 of 26 PagelD# 701

As of the execution of the declaration, Plaintiff had not received a mailed copy of ECF No.
62, 63, 64, or 65 at his address of record. Ex. A J 10. The record does not show the date on which
the Clerk mailed the orders.

Entry of an order, service by mail, actual notice, and the opportunity to prepare a required
submission are different events. ECF No. 64 fixed the submission date without providing a period
measured from Plaintiff's receipt of notice.

B. The rules-based and due-process grounds

Formal service. Rule 77(d)(1) requires the Clerk to serve notice of entry of an order as
provided in Rule 5(b). Rule 5(b)(2)(C) provides that service by mail "is complete upon mailing.”
Fed. R. Civ. P. 5(b)(2)(C); Fed. R. Civ. P. 77(d)(1). Completion of service upon mailing fixes the
service date. It does not fix the date of receipt or the date of awareness. ECF No. 64 was entered
September 9. ECF No. 64 set September 11 as the performance date. No mailed copy had reached
Plaintiff by the time he executed his declaration. Ex. A ¥ 10.

Actual notice under Rule 83(b). A judge may regulate practice "in any manner consistent
with federal law, rules adopted under 28 U.S.C. §§ 2072 and 2075, and the district's local rules."
Fed. R. Civ. P. 83(b). The same rule provides: "No sanction or other disadvantage may be imposed
for noncompliance with any requirement not in federal law, federal rules, or the local rules unless
the alleged violator has been furnished in the particular case with actual notice of the requirement.”
Id. No federal rule requires a redlined comparison with a motion for leave to amend. No Local Civil
Rule of this Court requires one. The absence of a generally applicable redline requirement
identifies ECF No. 64 as a case-specific direction governed by Rule 83(b). Plaintiff obtained actual
notice of that direction at about 9:09 p.m. on the compliance date. Ex. A 8. That notice informed

him of an obligation already due that day.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 6 of 26 PagelD# 702

Opportunity to perform. Rule 83(b) addresses actual notice of a case-specific
requirement. The opportunity to act after notice is a related but distinct question. Notice must be
"reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties" of the
requirement and "must afford a reasonable time for those interested to make their appearance."
Mullane v. Cent. Hanover Bank & Tr. Co., 339 U.S. 306, 314 (1950). Whether a party has had a
reasonable opportunity depends on the circumstances presented and the reasons offered. Ungar v.
Sarafite, 376 U.S. 575, 589-91 (1964). Plaintiff challenges both the two-calendar-day period fixed
when the order issued and the opportunity remaining after actual notice. Actual notice at the end of
the compliance date does not establish that Plaintiff had a reasonable opportunity to prepare,
verify, and submit the required comparison. The Court's Electronic Document Submission System
marks accepted documents as filed on the date of submission. E.D. Va., Electronic Document
Submission System (EDSS) User Manual 5 (Apr. 2026); see Ex. A § 11. Plaintiff's objection
concerns the time available to prepare and submit the comparison. The date of the Clerk's later
docketing is not the basis of that objection.

Plaintiff requested expedited determination of the materials already submitted, after
completion of briefing. ECF No. 59 § 14; ECF No. 60 at 15-16. That request sought prompt
adjudication of an existing submission. That request did not seek an expedited obligation to prepare
additional material.

C. The remedy

Plaintiff requests vacatur of ECF No. 64. Plaintiff requests an order that ECF No. 59 shall
not be denied, deemed abandoned, excluded from consideration, or otherwise disadvantaged based

on the absence of a comparison document on September 11, 2026.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 7 of 26 PagelD# 703

If the Court treats the September 11 date as a deadline that survives review, Plaintiff
requests an extension under Rule 6(b)(1)(B) for excusable neglect. The determination "is at bottom
an equitable one, taking account of all relevant circumstances," including "the danger of prejudice
to the [nonmovant], the length of the delay and its potential impact on judicial proceedings, the
reason for the delay, including whether it was within the reasonable control of the movant, and
whether the movant acted in good faith." Pioneer Inv. Servs. Co. v. Brunswick Assocs. Ltd. P'ship,
507 U.S. 380, 395 (1993). The Fourth Circuit treats the reason for the delay as the most important
factor. Thompson v. E.I. DuPont de Nemours & Co., 76 F.3d 530, 533-34 (4th Cir. 1996).

Each factor is addressed on this record. Prejudice: no response to ECF No. 59 was yet due
on September 11, no Defendant had asserted that the submission was insufficient, and no order or
filing identifies harm from the absence of a comparison document. Length and impact: Plaintiff
sought relief on the first business day after actual notice. He requests suspension during review
and, if a comparison requirement is sustained, seven calendar days after actual notice of that
determination to comply. No response to ECF No. 59 was yet due on September 11. Plaintiff
requests no suspension of briefing on ECF No. 59. The requested pause concerns enforcement of
the comparison requirement and the specified discovery proceedings. Reason and control: Plaintiff
did not know the obligation existed until about 9:09 p.m. on the compliance date, and Plaintiff was
unwell from about September 7 through the afternoon of September 11. Ex. A §{{ 6, 8. Thompson
involved a party who knew the deadline and entrusted the filing to outgoing mail. 76 F.3d at 532—
34. This record involves a newly created obligation of which Plaintiff first learned at
approximately 9:09 p.m. on the compliance date, without a meaningful remaining opportunity to

perform. The two situations are distinct. Good faith: Plaintiff sought review on the first business

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 8 of 26 PagelD# 704

day after notice, disclosed the chronology under penalty of perjury, and committed to produce any
comparison the District Judge sustains within seven days of actual notice of that ruling.

Rule 6(d) does not supply this relief. Rule 6(d) adds three days to a period that runs from
service by mail. ECF No. 64 fixed a calendar date. Rule 6(d) does not move a fixed calendar date.

IV. THE INFORMATION-SUFFICIENCY DETERMINATION MUST BE
ASSESSED AGAINST ECF NOS. 59 AND 60

A. The procedural objection Plaintiff addressed

Meta's opposition to ECF No. 26 objected that Plaintiff attached "only his supplemental
allegations, 'incorporating by reference’ the remainder of his FAC," rather than "a copy of the
proposed amended pleading in its entirety." ECF No. 53 at 3 n.1. Plaintiff answered that objection
five days later. ECF No. 59 at 1-3; ECF No. 60 at 1-4. The asserted absence of a complete
proposed pleading was the subject of Meta's form objection. ECF No. 59 supplied that pleading.
ECF No. 60 explained the form of the submission and the substance of the proposed changes.
Plaintiff did not concede that ECF No. 26 was defective. ECF No. 59 4 1; ECF No. 60 at 4.

B. What the existing submission supplied

ECF No. 64 states that the Court lacked "sufficient information to issue an Order." The

submission before the Court on September 9 contained the following.

Record location Information available to the Court on September 9, 2026
ECF No. 59 §§ 3-5 ECF No. 5 identified as the operative pleading. The proposed
replacement identified. The same parties, six counts, and
categories of relief retained. Four categories of additional facts,
each cited to a section of the proposed pleading.

ECF No. 59 §q 7-13 Relationship of the motion to ECF Nos. 26 and 43. Procedural
posture. No answer, no scheduling order, no Rule 26(f) conference,
no discovery.

ECF No. 60 at 1-4 The five principal changes. The integrated form. The governing
standards under Rules 15(a)(2) and 15(d). The response to Meta's
form objection.

ECF No. 60 at 5—7 Timing, procedural stage, and absence of prejudice under Laber.
ECF No. 60 at 7-10 Section-by-section description of the material amendments:

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 9 of 26 PagelD# 705

source-level falsity, search identifiers versus report contents,
subsequent events, retained counts.

ECF No. 60 at 10-15 Absence of bad faith. Futility analysis under the Rule 12(b)(6)
standard. Rule 15(d) supplementation. Procedural effect of
granting leave.

ECF No. 60 at 15-16 The requested sequence: expedited determination after Local Civil
Rule 7(F)(1) briefing.

ECF No. 59-2 4] 2-10; The declaration concerning Plaintiff's legal name and Meta-

ECF No. 59-1 8 S account usage, and the corresponding pleaded facts.
ECF No. 5; ECF No. 1 The operative pleading and the original pleading, both on the
docket.

ECF No. 60 is a twenty-page filing. Pages 1 through 16 are the memorandum. Pages 17
through 20 are the certificate of service and the Local Civil Rule 83.1(N) certification. The
memorandum identifies the material amendments by category. The memorandum locates each
category in the proposed pleading by section. The memorandum states the governing standard for
each. The complete proposed pleading was attached as ECF No. 59-1 and again as ECF No. 60-1.
ECF No. 5 was on the docket. ECF No. 1 was on the docket.

C. The objection to the additional condition

A redline may assist comparison. Plaintiff does not challenge the authority of a court to
request one. Plaintiff objects to the condition imposed on this record. ECF No. 64 made
consideration of ECF No. 59 contingent on an additional submission due September 11. The
complete proposed pleading and the explanation in ECF No. 60 were already before the Court.

ECF No. 64 identifies the comparison it requires. On the record presented, ECF No. 64 does
not connect the additional comparison, the selected baseline, and the September 11 deadline to an
informational need that ECF No. 60 left unmet. Plaintiff does not contend that Rule 52 or Rule 72
required ECF No. 64 to state findings; Rule 52(a)(3) generally does not require findings on a
motion. Plaintiff contends that the premise the order states is not supported by the record it

addresses. ECF No. 64 issued one day after ECF Nos. 59 and 60 were docketed. No Defendant's

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 _ Filed 09/14/26 Page 10 of 26 PagelD#
706

response was due under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1). No Defendant had asserted that the submission
was insufficient.

Rule 83(b) permits a judge to regulate practice in a manner consistent with federal law, the
federal rules, and the local rules. Fed. R. Civ. P. 83(b). A district court's inherent authority to
manage its docket "must be a 'reasonable response to the problems and needs’ confronting the
court's fair administration of justice." Dietz v. Bouldin, 579 U.S. 40, 45 (2016) (citation omitted).
The exercise "cannot be contrary to any express grant of or limitation on the district court's power
contained in a rule or statute." Id.; see id. at 45-48. ECF No. 64 identifies one problem: insufficient
information. The record on September 9 contained the complete proposed pleading, the pleading it
replaces, the original pleading, a sixteen-page memorandum identifying and locating the material
amendments, and a declaration. The condition imposed was a two-day requirement to produce a
cumulative comparison against a pleading the motion does not seek to replace. That condition does
not respond to the problem stated. Plaintiff requests review of the additional condition in light of
that record, the selected comparator, and the notice-and-performance interval.

Rule 15(a)(2) directs that the court "should freely give leave when justice so requires." Fed.
R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2). The Supreme Court has identified the grounds on which leave is denied: undue
delay, bad faith, dilatory motive, repeated failure to cure, undue prejudice, and futility. Foman v.
Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 (1962); Laber v. Harvey, 438 F.3d 404, 426-27 (4th Cir. 2006) (en banc).
The absence of a comparison document does not itself establish futility, prejudice, or bad faith. To
the extent nonperformance by September 11 is proposed as a procedural basis for denying
consideration of ECF No. 59, the validity of the condition and Plaintiff's opportunity to satisfy it
require separate determination. Plaintiff requests that the Rule 15 merits and the asserted

September 11 default be addressed separately.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 _ Filed 09/14/26 Page 11 of 26 PagelD#
707

Any proposed claim-terminating consequence based on September 11 nonperformance
would require separate consideration of the circumstances of that nonperformance, the notice and
warning provided, and the availability of less severe alternatives. Ballard v. Carlson, 882 F.2d 93,
95-96 (4th Cir. 1989) (dismissal); Hathcock v. Navistar Int'l Transp. Corp., 53 F.3d 36, 40—41 (4th
Cir. 1995) (default judgment). ECF No. 64 is not a sanctions order and contains no warning.
Plaintiff cites those authorities only against a consequence that would operate as a case-dispositive
sanction.

Plaintiff requests that the information-sufficiency finding be set aside. Plaintiff requests
that ECF No. 59 proceed to determination on the existing submission.

V. ECF NO. 64 USES A DIFFERENT BASELINE FROM THE PLEADING
ECF NO. 59 SEEKS TO REPLACE
ECF No. 59 seeks to replace ECF No. 5. ECF No. 59 43; ECF No. 60 at 2, 15. ECF No. 64

requires comparison to ECF No. 1. The ordered comparison therefore combines changes already
made through the First Amended Complaint with the changes presently proposed through ECF No.
59.

An amended pleading supersedes the original as the operative pleading and renders the
original of no legal effect. Young v. City of Mount Ranier, 238 F.3d 567, 572—73 (4th Cir. 2001).
Plaintiff filed ECF No. 5 as of right on August 6, 2026. ECF No. 59 § 10. Every pending motion to
dismiss is directed to ECF No. 5. ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45. ECF No. 1 may supply historical context. It
does not supply the baseline that isolates the amendments presently proposed. ECF No. 59 presents
two questions: whether the proposed pleading should replace ECF No. 5 under Rule 15(a)(2), and
whether the post-August 6 events should be added under Rule 15(d). Comparing the proposed
pleading to ECF No. 1 combines amendments already made with amendments now requested. ECF

No. 64 does not identify why that cumulative comparison was necessary in addition to the proposed

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 _ Filed 09/14/26 Page 12 of 26 PagelD#
708

pleading and ECF No. 60's explanation of the current amendments. This is Plaintiff's first motion
for leave to amend. No prior amendment was allowed by leave. ECF No. 60 at 10.

Plaintiff requests vacatur of the ECF No. 1 comparison requirement as part of the principal
relief.

Alternative relief. If the District Judge sustains a comparison requirement, Plaintiff
requests an order identifying the required baseline. Plaintiff requests seven calendar days after
actual notice of that determination to produce it. Plaintiff requests express relief from the
September 11, 2026 date. The package submits neither comparison. It seeks a ruling on the
requirement and a prospective period if the requirement survives review.

VI. THE AMENDMENT REQUEST SHOULD BE DETERMINED BEFORE
DISCOVERY BRIEFING IS COMPLETED AGAINST THE PLEADING IT
WOULD REPLACE

A. Plaintiff maintains all three substantive positions

Plaintiff maintains that the First Amended Complaint states each of its six claims and
survives the pending motions to dismiss. ECF Nos. 20, 30, 51. Plaintiff maintains that amendment
is warranted under Rule 15(a)(2) for the reasons stated in ECF No. 60 at 4-14. Plaintiff maintains
that the post-August 6 events independently warrant supplementation under Rule 15(d) for the
reasons stated in ECF No. 60 at 14-15. The standards governing amendment and supplementation
"are nearly identical," and leave under either "should be freely granted." Franks v. Ross, 313 F.3d
184, 198 n.15 (4th Cir. 2002). Plaintiff renews the request for leave through ECF No. 59. Plaintiff
incorporates ECF No. 60 at 2-16 by reference. Foman, 371 U.S. at 182; Laber, 438 F.3d at 426-29.

Vacating ECF No. 64 removes the disputed condition. Granting ECF No. 59 is the separate

action that makes the proposed pleading operative. Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2), (d). Plaintiff requests

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 13 of 26 PagelD#
709

both. Vacatur alone preserves consideration of ECF No. 59. It does not make the proposed pleading
operative.

B. The consequence of the existing sequence

ECF No. 60 requested prompt determination so the parties could address one complete
operative pleading. ECF No. 64 imposed another submission requirement before determination of
that request. ECF No. 65 established discovery briefing while the request remained unresolved.
Plaintiff seeks a sequence in which the pleading determination precedes completion of briefing on
the discovery directed to those allegations.

ECF No. 54 remains supported by the operative First Amended Complaint and the existing
record. ECF No. 15 does as well. The First Amended Complaint pleads the three identifiers, the
letters’ wording, and the distinction between the letters and the source records. The proposed
pleading adds allegations bearing on the same requested discovery. Section S of the proposed
pleading alleges, on Plaintiff's personal knowledge, that Plaintiff never used "Marvelle J.
Ballentine" to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any Meta account. ECF No. 59-
1 § S; ECF No. 59-2 4 2-10; ECF No. 60 at 7. Section S alleges, on information and belief, that
neither report as originally received by NCMEC contained or otherwise identified Plaintiff by that
name and that neither concerned Plaintiff personally. ECF No. 59-1 § S; ECF No. 60 at 7-8.
Section O adds NCMEC's August 12, 2026 statements and counsel's August 13, 2026 response.
ECF No. 59-1 § O; ECF No. 60 at 9.

The interrogatories are directed to those propositions. ECF No. 15 proposes three
interrogatories to NCMEC, each answerable "Yes," "No," or "Unable to determine after reasonable
inquiry," asking whether either report, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise

identified "Marvelle J. Ballentine," "Jay Ballentine," or jaychizza@icloud.com. ECF No. 15-1.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 14 of 26 PagelD#
710

ECF No. 54 proposes four interrogatories to Meta in the same form. ECF No. 54-1. The first asks
whether Meta submitted a CyberTipline report to NCMEC in connection with the Facebook
account terminated on or about July 4, 2022. Id. The remaining three ask whether any such report
contained any of the same three identifiers. Id. NCMEC's memorandum states that Plaintiff "does
not have access to those reports." ECF No. 11 at 9. The proposed pleading pleads what Plaintiff
knows and what Plaintiff alleges on information and belief as separate propositions. The
interrogatories are directed to the second category.

Briefing completed before determination of ECF No. 59 may require supplementation to
address the allegations subsequently made operative. Resolving ECF No. 59 first would permit one
round of briefing against the resulting operative pleading. Rule 15 governs when the proposed
pleading becomes operative. Rule 26 governs the discovery sought. Plaintiff does not contend that
the proposed pleading governs the action now. Plaintiff identifies its contents as the reason to
sequence the pleading determination before the discovery briefing.

C. Replacement schedule

Plaintiff requests suspension of the opposition and reply deadlines established by ECF No.
65 pending determination of ECF No. 59, followed by a replacement schedule addressed to the
resulting operative pleading. Plaintiff separately requests that determination of ECF Nos. 15 and 54
remain in abeyance until ECF No. 59 has been determined and the resulting court-authorized
briefing periods have concluded. ECF No. 15 is fully briefed. Its existing submissions should be
preserved, with any additional briefing limited to a material effect of the pleading determination.
ECF No. 54 has outstanding response and reply deadlines. Those deadlines should be replaced on

the triggering events stated below.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 _ Filed 09/14/26 Page 15 of 26 PagelD#
711

Plaintiff requests the ordinary intervals of Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1): fourteen days for the
response and six days for the reply. If ECF No. 59 is granted, service of the order granting leave and
deeming the Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint filed would start Meta's fourteen days
on ECF No. 54. If ECF No. 59 is denied, service of the order denying leave would start Meta's
fourteen days, with briefing addressed to the First Amended Complaint. If ECF No. 59 is granted in
part, the filing of the conforming pleading the order directs, within seven calendar days after
Plaintiff receives actual notice of the order directing that filing, would start Meta's fourteen days.
Because ECF No. 59 is not stayed and may be determined while these objections are pending, each
replacement response period and each initial supplemental-brief period should run from the later of
service of the order resolving these objections on the party required to act or the otherwise
applicable triggering event. Service of Meta's response would start Plaintiff's six days in each
branch. Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) supplies those intervals and permits a different court-ordered
arrangement. Each replacement date is defined by a future event so that the schedule operates
whenever the ruling issues.

ECF Nos. 15 and 54 should remain pending without withdrawal or refiling. The existing
briefing on ECF No. 15 (ECF Nos. 16, 31, 33, 36, 46, 52) should be preserved. The parties should
be permitted limited supplemental briefing on ECF No. 15 addressed to any material effect of the
pleading determination, on the same triggering events.

Alternative. If the Court permits Meta's briefing under ECF No. 65 to proceed, Plaintiff
separately requests that determination of ECF Nos. 15 and 54 be held in abeyance pending
determination of ECF No. 59. Upon any grant of ECF No. 59 in full or in part, Plaintiff requests
leave to submit supplemental briefing addressed to the resulting operative pleading before either

discovery motion is determined. The existing submissions on both motions should be preserved. A

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 16 of 26 PagelD#
712

ruling that permits Meta's briefing to continue does not dispose of the separate request to defer
adjudication of both motions.

D. Determination of ECF No. 59 before or within any claim-terminating

disposition

Three motions to dismiss directed to the First Amended Complaint are pending before the
District Judge. ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45. ECF No. 59 is pending before the Magistrate Judge. A
disposition of the motions to dismiss that terminated a claim while ECF No. 59 remained
undetermined would decide the sufficiency of a pleading Plaintiff has moved to replace. It would
do so without addressing the motion to replace it. Plaintiff requests that ECF No. 59 be determined
before, or expressly within, any disposition of ECF Nos. 10, 21, or 45 that would terminate any
claim. To the extent a ruling on ECF No. 59 would foreclose a claim, Plaintiff requests that the
ruling issue in a form permitting the review 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1) provides for dispositive matters.

VII. GROUNDS FOR INTERIM AND CONTINUING CASE-MANAGEMENT
RELIEF

The filing of Rule 72(a) objections does not suspend the order objected to. Plaintiff
therefore requests an interim order during review and an express ruling on continuing abeyance
when the objections are determined. Three requests rest on three different grounds. The first
ground supports suspension of ECF No. 64's enforcement during review. The remaining grounds
support adjustment of the discovery-briefing deadlines and interim and continuing abeyance of
discovery adjudication, respectively.

Suspension of ECF No. 64's enforcement during review. The District Judge holds the
objections. Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a). The objections challenge the September 11 requirement. A
denial, deemed abandonment, or exclusion of ECF No. 59 for September 11 nonperformance,

entered while those objections are pending, would decide the objected-to question first. Suspension

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 17 of 26 PagelD#
713

preserves the District Judge's review and preserves consideration of ECF No. 59 without an
intervening adverse consequence.

Adjustment of the unexpired September 17 and September 23 deadlines. Rule 6(b)(1)
(A) permits the court, for good cause, to extend a period "if a request is made, before the original
time or its extension expires." Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(b)(1)(A). This request precedes both deadlines.
Good cause is the pendency of ECF No. 59 and of these objections, and the reasons stated in Part
VI. Local Civil Rule 37(F) recognizes court-ordered extensions concerning discovery motions.

A limited pause in determination of ECF Nos. 15 and 54. A court has authority "to
control the disposition of the causes on its docket with economy of time and effort for itself, for
counsel, and for litigants," and exercises that authority by weighing the competing interests.
Landis v. N. Am. Co., 299 U.S. 248, 254-55 (1936). The party requesting the pause must show that
the balance favors it. Williford v. Armstrong World Indus., Inc., 715 F.2d 124, 127 (4th Cir. 1983).
The balance is as follows. Duration: interim relief preserves the identified proceedings during
district-judge review. The separately requested continuing abeyance runs through determination of
ECF No. 59, establishment of the resulting operative pleading, and conclusion of the resulting
court-authorized briefing periods. Plaintiff requests an express ruling on that continuing relief
when the Court determines the objections. Effect on Meta: Meta's response on ECF No. 54 is
deferred, not enlarged; Meta briefs once, against one pleading. Effect on NCMEC and Hall: ECF
No. 15 is fully briefed; the immediate relief defers adjudication of an already briefed motion and
imposes no briefing obligation; no discovery is proceeding; no scheduling order has issued. Effect
on Plaintiff: without abeyance, Plaintiff's reply on ECF No. 54 may become due before the
pleading determination and the District Judge's ruling on the requested sequence, and the discovery

motions may be determined against a pleading that a pending motion seeks to replace. Effect on the

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 _ Filed 09/14/26 Page 18 of 26 PagelD#
714

Court: one round of briefing against one pleading instead of two rounds against two. No Defendant
has identified prejudice from the sequence Plaintiff requests.

Plaintiff requests determination of the interim application before September 17, 2026.
Plaintiff also requests an express determination of continuing abeyance through resolution of ECF
No. 59 and the resulting briefing. Those case-management requests are independently supported
by the grounds stated above and do not depend entirely on sustaining the Rule 72(a) objections.
Plaintiff submits the interim application on the papers. That submission is limited to the interim
application.

VIll. ORAL ARGUMENT ON BOTH DISCOVERY MOTIONS SHOULD BE
RESTORED AFTER THE PLEADING DETERMINATION AND
BRIEFING

This Part states a separate objection and a separate request for a ruling.

A. The hearing chronology

No. 16 (memorandum), and ECF No. 17 (notice of hearing).

August 24, 2026 ECF No. 31, Plaintiff's declaration supporting ECF No. 15, was
docketed.

August 25, 2026 The Court set the September 25, 2026 hearing on ECF Nos. 15 and

26 before the Magistrate Judge.

August 31—September 1, | Plaintiff filed ECF No. 41, requesting leave to appear remotely at
2026 the September 25 hearing as to ECF Nos. 15 and 26.

September 3-4, 2026 Plaintiff filed ECF Nos. 54 (Meta interrogatories motion), 55
(memorandum), and 56 (notice of hearing for September 25).
September 8, 2026 The Court set the September 25, 2026 hearing on ECF No. 54.

ECF No. 26 (ECF No. 57), the request to vacate the hearing as to
ECF No. 26 only (ECF No. 58), the amendment motion (ECF Nos.

September 9, 2026 ECF No. 62 deemed ECF No. 26 withdrawn, vacated the hearing

26, and terminated the hearing on ECF No. 15. ECF No. 64

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 19 of 26 PagelD#
715

imposed the comparison requirement.
September 10, 2026 ECF No. 65 terminated the hearing on ECF No. 54 and set the
September 17 and September 23 deadlines.

ECF No. 31 was part of the record when the Court set the hearing on August 25. ECF No.
31 was part of the record when the Court terminated the hearing on September 9.

B. The scope of Plaintiff's requests and waivers

Plaintiff requested withdrawal of ECF No. 26 and termination of its hearing only. ECF Nos.
57, 598. ECF No. 62 granted that request and expressly preserved the other scheduled hearings.
Plaintiff's waiver at ECF No. 61 addressed the amendment motion, ECF No. 59. Plaintiff's waiver
at ECF No. 40 addressed the motions to dismiss, ECF Nos. 10 and 21. Those submissions did not
request termination of oral argument on ECF Nos. 15 and 54. ECF No. 41 requested leave to
participate in the September 25 hearing remotely.

ECF No. 63 denied ECF No. 41 as moot on the stated ground that ECF No. 26 had been
withdrawn. Plaintiff filed ECF No. 41 as to ECF No. 15 as well. ECF No. 63 then terminated the
ECF No. 15 hearing in its next decretal paragraph. ECF No. 62's preservation of the other hearings
did not bar a later order from changing the schedule. The objection is to the exercise of that
discretion on this record.

Plaintiff requests oral argument on both discovery motions. Plaintiff objects to their
disposition without argument under the present pleading and briefing sequence.

C. What oral argument would address

The hearing would address whether the requested interrogatories should be authorized and
on what terms. Plaintiff seeks written discovery responses through the proposed interrogatories.

The hearing is a discovery-motion hearing. Counsel would not supply sworn answers at it.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 _ Filed 09/14/26 Page 20 of 26 PagelD#
716

Argument would address the relationship between the three NCMEC interrogatories and
the four Meta interrogatories. Argument would address the relevance of each requested answer to
the claims in the operative pleading. Argument would address the distinction between the
requested identifying information and the contents of the reports. Argument would address the
declarations on file (ECF Nos. 31, 59-2) and Defendants’ filed descriptions of what the April 22,
2026 letters supplied. Argument would address any burden, privilege, or statutory restriction
Defendants assert in their briefing. NCMEC's memorandum states that Plaintiff "does not have
access to those reports." ECF No. 11 at 9. The interrogatories are drafted to require no report
content. ECF Nos. 15-1, 54-1. Argument would address the relationship between that objection and
that drafting.

D. The governing basis and the requested correction

Rule 78(b) permits a court, "[b]y rule or order," to provide for "submitting and determining
motions on briefs, without oral hearings." Fed. R. Civ. P. 78(b). Local Civil Rule 7(J) permits
determination without oral hearing. Plaintiff does not contend that calendaring created an
entitlement to argument. The preserved issue is whether terminating these hearings was an
appropriate exercise of discretion in the circumstances presented. Plaintiff had noticed argument
on both motions and had sought remote participation. The Court had preserved the hearing by order
the same day as to every motion other than ECF No. 26. A motion to replace the pleading against
which the discovery motions’ relevance is measured was pending.

Plaintiff requests modification of ECF Nos. 63 and 65 to provide oral argument on ECF
Nos. 15 and 54 after determination of ECF No. 59 and completion of the resulting briefing.

Plaintiff requests a newly scheduled date. Plaintiff does not request reinstatement of September 25,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 _ Filed 09/14/26 Page 21 of 26 PagelD#
717

2026. Reinstating that date while suspending the briefing that precedes it would place the hearing
before the briefing.

Plaintiff requests, as part of that relief, that notice of the new date be mailed at least twenty-
one days before the hearing. Plaintiff does not assert an entitlement to that interval. Plaintiff
receives notice by mail, resides outside the Commonwealth, and must arrange travel or renew a
request for remote appearance after the date is set. Twenty-one days accommodates mail transit,
the renewal of ECF No. 41 for the new date, and a ruling on it before the hearing.

Upon restoration of a hearing, Plaintiff requests reconsideration of the denial of ECF No.
41 as moot. Alternatively, Plaintiff requests leave to renew that request for the new date within
fourteen days after service of the notice of hearing. That request is separate from the request to hear
the motions.

IX. THE CASE-WIDE CERTIFICATION REQUIREMENT MUST REST ON
THE MAGISTRATE JUDGE'S DELEGATED AUTHORITY

ECF No. 63 at 1 and ECF No. 65 at 1 each provide: "should any party utilize generative
artificial intelligence for the preparation of any filing submitted to this Court, that party must
identify the use of the generative artificial intelligence in the filing as well as provide a certification
that said party has reviewed all citations for accuracy."

ECF Nos. 63 and 65 require disclosure and certification for "any filing submitted to this
Court" when generative artificial intelligence is used in its preparation. The requirement applies
throughout this action. It reaches filings concerning matters before the District Judge, including
these objections. The language contains no limitation to filings concerning matters assigned to the
Magistrate Judge.

A magistrate judge exercises authority conferred by 28 U.S.C. § 636 and assigned by the

district court. Section 636(b)(1)(A) permits determination of assigned nondispositive pretrial

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 _ Filed 09/14/26 Page 22 of 26 PagelD#
718

matters. Section 636(b)(3) permits assignment of additional duties consistent with the Constitution
and federal law. Local Civil Rule 72 authorizes duties permitted by governing law and provides for
assignment or referral by an order entered in the action or instructions of a district judge.

Rule 83(b) permits procedural directions consistent with federal law. It does not
independently enlarge the duties assigned under § 636. The Fourth Circuit has identified § 636 as
the source of a magistrate judge's authority and has distinguished that statutory authority from the
inherent Article III powers of a district court. Reddick v. White, No. 08-2286, slip op. at 5—7 (4th
Cir. Dec. 1, 2011) (per curiam) (unpublished). Authority to administer an assigned matter does not,
by itself, establish authority to impose a continuing requirement on every filing in the action.

Plaintiff requests determination of the assignment governing the Magistrate Judge's
authority in this action and whether that assignment supports the requirement's case-wide reach.
Plaintiff requests that the provisions be confined to filings concerning matters assigned to the
Magistrate Judge and that their application to filings concerning matters retained by the District
Judge be set aside. Plaintiff requests a determination of authority before approval of a compliance
method.

Alternative relief: specification and compliance

The orders require identification of generative-AI use "in the filing" and a certification of
citation review. They prescribe no location or form for either. They do not address citations within
attached materials. They do not state whether research, drafting, revision, proofreading, or
formatting assistance each triggers the obligation, whether the system must be identified or its
contribution described, whether declarations, proposed orders, and previously created third-party
exhibits are covered, whether "all citations" includes record references, quotations, and pinpoints,

or whether a separate declaration under 28 U.S.C. § 1746 is required.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 23 of 26 PagelD#
719

Plaintiff supplies the following disclosures and certifications while seeking review. For any
requirement that remains in effect, Plaintiff requests approval of this method or specification of a
different method. Each docketed filing that Plaintiff submits with generative-AI assistance carries,
following its signature block, a signed section titled "Generative-Artificial-Intelligence Disclosure
and Citation Certification." That section states that generative AI was used, describes the nature of
the assistance, identifies each attachment submitted with the filing that the assistance covered, and
certifies that Plaintiff reviewed each citation to legal authority and each citation to the record in the
filing and its attachments for accuracy, stating the method of review. A memorandum docketed as
a separate entry carries its own section. A declaration states within its sworn text that generative AI
assisted with its form and that each fact stated is the declarant's own. Proposed orders are identified
in the certification of the motion they accompany and carry no separate certification on their face,
so that the document tendered for the Court's signature contains only the proposed order.
Previously created third-party documents attached as exhibits are identified as not prepared with
generative AI. The separate Local Civil Rule 83.1(N) certification is maintained.

Plaintiff requests that any materially additional disclosure or review obligation first
specified in resolving this Motion operate prospectively, with an opportunity to comply after
notice. Rule 83(b) bars a sanction or other disadvantage for noncompliance with a requirement not
in federal law, the federal rules, or the local rules absent actual notice of the requirement. Fed. R.
Civ. P. 83(b).

X. THE CONSEQUENCES AND DETERMINATIONS SOUGHT

The challenged procedures bear on five matters. The first is whether the proposed
allegations will be considered. The second is whether amendment and supplementation will be

determined on the Foman grounds or on a form condition. The third is the pleading against which

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 24 of 26 PagelD#
720

the discovery motions' relevance is measured. The fourth is whether Plaintiff will be heard on the
discovery issues the parties have briefed. The fifth is whether the Magistrate Judge's assigned
duties authorize a continuing certification requirement for every Al-assisted filing in this action.
Rule 61 directs the Court to disregard errors that do not affect a party's substantial rights. Fed. R.
Civ. P. 61. Each correction requested here is connected to adjudication: the determination of ECF
No. 59, the briefing on ECF Nos. 15 and 54, and the disposition of the pending motions to dismiss.

Timely, specific objections preserve each issue for review. A judgment entered while
objections remain pending operates as an implicit rejection of them, and that rejection is
reviewable. Wall v. Rasnick, 42 F.4th 214, 217-19 (4th Cir. 2022). Plaintiff requests express
resolution of each objection and each alternative.

Plaintiff has not produced the comparison ECF No. 64 required. Plaintiff has sought review
of the requirement instead. Plaintiff maintains ECF No. 59. Plaintiff maintains the positions
directed to the First Amended Complaint in ECF Nos. 20, 30, and 51. Plaintiff maintains the
withdrawal of ECF No. 26.

Plaintiff requests an order granting the relief stated in paragraphs 6 through 10 of the
Motion. The order should set aside ECF No. 64. The order should suspend enforcement of ECF No.
64 during review. The order should suspend the ECF No. 65 deadlines pending determination of
ECF No. 59 and establish replacement briefing on the triggering events identified in Part VI.C. The
order should preserve ECF Nos. 15 and 54 as pending motions, preserve their existing submissions,
and defer adjudication of both until ECF No. 59 has been determined and the resulting court-
authorized briefing periods have concluded. The order should expressly determine that case-
management relief independently of the disposition of the individual objections. The order should

restore oral argument on ECF Nos. 15 and 54 on a newly scheduled date after the pleading

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 68 Filed 09/14/26 Page 25 of 26 PagelD#
721

determination and resulting briefing. The order should direct determination of ECF No. 59 before
or within any claim-terminating disposition of ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45. The order should
determine the source and scope of the Magistrate Judge's authority to impose the case-wide
certification requirement. The order should set aside its application beyond that authority. For any
requirement remaining in effect, the order should approve or specify the compliance method. In the
alternative, Plaintiff requests identification of the comparison baseline, seven calendar days from

actual notice to produce it, and supplemental discovery briefing after any grant of ECF No. 59.

Date: September 13, 2026 Respectfully submitted,

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

Plaintiff used generative artificial intelligence in the preparation of this Memorandum. The

          DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO
               PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE A SUR-REPLY


           Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc., (“Meta”) by and through its undersigned counsel, hereby

  respectfully opposes Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine’s Motion for Leave to File a Sur-Reply, Dkt.

  No. 43 (“Mot. for Leave”). In support of its response, Meta states the following:

     I.       Legal Standard

           Courts in this District have held that “sur-replies are highly disfavored, as they usually are

  a strategic effort by the nonmoving party to have the last word on the matter.” Trustees of Columbia

  Univ. in City of New York v. Symantec Corp., No. 3:12-cv-808, 2019 WL 13189619, at *2 (E.D.

  Va. Oct. 10, 2019) (cleaned up and internal quotations omitted). As Plaintiff concedes, “an

  opposing party may not submit a sur-reply simply because the movant used their reply brief to

  further support an argument made in their opening brief or to respond to new arguments in the

  opposing party ’s opposition.” Taylor v. Revature, LLC¸ No. 1:22-cv-1153-RDA-WBP, 2025 WL




                                                     1

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD             Document 69       Filed 09/15/26       Page 2 of 5 PageID# 727




  711961, at *4 (E.D. Va. Mar. 5, 2025) (internal quotations and punctuation omitted); See Mot. for

  Leave, at 2.

      II.      Argument

            Plaintiff seeks leave to file a sur-reply in response to Meta’s Motion to Dismiss the First

  Amended Complaint (“FAC”), Dkt. No. 21 (“Motion to Dismiss”), asserting that Meta’s Reply in

  Support of its Motion to Dismiss (Dkt. No. 39) (“Reply”) “introduced a new proposition,” namely

  that “Plaintiff has not identified any non-speculative opportunity for him to provide testimony.”

  Dkt. No. 43 at 3 (quoting Meta’s Reply in Support of its Motion to Dismiss). But Meta’s argument

  that Plaintiff failed to sufficiently allege a non-speculative opportunity for him to testify merely

  develops the argument Meta made in its Motion to Dismiss that Plaintiff failed to sufficiently allege

  injury under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2). In its Motion to Dismiss, Meta expressly argued that Plaintiff

  failed to allege injury because “Plaintiff fails to plead any facts showing that the discovery actually

  impacted his ability to testify or pursue his claim.” See Dkt. No. 22 at 12 (emphasis added); see

  also id. at 2.

            In his opposition to Meta’s Motion to Dismiss (Dkt. No. 30) (“Opposition”), Plaintiff

  argued that, even if physical presence in court was required to state a claim for the “attending

  court” prong of Section 1985(2), such physical presence would “not dispose of the testimony

  branch,” apparently conceding that Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim relies solely on “Plaintiff’s

  prospective-witness status.” Dkt. No. 30 at 20-21. In response, Meta’s Reply further developed

  Meta’s argument that the FAC fails to allege injury because the FAC includes no non-speculative

  allegations that Plaintiff would testify in any action. See Dkt No. 39 at 7. This is not a new argument

  raised in reply, but rather a further development of an argument made in Meta’s Motion to Dismiss

  in response to Plaintiff’s Opposition. Accordingly, a sur-reply would be improper. See Johnson v.



                                                     2

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD              Document 69        Filed 09/15/26      Page 3 of 5 PageID# 728




  Henrico Cnty. Bd. of Supervisors, No. 3:23-cv-679, 2025 WL 310122, at *1, n.3 (E.D. Va. Jan. 27,

  2025) (refusing to “consider Plaintiff’s Sur-Reply” where defendant’s reply “introduced no new

  arguments or new material for which a sur-reply would be warranted”).

             Additionally, Plaintiff’s proposed sur-reply simply reiterates allegations from the FAC,

  pointing to Plaintiff’s allegation that he “expected to testify under oath at deposition” in the

  underlying actions between Plaintiff and Meta and asserting that solely because of this alleged

  expectation, “Plaintiff was a prospective witness” in those actions. As Meta’s Motion to Dismiss

  and Reply point out, Plaintiff’s allegations that he may have testified at some point in the

  underlying actions do not identify any non-speculative opportunity to testify. This is particularly

  true given that, at the time the alleged letters at issue were sent, Plaintiff’s claims in the underlying

  actions had not even survived initial motions to dismiss testing the viability of his allegations.

      III.      Conclusion

             For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court deny Plaintiff’s Motion

  for Leave to File a Sur-reply.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 71 Filed 09/17/26 Page 1 of 8 PagelD# 732

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA

ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
V. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

EXHIBIT A

PLAINTIFE’S SUR-REPLY TO DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S
REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO DISMISS

Meta’s Reply largely reiterates its opening arguments. One argument appears for the first
time at page 7. Meta now contends that Plaintiff “has not identified any non-speculative
opportunity for him to provide testimony in any action” and that the FAC fails to identify “any
actual testimony in federal court that Plaintiff has or likely will offer.” ECF No. 39 at 7. The First

Amended Complaint alleges precisely what Meta says is absent.

I. META’S NEW ARGUMENT IS CONTRADICTED BY THE FIRST AMENDED
COMPLAINT

Start with the pleading. Paragraph 31 of the FAC alleges:

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 71 Filed 09/17/26 Page 2 of 8 PagelD# 733

Plaintiff was a prospective witness in both actions concerning his account history,
the July 4, 2022 enforcement event, the absence of any law-enforcement contact
with Plaintiff, and his damages. Plaintiff expected to testify under oath at deposition
and at trial concerning those subjects.

ECF No. 5 ¥ 31. That paragraph identifies the witness, the actions, the subjects of the
testimony, and the settings in which it was expected to be given.

The FAC then pleads what Defendants sought to do about that testimony and what they
knew. The purpose of the alleged understanding was “to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from
continuing to attend the 376 Action and the 286 Action as a party, and from testifying freely, fully,
and truthfully as a prospective witness in those pending federal proceedings, including concerning
the CyberTipline-reporting question.” Id. ¥ 158. The intimidation “was directed both at Plaintiff’s
continued attendance as a party in the two pending federal actions and at Plaintiff’s own
prospective sworn testimony concerning his account, the July 4, 2022 enforcement event, the
absence of any law-enforcement contact with Plaintiff, and his damages.” Id. § 159. And
Defendants “knew that Plaintiff was pro se; that the noticed depositions depended on Plaintiff’s
personal preparation and examination; that the CyberTipline issue was central to the noticed
examinations; and that Plaintiff was a prospective witness concerning his account, the enforcement
event, and his damages.” Id. § 160. Count IV incorporates those allegations, id. { 234, and
separately repeats the alleged purpose and injury, id. {J 237, 239.

Meta’s argument therefore does not identify an omitted allegation. It asks the Court to
disregard an allegation that is already there.

Rule 12(b)(6) does not permit that. The Court “must accept as true all of the factual
allegations contained in the complaint,” and must draw “all reasonable inferences” in Plaintiff’s
favor. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co. v. Kolon Indus., Inc., 637 F.3d 435, 440 (4th Cir. 2011); King

v. Rubenstein, 825 F.3d 206, 212 (4th Cir. 2016). Meta cites no authority imposing an additional

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 71 Filed 09/17/26 Page 3 of 8 PagelD# 734

requirement that a § 1985(2) plaintiff identify a future testimony event certain or likely to occur.
Meta’s argument instead asks the Court to find that Plaintiff’s expected testimony was unlikely to
happen. But a plaintiff “need not demonstrate that her right to relief is probable or that alternative
explanations are less likely.” Houck v. Substitute Tr. Servs., Inc., 791 F.3d 473, 484 (4th Cir. 2015).
The question “is not whether there are more likely explanations” for the facts alleged. Woods v.
City of Greensboro, 855 F.3d 639, 649-50 (4th Cir. 2017).

The point can be stated simply. Whether Plaintiff ultimately would have testified is a
factual question concerning what later occurred. The Rule 12 question presented by Meta’s new
argument is whether the FAC plausibly alleges that Plaintiff was a prospective witness and that
the alleged object was to deter his testimony. Paragraphs 31 and 158 through 160 expressly plead

those facts.

Il. META USES LATER PROCEDURAL EVENTS TO NEGATE THE
CIRCUMSTANCES ALLEGED TO EXIST WHEN THE CONDUCT OCCURRED

Meta’s argument depends on two events. The first is the dismissal of the 286 Action. The
second is a motion to dismiss now pending in the 376 Action, which Meta says, “if granted, will
entirely dispose of Plaintiff’s claims before discovery commences.” ECF No. 39 at 7. From those
two events Meta concludes that “it is likely that no such potential testimony will ever come to
fruition.” Id.

Both events postdate the conduct alleged. The FAC pleads the circumstances that existed
on April 22, 2026, when the letters issued. Both federal actions were pending. ECF No. 5 { 27.
Plaintiff was a prospective witness in both. Id. ¥ 31. Plaintiff had noticed Accenture’s Rule 30(b)
(6) deposition for April 29 and 30, 2026, with CyberTipline reporting as a matter for examination.

Id. §§ 51-52. Plaintiff had noticed Anderson’s deposition for April 28, 2026. Id. 4 53. Plaintiff had

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 71 Filed 09/17/26 Page 4 of 8 PagelD# 735

retained a court reporter and a videographer. Id. 4] 54. The alleged purpose of the understanding
was to deter that prospective sworn testimony. Id. {{ 158-164.

A later procedural development does not erase the circumstances the FAC alleges existed
when Defendants acted. Both actions were then pending. Plaintiff was then a prospective witness
in both. Depositions were then noticed and imminent. Plaintiff then expected to testify under oath
at deposition and trial. The alleged agreement was then directed at deterring that prospective
testimony. The FAC alleges the circumstances that existed when the challenged conduct occurred.
Later procedural developments do not negate those pleaded historical facts on a Rule 12(b)(6)
motion.

Nor can the possibility that a pending Rule 12 motion may later terminate another action
be converted, on this Rule 12 motion, into a factual determination that Plaintiff’s pleaded
prospective testimony was speculative. The 376 Action has not been dismissed. Meta’s prediction
that Plaintiff’s anticipated testimony is unlikely ever to occur remains a prediction about the future
posture of another case. A prediction about the future of another case is not a ground for dismissing
a well-pleaded allegation about the past in this one.

Ill, META’S REPLY ITSELF DEMONSTRATES WHY ITS NEW CERTAINTY
THEORY FAILS

Meta’s Reply addresses the 376 Action twice. Read together, the two passages establish
one thing: the future posture of that action is unresolved.

At pages 3 and 4, answering Plaintiff’s point that the letters displaced the discovery he had
noticed, Meta says that “to the extent any of Plaintiff’s claims in Ballentine 2 survive defendants’
motion to dismiss, Plaintiff can again seek the discovery he claims was ‘displaced’ or ‘substituted’

by the letters.” ECF No. 39 at 3-4. At page 7, answering Plaintiff’s prospective-witness allegation,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 71 Filed 09/17/26 Page 5 of 8 PagelD# 736

Meta says that because the same motion to dismiss is pending, “it is likely that no such potential
testimony will ever come to fruition.” Id. at 7.

Put those statements side by side. On pages 3 and 4, Meta acknowledges that the 376
Action may survive and that discovery may resume. On page 7, Meta relies on the same unresolved
motion to argue that Plaintiff’s potential testimony is unlikely ever to occur. Meta itself recognizes
that the posture of the 376 Action remains unresolved. A pending motion to dismiss therefore
supplies no factual basis at Rule 12 to declare the FAC’s expressly pleaded prospective testimony
nonexistent or insufficiently concrete.

The statute confirms the point. Section 1985(2) addresses a conspiracy to “deter, by force,
intimidation, or threat, any party or witness in any court of the United States from attending such
court, or from testifying to any matter pending therein, freely, fully, and truthfully.” 42 U.S.C. §
1985(2). The statute expressly protects a party or witness from being deterred from testifying to a
matter pending in federal court. The FAC alleges that both matters were pending, ECF No. 5 { 27;
that Plaintiff was a prospective witness who expected to testify under oath at deposition and trial,
id. 431; the subjects of that testimony, id. J 31, 159; and an alleged purpose to deter it, id. {4 158,
237. Meta cites no authority imposing an additional requirement that the FAC identify a future

testimony event certain or likely to occur.

CONCLUSION

Meta’s new argument supplies no basis for dismissal. The FAC expressly pleads Plaintiff’s
prospective-witness status, the subjects of his anticipated sworn testimony, Defendants’
knowledge of that status, and the alleged purpose of deterring that testimony while both federal
actions were pending. The Court should reject the argument first advanced at page 7 of Meta’s

Reply and deny Meta’s Motion to Dismiss.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 71 Filed 09/17/26 Page 6 of 8 PagelD# 737

Date: September 1, 2026 Respectfully submitted,

YD

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se
1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847

Alexandria, Virginia 22307
(407) 794-6503
jayballentine@protonmail.com

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD              Document 73      Filed 09/17/26     Page 1 of 7 PageID# 745




                            IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
                           FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
                                       Alexandria Division


  MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE.,                              )
                                                        )
                   Plaintiff,                           )
                                                        ) Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
                           v.                           )
                                                        )
  KATIE HALL, NATIONAL                                  )
  CENTER FOR MISSING &                                  )
  EXPLOITED CHILDREN;                                   )
  META PLATFORMS, INC. and                              )
  JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,                                   )
                                                        )
                   Defendants.                          )

       DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO
           PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO SERVE FOUR LIMITED
      INTERROGATORIES ON META PLATFORMS, INC. BEFORE THE RULE 26(f)
                               CONFERENCE

     Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc., (“Meta”) by and through its undersigned counsel, hereby

  respectfully opposes Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine’s Motion for Leave to Serve Four Limited

  Interrogatories on Meta Before the Rule 26(f) Conference. Dkt. No. 54. In support of its response,

  Meta states the following:

     I.      Procedural History

          In this action, Plaintiff seeks to hold Defendants National Center for Missing & Exploited

  Children (“NCMEC”) and Katie Hall (collectively, the “NCMEC Defendants”) liable for

  responding to draft subpoenas that Plaintiff sent to NCMEC, which each requested “a document

  sufficient to show whether NCMEC received or maintains any CyberTipline report concerning (1)

  Marvelle    J.    Ballentine;   (2)    Jay   Ballentine,   and/or   the   account-level   identifier

  jaychizza@icloud.com.” FAC ¶ 56. He also seeks to hold Meta liable for purportedly conspiring

  with the NCMEC Defendants to send the responses to the draft subpoenas.


                                                    1

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD               Document 73        Filed 09/17/26      Page 2 of 7 PageID# 746




              Plaintiff first raised his claims against the NCMEC Defendants in a separate action in this

  district. See Ballentine v. Nat’l Ctr. for Missing & Exploited Children, et al., No. 1:26-cv-1341,

  Dkt. No. 1 (E.D. Va. May 19, 2026). After moving to dismiss Plaintiff’s Complaint there, the

  NCMEC Defendants filed a Motion to Stay Discovery. Id., Dkt. No. 11 at 3-4. The court granted

  their motion, staying all discovery pending resolution of the NCMEC Defendants’ Motion to

  Dismiss. Id., Dkt. No. 15. Plaintiff then voluntarily dismissed that action and reasserted his claim

  against the NCMEC Defendants in the instant action, adding Meta as a Defendant. Id., Dkt. No.

  21.

              After the NCMEC Defendants renewed their Motion to Dismiss, Plaintiff filed a motion

  seeking leave to serve three interrogatories on NCMEC prior to any Rule 26(f) conference. See

  Dkt. No. 15. The three proposed interrogatories asked whether NCMEC received a CyberTipline

  report associated with each of the three identifiers listed in the proposed subpoenas Plaintiff sent

  to NCMEC. Id. NCMEC opposed Plaintiff’s request. See Dkt. No. 33.

              Similarly, after Meta filed its Motion to Dismiss (Dkt. No. 21), Plaintiff filed the instant

  motion, seeking leave to serve four interrogatories on Meta prior to any Rule 26(f) conference,

  closely mirroring his prior requests directed to NCMEC. Dkt. No. 54. Plaintiff’s proposed

  interrogatories to Meta ask whether Meta submitted any CyberTipline regarding his Facebook

  account and, whether any such report submitted by Meta identified any of the three identifiers

  provided by Plaintiff. Id.

        II.      Legal Standard

              Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1) provides that a “party may not seek discovery from any source

  before the parties have conferred as required by Rule 26(f), except. . . when authorized. . . by court

  order.” “A district court has wide latitude in controlling discovery.” Rowland v. Am. Gen. Fin.,

  Inc., 340 F.3d 187, 195 (4th Cir. 2003). “In rare circumstances, the court may authorize expedited


                                                       2

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 73       Filed 09/17/26      Page 3 of 7 PageID# 747




  discovery upon a showing of good cause.” Thornock v. JES Found. Repair & Groundworks, No.

  7:23-CV-00638, 2023 WL 12012073, at *1 (W.D. Va. Oct. 25, 2023) (internal quotation marks

  omitted).

            Although “the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure do not specify a standard for assessing

  when to grant Motions for Expedited Discovery, and the Fourth Circuit has not established one,”

  courts in this district have applied “a modified preliminary injunction test to assess whether

  expedited discovery is warranted.” Arthur J. Gallagher & Co. v. Markfeld, No. 3:25-cv-885, 2026

  WL 2186600, at *9 (E.D. Va. July 29, 2026) (internal quotation marks omitted). Under this test the

  court considers “whether the Plaintiff has made a strong showing of merits,” and whether

  irreparable harm exists absent expedited discovery. Id. (internal quotation marks omitted). Such

  “relief outside of the federal rules should be limited to unusual circumstances.” Id.

     III.      Argument

            Plaintiff’s Motion does not establish that this case presents an “unusual circumstance”

  warranting expedited discovery outside the federal rules. Indeed, the opposite is true: Plaintiff has

  not shown a strong likelihood of success on the merits or any irreparable harm if his request for

  early discovery is denied.

            A. Plaintiff Is Not Likely To Succeed on the Merits

            Meta’s Motion to Dismiss demonstrates that Plaintiff cannot show a strong likelihood of

  success on the merits as to his claims against Meta. See Dkt. Nos. 21, 22, 30, 39. As Meta explained

  in its Motion to Dismiss, the FAC’s allegations fail to state any claim for relief against Meta

  because, among other things, Plaintiff fails to plausibly allege the existence of a conspiracy

  between Meta and the NCMEC Defendants. Even if the discovery Plaintiff requests could be

  considered in resolving Meta’s Motion to Dismiss (it cannot), the information sought cannot rescue

  the FAC’s deficient allegations.


                                                   3

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 73        Filed 09/17/26      Page 4 of 7 PageID# 748




         Courts have recognized that discovery prior to resolution of case-dispositive motions to

  dismiss are inappropriate, as is the case here. See, e.g., Rivers v. United States, No. 6:18-cv-00061,

  2020 WL 1469475, at *1 (W.D. Va. Jan. 24, 2020) (finding that “early discovery is not reasonable

  at this stage of the proceeding” and “good cause” exists “to stay all discovery” until after the court

  “determines which of Plaintiff’s claims, if any, survive” the pending motions to dismiss); cf.

  Colonial River Wealth Advisors, LLC v. Cambridge Inv. Rsch., Inc., No. 3:22-cv-717, 2023 WL

  4936708, at *1 (E.D. Va. June 5, 2023) (staying discovery pending resolution of motion to dismiss

  where the motion “would dispose of all the claims against [defendant]” and the “moving

  Defendants have made a colorable showing raising doubts as to the viability of Plaintiff’s

  complaint”). And, because Meta’s Motion to Dismiss tests only the sufficiency of the allegations

  in the FAC, any discovery would have no bearing on the resolution of Meta’s Motion to Dismiss.

  Meade v. Hicks, No. 3:21-cv-222, 2022 WL 433004, at *4 (E.D. Va. Feb. 11, 2022) (noting that

  “at the motion to dismiss stage, the Court generally only considers the well-pleaded factual

  allegations in the complaint”).

         B. Plaintiff Cannot Establish Irreparable Harm

         Plaintiff also cannot establish any irreparable harm from not receiving the discovery he

  requests now. In the event that either of Plaintiff’s claims against Meta survive Meta’s Motion to

  Dismiss, Plaintiff would be free to then seek discovery, after the parties have conferred pursuant

  to Rule 26(f).

     Notably, a different court in this district previously stayed all discovery pending resolution of

  the NCMEC Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss the first lawsuit that Plaintiff filed against them based

  on the same responses to Plaintiff’s draft subpoenas that are at issue in the present action.

  Ballentine v. Nat’l Ctr. for Missing & Exploited Children, et al., No. 1:26-cv-1341-MSN/WBP,




                                                    4

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 73         Filed 09/17/26      Page 5 of 7 PageID# 749




  Dkt. No. 15. Allowing Plaintiff to obtain early discovery in this new action (against either Meta or

  the NCMEC Defendants) would improperly reward Plaintiff’s procedural gamesmanship in

  voluntarily dismissing his first action only to re-file a substantially similar action to avoid both the

  stay of discovery and Rule 15’s requirement that he obtain leave before amending his complaint.

         C. Plaintiff’s Proffered Justification for Seeking Early Discovery Lacks Merit.

         Plaintiff appears to argue that any decision on Meta’s Motion to Dismiss without the

  requested discovery would be prejudicial to Plaintiff because Meta’s Motion to Dismiss

  purportedly raised a new factual issue; namely, whether NCMEC’s responses to Plaintiff’s draft

  subpoenas provided the “exact discovery” that Meta objected to in parallel cases that Plaintiff

  brought against Meta. Dkt. No. 55 at 4-5. But he is wrong. Meta’s Motion to Dismiss did not raise

  a new factual issue, it responded to Plaintiff’s allegations. Specifically, the FAC itself alleges that

  the “April 21, 2026 motions [i.e., Meta’s motions to stay discovery in the separate actions] were

  directed at the same discovery the April 9, 2026 materials [i.e., the proposed subpoenas to

  NCMEC] described.” FAC ¶ 127. The FAC further alleges that NCMEC’s letters “supplied. . . the

  precise subject scheduled for sworn examination” in Plaintiff’s upcoming deposition, which the

  motions to stay sought to prevent. FAC ¶ 133. To the extent Plaintiff disagrees with Meta’s

  characterizations of his FAC, he was free to raise that—and did in fact do so—in his Opposition

  to Meta’s Motion to Dismiss. See Dkt. No. 30 at 6 (arguing that the FAC did not admit that the

  letters from “NCMEC supplied exactly what Plaintiff requested”). That issue can be resolved based

  on the parties’ briefing on Meta’s Motion to Dismiss. Any further factual development would be

  wholly irrelevant for the purpose of evaluating the Motion to Dismiss, since the Court cannot

  consider evidence outside the pleadings. See Meade, 2022 WL 433004, at *4.




                                                     5

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD         Document 73       Filed 09/17/26      Page 6 of 7 PageID# 750




           Because the requested discovery does not impact the resolution of Meta’s Motion to

  Dismiss, the pendency of that motion cannot give rise to irreparable harm warranting premature

  discovery.

     IV.       Conclusion

     For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court deny Plaintiff’s Motion

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 1 of 7 PagelD# 752

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
Alexandria Division

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE, )
)
Plaintiff, )
)
