OPPOSITION OF DEFENDANTS KATIE HALL, ESQ. &
THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN
TO PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

Defendants Katie Hall, Esq. and the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children
[collectively, “NCMEC”], by and through undersigned counsel and pursuant to the Rules and
Orders of this Honorable Court, hereby respectfully opposes Plaintiffs “Motion for Leave to File
Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint and Request for Expedited Determination on the
Papers” [Doc. 59]. Plaintiff’s Motion should be denied, on the basis of futility, because Plaintiff
did not comply with the Court’s Order to provide a redline version, and because the proposed
Second Amended Complaint appears to be an attempt to present argument as to the pending
Motion to Dismiss, which Plaintiff has already opposed (and successfully moved to vacate the
hearing as to). Additionally, allowing further amendment would be prejudicial to NCMEC, as
the proposed pleading—if allowed—would represent Plaintiff's fifth version of a complaint as to

this dispute.' In further support, NCMEC states as follows:

1 As detailed below, Plaintiff filed (1) his original complaint; (2) moved to amend that complaint, then
voluntarily dismissed the action when NCMEC opposed the motion to amend, while a motion to dismiss
was pending; (3) filed his original complaint in this action; (4) filed a first amended complaint; and (5)
seeks leave to file the second amended complaint.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 2 of 7 PagelD# 753

I. PROCEDURAL SETTING

The above-captioned matter is the Pro Se Plaintiff’s second lawsuit arising out of the
same operative events. In the first, Marvelle J. Ballentine vy. NCMEC, et al., Case No. 1:26-cv-
01341-MSN-WBP (E.D. Va. 2026), NCMEC filed a motion to dismiss. Plaintiff opposed that
motion, which was set for a hearing on August 16, 2026 before the Honorable Michael S.
Nachmanoff. Plaintiff filed a motion for leave to file a “First Amended and Supplemental
Complaint” on July 26, 2026, which was opposed by NCMEC on July 29, 2026. In lieu of
allowing the Court to rule on either the Motion to Dismiss or the motion to amend the complaint,
Plaintiff voluntarily dismissed the action on the same day that NCMEC filed its opposition (July
29, 2026).

The following day, Plaintiff filed the original Complaint [Doc. 1] in this matter. Prior to
filing of any responsive pleading, Plaintiff filed a First Amended Complaint on August 6, 2026
[Doc. 5]. On August 12, 2026, Defendant the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children
filed a motion to dismiss [Doc. 10], which motion was joined by Defendant Hall on September 2,
2026 [Doc. 45]. Plaintiff has opposed both motions to dismiss via “Protective Oppositions.”
[Docs. 30, 51]

On September 8, 2026, Plaintiff filed the Motion at issue, his “Motion for Leave to File
Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint and Request for Expedited Determination on the
Papers.” [Doc. 59] While the First Amended Complaint was 260 paragraphs and 49 pages long,
the proposed “Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint” is 297 paragraphs and 50 pages

long, and would represent Plaintiff’s fifth attempt to set forth a claim as to the events at issue.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 3 of 7 PagelD# 754

On September 9, 2026, the Court ordered Plaintiff to provide a redlined version of the proposed
Second Amended Complaint no later than September 11, 2026, which was to “clearly indicate
the changes, deletions, and additions that were made to Plaintiffs Complaint.” [Doc. 63] The
Order noted that the Court “does not possess sufficient information to issue an Order on this
matter.” [Id.]

Plaintiff did not file the redlined version of the proposed pleading as ordered. On
September 14, 2026, Plaintiff instead filed “Rule 72(a) Objections” to, inter alia, the Court’s
order to provide a redlined version of the proposed Second Amended Complaint, in which
Plaintiff objected to the redline requirement, the deadline imposed by the Court, and various
other orders. [Doc. 66] (NCMEC notes that Plaintiff represents that because he does not receive
notices of electronic filing, Plaintiff was unaware of the Order requiring a redline version of the
document until 9:00 P.M. on September 11, 2026.)

Il. STANDARD OF REVIEW

Under Rule 15(a), leave to amend is to be granted freely, “absent bad faith, undue
prejudice to the opposing party, or futility of amendment.” Hardee v. Mun. Jail Va. Beach
Sheriff's Off, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 184735, *5 (E.D. Va. 2025) (quoting United States v.
Pittman, 209 F.3d 314, 317 (4th Cir. 2000)); Save Our Sound OBX, Inc. v. N.C. DOT, 914 F.3d
213, 228 (4th Cir. 2019) (same). A proposed amendment is futile “when it is clearly insufficient
or frivolous on its face... [or] if the claim it presents would not survive a motion to dismiss.”
Id., United States ex rel. Wilson v. Kellogg Brown & Root, Inc., 525 F.3d 370, 375 (4th Cir.
2008). In determining futility, the Court is empowered to “apply common sense.” Nasim v.

Warden, Md. House of Corr., 64 F.3d 951, 954 (4th Cir. 1995).

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 4 of 7 PagelD# 755

HI. ARGUMENT

As a threshold matter, NCMEC respectfully submits that the Motion should be denied
due to Plaintiff’s failure to comply with the Court’s Order to provide a redlined version of the
pleading. As noted, both the First Amended Complaint and proposed Second Amended
Complaint are approximately fifty pages long—and despite numerous efforts, undersigned
counsel has been unable to “reverse-engineer” a redline comparison of the two documents via
either Adobe or Word. That requirement is neither onerous, nor novel; while Plaintiff’s failure to
timely file the ordered document is understandable based on his representations as to not
receiving notifications, his refusal to do so is puzzling at best, as such a document would allow
the litigants and the Court the opportunity to easily see what changes have been made. Given the
procedural uncertainty due to Plaintiff’s objection to the Court’s order as to a redline version of
the document, and given the time constraints in which NCMEC is required to file an Opposition,
NCMEC requests the opportunity to supplement or amend this Opposition, if and when Plaintiff
submits the redline version of the proposed Second Amended Complaint.

Based on the representations in Plaintiff’s Memorandum in Support of the Motion for
Leave [Doc. 60], however, NCMEC respectfully submits that leave to amend at this stage would
be futile and unnecessary. In Plaintiffs’ Memorandum, he asserts that:

The SAC [Second Amended Complaint] does five principal things. First, the

SAC strengthens the falsity allegations in three respects... [and] pleads source-

level falsity concerning the asserted association between the two CyberTipline

reports and “Marvelle J. Ballentine”... pleads “person-level falsity” concerning

the implication that the reports concern Plaintiff personally... pleads defamation

by implication arising from the letters combined working and omitted

limitations... pleads that Plaintiff never used that name to create, identify, or

operate any Meta account... pleads, on information and belief, that neither report,

as NCMEC originally received it, identified Plaintiff by that name or concerned

Plaintiff personally. Second, the SAC pleads the distinction between the three

search identifiers Plaintiff supplied and the contents of the two reports. Third,
the SAC incorporates the post-filing events underlying Plaintiffs pending Rule

4

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 5 of 7 PagelD# 756

15(d) motion... Fourth, the SAC pleads later statements and filings by

Defendants and their counsel... Those statements and filings bear on Defendants’

subsequent knowledge, continuing positions, and the unresolved reference of the

April 22, 2026 letters. Fifth, the SAC strengthens the factual allegations

supporting Counts J through VI without changing any count.

Doc. 60 at p. 2-3 (emphasis added for ease of review). Taking these arguments in order:

As to the first purported change, that is apparently in response to NCMEC’s pending
Motion to Dismiss, in which NCMEC asserts, inter alia, that the allegedly-actionable
statement—that NCMEC received CyberTipline Reports for any of the three identifiers in
Plaintiff’s subpoena to NCMEC—are true, and that Plaintiff cannot plausibly assert falsity,
because he does not have access to those reports. No allegations Plaintiff can make can change
that fact; if Plaintiff had access to the CyberTipline reports, they presumably would be exhibits to
the pleading, or provided under seal to the Court for review.

As to the second purported change, Plaintiff has filed “protective oppositions” to the
motions to dismiss, and fought against having a hearing held on NCMEC’s Motions to Dismiss.
He has had the opportunity to argue as to any distinctions he sees fit; there is no reason an
amended pleading is needed to accomplish that goal.

As to the third and fourth purported change, Plaintiff attempts to “incorporate post-filing
events underlying Plaintiff’s pending Rule 15(d) motion” and “later statements and filings by
Defendants and their counsel...” To be clear, no defendant has individually filed any document
in this matter—i.e., all filings have been by counsel— and it remains entirely unclear how an
argument in a motion to dismiss, or opposition to a motion, could form the basis of any pleading.

Plaintiff alleges that the fifth purported change “strengthens the factual allegations...

without changing any count.” Given the length of the proposed document, and the fact that the

format of the factual allegations have changed, it is unclear how the factual allegations have been

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 6 of 7 PagelD# 757

strengthened. However, this again appears to relate to argument as to the motions to dismiss,
which presumably were presented in the “protective oppositions,” or could have been presented
at a hearing, had Plaintiff not moved to have those hearings vacated.

Additionally, NCMEC respectfully submits that amendment would not impact the
arguments set forth in NCMEC’s pending Motions to Dismiss, and thus would be futile.
Specifically, NCMEC has argued that (1) the claims are barred by the litigation privilege, in that
the allegedly-actionable statements were made in a subpoena response; (2) that NCMEC has
statutory immunity to several of Plaintiff’s causes of action; (3) that Plaintiff cannot plausibly
assert that the statements are false, as he does not have access to the CyberTipline reports; (4) the
allegedly-defamatory meaning cannot be imputed from the language utilized in the statements at
issue; and (5) that the “insulting words” claim fails for the same reason. None of the broadly-
described changes impact those arguments, and as noted, Plaintiff has filed oppositions to those
motions and intentionally avoided the opportunity to present oral argument.

Finally, NCMEC respectfully submits that allowing leave to file a second amended
complaint would be prejudicial to NCMEC. As noted above, NCMEC has been forced to file
numerous motions in the prior iteration of this lawsuit, and in the present suit, and Plaintiff has
resisted on multiple occasions NCMEC’s opportunity to have the Court rule on motions to
dismiss. In the event that the Motion for Leave is granted, NCMEC will be forced to file a third
motion to dismiss, as to a dispute that NCMEC respectfully submits lacks merit. Given
Plaintiff’s multiple prior amendments—in this case and the prior iteration—NCMEC respectfully
submits that it will continue to suffer unfair prejudice if amendment is allowed prior to this

Honorable Court ruling on the pending motions to dismiss.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 74 _ Filed 09/18/26 Page 7 of 7 PagelD# 758

IV. CONCLUSION

In light of the foregoing, NCMEC respectfully submits that Plaintiff's Motion for Leave
to File a Second Amended Complaint be denied, on the basis of futility, or in the alternative that
the Motion be held in abeyance until the Court has had the opportunity to rule on the pending
Motions to Dismiss, in the event the Court believes that any defects in the pleadings could be

addressed via amendment.

Respectfully submitted,
JORDAN COYNE LLP

/s/ Padraic K. Keane
10201 Fairfax Boulevard, Suite 520
Fairfax, VA 22030
(703) 246-0900
Fax: (703) 591-3673

PLAINTIFF'S REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION FOR LEAVE
TO FILE SUR-REPLY
Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine respectfully submits this Reply in support of his Motion for
Leave to File Sur-Reply, ECF No. 43. Meta's Opposition confirms that leave is warranted.
Meta has stated its argument three ways. The opening memorandum argued that Plaintiff
pleaded no facts showing that the challenged conduct "actually impacted his ability to testify or
pursue his claim." ECF No. 22 at 12. The Reply advanced a different proposition: Plaintiff
identified no "non-speculative opportunity" to testify and no testimony he "has or likely will
offer." ECF No. 39 at 7. The Reply rested that proposition on procedural developments in the
underlying actions that came after the letters. The Opposition calls the proposition a "further
development" of the opening argument. The Opposition then adds a third formulation: Plaintiff's
claims "had not even survived initial motions to dismiss" when the letters issued. ECF No. 69 at 2-

3. The opening memorandum imposed neither requirement. Plaintiff has had no authorized
opportunity to answer either one.
Meta's remaining objection confirms the point. Meta faults the proposed sur-reply for
"simply reiterat[ing] allegations from the FAC." ECF No. 69 at 3. But the Reply asserts that the
FAC lacks sufficiently concrete prospective testimony. The direct answer to that assertion is the
FAC itself: Plaintiff's prospective-witness status, the subjects of his expected sworn testimony,
and Defendants' alleged knowledge and purpose concerning that testimony. The proposed sur-
reply identifies those allegations and addresses nothing else.
The Court should grant ECF No. 43 and deem the proposed Sur-Reply filed.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA

ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Ivan D. Davis

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;

EXHIBIT A

PLAINTIFF’S PROPOSED SUPPLEMENTAL MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF
ECF NO. 15 ADDRESSING NCMEC’S RENEWED TRUTH
AND LACK-OF-ACCESS ARGUMENTS

This memorandum supplements the briefing on Plaintiff’s pending Rule 26(d)(1) motion.
ECF No. 15. It addresses the opposition Defendants Katie Hall and NCMEC filed on September
18, 2026. ECF No. 74. It changes nothing about the discovery requested.

I. NCMEC Again Relies on Plaintiff’s Lack of Access to Support Dismissal.

ECF No. 74 states that Plaintiff “cannot plausibly assert falsity, because he does not have
access to those reports.” ECF No. 74 at 5. ECF No. 74 continues: “[n]Jo allegations Plaintiff can
make can change that fact.” Id. The word “fact” refers to Plaintiff’s lack of access. NCMEC
invokes the reports’ asserted contents to defeat the claims. NCMEC invokes Plaintiff’s inability to

inspect the reports to defeat any challenge. One informational gap does both jobs.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 78-1 Filed 09/18/26 Page 2 of 7 PagelD#
785

The categorical position is wrong. Allegations pled on information and belief “are not
categorically insufficient to state a claim for relief where the proof supporting the allegation is
within the sole possession and control of the defendant or where the belief is based on sufficient
factual material that makes the inference of culpability plausible.” Lowy v. Daniel Defense, LLC,
No. 24-1822, slip op. at 34-35 (4th Cir. Feb. 11, 2026) (quoting Ahern Rentals, Inc. v.
EquipmentShare.com, Inc., 59 F.4th 948, 954 (8th Cir. 2023)). Lowy is a published decision. Lowy
reversed a dismissal entered in this Division on the papers.

Lowy does not itself authorize discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference. Lowy forecloses
the categorical premise: that lack of access defeats Plaintiff’s allegations as a class. ECF No. 74
asks the Court to adopt that premise. NCMEC opposes the three answers directed to it. ECF No. 15
requests those answers. The premise should be tested, not assumed.

Il. NCMEC’s “Any” Formulation Permits Materially Different Source Facts.

ECF No. 74 describes the statements at issue as concerning CyberTipline reports received
“for any of the three identifiers in Plaintiff’s subpoena to NCMEC.” ECF No. 74 at 5. That sentence
is NCMEC’s litigation characterization. It is not the text of the April 22, 2026 letters.

First, “any” identifies no particular matching term. A report satisfies the formulation if it
matched one identifier out of three.

Second, the formulation is consistent with the absence of “Marvelle J. Ballentine” from
both reports as originally received. A report matching only “Jay Ballentine,” or only the email
address, satisfies the formulation.

Third, NCMEC’s August 12 memorandum supplied a different alternative: “a person with
the same name.” ECF No. 11 at 9. A report concerning a different person with the same name

would not concern Plaintiff.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 78-1 Filed 09/18/26 Page 3 of 7 PagelD#
786

Fourth, the three interrogatories address the facts both formulations leave unspecified. Each
asks whether either report, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise identified
one named identifier. ECF No. 15-1 at 1-2.

The two open questions are distinct. The absence of “Marvelle J. Ballentine” from a report
would not, by itself, establish that the report did not concern Plaintiff through his alias or his email
address. The name question concerns the reports’ original identifying information. The different-
person question concerns personal identity. Each answer narrows one of them. Neither formulation
NCMEC has offered resolves either one. NCMEC defends a disjunction. The interrogatories ask
which branch or branches of it are true.

II. _Plaintiff’s Declaration Supplies a Concrete Basis for the Source Question.

Plaintiff has sworn to his account-naming history. Plaintiff did not use “Marvelle J.
Ballentine” to create, identify, or operate any Meta account. Plaintiff used “Jay Ballentine.”
Plaintiff supplied his full legal name in the April 9, 2026 materials because it is his legal name. ECF
No. 31 44 3-8.

Those facts distinguish two sources. One is information Plaintiff supplied through litigation
materials. The other is identifying information contained in the reports when NCMEC originally
received them. Interrogatory No. 1 tests that distinction. It excludes the April 9 materials, court
filings, public sources, and information obtained or added after original receipt. ECF No. 15-1 at 1.

The request is not open-ended. It names two identified reports, three identifiers, one fixed
point in time, and stated exclusions. It permits three answers. It seeks no explanation and no report
content.

The declaration has limits, and the request respects them. The declaration establishes

Plaintiff’s own account practices. It does not identify the submitting provider or every possible

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 78-1 Filed 09/18/26 Page 4 of 7 PagelD#
787

source of a report’s contents. The interrogatories put the source question to the entity that holds the
reports.

IV. NCMEC Identifies the Reports as Material Evidence; Plaintiff Seeks Less than

Production.

ECF No. 74 states that if Plaintiff had access to the reports, they “presumably would be
exhibits to the pleading, or provided under seal to the Court for review.” ECF No. 74 at 5. That
sentence treats the reports as the evidence bearing on this dispute. That sentence identifies a sealed-
review path. NCMEC holds the reports. No defendant in either action has filed a CyberTipline
report, openly or under seal.

The sentence also demands proof at the pleading stage. Plaintiffs are not required “to prove
[their] case in the complaint,” and the requirement of factual detail is “tempered by the recognition
that a plaintiff may only have so much information at [her] disposal at the outset.” Lowy, slip op. at
22 (quoting Robertson v. Sea Pines Real Est. Cos., 679 F.3d 278, 291 (4th Cir. 2012)). A court may
consider the April 22 letters for their language without accepting their assertions as true. Goines v.
Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd., 822 F.3d 159, 167-69 (4th Cir. 2016). Pleading the letters does not make
the letters proof of their own truth.

The consequences NCMEC seeks sharpen the timing. NCMEC requests dismissal with
prejudice. ECF No. 11 at 17, NCMEC opposes amendment as futile and asks that leave await
rulings on the motions to dismiss. ECF No. 74 at 5—7. Both requests rest on what the reports are
said to establish. Plaintiff has asked three questions about those reports. NCMEC opposes the

answe!s.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 78-1 Filed 09/18/26 Page 5 of 7 PagelD#
788

The scope of this argument is narrow. Plaintiff draws no waiver from NCMEC’s sealed-
review reference. Plaintiff requests no adverse inference from nonproduction. This motion requests
neither the reports nor a sealing procedure. It requests three answers.

V. Three Sworn Answers Test NCMEC’s Chosen Premise with Defined Burden.

The pending interrogatories read in full:

INTERROGATORY NO. 1: Excluding information supplied by Plaintiff in the

April 9, 2026 materials, court filings, public sources, and information obtained or

added after original receipt by NCMEC, did either of the two CyberTipline reports

referenced in NCMEC’s April 22, 2026 letters, as originally received by NCMEC,
contain or otherwise identify “Marvelle J. Ballentine”?

INTERROGATORY NO. 2: Subject to the same exclusions, did either report, as
originally received by NCMEC, contain or otherwise identify “Jay Ballentine”?

INTERROGATORY NO. 3: Subject to the same exclusions, did either report, as
originally received by NCMEC, contain’ or _ otherwise _ identify
jaychizza@icloud.com?

ECF No. 15-1 at 1-2. NCMEC shall answer each interrogatory only “Yes,” “No,” or
“Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry.” Id. at 1. The interrogatories seek no explanation
and no report content. Id. Each asks about either report. None requires a report-by-report mapping.
None asks why a match occurred.

Rule 26(d)(1) permits discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference by court order.
Relevance, timing, access, and burden point the same way. NCMEC selected the two reports and
the three identifiers as the factual basis of its defense. NCMEC holds the reports. NCMEC seeks

claim-terminating relief now. The burden is three sworn one-sentence answers under Rule 33,

within the response period requested in ECF No. 15 or the period the Court directs.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 78-1 Filed 09/18/26 Page 6 of 7 PagelD#
789

The answers have defined value and defined limits. Each answer fixes or narrows one
original-source fact. No answer determines ownership of an alias, defamatory meaning, or liability.
Plaintiff does not contend that every ground in the motions to dismiss requires discovery. Plaintiff
requests resolution of the source question before any relief that depends on accepting NCMEC’s
account of what the reports establish.

CONCLUSION

The Court should grant ECF No. 15 on its existing terms and consider ECF No. 74 as
further support for the present need for the three answers. NCMEC’s “any” formulation leaves the

identifying facts unspecified. ECF No. 15 asks for those facts, under oath, without requesting the

reports.

Date: September 18, 2026 Respectfully submitted,

rp

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847
Alexandria, Virginia 22307

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFE’S MOTION FOR LEAVE
TO FILE A SUPPLEMENTAL MEMORANDUM ADDRESSING ECF NO. 74

Plaintiff seeks leave to file one supplemental memorandum in support of his pending Rule
26(d)(1) motion. ECF No. 15. The ground is a filing Defendants made after the discovery briefing
closed. Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) requires leave for further briefs. This memorandum states why
leave should be granted.

I. NCMEC’s September 18 Filing Renews the Premise of the Pending Discovery

Motion.

The sequence is short. Plaintiff filed ECF No. 15 on August 20, 2026, requesting leave to
serve three source-identification interrogatories before the Rule 26(f) conference. Plaintiff filed a
sworn declaration stating his account-naming history. ECF No. 31. Plaintiff then moved for leave

to file a Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint containing corresponding source-

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 79 Filed 09/18/26 Page 2 of 4 PagelD# 794

identification allegations. ECF Nos. 59-60. On September 18, 2026, Defendants Katie Hall and
NCMEC opposed that motion. ECF No. 74.

ECF No. 74 renews two propositions. It describes the statements at issue as concerning
reports received “for any of the three identifiers in Plaintiff’s subpoena to NCMEC.” ECF No. 74 at
5. It states that Plaintiff “cannot plausibly assert falsity, because he does not have access to those
reports,” and that “[n]o allegations Plaintiff can make can change that fact.” Id. ECF No. 74 applies
those propositions to the proposed source-identification allegations. ECF No. 74 at 4-6.

ECF No. 74 is not one more filing that mentions the reports. ECF No. 74 renews the
position that the reports’ asserted contents defeat Plaintiff’s claims while Plaintiff’s inability to
inspect the reports defeats any challenge. That is the premise the three interrogatories were drafted
to test. The renewal came after the discovery briefing closed. The renewal is the ground for
supplementation.

Il. The Supplement Addresses the Decision Before the Court.

Two decisions are distinct. The first is whether this subsequent development may be added
to the briefing on ECF No. 15. The second is whether the requested discovery should be authorized.
This motion presents only the first. Exhibit A addresses the second, and the Court will resolve it in
ruling on ECF No. 15.

The supplement’s contribution is specific. It places NCMEC’s September 18 formulations
beside the exact questions already proposed. It explains why the three answers address NCMEC’s
own asserted premise. The Court deciding ECF No. 15 should have that development before it.

II. The Supplement Permits Focused Adjudication Without Expanding

Discovery.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 79 Filed 09/18/26 Page 3 of 4 PagelD# 795

Exhibit A has one confined subject: ECF No. 74’s renewed truth and lack-of-access
arguments. Exhibit A relies on docket materials only: ECF Nos. 11, 15-1, 31, and 74. Exhibit A
attaches no new declaration. Exhibit A changes no interrogatory, no exclusion, and no permitted
answer. The substantive discovery argument appears in Exhibit A, not here.

Plaintiff requests leave to file Exhibit A and its consideration with ECF No. 15. Any

responsive submission is for the Court’s direction. Leave should be granted.

9/21/2026
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Ivan D. Davis

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

PLAINTIFE’S REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION UNDER FEDERAL
RULE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE 26(d)(1) FOR LEAVE TO SERVE
FOUR LIMITED INTERROGATORIES ON META PLATFORMS, INC.
BEFORE THE RULE 26(f) CONFERENCE

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine respectfully submits this Reply in support of his Motion
Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(d)(1) for Leave to Serve Four Limited Interrogatories on
Meta Platforms, Inc. Before the Rule 26(f) Conference (ECF No. 54), and in reply to Defendant
Meta Platforms, Inc.’s Response in Opposition (ECF No. 73).

I. INTRODUCTION

Meta’s Opposition runs seven pages. ECF No. 73. It does not dispute that Meta’s
Memorandum described the April 22, 2026 letters as “the exact discovery” Plaintiff had sought
from Meta. ECF No. 22 at 9. It identifies no specific burden in answering four closed questions

about Meta’s own records. It asserts no privilege. It does not address the three-answer format, the

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 81 Filed 09/21/26 Page 2 of 9 PagelD# 800

bounded period, or the Motion’s exclusion of all other discovery. ECF No. 54 at 2. Neither the
Opposition nor Meta’s dismissal briefing states whether Meta submitted a CyberTipline report
within the account and date parameters specified in Interrogatory No. 1. ECF Nos. 22, 39, 73. The
four interrogatories ask whether such a submission occurred and, if so, whether it contained or
otherwise identified the specified terms. ECF No. 54 at 1-2.

II. META HAS NOT ESTABLISHED THAT ITS PRELIMINARY-
INJUNCTION FRAMEWORK CONTROLS THIS REQUEST

Meta asks the Court to apply a modified preliminary-injunction test to this request. ECF
No. 73 at 2-3. Its principal authority, Arthur J. Gallagher & Co. v. Markfeld, addressed expedited
discovery in a preliminary-injunction proceeding. No. 3:25-cv-00885-RCY, ECF No. 70 at 1, 17—
18 (E.D. Va. July 29, 2026). Shenzhenshibairihongmaoyiyouxiangongsi v. Novoluto GmbH
likewise applied that framework to discovery sought for a pending preliminary injunction. No.
3:25-cv-00844-RCY, ECF No. 44 at 3-6 (E.D. Va. Mar. 9, 2026). Neither decision addressed the
four-question request presented here. Plaintiff identified that difference in ECF No. 55 at 4. The
Court retains authority under Rule 26(d)(1) to authorize discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference
and to confine that discovery to relevant, proportional inquiries under Rule 26(b)(1).

Plaintiff’s merits showing rests on the circumstances pleaded in the First Amended
Complaint, not on the proposition that the requested answers would establish a conspiracy. The
FAC alleges common receipt of case-specific materials, imminent examinations concerning
CyberTipline reporting, motions directed at that discovery, and two case-specific letters issued the
following day without compulsory process and without identifying the reporting provider or
account connection. FAC 4 126—135. Plaintiff relies on that combined sequence to support the
pleaded inference of agreement. ECF No. 30 at 12-14. Meta disputes that inference, in part by

characterizing its conduct and NCMEC’s conduct as contradictory because Meta sought to prevent

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 81 Filed 09/21/26 Page 3 of 9 PagelD# 801

discovery that NCMEC supposedly supplied. ECF No. 22 at 9-10. The distinction between an
assertion about the discovery’s subject and the source-specific information sought is therefore
relevant to an argument Meta advances.

The reason for seeking the answers now is correspondingly specific. Meta invokes that
characterization in support of dismissal with prejudice, while the letters do not identify Meta as the
submitting provider or connect either report to Plaintiffs Facebook account. ECF No. 22 at 7, 9-
11, 14. Plaintiff’s existing declaration supplies a concrete basis for examining the listed identifiers:
Plaintiff states that he did not use his legal name to identify or operate a Meta account and included
it in the April 9 materials because it is his litigation name. ECF No. 31 4 3, 6—7. That declaration
does not establish what any report contained. It explains why the requested inquiry concerns
identified facts rather than an unrestricted search for a claim. ECF No. 55 at 3-4.

Novoluto supports considering informational imbalance and tailoring discovery to an
identified adjudicative need, but its irreparable-harm finding also rested on threatened marketplace
injuries and shifting seller identities. Novoluto, No. 3:25-cv-00844-RCY, ECF No. 44 at 5-6.
Plaintiff does not contend that a pending dismissal motion alone establishes irreparable harm or an
automatic entitlement to discovery. The requested exercise of discretion rests on the particular
factual issue, Plaintiff’s existing showing, the parties’ relative access to the information, and the
confined scope of four interrogatories. ECF No. 55 at 3—7.

Til. META’S CHARACTERIZATION OF THE LETTERS IS NOT AN
ESTABLISHED FACT
Meta’s Rule 12 papers tell the Court that NCMEC “provided him with exactly what he

asked for,” ECF No. 22 at 11, that the letters were “the exact discovery” Meta’s April 21 motion
practice sought to prevent, id. at 9, and that NCMEC was “responding to proposed subpoenas from

Plaintiff requesting the provided information,” ECF No. 39 at 5-6. Meta may argue from the

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 81 Filed 09/21/26 Page 4 of 9 PagelD# 802

wording of the First Amended Complaint and the letters. Meta may not convert its characterization
of those documents into an established fact about reports the documents neither identify nor
produce. A court may consider a document without accepting its assertions, or a party’s assertions
about it, as true. Goines v. Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd., 822 F.3d 159, 166-69 (4th Cir. 2016). Plaintiff
has contested the asserted equivalence. ECF No. 30 at 6. The letters identify no reporting provider,
no account, and no enforcement event. ECF No. 22 at 7 (quoting FAC 4 92). The letters and the
cited paragraphs do not establish that Meta submitted a report concerning the account at issue.
Whether such a submission occurred is a question for inquiry into Meta’s reporting records, not a
fact established by its characterization of the letters. The four interrogatories address that inquiry.

The answers would be material without being conclusive. A “Yes” to Interrogatory No. 1
would establish that Meta submitted a report within the stated parameters. It would not, by itself,
establish that the submission was either report referenced in the April 22 letters. Interrogatories
Nos. 2 through 4 would identify whether a qualifying Meta submission contained or otherwise
identified the specified terms. ECF No. 54 at 1-2. No answer would adjudicate conspiracy,
intimidation, defamation, or liability. ECF No. 55 at 7. Plaintiff maintains that the FAC
independently pleads an agreement through the circumstances stated in FAC {J 124-138. The
requested discovery addresses the reporting facts relevant to Meta’s characterization of that alleged
conduct.

IV. THE SAME SUBJECT IS NOT THE SAME ANSWER

Meta reads two paragraphs of the First Amended Complaint as pleading the equivalence.
ECF No. 73 at 5. They do not. Paragraph 127 alleges that “the April 21, 2026 motions were directed
at the same discovery the April 9, 2026 materials described.” That is an allegation about what the

motions targeted. Paragraph 133 alleges that the letters “supplied, outside the discovery process, an

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 81 Filed 09/21/26 Page 5 of 9 PagelD# 803

unsworn and source-free assertion concerning the precise subject scheduled for sworn
examination.” The Opposition quotes that paragraph as alleging that the letters “supplied. . . the
precise subject scheduled for sworn examination.” ECF No. 73 at 5. The ellipsis removes the words
“outside the discovery process, an unsworn and source-free assertion concerning.” Paragraph 133
alleges an unsworn assertion about the subject of the contemplated examination. Paragraph 135
alleges that the assertion “purported to answer” the report-existence question. Neither paragraph
concedes that the letters identified Meta as the submitting provider or connected either report to
Plaintiff’s Facebook account. Meta’s shortened quotation does not supply those missing
propositions.

Meta proposes that “[t]hat issue can be resolved based on the parties’ briefing.” ECF No. 73
at 5. The Court can determine from the FAC whether the cited paragraphs admit that Meta
submitted an account-related report. They do not. Whether Meta actually made such a submission
is a separate factual question that those paragraphs and the April 22 letters leave unanswered. The
four interrogatories address that question; they are not needed to establish what the FAC says.

V. THE CITED DECISIONS CONFIRM DISCRETION; THEY DO NOT
DECIDE THIS REQUEST

Rivers denied the early discovery requested there and stayed all discovery on the
defendants’ motion. ECF No. 73 at 4. Colonial River, as Meta quotes it, stayed discovery on a stay
motion after the court found the movants had made a colorable showing. Id. Those decisions
confirm the Court’s discretion to defer discovery. They do not establish that a pending dismissal
motion categorically defeats a request under Rule 26(d)(1). The question remains whether the
grounds stated in ECF No. 55 justify these four interrogatories now: one defendant, one identified
account, one bounded period, three permitted responses, and no production of any report. ECF No.

34 at 1-2.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 81 Filed 09/21/26 Page 6 of 9 PagelD# 804

The Opposition calls the dismissal of Case No. 1:26-cv-01341 “procedural
gamesmanship.” ECF No. 73 at 5. Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) conferred that dismissal as of right. The stay
entered in that action governed discovery in that action. It did not decide the four interrogatories
now proposed. It did not address Meta’s subsequently filed characterization of the April 22 letters.
The First Amended Complaint here was filed as of right under Rule 15(a)(1). ECF No. 59 10.
Plaintiff then sought leave to supplement under Rule 15(d), ECF No. 26, and now seeks leave to
file an amended and supplemental pleading, ECF No. 59. The present request is evaluated on the
present record.

VI. CONCLUSION

The Opposition identifies no specific burden, asserts no privilege, and contests neither the
scope nor the format of the four interrogatories. The answers are relevant to a characterization Meta
placed in its own Rule 12 briefing. Meta seeks dismissal with prejudice while the source-side facts
remain in Meta’s records. The request is confined to four answers about those records. The Motion
should be granted.

Date: September 21, 2026 Respectfully submitted,

rp

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847
Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503
jayballentine@protonmail.com

IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
                       FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
                                   Alexandria Division


MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE.,                            )
                                                    )
               Plaintiff,                           )
                                                    ) Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
                       v.                           )
                                                    )
KATIE HALL, NATIONAL                                )
CENTER FOR MISSING &                                )
EXPLOITED CHILDREN;                                 )
META PLATFORMS, INC. and                            )
JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,                                 )
                                                    )
               Defendants.                          )

    DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO
  PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

        Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc., (“Meta”) by and through its undersigned counsel, hereby

respectfully opposes Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine’s Motion for Leave to File a Second Amended

Complaint pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d), Dkt. No. 59. Meta hereby joins,

adopts and incorporates all applicable arguments and requested relief contained in Defendants

Katie Hall and National Center for Missing & Exploited Children’s (“NCMEC Defendants”)

Opposition to Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File a Second Amended Complaint (Dkt. No. 74). In

further support, Meta states as follows:

   I.      Procedural History

        As described in Meta’s Motion to Dismiss the First Amended Complaint (“FAC”), Plaintiff

has filed a series of actions against Meta across several different courts, all stemming from the

alleged disablement of his Facebook account. See Dkt. No. 22 at 3-5. Across all of these actions,

Plaintiff has routinely filed amended complaints (or sought leave to do so), consistently delaying



                                                1

decision on motions to dismiss across those actions. Indeed, since September 9, 2025 (when

Plaintiff filed his first complaint against Meta in the United States District Court for the Northern

District of California), Plaintiff has filed 12 distinct complaints against Meta across four different

courts.

          Plaintiff’s present request for leave to amend continues his strategy of seeking repeated

amendments to delay decision on motions to dismiss. Indeed, in this court alone, Plaintiff has:

             •   Filed a complaint based on the allegations raised in the FAC against NCMEC and
                 Defendant Katie Hall (together, the “NCMEC Defendants) in a distinct action
                 (Ballentine v. Nat’l Ctr. for Missing & Exploited Children, No. 1:26-cv-1341 (E.D.
                 Va.);
             •   Filed a motion for leave to amend that complaint to add claims against Meta;
             •   Voluntarily dismissed that action after the NCMEC Defendants opposed his request
                 for leave to amend;
             •   Filed the complaint and FAC against the NCMEC Defendants and Meta in the
                 instant action; and
             •   Following motions to dismiss, filed a motion for leave to file supplement his
                 pleading, withdrew that motion, and filed the instant motion for leave to amend.

See Dkt. No. 22 at 5; Dkt. No. 57; Dkt. No. 59.

   II.       Plaintiff’s Supplemental Allegations are Futile

          “[T]he standards used by a district court in ruling on a motion to amend or on a motion to

supplement [a complaint] are nearly identical.” Franks v. Ross, 313 F.3d 184, 198, n. 15 (4th Cir.

2002). In either case, “leave to amend a pleading should be denied. . . when the amendment would

be futile.” Brannen v. Selene Finance, LP, No. 2:18-cv-602, 2019 WL 13251099, at *2, 5 (E.D.

Va. Nov. 14, 2019) (denying leave to file supplemental complaint where “it would be futile to

permit” Plaintiff’s “supplemental pleading” where his “right to relief” remained “a matter of pure

speculation”).




                                                  2

As to Plaintiff’s supplemental allegations regarding the NCMEC Defendants, Meta fully

adopts the arguments in NCMEC’s Opposition, which explain why the supplemental allegations

are “futile,” “unnecessary,” and a further attempt to prolong the litigation. Dkt. No. 74 at 4-5.

          As to Plaintiff’s supplemental allegations regarding Meta, Plaintiff seeks to add allegations

that in a motion to dismiss in a separate action brought by Plaintiff (Ballentine v. Meta Platforms,

Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL (N.D. Cal.)), Meta described Plaintiff’s litigation against the

NCMEC Defendants as one of several actions Plaintiff has brought arising from the alleged

disablement of his Facebook account. See Dkt. No. 60 at 9. Plaintiff asserts that Meta’s citation

there of the present action is “a subsequent fact bearing on Meta’s knowledge, state of mind, and

awareness of the relationship between the two proceedings.” Id.

          But Meta’s knowledge, as of August 13, 2026, that Plaintiff sued NCMEC has no relevance

whatsoever to Plaintiff’s claims against Meta. Those claims are premised on Plaintiff’s assertion

that Meta somehow conspired with NCMEC in connection with letters that NCMEC sent to

Plaintiff on April 22, 2026. Plaintiff’s proffered supplemental allegations regarding Meta’s

knowledge of Plaintiff’s suit against NCMEC are plainly irrelevant to Plaintiff’s claims against

Meta or the issues raised in Meta’s motion to dismiss. Therefore, amendment would be futile and

Plaintiff’s motion should be denied. See Dacha v. Moody, No. 3:24-cv-713, 2026 WL 625494, at

*15 (E.D. Va. Mar. 5, 2026) (denying motion to supplement under Rule 15(d) because

supplementation with allegations that could not plausibly serve “as a factual basis for any claim”

against defendants “would be futile”).

   III.      Conclusion

          For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court deny Plaintiff’s Motion

for Leave to File a Second Amended Complaint.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Ivan D. Davis

KATIE HALL, individually;

NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;

and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

[PROPOSED] ORDER OF DISQUALIFICATION AND TRANSFER

This matter is before the Court on Plaintiff’s Motion to Disqualify Magistrate Judge Ivan D.
Davis Under 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) and § 455(a), and for Priority Determination (the “Motion”),
the Memorandum in Support, Exhibits A and B, and the Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine.
Plaintiff has waived oral argument, and the Court determines the Motion on the papers under Local
Civil Rule 7(J) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 78(b).

Upon consideration of the Motion and the record, and upon the undersigned’s review of the
undersigned’s personal financial interests under 28 U.S.C. § 455(c), the Court states for the record
that the asset reported as “FB common stock” on the undersigned’s financial disclosure reports for
calendar years 2024 and 2025 is common stock of Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc.; that the
undersigned held that interest directly, and not through a mutual or common investment fund

within the meaning of 28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4)(i), during the undersigned’s participation in this

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 86-4 Filed 10/13/26 Page 2 of 2 PagelD#
849

action, including on the dates on which ECF Nos. 62, 63, 64, 65, 82, and 84 were entered; and that
the conditions of 28 U.S.C. § 455(f) have not been satisfied. Accordingly, it is hereby

ORDERED that the Motion is GRANTED; it is further

ORDERED that the undersigned is DISQUALIFIED from further participation in this
action under 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) and, independently, under 28 U.S.C. § 455(a); it is further

ORDERED that the Clerk shall reassign all matters referred to the undersigned in this
action to another Magistrate Judge of this Court in accordance with the Court’s assignment
procedures, or return those matters to the District Judge as the District Judge may direct; it is
further

ORDERED that the undersigned shall take no further action in this matter other than the
ministerial steps necessary to effect this Order; it is further

ORDERED that nothing in this Order determines the retrospective relief requested by
Plaintiff from the District Judge concerning any order previously entered by the undersigned; and
it is further

ORDERED that the Clerk shall forward a copy of this Order to all counsel of record and to
Plaintiff.

ENTERED this day of , 2026.

Alexandria, Virginia

Ivan D. Davis United States Magistrate Judge

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 86 Filed 10/13/26 Page 1 of 9 Pagélij# 823

10/13/2026
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Ivan D. Davis

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

PLAINTIFE’S MOTION TO DISQUALIFY MAGISTRATE JUDGE IVAN D. DAVIS
UNDER 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) AND § 455(a), AND FOR PRIORITY DETERMINATION

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine, proceeding pro se, moves under 28 U.S.C. § 455 for the
disqualification of Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis from further participation in this action and for
priority determination of this Motion. The grounds are stated below and in the accompanying
Memorandum in Support. Exhibit A, Exhibit B, and the Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine
accompany this Motion.

I. STATUTORY BASIS AND RELIEF
This Motion rests on 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4). That subsection requires a magistrate judge to

disqualify himself when he knows that he has a financial interest in a party to the proceeding. The
Motion rests independently on 28 U.S.C. § 455(a), which requires disqualification in any

proceeding in which the judge’s impartiality might reasonably be questioned. Sections 455(c),

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 86 Filed 10/13/26 Page 2 of 9 PagelD# 824

455(d)(4), 455(e), and 455(f) govern the duty to inform, the definition of financial interest,
nonwaiver, and the divestiture exception.

The Motion presents one question of fact and one question of law. The question of fact is
whether a financial interest in Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta’’) was held during Magistrate
Judge Davis’s participation in this action. The question of law is whether, on the facts determined,
§ 455 requires disqualification.

The Motion alleges no bias, hostility, improper motive, bad faith, or intentional
nondisclosure. It rests on two signed financial disclosure reports and the docket.

II. FINANCIAL-DISCLOSURE FACTS
Exhibit A is Magistrate Judge Davis’s Financial Disclosure Report (AO Form 10) for

calendar year 2025. Judge Davis electronically signed it on May 14, 2026 and on May 26, 2026.
Ex. A at 1. Part VII, line 6, identifies “FB common stock” with a gross year-end value of $15,001—
$50,000 and dividend income of $1,000 or less. Ex. A at 2. No transaction is reported on that line.
The same report records purchases and sales of other securities during 2025. Ex. A at 3 (Part VU,
lines 37-40).

Exhibit B is Magistrate Judge Davis’s Financial Disclosure Report for calendar year 2024,
dated August 18, 2025. Part VII, line 6, identifies “FB common stock” with value code K
($15,001-$50,000) and income code A ($1,000 or less). Ex. B at 4. No transaction is reported on
that line.

Both reports identify common-stock holdings by trading symbol. Ex. A at 2—3 (Part VII,
lines 4-6, 16-34); Ex. B at 4-6 (Part VII, lines 4-6, 16-18, 20-35). “FB” was the Nasdaq trading
symbol for the Class A common stock of Facebook, Inc. Facebook, Inc. changed its corporate

name to Meta Platforms, Inc. on October 28, 2021. The trading symbol for the same stock changed

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 86 Filed 10/13/26 Page 3 of 9 PagelD# 825

to “META” in June 2022. The Memorandum in Support, Part II.B, identifies the public filings with
the Securities and Exchange Commission that establish those facts.

The reports establish that Judge Davis reported holding “FB common stock” at the close of
2024 and at the close of 2025. Whether that holding continued through the period of Judge Davis’s
participation in this action is an inference from the reports. It is not an established fact. This Motion
asks the Court to determine it.

II. PARTICIPATION IN THE ACTION
Plaintiff filed this action on July 30, 2026, naming Meta as a defendant. ECF No. 1. The

First Amended Complaint names Meta. ECF No. 5. Meta appeared through counsel, moved to
dismiss, and filed its corporate disclosure statement on August 21, 2026. ECF Nos. 21, 22, 24.

The Clerk’s docket assigns Magistrate Judge Davis to this action. On August 25, 2026, the
Clerk set Plaintiff’s motions at ECF Nos. 15 and 26 for hearing before Judge Davis on September
25, 2026. On September 8, 2026, the Clerk set ECF No. 54 for hearing before Judge Davis on the
same date.

Judge Davis entered six orders. ECF No. 62 (Sept. 9, 2026) treated ECF No. 26 as
withdrawn. ECF No. 63 (Sept. 9, 2026) denied ECF No. 41 as moot, terminated the hearing on ECF
No. 15, and required any party using generative artificial intelligence to identify that use and certify
citation review. ECF No. 64 (Sept. 9, 2026) required Plaintiff to file, by September 11, 2026, a
redlined version of the proposed amended complaint showing changes against the original
Complaint, ECF No. 1. ECF No. 65 (Sept. 10, 2026) terminated the hearing on ECF No. 54, set
Meta’s response and Plaintiff’s reply dates, and restated the certification requirement. ECF No. 82
(Sept. 22, 2026) granted ECF No. 78 and restated the certification requirement. ECF No. 84 (Oct.

7, 2026) is described next.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 86 Filed 10/13/26 Page 4 of 9 PagelD# 826

ECF No. 84 denied as premature Plaintiff's motions for leave to serve limited
interrogatories on NCMEC (ECF No. 15) and on Meta (ECF No. 54). ECF No. 84 describes those
motions as “requests for expedited discovery concerning Defendants National Center for Missing
& Exploited Children ((“NCMEC’) and Meta Platforms, Inc., respectively.” ECF No. 84 at 1. ECF
No. 84 also denied Plaintiff’s motion for leave to file a Second Amended and Supplemental
Complaint (ECF No. 59), stating that Plaintiff “has failed” to produce the redline required by ECF
No. 64. ECF No. 84 at 2.

Every order listed above was entered after Meta became a party. ECF No. 84 expressly
addresses discovery directed to Meta.

IV. TIMELINESS

Plaintiff was unaware of the reported financial interest when ECF No. 84 was entered on
October 7, 2026, and at every earlier point in this action, and promptly presented this Motion after
learning of it through the Financial Disclosure Reports database maintained by the Administrative
Office of the United States Courts. Ballentine Decl. §] 2—3. Kolon Indus. Inc. v. E.I. du Pont de
Nemours & Co., 748 F.3d 160, 169-71 (4th Cir. 2014), applies the prompt-presentation
requirement to motions under § 455(b); the judge’s independent obligation under § 455 does not
eliminate that requirement.

V. REQUESTED DETERMINATION

Plaintiff requests that the Court state on the record: (a) whether the asset reported as “FB
common stock” on Exhibits A and B is common stock of Meta Platforms, Inc.; (b) whether that
interest was held on July 30, 2026, and on each date on which ECF Nos. 62, 63, 64, 65, 82, and 84
were entered; (c) the date and manner of any divestiture; (d) whether the interest is held directly or
through a mutual or common investment fund within the meaning of 28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4)(i); and

(e) any other fact the Court considers material to the application of 28 U.S.C. § 455(f).

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 86 Filed 10/13/26 Page 5 of 9 PagelD# 827

Upon determination of those facts, Plaintiff requests a determination whether 28 U.S.C. §
455(b)(4) or § 455(a) requires disqualification. If disqualification is required, Plaintiff requests an
order of disqualification and the ministerial steps necessary to return or transfer the referred matters
through the Court’s assignment procedures.

VI. RELATED PROCEEDINGS
Plaintiff’s Rule 72(a) objections to ECF Nos. 63, 64, and 65 (ECF No. 66), Plaintiff’s

motion to set aside ECF No. 64 (ECF No. 67), and Plaintiff’s motion for leave to file a notice of
subsequent record development (ECF No. 76) are pending before District Judge Alston. On
October 12, 2026, Plaintiff submitted through the Court’s Electronic Document Submission
System a Notice of Waiver of Oral Argument as to ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 76, requesting
determination of those motions on the papers under Local Civil Rule 7(J).

Concurrently with this Motion, Plaintiff submits Rule 72(a) objections to ECF No. 84 anda
separate application to District Judge Alston to withdraw or modify the referral and for targeted
vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84. Those filings seek the retrospective and case-management
remedies. This Motion does not. This Motion asks Judge Davis to determine the statutory
disqualification question and the facts on which it depends. Neither this Motion nor the companion
filings extends the time to object under Rule 72(a) or replaces any pending objection.

Plaintiff reserves review under Rule 72(a) of any order disposing of this Motion.

VII. CONCLUSION AND RELIEF REQUESTED

Plaintiff requests that the Court:
Al.  Disqualify Magistrate Judge Davis under 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4), and alternatively

under 28 U.S.C. § 455(a), upon determination of the facts identified in Part V;

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 86 Filed 10/13/26 Page 6 of 9 PagelD# 828

A2. — State on the record whether the reported interest was held during the challenged
participation, the date and manner of any divestiture, and the facts necessary to determine any
claimed exception under 28 U.S.C. § 455(f);

A3. Determine this Motion before taking any further substantive action in this matter;

A4. — Upon disqualification, return or transfer the referred matters through the Court’s
assignment procedures; and

A5. Determine this Motion on the papers, in a written disposition sufficient to identify
the grounds of decision.

Plaintiff waives oral argument and requests determination on the papers under Local Civil
Rule 7(J) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 78(b). A Notice of Waiver of Oral Argument under

Local Civil Rule 7(E) accompanies this Motion. A proposed order accompanies this Motion.

Date: October 13, 2026 Respectfully submitted,

—rD

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847
Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503
jayballentine@protonmail.com

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 86 Filed 10/13/26 Page 7 of 9 PagelD# 829

CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE

I hereby certify that on October 13, 2026, I submitted the following documents to the Clerk
of Court for filing through the Court’s Electronic Document Submission System (EDSS):

1. Plaintiff’s Motion to Disqualify Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis Under 28 U.S.C. §
