Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 1 of 15 Patje|D# 850

10/13/2026
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Ivan D. Davis

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION TO DISQUALIFY
MAGISTRATE JUDGE IVAN D. DAVIS UNDER 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) AND § 455(a),
AND FOR PRIORITY DETERMINATION

I. INTRODUCTION

Magistrate Judge Davis’s two most recent annual financial disclosure reports list “FB
common stock.” Ex. A at 2 (Part VII, line 6); Ex. B at 4 (Part VII, line 6). Each report assigns the
holding a year-end value of $15,001 to $50,000. Judge Davis signed the 2025 report on May 14,
2026 and May 26, 2026. Ex. A at 1. “FB” was the trading symbol of Facebook, Inc. Facebook, Inc.
is Meta Platforms, Inc. Meta is a defendant in this action.

Plaintiff filed this action on July 30, 2026. Judge Davis has since entered six orders. The
last of them, ECF No. 84, denied discovery directed to Meta and denied leave to amend. Section

455(b)(4) requires a magistrate judge who knows that he has a financial interest in a party to

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 2 of 15 PagelD# 851

disqualify himself. Section 455(d)(4) defines a financial interest as ownership of a legal or
equitable interest “however small.” Section 455(e) bars the parties from waiving that ground.

The reports establish the holding at the end of 2024 and at the end of 2025. They do not
establish the holding in August, September, or October 2026. The present record cannot resolve
that fact. The Court can. This Motion asks that the fact be stated on the record and that the statute be
applied to it.

II. STATEMENT OF FACTS

A. The disclosure reports. Exhibit A is the Financial Disclosure Report (AO Form
10) of “Davis, Ivan,” Magistrate Judge, U.S. District Court, Virginia Eastern, for calendar year
2025. It bears two electronic signatures: May 14, 2026 at 1:34 p.m. and May 26, 2026 at 9:57 a.m.
Ex. A at 1. Each signature follows this certification: “I certify that all information given above
(including information pertaining to my spouse and minor or dependent children, if any) is
accurate, true, and complete to the best of my knowledge and belief.” Id. Part VII, line 6, reads:
“FB common stock,” income “$1,000 or less,” income type “Dividend,” gross value “$15,001 -
$50,000,” value method “Cash/Market.” Ex. A at 2. Line 6 reports no transaction. Lines 37 through
40 report sales and purchases of four other securities on August 21, 2025. Ex. A at 3.

Exhibit B is the Financial Disclosure Report of “Davis, Ivan D.,” U.S. Magistrate Judge,
full-time, for the reporting period January 1, 2024 to December 31, 2024, dated August 18, 2025.
Ex. B at 1. Part VII, line 6, reads: “FB common stock,” income code A, income type “Dividend,”
value code K, value method T. Ex. B at 4. The report’s legend defines code A as “$1,000 or less,”
code K as “$15,001 - $50,000,” and code T as “Cash Market.” Id. Line 6 reports no transaction. The
report’s certification, signed “s/ Ivan D. Davis,” uses the same “accurate, true, and complete to the

best of my knowledge and belief” language. Ex. B at 8.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 3 of 15 PagelD# 852

Both reports identify common-stock holdings by trading symbol. Ex. A at 2—3 (lines 4-6,
16-34); Ex. B at 4-6 (lines 4-6, 16-18, 20-35). Both reports list mutual funds and exchange-traded
funds as separate line items. Ex. A at 2—3 (lines 2, 3, 11, 12, 18, 35); Ex. B at 4—6 (lines 2, 3, 11, 12,
18, 36). Both reports list an IRA as a separate line item. Ex. A at 3 (line 36); Ex. B at 6 (line 37).

B. Facebook, Inc. is Meta Platforms, Inc. The Class A common stock of Facebook,
Inc. traded on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the symbol “FB.” Meta Platforms, Inc., Annual
Report (Form 10-K) for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2021 (filed Feb. 3, 2022) (cover page). On
October 28, 2021, Facebook, Inc. amended its certificate of incorporation to change its name to
Meta Platforms, Inc. Facebook, Inc., Current Report (Form 8-K) (Oct. 28, 2021); Meta Platforms,
Inc., Annual Report (Form 10-K) for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2021 (filed Feb. 3, 2022). In
June 2022, the trading symbol for the same Class A common stock changed from “FB” to
“META.” Meta Platforms, Inc., Annual Report (Form 10-K) for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31,
2022 (filed Feb. 2, 2023) (cover page). Federal courts treat the two names as one company. Mirror
Worlds Techs., LLC v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 122 F.4th 860 (Fed. Cir. 2024) (identifying Meta
Platforms, Inc. as the company formerly known as Facebook, Inc.).

The reports for 2024 and 2025 continue to describe the asset as “FB common stock.” The
description supports an inference that line 6 denotes common stock of Meta Platforms, Inc.
Plaintiff asks the Court to confirm that inference. Mot. Part V(a).

C. Meta’s party status and Judge Davis’s participation. Meta has been a named
defendant since July 30, 2026. ECF Nos. 1, 5. Meta moved to dismiss and filed its corporate
disclosure statement on August 21, 2026. ECF Nos. 21, 22, 24. Magistrate Judge Davis is the
assigned magistrate judge. Hearings on Plaintiff’s motions were set before him on August 25 and

September 8, 2026. He entered ECF Nos. 62, 63, and 64 on September 9, 2026; ECF No. 65 on

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 4 of 15 PagelD# 853

September 10, 2026; ECF No. 82 on September 22, 2026; and ECF No. 84 on October 7, 2026.
ECF No. 84 denied ECF Nos. 15 and 54 as premature, describing them as requests for expedited
discovery concerning NCMEC and “Meta Platforms, Inc., respectively,” and denied ECF No. 59
for noncompliance with ECF No. 64. ECF No. 84 at 1-2. The docket reflects no disclosure of the
reported holding to the parties.

D. Discovery and submission. Plaintiff was unaware of the reported financial interest
when ECF No. 84 was entered and promptly presented this Motion after learning of it. Ballentine
Decl. { 2. Plaintiff retrieved Exhibits A and B from the Financial Disclosure Reports database
maintained by the Administrative Office of the United States Courts. Id. 44] 3—4.

E. Related proceedings. ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 76 are pending before District Judge
Alston. On October 12, 2026, Plaintiff submitted through the Court’s Electronic Document
Submission System a Notice of Waiver of Oral Argument as to ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 76,
requesting determination of those motions on the papers under Local Civil Rule 7(J). Concurrently
with this Motion, Plaintiff submits Rule 72(a) objections to ECF No. 84 and an application to
District Judge Alston concerning the referral and retrospective relief. This Memorandum does not
repeat the arguments in those filings.

Til. ARGUMENT

A. Direct Ownership of Common Stock in a Party Requires Disqualification
Under § 455(b)(4).
1. The statutory elements. Section 455 applies to “[a]ny justice, judge, or magistrate

judge of the United States.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(a). Section 455(b)(4) requires disqualification where
the judge “knows that he, individually or as a fiduciary, or his spouse or minor child residing in his
household, has a financial interest in the subject matter in controversy or in a party to the

proceeding.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4). The elements are a covered officer, a financial interest,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 5 of 15 PagelD# 854

knowledge, and a party. Judge Davis is a covered officer. Meta is a party. ECF Nos. 1, 5, 21, 24.
The remaining elements are the financial interest and knowledge.

2. Common stock is a financial interest regardless of amount. Section 455(d)(4)
defines “financial interest” as “ownership of a legal or equitable interest, however small.” The
Fourth Circuit reads those words as written. “If a judge has an ownership interest in a party or in the
subject matter in controversy, it matters not at all whether the interest is a large or infinitesimally
small amount.” In re Va. Elec. & Power Co., 539 F.2d 357, 368 (4th Cir. 1976). “[I]t is well-
established that the ownership of stock constitutes a ‘financial interest’” under § 455(b)(4). Cent.
Tel. Co. of Va. v. Sprint Commc’ns Co. of Va., Inc., 715 F.3d 501, 515 (4th Cir. 2013) (quoting
Shell Oil Co. v. United States, 672 F.3d 1283, 1289 (Fed. Cir. 2012)). The Fourth Circuit “read[s] §
455(b)(4) to require a judge who is a stockholder in a party to a case to disqualify himself from
participation in the case even when he is not the fact-finder.” Gladhill v. Gen. Motors Corp., 743
F.2d 1049, 1051 (4th Cir. 1984). Gladhill concerned a juror who owned stock in a party. The court
cited § 455(b)(4) as the legislative rule confirming that a stockholder in a party may not sit. Id. The
reported holding here is common stock. The statute makes its amount irrelevant.

3. The fund exception does not appear on the face of the reports. Section 455(d)(4)
(i) provides that “[o]wnership in a mutual or common investment fund that holds securities is not a
‘financial interest’ in such securities unless the judge participates in the management of the fund.”
In Central Telephone, the judge held the shares in an IRA “along with the assets of many others
who hold similar accounts,” and the fund managers made the buy and sell decisions “without input
from the presiding judge.” 715 F.3d at 516. The Fourth Circuit held that the exception applied and
that no financial interest existed. Id. The reports here describe line 6 as “common stock.” They list

the judge’s funds separately. They list the judge’s IRA separately. Ex. A at 2-3; Ex. B at 4-6. On its

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 6 of 15 PagelD# 855

face, line 6 is a direct holding. Whether the stock is held through an arrangement that qualifies
under § 455(d)(4)(i) is a fact within Judge Davis’s knowledge. The Motion asks that it be stated.
Mot. Part V(d).

A, Knowledge. Section 455(b)(4) applies when the judge “knows” of the interest.
Liljeberg v. Health Servs. Acquisition Corp., 486 U.S. 847, 859 (1988). Section 455(c) directs a
judge to “inform himself about his personal and fiduciary financial interests.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(c).
Two facts bear on knowledge. The first is knowledge of the holding. Judge Davis certified on May
14 and May 26, 2026 that the 2025 report was “accurate, true, and complete to the best of my
knowledge and belief.” Ex. A at 1. He certified the 2024 report in the same terms on August 18,
2025. Ex. B at 8. Those certifications support an inference that Judge Davis knew, as of May 26,
2026, that he had reported holding FB common stock at the close of 2025. The second is
knowledge that the issuer is a party. Meta’s name appears in the caption of every filing. ECF No. 84
names “Meta Platforms, Inc.” and rules on discovery directed to Meta. ECF No. 84 at 1. The docket
establishes Meta’s participation. Whether Judge Davis connected the reported holding with the
party is a fact the Motion asks the Court to state. In Central Telephone, the appellant relied on the
judge’s financial disclosure form to establish knowledge. 715 F.3d at 515. The Fourth Circuit did
not reach that question because the fund exception applied. Id. at 516. No fund exception appears
here.

5. Nonwaiver. Section 455(e) bars a judge from accepting from the parties a waiver of
any ground enumerated in subsection (b). “Under § 455(e), the judge may not even accept a waiver
of this disqualification from the parties.” Gladhill, 743 F.2d at 1051; see also Centripetal
Networks, Inc. v. Cisco Sys., Inc., 38 F.4th 1025 (Fed. Cir. 2022) (“Recusal under § 455(a) may be

waived, but recusal under § 455(b) cannot be waived.”). Plaintiff offers no waiver. No party can.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 7 of 15 PagelD# 856

B. Section 455(a) Independently Requires Consideration of Disqualification.

Section 455(a) requires disqualification in any proceeding in which the judge’s
“impartiality might reasonably be questioned.” The test is objective. “The critical question
presented by this statute ‘is not whether the judge is impartial in fact. It is simply whether another,
not knowing whether or not the judge is actually impartial, might reasonably question his
impartiality on the basis of all the circumstances.’” United States v. DeTemple, 162 F.3d 279, 286
(4th Cir. 1998) (quoting Hathcock v. Navistar Int’! Transp. Corp., 53 F.3d 36, 41 (4th Cir. 1995)).
The observer is “a person outside the judicial system,” and “not a person unduly suspicious or
concemed about a trivial risk that a judge may be biased.” Id. at 287. Section 455(a) requires no
knowledge. Congress “intended to require knowledge under subsection (b)(4) and not to require
knowledge under subsection (a).” Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at 859. The provision’s purpose “does not
depend upon whether or not the judge actually knew of facts creating an appearance of impropriety,
so long as the public might reasonably believe that he or she knew.” Id. at 860.

Facts that fall short under § 455(b) remain relevant under § 455(a). “Even where the facts
do not suffice for recusal under § 455(b), however, those same facts may be examined as part of an
inquiry into whether recusal is mandated under § 455(a).” In re Certain Underwriter Defs., 294
F.3d 297, 306 (2d Cir. 2002). The Second Circuit applied that rule to a district judge whose spouse
held stock in a defendant during part of the case. Litovich v. Bank of Am. Corp., 106 F.4th 218 (2d
Cir. 2024) (per curiam). The record there did not show when the judge learned of the holding, and
the court assumed he learned of it only after judgment. The court held that “it is reasonable to
question the partiality of a judge presiding over a case in which his spouse holds an ownership
interest in a party,” and it vacated the judgment. Id. Litovich is persuasive authority. Its reasoning

applies with greater force to a judge’s own reported holding.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 8 of 15 PagelD# 857

Central Telephone reached a different result on different facts. There, the shares came into
the judge’s portfolio through mergers of which he was unaware, were held in an IRA managed by
others, and were disclosed to the parties and sold promptly after the judge learned of them. 715
F.3d at 516-17. None of those facts appears here. The reports list the stock as a direct holding.
Judge Davis certified the holding in two consecutive annual reports, most recently in May 2026.
The docket reflects no disclosure to the parties.

Plaintiff does not contend that any ruling in this action evidences bias. Adverse rulings are
not the basis of this Motion. Section 455(a) “forbids more than actual bias.” DeTemple, 162 F.3d at
286. It asks what an informed outside observer would think of a judge deciding discovery directed
to a company whose stock the judge reported owning five months earlier. That observer would
question it.

C. Section 455(f) Does Not Eliminate the Need to Determine the Relevant Facts.

Section 455(f) relieves a judge of disqualification in defined circumstances. The matter
must have been assigned to the judge. The disqualifying interest must appear or be discovered
“after the matter was assigned to him or her.” Substantial judicial time must have been “devoted to
the matter.” The interest must be a financial interest in a party “other than an interest that could be
substantially affected by the outcome.” And the judge must “divest[] himself or herself of the
interest that provides the grounds for the disqualification.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(f); see Certain
Underwriter, 294 F.3d at 303. Each condition is a question of fact. The present record does not
resolve them.

Substantial judicial time. The Second Circuit measures substantial judicial time by
“examining the time and effort a district court invests in a matter,” not by counting calendar days.
Certain Underwriter, 294 F.3d at 304. The exception is unavailable “where the docket reflects little

time devoted to the matter.” Id. at 304-05 (describing Tramonte v. Chrysler Corp., 136 F.3d 1025,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 9 of 15 PagelD# 858

1031-32 (5th Cir. 1998)). The docket shows six orders by Judge Davis between September 9 and
October 7, 2026. Each is one or two pages. No hearing was held. ECF Nos. 63, 65. No report and
recommendation issued. Whether that participation is “substantial” within § 455(f) is for the Court
to determine on the record.

Appearance or discovery after assignment. Judge Davis signed the 2025 report on May 14
and May 26, 2026. This action was filed on July 30, 2026. The holding was reported before the
assignment existed. The record does not show when, if ever, Judge Davis identified the reported
holding as an interest in a party to this action. Plaintiff does not contend that § 455(f) is unavailable
merely because the stock was acquired or reported before assignment. Plaintiff contends that the
Court must state the timing before § 455(f) can be applied.

Nature of the interest. The reported value is $15,001 to $50,000. Plaintiff does not contend
that the outcome of this action could substantially affect the value of a holding in that range in a
company of Meta’s size. This condition does not by itself foreclose § 455(f).

Divestiture. The Federal Circuit, reviewing a judgment of this District, held that “to ‘divest’
oneself of ‘ownership’ of a legal or equitable interest is possible only if one is ‘deprived or
dispossesse[d]’ of ownership—something that is possible only if the interest is sold or given
away.” Centripetal, 38 F.4th 1025. Placing the stock in a blind trust did not qualify. Id. The court
vacated the rulings entered after the judge learned of the interest and directed reassignment,
observing that “[a]llowing the same judge to reaffirm his own rulings would severely undermine §
455, which is why cases are routinely reassigned upon vacatur of judgment under § 455.” Id. No
divestiture appears in this record. Plaintiff does not assume that one occurred. Plaintiff does not
assume that none occurred. The Motion asks the Court to state whether one occurred and when.

Mot. Part V(c).

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 10 of 15 PagelD#
859

Two further points follow. First, divestiture under § 455(f) does not by itself resolve the
effect of participation before it. “While Section 455(f) allows a judge to divest a newly-discovered
disqualifying interest and continue to preside over a case, that divestiture cannot cure
circumstances in which recusal was required years before and important decisions have been
rendered in the interim.” Litovich, 106 F.4th 218 (quoting Chase Manhattan Bank v. Affiliated FM
Ins. Co., 343 F.3d 120, 131 (2d Cir. 2003)). Whether curative divestiture is available once “a
litigation has advanced to substantive disputes” is “a determination that must be analyzed on a
case-by-case basis.” Id. Second, whether an order entered during a period of disqualification
should stand is a separate question from whether the judge may continue. The considerations for
that question are “the risk of injustice to the parties in the particular case, the risk that the denial of
relief will produce injustice in other cases, and the risk of undermining the public’s confidence in
the judicial process.” Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at 864. That question is presented to the District Judge in
the companion application. It is not presented here.

D. The Motion Was Presented Promptly After Discovery.

“Timeliness is an essential element of a recusal motion.” United States v. Owens, 902 F.2d
1154, 1155 (4th Cir. 1990). A party “must raise the disqualification of the ... [judge] at the earliest
moment after knowledge of the facts.” Id. at 1156 (quoting Satterfield v. Edenton-Chowan Bd. of
Educ., 530 F.2d 567, 574-75 (4th Cir. 1975)). The rule exists “to prevent waste and delay” and to
prevent a party from awaiting an outcome before moving. Id. The Fourth Circuit applies that
requirement to motions under § 455(b) as well as § 455(a), and the judge’s independent obligation
does not excuse a party’s delay. Kolon Indus. Inc. v. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co., 748 F.3d 160,
169-71 (4th Cir. 2014). Plaintiff was unaware of the reported interest when ECF No. 84 was
entered and at every earlier point in this action, and presented this Motion promptly after learning

of it, with no intervening ruling. Ballentine Decl. 2. That presentation satisfies Owens and Kolon.

10

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 11 of 15 PagelD#
860

E. The Court Should Determine the Facts, Apply the Statute, and Transfer the
Referred Matters If Disqualification Is Required.

The Motion asks for five things. First, a statement on the record of the facts identified in
Part V of the Motion: the identity of the issuer, the dates of ownership, any divestiture, the manner
of holding, and any fact bearing on § 455(f). Second, a determination whether § 455(b)(4) or 8
455(a) requires disqualification on those facts. Third, priority determination, so that no further
substantive action is taken before the statutory question is resolved. Fourth, upon disqualification,
return or transfer of the referred matters through the Court’s assignment procedures. Fifth, a
written disposition sufficient to identify the grounds of decision.

The Motion does not ask Judge Davis to vacate any order. Vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84 is
requested from District Judge Alston in the companion application, under the considerations
identified in Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at 864. The Motion does not ask Judge Davis to decide any
contested substantive matter after disqualification. The reassignment practice described in
Centripetal serves the same purpose here: the judge whose participation is questioned does not
revisit his own rulings.

IV. CONCLUSION

Two signed reports identify a holding of FB common stock. FB common stock is Meta
common stock. Meta is a party. Judge Davis has entered six orders in this action, one of which
decided discovery directed to Meta. Whether the holding continued into that period is the fact on
which § 455(b)(4) turns. Section 455(a) requires an objective assessment of the same
circumstances, whether or not knowledge is established. The Court should state the facts on the
record, apply § 455 to them, disqualify if the statute requires it, and transfer the referred matters

through the Court’s assignment procedures.

10/13/2026
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

PLAINTIFE’S RULE 72(a) OBJECTIONS TO ECF NO. 84 AND MOTION TO SET
ASIDE THE AMENDMENT AND DISCOVERY DENIALS AND FOR COORDINATED
DETERMINATION OF THE PENDING OBJECTIONS

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine objects under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A), Federal Rule of
Civil Procedure 72(a), and Local Civil Rule 72 to the Order entered October 7, 2026 (ECF No. 84).
Local Civil Rule 72 treats these objections as a motion under Local Civil Rule 7. Plaintiff files them
in that form. A Memorandum in Support accompanies this Motion under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1)
and states the grounds. Plaintiff incorporates it by reference. No comparison document

accompanies this filing.

I. THE ORDER AND THE TWO DISPOSITIONS CHALLENGED
1. ECF No. 84 was signed by Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis and entered October 7, 2026.

It makes two dispositions.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 89 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 2 of 12 PagelD# 871

2. Discovery. ECF No. 84 denies “as premature” Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to Serve
Three Limited Interrogatories on NCMEC before the Rule 26(f) Conference (ECF No. 15) and
Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to Serve Four Limited Interrogatories on Meta Platforms, Inc. before
the Rule 26(f) Conference (ECF No. 54). ECF No. 84 at 1. The Order states: “At this time, the
Court cannot issue an order concerning Plaintiff’s Motions because discovery has not officially
begun in this case. Pursuant to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, discovery officially begins
when the District Judge issues a Scheduling Order and currently there is no Scheduling Order in
this case.” Id. at 1-2.

3. Amendment. ECF No. 84 denies Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File Second Amended
and Supplemental Complaint Pursuant to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a)(2) and 15(d), and
Request for Expedited Determination on the Papers (ECF No. 59). The Order states: “Plaintiff was
given ample opportunity to comply with the Court’s September 9, 2026 Order [Dkt. No. 64] by
producing a redlined Second Amended Complaint but has failed to do so as of the date of this
Order.” ECF No. 84 at 2.

4. The motions to dismiss filed by NCMEC (ECF No. 10), Meta (ECF No. 21), and Hall
(ECF No. 45) remain pending before the District Judge against the First Amended Complaint (ECF
No. 5).

II. THE OBJECTIONS

5. First objection: the discovery ruling rests on a legal premise the rule does not permit.
Rule 26(d)(1) bars discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference “except ... when authorized by
these rules, by stipulation, or by court order.” ECF Nos. 15 and 54 requested that court order. ECF
No. 84 treated the absence of a Scheduling Order and of ordinary discovery as preventing the Court
from issuing one. That premise removes the exception the motions invoked. The ruling is contrary

to law. It evaluated neither request under any standard for preconference discovery.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 89 Filed 10/13/26 Page 3 of 12 PagelD# 872

6. Second objection: the comparison condition must be reviewed together with its
enforcement. ECF No. 64 found that the Court “does not possess sufficient information to issue an
Order” on ECF No. 59, and required a marked comparison of the proposed pleading against the
original Complaint (ECF No. 1) by September 11, 2026. ECF No. 59 seeks to replace the First
Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5), not ECF No. 1. The complete proposed pleading (ECF No. 59-
1), a supporting declaration (ECF No. 59-2), and a memorandum identifying the material
amendments by category and section (ECF No. 60) were before the Court. Plaintiff’s objections to
the informational premise, the selected baseline, and the compliance period (ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68)
were pending and undecided when ECF No. 84 enforced the condition by denying ECF No. 59.

7. Third objection: the initial failure and the continued nonproduction required assessment
against the relief Plaintiff had requested. Plaintiff first received actual notice of ECF No. 64 at
about 9:09 p.m. on September 11, 2026, the compliance date. ECF No. 68-1 § 3-10. Two days
later Plaintiff sought review of the condition, suspension of its enforcement, relief from the expired
deadline under Rule 6(b)(1)(B), and a prospective compliance procedure keyed to a ruling on the
baseline. ECF No. 67 {{ 6-9. No comparison was produced through October 7, 2026. The requests
for relief were never decided. ECF No. 84 treated elapsed time as resolving them. Plaintiff objects
to the finding of “ample opportunity” to the extent it rests on a misunderstanding of the notice
chronology, and separately objects to the judgment that nonproduction justified denying a
completed Rule 15 submission on this record, without a warning in ECF No. 64 and without
addressing the less severe course already proposed.

8. Fourth objection: the rulings affect substantial rights. The amendment denial excludes
identified allegations and subsequent events from the pleading against which three dismissal

motions will be decided. ECF No. 59-1 §8§ O, P-S; ECF No. 60 at 7-15. The discovery denials

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 89 Filed 10/13/26 Page 4 of 12 PagelD# 873

reject seven closed answers about records Defendants control, on which Defendants’ dismissal
arguments rely, on the erroneous premise stated in the first objection. Fed. R. Civ. P. 61.

9. Fifth objection: statutory disqualification based on subsequently obtained financial
disclosures. Plaintiff separately objects to ECF No. 84 under 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) and § 455(a).
The annual financial disclosure reports of Magistrate Judge Davis submitted as Exhibits A and B to
the concurrent Plaintiff’s Motion to Disqualify Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis Under 28 U.S.C. 8
455(b)(4) and 8 455(a), and for Priority Determination identify “FB common stock,” the reported
Meta interest, at year-end 2025 (Exhibit A) and year-end 2024 (Exhibit B). Plaintiff advances
continued qualifying ownership during the relevant participation as an inference requiring
determination, not as an established fact. Plaintiff was unaware of the reported interest when ECF
No. 84 was entered and presents this ground promptly after learning of it. Declaration of Marvelle
J. Ballentine in Support of Plaintiff’s Motion to Disqualify Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis {{ 2-4.
Plaintiff requests consideration of that Declaration and Exhibits A and B and vacatur of ECF No.
84 upon the necessary statutory and remedial findings, either on these objections or through the
concurrent targeted-vacatur application. This objection supplements, and does not replace, the
preceding four objections.

TI. STANDARD OF REVIEW AND ALTERNATIVE CLASSIFICATION

10. The District Judge “must consider timely objections and modify or set aside any part of
the order that is clearly erroneous or is contrary to law.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a); 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)
(1)(A). The first objection presents legal error. The third presents a factual component and a
discretionary component. The second and fourth concern the exercise of discretion and its effect.
The fifth presents an additional statutory issue that requires consideration of the financial evidence
identified in paragraph 9 and a separate remedial determination under 28 U.S.C. § 455. To the

extent the Court treats any portion of ECF No. 84 as dispositive of a claim or defense, Plaintiff

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 89 Filed 10/13/26 Page 5 of 12 PagelD# 874

alternatively requests treatment of that portion under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(B)-(C) and de novo
determination under Rule 72(b)(3). Plaintiff does not contend that ECF No. 84 terminated any
claim.

IV. TIMELINESS, RELATED MATTERS, AND THE INDEPENDENCE OF THESE
OBJECTIONS
11. ECF No. 84 was entered October 7, 2026. The Court serves orders on Plaintiff by mail.

ECF No. 68-1 { 3. Plaintiff submitted this Motion through the Court’s Electronic Document
Submission System on October 13, 2026. That submission is within fourteen days of the entry date
itself, without the additional time Rule 6(d) provides for mail service. Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(1), 72(a).

12. Plaintiff’s Rule 72(a) Objections to ECF Nos. 63-65 (ECF No. 66), his Motion to Set
Aside ECF No. 64 (ECF No. 67), the Memorandum in Support (ECF No. 68), and his Motion for
Leave to File Notice of Subsequent Record Development (ECF No. 76) remain pending before the
District Judge. ECF Nos. 66 and 67 remain the vehicle challenging ECF Nos. 63, 64, and 65. These
objections challenge ECF No. 84. They do not restart the time to challenge the September orders,
and they withdraw nothing stated in ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68, or 76. On October 12, 2026, Plaintiff
submitted through the Court’s Electronic Document Submission System a Notice of Waiver of
Oral Argument as to ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 76, requesting determination of those motions on the
papers under Local Civil Rule 7(J).

13. Plaintiff concurrently presents a motion under 28 U.S.C. § 455 concerning the
Magistrate Judge’s disqualification and a motion to the District Judge for targeted vacatur and
withdrawal or modification of the referral. Those applications neither replace these objections nor
extend their filing period. The grounds and affirmative relief presented in these objections remain

independently maintained.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 89 Filed 10/13/26 Page 6 of 12 PagelD# 875

14. A separate Notice of Waiver of Oral Argument accompanies this Motion and requests
determination of these objections, this Motion, and the interim application on the papers. That
notice does not waive Plaintiff’s pending request to restore oral argument on ECF Nos. 15 and 54.
ECF No. 67 § 6(d).

V. INTERIM RELIEF REQUESTED
15. The filing of Rule 72(a) objections does not itself suspend the order objected to.

Plaintiff therefore requests an interim order, in the form of the accompanying Proposed Interim
Order, on an expedited basis. Each part is requested separately and may be granted without the
others:

(a) suspending enforcement of the comparison condition in ECF No. 64 pending the
Court’s determination of ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68, and 76 and of these objections;

(b) providing that, while that suspension operates, ECF No. 59 and the proposed pleading at
ECF No. 59-1 shall not be denied, stricken, deemed abandoned, excluded, or otherwise adversely
treated on the ground of nonproduction of the comparison directed by ECF No. 64;

(c) directing that the amendment-related issues presented in ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 76 and in
these objections be determined before, or expressly within, any disposition of ECF Nos. 10, 21, or
45 that would terminate a claim and that depends on the identity of the operative pleading;

(d) directing that the discovery objections presented here be determined before, or
expressly within, any adjudication that relies on the factual premises the interrogatories in ECF
Nos. 15-1 and 54-1 address;

(e) preserving the fifth objection and the concurrent targeted-vacatur application for
coordinated determination, without treating ownership of the reported interest or disqualification
as established; and

(f) expedited consideration of this request.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 89 Filed 10/13/26 Page 7 of 12 PagelD# 876

VI. RELIEF ON THE OBJECTIONS

16. Plaintiff requests an order, in the form of the accompanying Proposed Order:

(a) sustaining these objections and setting aside the rulings in ECF No. 84 denying ECF
Nos. 59, 15, and 54;

(b) granting ECF No. 76 and deeming the Notice at ECF No. 76-1 filed and considered;
determining the comparison-related objections in ECF Nos. 66 and 67 and the supporting issues in
ECF No. 68; and expressly reserving every other issue presented in ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 68 that
the order does not decide;

(c) removing the comparison condition in ECF No. 64 as a prerequisite to consideration of
ECF No. 59, and vacating the September 11, 2026 deadline;

(d) granting ECF No. 59 under Rules 15(a)(2) and 15(d); deeming ECF No. 59-1 filed as the
Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint and the operative pleading; directing separate
docketing; setting the time for responses; and directing how ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45 will be
handled in light of the operative pleading;

(e) alternatively to (d), restoring ECF No. 59 to pending status for determination under
Rules 15(a)(2) and 15(d) on its existing authorized submissions, including ECF Nos. 59, 59-1, 59-
2, 60, 74, 78, 78-1, 83, and, if leave is granted, 76 and 76-1, without an additional comparison;

(f) granting ECF Nos. 15 and 54 and authorizing service of the interrogatories at ECF Nos.
15-1 and 54-1 on the terms stated in those motions, with answers due seven calendar days after
service or within another period the Court directs;

(g) alternatively to (f), restoring ECF Nos. 15 and 54 to pending status for determination
under Rule 26(d)(1), with their authorized briefing preserved and their grounds based on the First

Amended Complaint intact independently of the disposition of ECF No. 59, including ECF Nos.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 89 Filed 10/13/26 Page 8 of 12 PagelD# 877

15, 15-1, 16, 31, 33, 36, 46, 52, 78, and 78-1 as to ECF No. 15, and ECF Nos. 54, 54-1, 55, 73, and
81 as to ECF No. 54; and

(h) determining the fifth objection in coordination with the concurrent Plaintiff’s Motion
for Targeted Vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84, Withdrawal or Modification of the Magistrate-Judge
Referral, and Related Interim Relief, and identifying in the order which issues are decided, which
are reserved, and which are moot because complete relief has been granted on the preceding
objections. The pendency of the financial-conflict applications does not prevent the District Judge
from granting independently warranted relief on the preceding objections, and Plaintiff requests
that relief under paragraphs (a) through (g) without awaiting resolution of the financial-conflict
applications.

VII. POSITIONS PRESERVED
17. Plaintiff maintains that the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) independently states

each of its six claims and survives ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45. Plaintiff maintains his entitlement to
amend and to supplement through ECF No. 59. Plaintiff maintains that ECF Nos. 15 and 54 are
supported on the First Amended Complaint and the existing record, whether or not leave to amend
is granted.

18. Nothing in this Motion revives ECF No. 26, which remains withdrawn (ECF No. 62), or
affects ECF Nos. 43, 70, and 71. Nothing in this Motion withdraws the objections in ECF Nos. 66
and 67 concerning the generative-artificial-intelligence provisions, the termination of oral
argument, or the remote-appearance motion (ECF No. 41), or resolves them by implication. The
hearings previously set on ECF Nos. 15 and 54 were terminated (ECF Nos. 63, 65); Plaintiff’s
request to restore argument on those motions (ECF No. 67 § 6(d)) remains pending.

VII. SUPPORTING RECORD

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 89 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 9 of 12 PagelD# 878

19. Plaintiff submits with this Motion: the Memorandum in Support; a Proposed Interim
Order; a Proposed Order; an Alternative Proposed Order; and a Notice of Waiver of Oral
Argument. The first four objections rely on the existing record, including ECF Nos. 68-1, 59-2, and
31 and the docket. The fifth objection additionally relies on the Declaration of Marvelle J.
Ballentine in Support of Plaintiff’s Motion to Disqualify Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis and its
Exhibit A (Financial Disclosure Report, Calendar Year 2025) and Exhibit B (Financial Disclosure
Report, Calendar Year 2024), submitted with the concurrent disqualification motion and not yet
assigned docket numbers.

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter the Proposed Interim
Order and, upon determination of these objections, the Proposed Order or, in the alternative, the

Alternative Proposed Order, granting the relief stated in paragraphs 15 through 16.

[PROPOSED] ORDER ON PLAINTIFF’S RULE 72(a) OBJECTIONS TO ECF NO. 84
AND ON THE PENDING OBJECTIONS CONCERNING ECF NO. 64

This matter is before the Court on Plaintiff’s Rule 72(a) Objections to ECF No. 84 and
Motion to Set Aside the Amendment and Discovery Denials and for Coordinated Determination of
the Pending Objections (ECF No. __), Plaintiff’s Rule 72(a) Objections to ECF Nos. 63-65 and
Motion to Set Aside ECF No. 64 (ECF Nos. 66, 67) with the Memorandum in Support (ECF No.
68), and Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File Notice of Subsequent Record Development (ECF No.
76). Having considered the objections, the briefing, and the record under Federal Rule of Civil
Procedure 72(a) and 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A), it is hereby

A. Disposition of the Objections
ORDERED that Plaintiff’s objections to ECF No. 84 are SUSTAINED to the extent set

forth in this Order; it is further

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document90-1 Filed 10/13/26 Page 2 of 4 PagelD#
895

ORDERED that the ruling in ECF No. 84 denying Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File
Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint (ECF No. 59) is SET ASIDE, and the rulings in
ECF No. 84 denying Plaintiff’s motions for leave to serve limited interrogatories before the Rule
26(f) conference (ECF Nos. 15 and 54) are SET ASIDE; it is further

ORDERED that ECF No. 76 is GRANTED; the Notice at ECF No. 76-1 is deemed filed
and has been considered in connection with ECF Nos. 66 and 67; it is further

ORDERED that ECF Nos. 66 and 67 are SUSTAINED to the extent set forth in Part B, and
that every other issue presented in ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 68 not expressly decided in this Order
remains pending and preserved;

B. The Comparison Condition and ECF No. 59
ORDERED that the requirement in ECF No. 64 that Plaintiff provide a comparison of the

proposed pleading against the Complaint (ECF No. 1) is VACATED as a condition of
consideration of ECF No. 59, and that the September 11, 2026 deadline in ECF No. 64 is of no
further effect; it is further

ORDERED that ECF No. 59 is GRANTED under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a)
(2) and 15(d); that the proposed pleading at ECF No. 59-1 is deemed filed as of the date of this
Order as Plaintiff’s Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint and is the operative pleading in
this action; and that the Clerk is DIRECTED to docket ECF No. 59-1 separately as the Second
Amended and Supplemental Complaint; it is further

ORDERED that Defendants shall respond to the Second Amended and Supplemental
Complaint within the time provided by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a)(3), unless the Court
directs otherwise under the following paragraph; it is further

ORDERED that, within fourteen (14) days of the entry of this Order, each Defendant shall

file a statement advising whether it elects to stand on its pending motion to dismiss (ECF No. 10,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document90-1 Filed 10/13/26 Page 3 of 4 PagelD#
896

21, or 45, as applicable) and supporting memorandum as directed to the Second Amended and
Supplemental Complaint, or to file a new response under Rule 15(a)(3). Upon receipt of those
statements the Court will direct any further briefing. ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45 remain pending until
so directed;

C. ECE Nos. 15 and 54

ORDERED that Plaintiff’s motions for leave to serve limited interrogatories before the
Rule 26(f) conference (ECF Nos. 15 and 54) are GRANTED under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure
26(d)(1); that Plaintiff may serve on Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children
the three interrogatories set out at ECF No. 15-1, and on Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. the four
interrogatories set out at ECF No. 54-1, on the terms stated in those documents; and that each
responding Defendant shall serve its answers under oath, limited to “Yes,” “No,” or “Unable to
determine after reasonable inquiry,” within seven (7) calendar days after service of the
interrogatories. This authorization is limited to the interrogatories identified; it does not open
general discovery, and no other discovery is authorized by this Order;

D. Preservation and Transition

ORDERED that nothing in this Order revives ECF No. 26, which remains withdrawn (ECF
No. 62), or affects ECF Nos. 43, 70, and 71; it is further

ORDERED that the objections in ECF Nos. 66 and 67 concerning the generative-artificial-
intelligence provisions of ECF Nos. 63 and 65, the termination of oral argument, and the remote-
appearance motion (ECF No. 41) are not resolved by implication and remain pending; Plaintiff’s
request to restore oral argument on ECF Nos. 15 and 54 is DENIED AS MOOT in light of Part C,
without prejudice to the remaining objections; it is further

ORDERED that the Interim Order entered at ECF No.___ expires upon entry of this Order;

it is further

897

E. The Fifth Objection and the Financial-Conflict Applications
ORDERED that the fifth objection presented in Plaintiff’s objections to ECF No. 84, which

rests on 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) and § 455(a) and on the financial disclosure reports submitted as
Exhibits A and B to Plaintiff’s Motion to Disqualify Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis, is not rejected
by implication by the relief granted in Parts A through D, and that Plaintiff’s Motion for Targeted
Vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84, Withdrawal or Modification of the Magistrate-Judge Referral, and
Related Interim Relief (ECF No. ___) remains pending for determination; it is further

Targeted Vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84, Withdrawal or Modification of the Magistrate-Judge
Referral, and Related Interim Relief (ECF No.___), which requests presented in the fifth objection
and in that motion are decided, which are reserved, and which are moot because complete relief has

during the Magistrate Judge’s participation, or disqualification under 28 U.S.C. § 455, as

10/13/2026
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

PLAINTIFE’S RULE 72(a) OBJECTIONS TO ECF NO. 84 AND MOTION TO SET
ASIDE THE AMENDMENT AND DISCOVERY DENIALS AND FOR COORDINATED
DETERMINATION OF THE PENDING OBJECTIONS

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine objects under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A), Federal Rule of
Civil Procedure 72(a), and Local Civil Rule 72 to the Order entered October 7, 2026 (ECF No. 84).
Local Civil Rule 72 treats these objections as a motion under Local Civil Rule 7. Plaintiff files them
in that form. A Memorandum in Support accompanies this Motion under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1)
and states the grounds. Plaintiff incorporates it by reference. No comparison document

accompanies this filing.

I. THE ORDER AND THE TWO DISPOSITIONS CHALLENGED
1. ECF No. 84 was signed by Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis and entered October 7, 2026.

It makes two dispositions.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document90_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 2 of 12 PagelD# 883

2. Discovery. ECF No. 84 denies “as premature” Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to Serve
Three Limited Interrogatories on NCMEC before the Rule 26(f) Conference (ECF No. 15) and
Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to Serve Four Limited Interrogatories on Meta Platforms, Inc. before
the Rule 26(f) Conference (ECF No. 54). ECF No. 84 at 1. The Order states: “At this time, the
Court cannot issue an order concerning Plaintiff’s Motions because discovery has not officially
begun in this case. Pursuant to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, discovery officially begins
when the District Judge issues a Scheduling Order and currently there is no Scheduling Order in
this case.” Id. at 1-2.

3. Amendment. ECF No. 84 denies Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File Second Amended
and Supplemental Complaint Pursuant to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a)(2) and 15(d), and
Request for Expedited Determination on the Papers (ECF No. 59). The Order states: “Plaintiff was
given ample opportunity to comply with the Court’s September 9, 2026 Order [Dkt. No. 64] by
producing a redlined Second Amended Complaint but has failed to do so as of the date of this
Order.” ECF No. 84 at 2.

4. The motions to dismiss filed by NCMEC (ECF No. 10), Meta (ECF No. 21), and Hall
(ECF No. 45) remain pending before the District Judge against the First Amended Complaint (ECF
No. 5).

II. THE OBJECTIONS

5. First objection: the discovery ruling rests on a legal premise the rule does not permit.
Rule 26(d)(1) bars discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference “except ... when authorized by
these rules, by stipulation, or by court order.” ECF Nos. 15 and 54 requested that court order. ECF
No. 84 treated the absence of a Scheduling Order and of ordinary discovery as preventing the Court
from issuing one. That premise removes the exception the motions invoked. The ruling is contrary

to law. It evaluated neither request under any standard for preconference discovery.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document90_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 3 of 12 PagelD# 884

6. Second objection: the comparison condition must be reviewed together with its
enforcement. ECF No. 64 found that the Court “does not possess sufficient information to issue an
Order” on ECF No. 59, and required a marked comparison of the proposed pleading against the
original Complaint (ECF No. 1) by September 11, 2026. ECF No. 59 seeks to replace the First
Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5), not ECF No. 1. The complete proposed pleading (ECF No. 59-
1), a supporting declaration (ECF No. 59-2), and a memorandum identifying the material
amendments by category and section (ECF No. 60) were before the Court. Plaintiff’s objections to
the informational premise, the selected baseline, and the compliance period (ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68)
were pending and undecided when ECF No. 84 enforced the condition by denying ECF No. 59.

7. Third objection: the initial failure and the continued nonproduction required assessment
against the relief Plaintiff had requested. Plaintiff first received actual notice of ECF No. 64 at
about 9:09 p.m. on September 11, 2026, the compliance date. ECF No. 68-1 § 3-10. Two days
later Plaintiff sought review of the condition, suspension of its enforcement, relief from the expired
deadline under Rule 6(b)(1)(B), and a prospective compliance procedure keyed to a ruling on the
baseline. ECF No. 67 {{ 6-9. No comparison was produced through October 7, 2026. The requests
for relief were never decided. ECF No. 84 treated elapsed time as resolving them. Plaintiff objects
to the finding of “ample opportunity” to the extent it rests on a misunderstanding of the notice
chronology, and separately objects to the judgment that nonproduction justified denying a
completed Rule 15 submission on this record, without a warning in ECF No. 64 and without
addressing the less severe course already proposed.

8. Fourth objection: the rulings affect substantial rights. The amendment denial excludes
identified allegations and subsequent events from the pleading against which three dismissal

motions will be decided. ECF No. 59-1 §8§ O, P-S; ECF No. 60 at 7-15. The discovery denials

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document90_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 4 of 12 PagelD# 885

reject seven closed answers about records Defendants control, on which Defendants’ dismissal
arguments rely, on the erroneous premise stated in the first objection. Fed. R. Civ. P. 61.

9. Fifth objection: statutory disqualification based on subsequently obtained financial
disclosures. Plaintiff separately objects to ECF No. 84 under 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) and § 455(a).
The annual financial disclosure reports of Magistrate Judge Davis submitted as Exhibits A and B to
the concurrent Plaintiff’s Motion to Disqualify Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis Under 28 U.S.C. 8
455(b)(4) and 8 455(a), and for Priority Determination identify “FB common stock,” the reported
Meta interest, at year-end 2025 (Exhibit A) and year-end 2024 (Exhibit B). Plaintiff advances
continued qualifying ownership during the relevant participation as an inference requiring
determination, not as an established fact. Plaintiff was unaware of the reported interest when ECF
No. 84 was entered and presents this ground promptly after learning of it. Declaration of Marvelle
J. Ballentine in Support of Plaintiff’s Motion to Disqualify Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis {{ 2-4.
Plaintiff requests consideration of that Declaration and Exhibits A and B and vacatur of ECF No.
84 upon the necessary statutory and remedial findings, either on these objections or through the
concurrent targeted-vacatur application. This objection supplements, and does not replace, the
preceding four objections.

TI. STANDARD OF REVIEW AND ALTERNATIVE CLASSIFICATION

10. The District Judge “must consider timely objections and modify or set aside any part of
the order that is clearly erroneous or is contrary to law.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a); 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)
(1)(A). The first objection presents legal error. The third presents a factual component and a
discretionary component. The second and fourth concern the exercise of discretion and its effect.
The fifth presents an additional statutory issue that requires consideration of the financial evidence
identified in paragraph 9 and a separate remedial determination under 28 U.S.C. § 455. To the

extent the Court treats any portion of ECF No. 84 as dispositive of a claim or defense, Plaintiff

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document90_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 5 of 12 PagelD# 886

alternatively requests treatment of that portion under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(B)-(C) and de novo
determination under Rule 72(b)(3). Plaintiff does not contend that ECF No. 84 terminated any
claim.

IV. TIMELINESS, RELATED MATTERS, AND THE INDEPENDENCE OF THESE
OBJECTIONS
11. ECF No. 84 was entered October 7, 2026. The Court serves orders on Plaintiff by mail.

ECF No. 68-1 { 3. Plaintiff submitted this Motion through the Court’s Electronic Document
Submission System on October 13, 2026. That submission is within fourteen days of the entry date
itself, without the additional time Rule 6(d) provides for mail service. Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(1), 72(a).

12. Plaintiff’s Rule 72(a) Objections to ECF Nos. 63-65 (ECF No. 66), his Motion to Set
Aside ECF No. 64 (ECF No. 67), the Memorandum in Support (ECF No. 68), and his Motion for
Leave to File Notice of Subsequent Record Development (ECF No. 76) remain pending before the
District Judge. ECF Nos. 66 and 67 remain the vehicle challenging ECF Nos. 63, 64, and 65. These
objections challenge ECF No. 84. They do not restart the time to challenge the September orders,
and they withdraw nothing stated in ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68, or 76. On October 12, 2026, Plaintiff
submitted through the Court’s Electronic Document Submission System a Notice of Waiver of
Oral Argument as to ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 76, requesting determination of those motions on the
papers under Local Civil Rule 7(J).

13. Plaintiff concurrently presents a motion under 28 U.S.C. § 455 concerning the
Magistrate Judge’s disqualification and a motion to the District Judge for targeted vacatur and
withdrawal or modification of the referral. Those applications neither replace these objections nor
extend their filing period. The grounds and affirmative relief presented in these objections remain

independently maintained.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document90 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 6 of 12 PagelD# 887

14. A separate Notice of Waiver of Oral Argument accompanies this Motion and requests
determination of these objections, this Motion, and the interim application on the papers. That
notice does not waive Plaintiff’s pending request to restore oral argument on ECF Nos. 15 and 54.
ECF No. 67 § 6(d).

V. INTERIM RELIEF REQUESTED
15. The filing of Rule 72(a) objections does not itself suspend the order objected to.

Plaintiff therefore requests an interim order, in the form of the accompanying Proposed Interim
Order, on an expedited basis. Each part is requested separately and may be granted without the
others:

(a) suspending enforcement of the comparison condition in ECF No. 64 pending the
Court’s determination of ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68, and 76 and of these objections;

(b) providing that, while that suspension operates, ECF No. 59 and the proposed pleading at
ECF No. 59-1 shall not be denied, stricken, deemed abandoned, excluded, or otherwise adversely
treated on the ground of nonproduction of the comparison directed by ECF No. 64;

(c) directing that the amendment-related issues presented in ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 76 and in
these objections be determined before, or expressly within, any disposition of ECF Nos. 10, 21, or
45 that would terminate a claim and that depends on the identity of the operative pleading;

(d) directing that the discovery objections presented here be determined before, or
expressly within, any adjudication that relies on the factual premises the interrogatories in ECF
Nos. 15-1 and 54-1 address;

(e) preserving the fifth objection and the concurrent targeted-vacatur application for
coordinated determination, without treating ownership of the reported interest or disqualification
as established; and

(f) expedited consideration of this request.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document90_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 7 of 12 PagelD# 888

VI. RELIEF ON THE OBJECTIONS

16. Plaintiff requests an order, in the form of the accompanying Proposed Order:

(a) sustaining these objections and setting aside the rulings in ECF No. 84 denying ECF
Nos. 59, 15, and 54;

(b) granting ECF No. 76 and deeming the Notice at ECF No. 76-1 filed and considered;
determining the comparison-related objections in ECF Nos. 66 and 67 and the supporting issues in
ECF No. 68; and expressly reserving every other issue presented in ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 68 that
the order does not decide;

(c) removing the comparison condition in ECF No. 64 as a prerequisite to consideration of
ECF No. 59, and vacating the September 11, 2026 deadline;

(d) granting ECF No. 59 under Rules 15(a)(2) and 15(d); deeming ECF No. 59-1 filed as the
Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint and the operative pleading; directing separate
docketing; setting the time for responses; and directing how ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45 will be
handled in light of the operative pleading;

(e) alternatively to (d), restoring ECF No. 59 to pending status for determination under
Rules 15(a)(2) and 15(d) on its existing authorized submissions, including ECF Nos. 59, 59-1, 59-
2, 60, 74, 78, 78-1, 83, and, if leave is granted, 76 and 76-1, without an additional comparison;

(f) granting ECF Nos. 15 and 54 and authorizing service of the interrogatories at ECF Nos.
15-1 and 54-1 on the terms stated in those motions, with answers due seven calendar days after
service or within another period the Court directs;

(g) alternatively to (f), restoring ECF Nos. 15 and 54 to pending status for determination
under Rule 26(d)(1), with their authorized briefing preserved and their grounds based on the First

Amended Complaint intact independently of the disposition of ECF No. 59, including ECF Nos.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document90 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 8 of 12 PagelD# 889

15, 15-1, 16, 31, 33, 36, 46, 52, 78, and 78-1 as to ECF No. 15, and ECF Nos. 54, 54-1, 55, 73, and
81 as to ECF No. 54; and

(h) determining the fifth objection in coordination with the concurrent Plaintiff’s Motion
for Targeted Vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84, Withdrawal or Modification of the Magistrate-Judge
Referral, and Related Interim Relief, and identifying in the order which issues are decided, which
are reserved, and which are moot because complete relief has been granted on the preceding
objections. The pendency of the financial-conflict applications does not prevent the District Judge
from granting independently warranted relief on the preceding objections, and Plaintiff requests
that relief under paragraphs (a) through (g) without awaiting resolution of the financial-conflict
applications.

VII. POSITIONS PRESERVED
17. Plaintiff maintains that the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) independently states

each of its six claims and survives ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45. Plaintiff maintains his entitlement to
amend and to supplement through ECF No. 59. Plaintiff maintains that ECF Nos. 15 and 54 are
supported on the First Amended Complaint and the existing record, whether or not leave to amend
is granted.

18. Nothing in this Motion revives ECF No. 26, which remains withdrawn (ECF No. 62), or
affects ECF Nos. 43, 70, and 71. Nothing in this Motion withdraws the objections in ECF Nos. 66
and 67 concerning the generative-artificial-intelligence provisions, the termination of oral
argument, or the remote-appearance motion (ECF No. 41), or resolves them by implication. The
hearings previously set on ECF Nos. 15 and 54 were terminated (ECF Nos. 63, 65); Plaintiff’s
request to restore argument on those motions (ECF No. 67 § 6(d)) remains pending.

VII. SUPPORTING RECORD

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document90_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 9 of 12 PagelD# 890

19. Plaintiff submits with this Motion: the Memorandum in Support; a Proposed Interim
Order; a Proposed Order; an Alternative Proposed Order; and a Notice of Waiver of Oral
Argument. The first four objections rely on the existing record, including ECF Nos. 68-1, 59-2, and
31 and the docket. The fifth objection additionally relies on the Declaration of Marvelle J.
