UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a)(2), 15(d), 20(a)(2), and 21 for leave to file the Second Amended Complaint attached as Exhibit A. Under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1), a Memorandum in Support accompanies this Motion and states the grounds. Plaintiff incorporates it by reference. A Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine and a Proposed Order also accompany this Motion.

I.	THE SUBMISSION

1.	Exhibit A is the complete proposed Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”). It is one integrated pleading. It incorporates no prior pleading by reference.

2.	Exhibit B is a comparison of Exhibit A against the Complaint (ECF No. 1). It marks each addition and deletion. It is the comparison described in the Court’s September 9, 2026 Order (ECF No. 64).

3.	Exhibit C is a comparison of Exhibit A against the operative First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5). It marks each addition and deletion made to the operative pleading.

4.	Plaintiff submits a complete proposed Second Amended Complaint, together with comparisons against both the original Complaint (ECF No. 1) and the operative First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5), to facilitate the Court’s review of the proposed amendments.

II.	THE PRIOR MOTION AND ITS DISPOSITION

5.	On September 8, 2026, Plaintiff moved for leave to file a second amended and supplemental complaint (ECF No. 59). On September 9, 2026, the Court ordered Plaintiff to provide a redlined version of the proposed pleading showing the changes made to the Complaint (ECF No. 1), no later than September 11, 2026 (ECF No. 64).

6.	On October 7, 2026, the Court denied ECF No. 59. The Order stated one ground: “Plaintiff was given ample opportunity to comply with the Court’s September 9, 2026 Order [Dkt. No. 64] by producing a redlined Second Amended Complaint but has failed to do so as of the date of this Order.” ECF No. 84 at 2. The Order made no finding of futility, prejudice, bad faith, or undue delay. It did not address the merits of any claim or any argument raised in the pending motions to dismiss.

7.	Defendants Hall and the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) requested, in opposing ECF No. 59, “the opportunity to supplement or amend this Opposition, if and when Plaintiff submits the redline version of the proposed Second Amended Complaint.” ECF No. 74 at 4. Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) has stated that “nothing in Magistrate Judge Davis’s order expressly precludes Plaintiff from renewing his request to amend by curing his failure to comply with the Court’s order requiring Plaintiff submit a redlined version of the proposed amended complaint.” ECF No. 101 at 6.

8.	This Motion supplies the comparison. It presents the request for leave anew, on the complete record.

III.	THE PROPOSED PLEADING

9.	The First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) is the operative pleading. The SAC replaces it with one integrated pleading.

10.	The SAC adds one defendant: Panayiota Souras, also known as Yiota G. Souras, NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, sued individually. Ex. A ¶¶ 14, 21, 91–104. The First Amended Complaint identified among the John/Jane Doe Defendants “the NCMEC personnel who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters.” ECF No. 5 ¶ 25. The SAC alleges, on information and belief, that Souras participated in that approval or authorization. The SAC names Souras in Counts I, II, IV, V, and VI. Ex. A, Counts I, II, IV, V, VI.

11.	The SAC adds no cause of action. It retains the six-count structure of the First Amended Complaint. Count I and Count II plead defamation per se and defamation by implication against Hall, Souras, and NCMEC, one count for each of the two April 22, 2026 letters. Count III pleads intentional infliction of emotional distress against Hall and NCMEC. Count IV pleads conspiracy under the first clause of 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) against all Defendants. Count V pleads Virginia common-law conspiracy against all Defendants. Count VI pleads insulting words under Va. Code § 8.01-45 against Hall, Souras, and NCMEC. Ex. A, Counts I–VI.

12.	The SAC pleads additional facts in four categories. First, facts concerning Souras’s responsibilities and her alleged participation in the review, approval, and authorization of the April 22, 2026 letters. Ex. A § J. Second, facts concerning Plaintiff’s legal name and Plaintiff’s Meta accounts, and, on information and belief, the contents of the two CyberTipline reports the letters reference. Ex. A § T. Third, facts concerning the letters’ wording, omitted limitations, and the meaning a reasonable reader would take from them. Ex. A §§ K, L. Fourth, events occurring after the First Amended Complaint was filed: NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum, the August 13, 2026 correspondence with counsel for NCMEC and Hall, Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California, and Hall’s September 2, 2026 filings. Ex. A § P.

13.	The proposed Second Amended Complaint retains federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(1), supplemental jurisdiction under § 1367(a), and restores § 1332(a)(1) as an alternative basis for original jurisdiction over the state-law claims, as supported by the citizenship and amount-in-controversy allegations. Ex. A ¶¶ 9–11.

14.	The SAC combines amendment under Rule 15(a)(2) with supplementation under Rule 15(d) in one pleading. The amended matter and the supplemental matter concern the same two April 22, 2026 letters, the same six claims, and the same course of conduct.

IV.	GROUNDS

15.	Rule 15(a)(2) provides that the Court “should freely give leave when justice so requires.” Rule 15(d) permits a supplemental pleading “setting out any transaction, occurrence, or event that happened after the date of the pleading to be supplemented.” Rule 20(a)(2) permits joinder of a defendant against whom a right to relief is asserted “with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences” where “any question of law or fact common to all defendants will arise in the action.” Rule 21 provides that the Court “may at any time, on just terms, add or drop a party.”

16.	No Defendant has answered. No scheduling order has issued under Rule 16(b). Discovery has not begun. ECF No. 108 at 2. Rule 15(a)(2) alone supplies the standard for amendment.

17.	The claims against Souras arise from the same two letters as every claim in the First Amended Complaint. The questions whether the letters were issued before formal service, what the letters conveyed, whether the imputation was false, and who within NCMEC approved the letters are common to Souras, Hall, and NCMEC.

18.	The amendment prejudices no Defendant. It adds no theory of recovery. It is offered before any answer, before any scheduling order, and before any discovery. Defendants have briefed the subjects the SAC addresses. ECF Nos. 11, 22, 39, 45.

19.	The amendment is not futile. The SAC pleads facts that, accepted as true, state each of the six existing claims, including the claims against Souras. The Memorandum in Support addresses each dismissal theory Defendants have asserted.

20.	The post-filing events in Section P are transactions, occurrences, and events that happened after August 6, 2026. They concern the same letters, the same Defendants, and the same claims. Rule 15(d) permits their inclusion in the operative pleading.

V.	RELATIONSHIP TO PENDING PAPERS

21.	Plaintiff’s pending objections and applications concerning ECF Nos. 64 and 84 remain submitted in their respective proceedings. Granting this Motion would provide the immediate relief of permitting the proposed superseding pleading. Plaintiff requests no determination through this Motion concerning the continued justiciability or disposition of the remaining objections or retrospective-relief requests, which remain subject to the effect of any relief actually granted.

22.	The pending motions to dismiss directed to the First Amended Complaint (ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45) are procedural context. This Motion requests no disposition of those motions.

VI.	RELIEF REQUESTED

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter an order: (a) granting Plaintiff leave under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a)(2), 15(d), 20(a)(2), and 21 to file the Second Amended Complaint attached as Exhibit A, deeming Exhibit A filed as of the date of the order, and deeming it the operative pleading in this action; (b) directing the Clerk, to the extent administratively necessary, to docket the Second Amended Complaint separately as the operative complaint; (c) directing the Clerk to issue a summons for Defendant Panayiota Souras under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(b) upon Plaintiff’s presentation of a completed summons form; (d) providing that Defendants Hall, NCMEC, and Meta shall respond to the Second Amended Complaint within the time prescribed by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a)(3) or such other time as the Court directs, and that Defendant Souras shall respond within the time prescribed by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(a) following service; and (e) granting such further relief as the Court deems just.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine submits this Memorandum in Support of his Motion for Leave to File Second Amended Complaint. The proposed pleading is Exhibit A to the Motion. Exhibit B compares Exhibit A against the Complaint (ECF No. 1). Exhibit C compares Exhibit A against the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5). The Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine (“Ballentine Decl.”) accompanies the Motion.

I.	INTRODUCTION

The Court denied Plaintiff’s prior motion for leave (ECF No. 59) for one stated reason: the absence of a redlined comparison. ECF No. 84 at 2. The Order did not find the proposed amendment futile. It did not find prejudice, bad faith, or undue delay. It did not reach the merits of any claim. Meta has said as much: the Court’s orders did not “address the merits of any of Plaintiff’s claims or the arguments raised in Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss,” and nothing in ECF No. 84 “expressly precludes Plaintiff from renewing his request to amend by curing” the omission. ECF No. 101 at 6. NCMEC asked for the chance to respond once a redline was filed. ECF No. 74 at 4. This Motion supplies two comparisons, one against ECF No. 1 and one against ECF No. 5, and presents the request for leave on the complete record.

The proposed Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”) does four things. It names NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, Panayiota Souras, and alleges, on information and belief, that she participated in the approval or authorization described in the First Amended Complaint (“FAC”), which identified among the Doe Defendants “the NCMEC personnel who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters.” ECF No. 5 ¶ 25. It pleads additional facts bearing on falsity, defamatory meaning, and the Defendants’ knowledge. It incorporates events that occurred after August 6, 2026. It keeps the same six counts and the same categories of relief. Leave should be granted under Rules 15(a)(2), 15(d), 20(a)(2), and 21.

II.	BACKGROUND

A.	The Pleadings and the Pending Motions to Dismiss

Plaintiff filed the Complaint on July 30, 2026 (ECF No. 1) and the FAC, as of right, on August 6, 2026 (ECF No. 5). NCMEC moved to dismiss on August 12, 2026 (ECF Nos. 10, 11). Meta moved to dismiss on August 21, 2026 (ECF Nos. 21, 22) and replied on August 31, 2026 (ECF No. 39). Hall moved to dismiss on September 2, 2026, adopting and joining NCMEC’s motion and memorandum (ECF No. 45). No Defendant has answered. No scheduling order has issued. On October 29, 2026, the Court stated that “the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2.

B.	ECF Nos. 59, 64, and 84

On September 8, 2026, Plaintiff moved for leave to file a second amended and supplemental complaint, attaching the complete proposed pleading as Exhibit A (ECF Nos. 59, 59-1, 60). On September 9, 2026, the Court found that it “does not possess sufficient information to issue an Order on this matter” and directed Plaintiff to provide, by September 11, 2026, a redlined version that “must clearly indicate the changes, deletions, and additions that were made to Plaintiff’s Complaint [Dkt. No. 1].” ECF No. 64. NCMEC and Hall opposed ECF No. 59 on September 18, 2026 (ECF No. 74). Meta opposed on September 22, 2026 (ECF No. 83). On October 7, 2026, the Court denied ECF No. 59 on the ground that Plaintiff “was given ample opportunity to comply with the Court’s September 9, 2026 Order [Dkt. No. 64] by producing a redlined Second Amended Complaint but has failed to do so as of the date of this Order.” ECF No. 84 at 2. Plaintiff’s Rule 72(a) objections to ECF Nos. 64 and 84 and related applications remain pending (ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68, 89, 90, 91, 93, 94).

C.	The Proposed Pleading

The SAC is one integrated pleading of 319 numbered paragraphs. It contains a Preliminary Statement, Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, Scope of Allegations, Facts in Sections A through T, six Counts, a Prayer for Relief, and a Demand for Jury Trial. Ex. A.

The SAC adds Souras as a defendant. It alleges that she served as NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer at its Alexandria headquarters; that she was responsible for NCMEC’s legal affairs, including litigation and compliance; that she practiced at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP before joining NCMEC in 2006; that Orrick represented Meta in the two underlying federal actions and received Plaintiff’s April 9, 2026 materials on Meta’s behalf; and that she has performed related functions in prior CyberTipline litigation. Ex. A ¶¶ 21, 91–96. It alleges, on information and belief, that Souras participated in the handling of the April 9, 2026 request, approved the wording of the April 22, 2026 letters, and authorized or directed Hall to issue them before formal service. Ex. A ¶¶ 99–101. It identifies the records, within NCMEC’s control, that would confirm or refute them. Ex. A ¶ 104. It pleads the mental states with which she acted and the purpose her participation served. Ex. A ¶ 102.

The SAC adds facts concerning Plaintiff’s legal name and his Meta accounts, and, on information and belief, the contents of the two CyberTipline reports the letters reference. Ex. A § T; Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 3–11. It adds facts concerning the letters’ content defects and the meaning a reasonable reader would take from them. Ex. A §§ K, L. It incorporates events after August 6, 2026: NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum, the August 13, 2026 correspondence with counsel for NCMEC and Hall, Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California, and Hall’s September 2, 2026 filings. Ex. A §§ P, S.

The proposed Second Amended Complaint retains federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(1), supplemental jurisdiction under § 1367(a), and restores § 1332(a)(1) as an alternative basis for original jurisdiction over the state-law claims, as supported by the citizenship and amount-in-controversy allegations. Ex. A ¶¶ 9–11.

III.	GOVERNING STANDARDS

A.	Amendment

Rule 15(a)(2) provides that the Court “should freely give leave when justice so requires.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2). Absent “undue delay, bad faith or dilatory motive on the part of the movant, repeated failure to cure deficiencies by amendments previously allowed, undue prejudice to the opposing party by virtue of allowance of the amendment, futility of amendment, etc.,” leave “should, as the rules require, be ‘freely given.’” Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 (1962). The Fourth Circuit reads Rule 15(a) “to provide that ‘leave to amend a pleading should be denied only when the amendment would be prejudicial to the opposing party, there has been bad faith on the part of the moving party, or the amendment would have been futile.’” Laber v. Harvey, 438 F.3d 404, 426 (4th Cir. 2006) (en banc) (quoting Johnson v. Oroweat Foods Co., 785 F.2d 503, 509 (4th Cir. 1986)). “Delay alone, however, is an insufficient reason to deny the plaintiff’s motion to amend.” Id. at 427. “Rather, the delay must be accompanied by prejudice, bad faith, or futility.” Edwards v. City of Goldsboro, 178 F.3d 231, 242 (4th Cir. 1999).

B.	Supplementation

Rule 15(d) permits the Court, “[o]n motion and reasonable notice,” to allow a party, “on just terms,” to serve “a supplemental pleading setting out any transaction, occurrence, or event that happened after the date of the pleading to be supplemented.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(d). “The court may permit supplementation even though the original pleading is defective in stating a claim or defense.” Id. The standards governing amendment and supplementation “are nearly identical. In either situation, leave should be freely granted, and should be denied only where ‘good reason exists . . . , such as prejudice to the defendants.’” Franks v. Ross, 313 F.3d 184, 198 n.15 (4th Cir. 2002) (citation omitted).

C.	Joinder of an Additional Defendant

Rule 20(a)(2) permits persons to be joined as defendants if “any right to relief is asserted against them jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences” and “any question of law or fact common to all defendants will arise in the action.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 20(a)(2). Rule 21 provides that “[o]n motion or on its own, the court may at any time, on just terms, add or drop a party.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 21. Rule 15(a) governs an amendment that adds a party. Galustian v. Peter, 591 F.3d 724, 730 (4th Cir. 2010) (“While some courts have concluded that Rule 15(a) does not apply to amendments seeking to add parties, . . . most courts, including this one, have concluded otherwise.”). A court deciding such a motion “must consider both the general principles of amendment provided by Rule 15(a) and also the more specific joinder provisions of Rule 20(a).” Hinson v. Norwest Fin. S.C., Inc., 239 F.3d 611, 618 (4th Cir. 2001).

D.	Futility

“Futility is apparent if the proposed amended complaint fails to state a claim under the applicable rules and accompanying standards.” Katyle v. Penn Nat’l Gaming, Inc., 637 F.3d 462, 471 (4th Cir. 2011). The applicable standard is Rule 12(b)(6). A complaint satisfies it when it pleads “sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)). The Court accepts the well-pleaded facts as true and draws reasonable inferences in the plaintiff’s favor. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co. v. Kolon Indus., Inc., 637 F.3d 435, 440 (4th Cir. 2011). The Court does not adopt a defendant’s characterization of a defendant-authored document as established fact at the pleading stage. Goines v. Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd., 822 F.3d 159, 167–69 (4th Cir. 2016).

IV.	ARGUMENT

A.	The Only Stated Ground for Denying ECF No. 59 Is Eliminated.

ECF No. 64 required a comparison against the Complaint (ECF No. 1). Exhibit B is that comparison. Exhibit C compares the SAC against the operative FAC (ECF No. 5), so that the Court and the Defendants can see exactly what the Motion proposes to change in the pleading now in effect. Exhibit A is the clean copy. Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 14–16.

That submission tracks the form this Court has prescribed for a renewed motion for leave. In Vogel v. RMAC Trust Series 2016-CTT, No. 1:24-cv-2182 (RDA/LRV) (E.D. Va. Apr. 11, 2025), the Court denied a motion for leave without prejudice and stated that if the plaintiffs wished to seek leave again, they “should be allowed to file a renewed motion to amend their Complaint, together with (1) a redlined copy of the proposed amended Complaint against the original Complaint, and (2) a clean copy of the proposed amended Complaint,” with a motion that “set[s] forth sufficient information for the Court to assess whether the Rule 15 standard is met.” Meta cited that order in opposing Plaintiff’s objections. ECF No. 101 at 4–5. This Motion follows it.

ECF No. 84 reached nothing else. It made no finding under Foman or Laber. Meta has told the Court that neither ECF No. 64 nor ECF No. 84 “dismissed any of Plaintiff’s claims nor did they address the merits of any of Plaintiff’s claims or the arguments raised in Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss,” and that “nothing in Magistrate Judge Davis’s order expressly precludes Plaintiff from renewing his request to amend by curing his failure to comply with the Court’s order requiring Plaintiff submit a redlined version of the proposed amended complaint.” ECF No. 101 at 6. NCMEC “request[ed] the opportunity to supplement or amend this Opposition, if and when Plaintiff submits the redline version of the proposed Second Amended Complaint.” ECF No. 74 at 4. The comparison is now before the Court and the Defendants. The Rule 15 question is presented on its merits for the first time.

B.	Rule 15(a)(2) Supplies the Governing Standard.

No scheduling order has issued under Rule 16(b). ECF No. 84 at 1–2; ECF No. 108 at 1–2. The good-cause requirement of Rule 16(b)(4) does not apply. Rule 15(a)(2) alone governs the amendment, and Rule 15(d) governs the supplemental matter under a standard that is “nearly identical.” Franks, 313 F.3d at 198 n.15.

C.	Joinder of Souras Satisfies Rules 20(a)(2) and 21.

Every claim against Souras arises from the same transaction as every claim in the FAC: the preparation, review, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of the two April 22, 2026 letters. Ex. A ¶¶ 10, 21, 91–104, 154, 199. Counts I, II, V, and VI assert rights to relief against Souras jointly and severally with Hall and NCMEC. Count IV asserts a right to relief against her jointly and severally with all Defendants. Ex. A, Prayer for Relief ¶¶ A, C, D, E. The questions common to Souras and the existing Defendants include whether the letters issued before formal service of any subpoena, what meaning a reasonable reader would take from the letters, whether the imputation was false, who within NCMEC’s Office of Legal Counsel reviewed and approved the letters, and whether the issuance fell within the responsibilities and functions described in 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(a). Ex. A §§ I, J, K, L, T. Rule 20(a)(2) is satisfied.

The FAC named among the Doe Defendants “the NCMEC personnel who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters,” stated that their identities “are maintained within the records of . . . NCMEC,” and stated that Plaintiff “will seek leave to amend to identify the Doe Defendants when their identities are ascertained.” ECF No. 5 ¶ 25. As Plaintiff states in his Declaration, the SAC alleges, on information and belief, that Souras participated in the approval or authorization described in ECF No. 5 ¶ 25, and Plaintiff discovered her connection to Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP this past weekend during deeper research. Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 12–13. The SAC names her on that allegation. It does so before any answer, before any scheduling order, and before any discovery. Joinder “on just terms” under Rule 21 requires nothing more.

Subject-matter jurisdiction over the claims against Souras is secure. Count IV, asserted against her, arises under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2). 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1343(a)(1). The state-law claims against her form part of the same case or controversy, and 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) extends supplemental jurisdiction to “claims that involve the joinder or intervention of additional parties.” Ex. A ¶ 10; see Hinson, 239 F.3d at 618.

D.	The Amendment Prejudices No Defendant.

“Whether an amendment is prejudicial will often be determined by the nature of the amendment and its timing.” Laber, 438 F.3d at 427. A prejudicial amendment is one that “raises a new legal theory that would require the gathering and analysis of facts not already considered by the [defendant, and] is offered shortly before or during trial.” Id. (alteration in original) (citation omitted). An amendment “is not prejudicial, by contrast, if it merely adds an additional theory of recovery to the facts already pled and is offered before any discovery has occurred.” Id.

The SAC does less than the amendment Laber describes as non-prejudicial. It adds no theory of recovery. It keeps the same six counts, the same two letters, and the same categories of relief. It is offered before any answer and before any discovery. ECF No. 108 at 2. No discovery has been taken that would have to be reopened. No trial date exists.

The Defendants have already briefed the subjects the SAC addresses: truth and substantial truth, the referent of the letters, privilege, 18 U.S.C. § 2258D, and the sufficiency of the conspiracy allegations. ECF Nos. 11, 22, 39, 45, 74, 83. The contents of the two CyberTipline reports, the internal routing of the April 9, 2026 request, and the approval records for the April 22, 2026 letters are within NCMEC’s records and, to the extent Meta submitted either report, Meta’s records. Ex. A ¶¶ 104, 152, 232. The August 2026 and September 2026 filings pleaded in Section P are Defendants’ own statements. “Because defendant was from the outset made fully aware of the events giving rise to the action, an allowance of the amendment could not in any way prejudice the preparation of the defendant’s case.” Davis v. Piper Aircraft Corp., 615 F.2d 606, 613 (4th Cir. 1980).

Joinder of Souras adds no prejudice to the existing Defendants. NCMEC has been a party since July 31, 2026. ECF No. 3. Souras is alleged to have acted as NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, within NCMEC’s Office of Legal Counsel, on the same letters NCMEC has defended since June 2026. Ex. A ¶¶ 19, 21, 98–101, 157. NCMEC is already sued for her conduct within the scope of her employment. Ex. A ¶ 19. Naming her individually requires no Defendant to gather facts it has not already considered.

NCMEC and Meta argue that the SAC would be a “fifth version of a complaint as to this dispute” and that further amendment would require “a third motion to dismiss.” ECF No. 74 at 1 n.1, 6; ECF No. 83 at 1–2. The Foman factor those arguments invoke is “repeated failure to cure deficiencies by amendments previously allowed.” 371 U.S. at 182. No amendment in this action has been allowed by leave. The FAC was filed as of right under Rule 15(a)(1). ECF No. 5. ECF No. 26 was withdrawn before decision. ECF No. 62. ECF No. 59 was denied on the comparison ground alone. ECF No. 84 at 2. No court has found deficient any pleading Plaintiff has filed concerning the April 22, 2026 letters. The complaint in the 1341 Action was voluntarily dismissed under Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) before any ruling. Ex. A ¶ 174. A defendant’s obligation to respond to an amended pleading under Rule 15(a)(3) is the ordinary consequence of amendment, not the prejudice Laber describes. The motions to dismiss now pending address the same letters, the same claims, and the same defenses the SAC addresses. ECF Nos. 11, 22, 45.

E.	There Is No Bad Faith or Dilatory Motive.

The record reflects the following. The Court denied ECF No. 59 on October 7, 2026. ECF No. 84. Plaintiff files this Motion on November 1, 2026, with the comparison ECF No. 64 described and a second comparison against the operative pleading. The SAC names a defendant alleged, on information and belief, to have participated in the approval or authorization the FAC described in August 2026. ECF No. 5 ¶ 25. It adds no claim. No Defendant has answered. No discovery has begun. Those facts reflect no bad faith and no dilatory motive.

F.	The Amendment Is Not Futile.

Futility turns on whether the SAC states a claim under Rule 12(b)(6). Katyle, 637 F.3d at 471. The Court accepts the well-pleaded facts as true. Kolon, 637 F.3d at 440. The Court need not resolve the pending Rule 12 arguments to find that the SAC is not futile. It need only find that the SAC pleads facts that, accepted as true, state the six claims notwithstanding the defenses asserted.

1.	The claims against Hall, NCMEC, and Meta.

The SAC pleads facts addressed to each dismissal theory the Defendants have asserted. ECF Nos. 11, 22, 39, 45.

First, the SAC distinguishes an advance notice of intended subpoenas from formally served compulsory process. The April 9, 2026 transmission was captioned “Advance Notice of Intended Subpoenas — Two Separate Matters,” enclosed signed subpoenas, and stated that formal service would occur after the notice period had run. Neither subpoena was served. No return, proof of service, or court order existed. Plaintiff neither waived service nor requested an early response. Ex. A §§ G, I (¶¶ 54–56, 72–75).

Second, the SAC pleads the voluntary and private issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters. The letters were addressed to Plaintiff alone, were not copied to any court or counsel, and were not filed in either action. They were not CyberTipline reports or referrals and were not undertaken as part of any effort to identify a child victim. Ex. A ¶¶ 79–80. The SAC pleads that the conduct was intentional, was undertaken with actual malice and reckless disregard of a substantial risk of injury without legal justification, and served the litigation-directed purpose alleged in Section Q. Ex. A ¶ 80.

Third, the SAC pleads source-level falsity. Plaintiff’s legal name is Marvelle J. Ballentine. Before April 22, 2026, he never used that name to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any Meta account. The Facebook account associated with the July 4, 2022 enforcement event was maintained under the name “Jay Ballentine.” On information and belief, neither report referenced in the letters, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise identified Plaintiff as “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” and neither concerned Plaintiff personally. Ex. A § T; Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 3–11.

Fourth, the SAC pleads person-level falsity and defamatory implication. The letters placed Plaintiff’s full legal name in the same sentence as “two CyberTipline reports,” joined Plaintiff’s three search identifiers disjunctively in the order he supplied them, identified no report number, date, provider, or matched identifier, and omitted every limiting statement. Ex. A §§ K, L (¶¶ 105–119). The SAC pleads the meaning a reasonable reader would take from the letters. Ex. A ¶¶ 117, 194.

Fifth, the SAC pleads facts supporting Hall’s knowledge, intent, recklessness, and actual malice as of April 22, 2026: her access to NCMEC’s legal-intake records showing no service; her selection of language characterizing the letters as responses to a subpoena; her disjunctive listing of Plaintiff’s own search terms without disambiguation; and her omission of every source-identifying detail. Ex. A §§ I, K, T; Ex. A ¶¶ 244–246. The later events in Section P are pleaded as bearing on subsequent knowledge, continuing position, the unresolved referent of the letters, and continuing injury, not as proof of what Hall knew on April 22, 2026. Ex. A ¶¶ 173, 185, 188, 289.

Sixth, the SAC pleads Plaintiff’s disclosed survivor status and Hall’s knowledge of it before April 22, 2026. Ex. A §§ C, G (¶¶ 39–45, 60); Ex. A ¶ 283.

Seventh, the SAC pleads the circumstantial facts supporting the alleged agreement: identical materials to NCMEC and to counsel for Meta and Accenture on April 9, 2026; motions on April 21, 2026 directed at the same discovery; imminent depositions; no formal service and no court order requiring a response; two case-keyed letters one day after those motions; issuance before the notice period expired; omission of every source-identifying detail; an unsworn assertion, outside the discovery process, on the subject scheduled for sworn examination; and issuance while the motions remained pending. Ex. A § O (¶¶ 141–151).

Eighth, the SAC pleads the object of the understanding and the deterrence directed at Plaintiff’s attendance as a party and his testimony as a prospective witness. Ex. A § Q (¶¶ 190–196).

Ninth, the SAC pleads overt acts by each Defendant and personal injury with physical manifestation, impaired capacity, and litigation-related consequences. Ex. A §§ R, S (¶¶ 197–213).

Meta’s opposition to ECF No. 59 argued that the allegation concerning Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California “has no relevance whatsoever to Plaintiff’s claims against Meta.” ECF No. 83 at 3. The SAC pleads that filing only as a subsequent fact bearing on Meta’s knowledge, state of mind, and awareness of the relationship between the two proceedings. Ex. A ¶¶ 185, 297. It states that no claim rests on the filing and that liability under Count IV rests on Sections O, Q, and R. Ex. A ¶ 297. The weight of one subsequent-knowledge allegation does not determine whether Count IV states a claim. Count IV rests on the agreement alleged in Section O, the purpose alleged in Section Q, the overt acts alleged in Section R, and the injury alleged in Section S. Ex. A ¶¶ 290–299.

2.	The claims against Souras.

The SAC pleads each element of each count against Souras. For Counts I and II, it pleads her participation in publication by approving the wording and authorizing or directing issuance (Ex. A ¶¶ 235, 259); falsity (¶¶ 242–243, 266–267); negligence and, separately, actual malice, with the facts from which each is inferred (¶¶ 247, 271); and scope of employment (¶¶ 249, 273). For Count IV, it pleads her knowing participation in implementing the agreement, her knowledge of the pending actions and the announced formal service, her sharing of the purpose, and her overt acts (¶¶ 102, 154, 199, 294, 296). For Count V, it pleads her part in the combination and its execution (¶¶ 302–303). For Count VI, it pleads her approval of the words communicated to Plaintiff and her knowledge or reckless disregard of their falsity (¶¶ 311, 316).

NCMEC has invoked 18 U.S.C. § 2258D. ECF No. 11 at 7. That section bars civil claims “against NCMEC, including any director, officer, employee, or agent of NCMEC, arising from the performance of the CyberTipline responsibilities or functions of NCMEC.” 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(a). It does not apply where the officer or employee “engaged in intentional misconduct,” acted “with actual malice,” acted “with reckless disregard to a substantial risk of causing injury without legal justification,” or acted “for a purpose unrelated to the performance of any responsibility or function under this section, section 2258A or 2258C of this title, or section 404 of the Missing Children’s Assistance Act (34 U.S.C. 11293).” 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(b). The SAC pleads, as to Souras, that her review, approval, and authorization “were not part of any effort to identify a child victim,” and that her participation “was intentional, was undertaken with actual malice and reckless disregard of a substantial risk of injury without legal justification, and served the litigation-directed purpose alleged in Section Q.” Ex. A ¶ 102. Those allegations track subsection (b). The SAC attaches the facts from which they are inferred: the letters were voluntary correspondence, issued before formal service, without any court order, addressed to Plaintiff alone, keyed to two pending federal actions in which the recipient’s own counsel had moved to stay the same discovery one day earlier. Ex. A §§ G, H, I, J, O. Whether the exception applies is a merits question. At the pleading stage the question is whether the SAC pleads facts that, taken as true, fall within subsection (b). It does.

The allegations of Souras’s participation are pleaded on information and belief, and the SAC says so in each instance. The Fourth Circuit has held that factual “allegations pled on information and belief are not categorically insufficient to state a claim for relief where the proof supporting the allegation is within the sole possession and control of the defendant or where the belief is based on sufficient factual material that makes the inference of culpability plausible.” Lowy v. Daniel Defense, LLC, No. 24-1822, slip op. at 34–35 (4th Cir. Feb. 11, 2026) (citation omitted). Such allegations “may not be wholly conclusory,” and must be “supported by . . . well-pled facts that exist independent of [the plaintiff’s] legal conclusions.” Kashdan v. George Mason Univ., 70 F.4th 694, 701 (4th Cir. 2023). The SAC satisfies both conditions. It pleads the facts on which the belief rests: Souras’s responsibility for NCMEC’s litigation and compliance matters; her documented performance of related functions in CyberTipline litigation; her former employment at Orrick, which represented Meta in both actions and received the April 9, 2026 materials for Meta; the arrival of the request at NCMEC’s Legal Department; the issuance of the response by Hall, as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel, on NCMEC letterhead in two pending federal actions; and the chronology in Sections G through I. Ex. A ¶¶ 91–98; Ex. A §§ G–I. It states that the identities of other reviewers, the internal routing, the communications, and any approval records are maintained in NCMEC’s records and cannot be reached without discovery. Ex. A ¶ 104. Those are well-pleaded facts independent of the legal conclusion. The inference that NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer reviewed and approved case-captioned legal correspondence issued by her office in two pending federal actions is plausible on those facts.

3.	The futility arguments already made do not establish futility.

NCMEC argued that “[n]o allegations Plaintiff can make can change” the asserted truth of the letters “because he does not have access to those reports.” ECF No. 74 at 5. That argument asks the Court to treat NCMEC’s characterization of its own letters as established fact. At the pleading stage the Court does not do so. Goines, 822 F.3d at 167–69. The SAC pleads, with the factual basis, that neither report as received identified Plaintiff as “Marvelle J. Ballentine” and that neither concerned Plaintiff personally. Ex. A ¶¶ 228–232. It pleads that NCMEC’s own memorandum framed the referent as Plaintiff, “a person with the same name,” or an e-mail address, and that counsel declined to answer which identifier, if any, appears in either report. Ex. A ¶¶ 176, 178–179, 215. Those allegations are accepted as true on a futility inquiry. Kolon, 637 F.3d at 440.

NCMEC also argued that the amendment is “unnecessary” because Plaintiff could present the same points in opposition briefs. ECF No. 74 at 5–6. A plaintiff’s ability to argue a point in a brief does not bear on whether the proposed pleading states a claim, which is the futility question. Katyle, 637 F.3d at 471. Facts belong in the pleading. The SAC places them there.

G.	Rule 15(d) Supports Incorporating the Subsequent Events into One Operative Pleading.

Section P pleads events after August 6, 2026: NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 memorandum stating that NCMEC “responded to the subpoenas without awaiting formal service” and that the linkage may involve “a person with the same name”; Plaintiff’s August 13, 2026 question to counsel and counsel’s response; Meta’s August 13, 2026 filing in the Northern District of California citing this action; and Hall’s September 2, 2026 filings adopting NCMEC’s positions. Ex. A ¶¶ 175–189. Count III pleads that the severe emotional distress on which it rests continued after the FAC was filed while the referent of the letters remained unresolved. Ex. A ¶ 289. Each is a “transaction, occurrence, or event that happened after the date of the pleading to be supplemented.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(d). Each concerns the same letters, the same Defendants, and the same claims. Each bears on knowledge, state of mind, the referent of the letters, or continuing injury. The Scope of Allegations limits their use: court filings are pleaded “solely as facts establishing timing, notice, knowledge, coordination, and admissions,” and “[n]one is conduct on which any claim rests.” Ex. A ¶ 25.

One integrated pleading serves efficient adjudication. Defendants respond to one pleading. The Court adjudicates one set of allegations. Rule 15(d) exists to permit that result, and the Fourth Circuit treats a pleading that both amends and supplements under the same standard. Franks, 313 F.3d at 198 n.15.

H.	Procedural Effect of Granting Leave.

Granting leave has the following consequences. First, the SAC supersedes the FAC. “[A]n amended pleading ordinarily supersedes the original and renders it of no legal effect.” Young v. City of Mount Ranier, 238 F.3d 567, 572 (4th Cir. 2001) (citation omitted). Second, Defendants Hall, NCMEC, and Meta respond within the time provided by Rule 15(a)(3) or such other time as the Court directs. Third, the Clerk issues a summons for Souras under Rule 4(b), and Plaintiff serves her under Rule 4.

Plaintiff’s pending objections and applications concerning ECF Nos. 64 and 84 remain submitted in their respective proceedings. Granting this Motion would provide the immediate relief of permitting the proposed superseding pleading. Plaintiff requests no determination through this Motion concerning the continued justiciability or disposition of the remaining objections or retrospective-relief requests, which remain subject to the effect of any relief actually granted.

The pending motions to dismiss directed to the FAC (ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45) are procedural context. This Motion requests no disposition of them. Their management after the SAC becomes the operative pleading remains within the Court’s discretion. NCMEC’s alternative request that leave be held in abeyance until the motions to dismiss are decided (ECF No. 74 at 7) would have the Court adjudicate a pleading the SAC replaces. Rule 15(d) permits supplementation “even though the original pleading is defective in stating a claim or defense.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(d). Deciding leave first permits the Court to adjudicate one complete pleading once.

V.	CONCLUSION

The SAC names a defendant alleged, on information and belief, to have participated in the approval or authorization the FAC described, adds facts, incorporates subsequent events, and keeps the same six claims. It is presented before any answer, before any scheduling order, and before any discovery, with the comparison the Court described in ECF No. 64 and a second comparison against the operative pleading. It prejudices no Defendant. It is not futile. The only stated ground for the prior denial is eliminated. Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter an order: (a) granting leave under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a)(2), 15(d), 20(a)(2), and 21 to file the Second Amended Complaint attached as Exhibit A, deeming it filed as of the date of the order, and deeming it the operative pleading; (b) directing the Clerk, to the extent administratively necessary, to docket it separately as the operative complaint; (c) directing the Clerk to issue a summons for Defendant Panayiota Souras upon Plaintiff’s presentation of a completed summons form; (d) providing that Defendants Hall, NCMEC, and Meta shall respond within the time prescribed by Rule 15(a)(3) or such other time as the Court directs, and that Defendant Souras shall respond within the time prescribed by Rule 12(a) following service; and (e) granting such further relief as the Court deems just.

Date: November 1, 2026		                      Respectfully submitted,

Marvelle J. Ballentine

EXHIBIT A

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; PANAYIOTA SOURAS, also known as YIOTA G. SOURAS, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

PLAINTIFF’S PROPOSED SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

•	On July 4, 2022, Meta Platforms, Inc. invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy against my Facebook account and cut off the contracts I performed through it. I sued them in September 2025. Meta filed a motion to dismiss. Meta did not staple a CyberTipline report to the motion.

•	When Meta’s co-defendants’ lawyers asserted that a “legitimate violation by Ballentine is consistent with the facts” while repeatedly putting my name beside the words “child sexual exploitation” in their papers, I sued them in February 2026. Defendants filed motions to dismiss. Defendants did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

•	I sent Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas to NCMEC in April concerning those two cases, and their attorney, Ms. Hall, sent me two letters associating my full legal name, “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” with two CyberTipline reports. I sued them in May 2026 because I have never even used my full legal name to operate any social media account. NCMEC and Hall filed motions to dismiss. NCMEC and Hall did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

•	I served Meta on July 31, 2026 concerning its role in the drafting, transmission, and delivery of the letters. It filed a motion to dismiss. Once again, it did not staple a CyberTipline report to the motion. Meta substituted the CyberTipline report with a chronicle of my prior lawsuits, their captions, and their procedural history.

•	I have sworn that I never used my full legal name to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any account on any Meta product or service that I used. The defense may move to dismiss this complaint. Whether or not they staple a CyberTipline report to the motions is to be determined.

•	That matters because the two letters signed by Hall on behalf of NCMEC stated:

“In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its written responses as detailed below.

NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.”

•	So, that leaves the remaining questions up for determination: Where did my legal name come from? How and why did it arrive on those letters? Did either of the two asserted CyberTipline reports, as originally received by NCMEC, actually identify “Marvelle J. Ballentine”? Did Meta submit either report? Why did NCMEC and Hall act before formal service? Why did they not wait the five days until April 27, when one court temporarily stayed discovery, or the nine days until May 1, when discovery in the other action was temporarily stayed? Where did the urgency come from?

•	I bring six counts: conspiracy under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and Virginia law against all Defendants, for letters sent to frighten me out of my own lawsuits; defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and insulting words against Hall and NCMEC, for what the letters said and to whom. This Complaint adds NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, Panayiota Souras, who, on information and belief, approved the wording of the letters and authorized Hall to send them before formal service. The defamation and insulting-words counts are also asserted against Souras; Count III remains against Hall and NCMEC.

JURISDICTION AND VENUE

•	This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(1). Count IV arises under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2).

•	This Court has supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) over the claims for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, common-law conspiracy, and insulting words. Those claims arise from the same nucleus of operative fact as Count IV: the preparation, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of the April 22, 2026 letters. They form part of the same case or controversy.

•	In the alternative, this Court has original jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1) over Counts I, II, III, V, and VI if complete diversity exists. Plaintiff is a citizen of the State of Florida. NCMEC, a District of Columbia non-profit corporation with its principal place of business in Virginia, is a citizen of the District of Columbia and Virginia. Meta, a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in California, is a citizen of Delaware and California. At all relevant times, Hall and Souras worked at NCMEC’s headquarters in Alexandria, Virginia. On information and belief, each is domiciled in, and therefore is a citizen of, a State other than Florida. Plaintiff cannot presently allege the citizenship of John/Jane Does 1-6, whose identities are unknown. This basis applies only if no Defendant is a citizen of Florida and each Doe Defendant’s citizenship is alleged or no Doe Defendant remains a party. The amount in controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.

•	Venue is proper in this district under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2). A substantial part of the events giving rise to the claims occurred here. Hall prepared or approved, signed, and issued the April 22, 2026 letters from NCMEC’s office in Alexandria, Virginia, within the Alexandria Division of this district. The letters were transmitted to Plaintiff’s commercial mail-receiving address in Alexandria, Virginia, where they were opened and processed.

•	This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Hall under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). Hall performed the challenged acts in Virginia. She prepared or approved, signed, issued, and caused the transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters from NCMEC’s Alexandria headquarters. The first third-party publication alleged in this Complaint occurred in Alexandria, when the commercial mail-receiving agency opened, reviewed, and scanned the letters. Each claim against Hall arises from her Virginia conduct.

•	This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Souras under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). Souras served as Chief Legal Officer of NCMEC at its Alexandria, Virginia headquarters. On information and belief, Souras reviewed, approved, and authorized the April 22, 2026 letters in the course of her work for NCMEC, and the letters issued from NCMEC’s Alexandria office and were transmitted to Plaintiff’s Alexandria address as a result. Each claim against Souras arises from that Virginia conduct.

•	This Court has general personal jurisdiction over NCMEC, a corporation with its principal place of business in Alexandria, Virginia. This Court also has specific personal jurisdiction over NCMEC under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). The April 22, 2026 letters were prepared or approved, signed, and issued from NCMEC’s Alexandria headquarters, and each claim against NCMEC arises from that Virginia conduct.

•	This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Meta Platforms, Inc. under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3) and the conspiracy-based attribution of forum contacts. Sections O through R allege the conspiracy. Meta knowingly participated through one or more authorized representatives or intermediaries. NCMEC and Hall committed the Virginia acts alleged in this Complaint in furtherance of that conspiracy. Meta received the April 9, 2026 materials directed to NCMEC’s Legal Department in Alexandria, Virginia. The understanding alleged in Section O contemplated that Hall would issue the case-specific correspondence from that Virginia office. Plaintiff’s claim against Meta arises from those Virginia acts.

•	The exercise of personal jurisdiction over each Defendant comports with the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

PARTIES

•	Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine, also known as Jay Ballentine, is an adult citizen of the State of Florida. At all relevant times Plaintiff maintained a mailing address at 1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847, Alexandria, Virginia 22307. A commercial mail-receiving agency operates that address and is authorized to receive and process mail on Plaintiff’s behalf.

•	Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) is a District of Columbia non-profit corporation. Its principal place of business is 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. NCMEC operates the CyberTipline under federal authorization in connection with 18 U.S.C. § 2258A. At all relevant times NCMEC employed Defendant Katie Hall as its Corporate Counsel. Hall was responsible for legal correspondence NCMEC issued in response to claimed legal process. NCMEC is sued for its own conduct, undertaken through Hall and one or more additional personnel. NCMEC is also sued vicariously for the conduct of Hall and Souras within the scope of their employment.

•	Defendant Katie Hall is an individual. At all relevant times she served as Corporate Counsel of NCMEC at 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. On information and belief, Hall is domiciled in a State other than Florida and is a citizen of that State. Hall prepared or approved, signed, issued, and caused the transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters. Hall is sued individually for her own tortious conduct.

•	Defendant Panayiota Souras, known publicly as Yiota G. Souras, is an individual. At all relevant times she served as Chief Legal Officer of NCMEC at 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. On information and belief, Souras is domiciled in a State other than Florida and is a citizen of that State. Souras was responsible for NCMEC’s legal affairs, including litigation and compliance, and managed NCMEC’s legal operations. Souras is sued individually for her own alleged participation in reviewing, approving, and authorizing the April 22, 2026 letters.

•	Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) is a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in Menlo Park, California. Meta was a defendant in the 376 Action and in the 286 Action, each identified in Section A, at all relevant times. Meta is an electronic service provider subject to the reporting duties of 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.

•	Meta owns and operates Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.

•	Defendants John/Jane Does 1-6 are persons not yet identified who participated in the communications, authorization, approval, preparation, or transmission alleged in this Complaint. Their roles include: the Meta representative or representatives who communicated with NCMEC concerning Plaintiff, the identifiers, the intended subpoenas, or the two federal actions; any Accenture representative who knowingly joined or implemented the understanding alleged in this Complaint; any NCMEC personnel, other than Hall and Souras, who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters; and any intermediary, including counsel or other agents acting for Meta, Accenture, or NCMEC, through whom the alleged communications occurred. Meta, Accenture, NCMEC, and their representatives hold the records that identify the Doe Defendants. Plaintiff will seek leave to amend when those identities are ascertained.

SCOPE OF ALLEGATIONS

•	This Complaint predicates no liability on the filing of any motion, brief, or other paper in any court. Court filings identified here are alleged solely as facts establishing timing, notice, knowledge, coordination, and admissions. The claims do not challenge NCMEC’s receipt, maintenance, or lawful referral of CyberTipline reports. The claims challenge the extra-judicial agreement alleged below and the preparation, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of external legal correspondence that falsely invoked compulsory process and served the litigation-directed purposes alleged below. No claim against Meta seeks liability for the July 4, 2022 account-level enforcement, for any content-related decision, for any failure to restore Plaintiff’s account, or for any treatment of third-party content. Those matters are alleged only to establish the subject matter of the pending federal actions, Defendants’ knowledge, Meta’s interest in whether a CyberTipline report exists, and the testimony Defendants sought to deter. The same is true of the memorandum, motion to stay, and opposition filed in the 1341 Action and the August 13, 2026 filing in the 376 Action, each identified in Section P. Each is alleged as an admission and as a fact establishing timing, coordination, and knowledge. None is conduct on which any claim rests.

FACTS

A.	The Federal Proceedings and Plaintiff’s Role as Party and Prospective Witness

•	Plaintiff filed Ballentine v. Accenture LLP, et al., Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI (M.D. Fla.) (the “286 Action”), on February 9, 2026. Plaintiff filed Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al., Case No. 6:26-cv-00376-AGM-DCI (M.D. Fla.) (the “376 Action”), on February 17, 2026. Each action was pending in a court of the United States at all relevant times.

•	The defendants in the 376 Action included Meta, Accenture, TaskUs, Inc., and Genpact Limited. Accenture is a limited liability partnership that provides platform policy enforcement services to Meta. The defendants in the 286 Action included Meta, Devin S. Anderson, and Christopher W. Keegan. Kirkland & Ellis LLP (“Kirkland”) represented Anderson and Keegan. Accenture, Anderson, Keegan, TaskUs, Inc., Genpact Limited, Kirkland, Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP (“Orrick”), Diana M. Fassbender, and Marianna Chapleau are not defendants here. Their conduct is alleged only to establish chronology, notice, knowledge, or the conduct of the Defendants, including the Doe Defendants.

•	Both actions arise from one event. On July 4, 2022, Meta issued an account-level enforcement notice against Plaintiff’s Facebook account. That notice interrupted Plaintiff’s ability to perform third-party contracts through the account.

•	Plaintiff proceeded pro se in both actions. Every act of prosecution depended on Plaintiff’s personal capacity and participation: discovery, deposition examination, briefing, and appearance.

•	Plaintiff was a prospective witness in both actions. He expected to testify under oath, at deposition and at trial, concerning his account history, the July 4, 2022 enforcement event, the absence of any law-enforcement contact with him, and his damages.

•	The dockets of the 376 Action and the 286 Action were publicly accessible through the federal Public Access to Court Electronic Records system.

B.	The Contested CyberTipline Question

•	One question has been contested since October 2025: whether Meta, or any person acting in connection with the July 4, 2022 account-enforcement event, transmitted a CyberTipline report under 18 U.S.C. § 2258A concerning Plaintiff or his account identifiers.

•	Before April 22, 2026, no CyberTipline report concerning Plaintiff had been identified, produced, or attributed to any provider in any forum.

•	Plaintiff’s first substantive act in the 376 Action was a motion for leave to serve a single early request for admission. The request asked whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff’s account. The court denied the motion.

•	From that denial forward, the defendants in the 376 Action knew what Plaintiff’s discovery would target: the existence or non-existence of a CyberTipline report.

•	The operative complaint in the 376 Action alleged that Meta filed no CyberTipline report. Its prayer sought a declaration that no CyberTipline report was filed regarding the July 4, 2022 enforcement event.

•	On April 9, 2026, Meta moved to dismiss the 376 Action (ECF No. 85). Meta described Plaintiff’s allegation that a CyberTipline report had been submitted and disseminated as “hypothetical (and elsewhere contradicted).” Meta identified the contradiction as Plaintiff’s allegation that “Meta filed no CyberTipline report.”

•	In the 286 Action, the existence or non-existence of a CyberTipline report bore on the claims then pending, including the falsity and factual basis of the statements challenged in that action.

C.	Plaintiff’s Disclosed Survivor Status

•	On September 9, 2025, Plaintiff filed a complaint in Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al., Case No. 3:25-cv-07671-CRB (N.D. Cal.) (the “California Action”).

•	That complaint contained a single footnote. The footnote states: “As a CSA survivor, Plaintiff gratefully acknowledges the unwavering support of his wife, whose steady presence made the psychological recovery, and subsequent preparation of this Complaint possible. He further acknowledges his children, especially his eldest, who endured his distance during the preparation of this filing after once celebrating his NRVTA graduation with pride. This work now returns to them, just as their father and husband does.”

•	The footnote disclosed that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse and had undergone a psychological recovery that made preparation of the complaint possible.

•	Before April 22, 2026, then, Plaintiff had disclosed that he is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse. He had described undergoing psychological recovery. He retained the functional capacity to prepare and prosecute his pending actions.

•	The publicly filed pleadings in the 286 Action disclosed on their face that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse. Those pleadings alleged that placing Plaintiff’s name near child-sexual-exploitation terminology had already caused Plaintiff emotional injury.

•	Meta, Anderson, and Keegan, through their respective counsel, received and litigated against the 286 Action pleadings containing those disclosures before April 21, 2026.

•	The Kirkland attorneys who appeared for Accenture in the 376 Action also represented Anderson and Keegan in the 286 Action. They therefore possessed the 286 Action pleadings before April 21, 2026. Accenture’s authorized representatives knew of the disclosures before April 21, 2026.

D.	CyberTipline Reporting by Meta-Operated Services

•	NCMEC receives CyberTipline reports from Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.

E.	Counsel Operating Across Both Actions

•	Fassbender, an attorney at Orrick, was counsel of record for Meta in the 286 Action and for Meta and Genpact Limited in the 376 Action.

•	Chapleau and Anderson, attorneys at Kirkland, were counsel of record for Accenture in the 376 Action. Kirkland, through Chapleau, also represented Anderson and Keegan in the 286 Action.

•	Anderson held two roles at once. In the 286 Action he was an individual defendant and a noticed deposition witness. In the 376 Action he was counsel of record for Accenture.

F.	The Deposition Program

•	On April 7, 2026, Plaintiff served a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition notice on Accenture in the 376 Action. The notice set a two-day examination for April 29 and April 30, 2026. Plaintiff served the notice on Chapleau and Anderson.

•	Matter for Examination No. 5 of that notice is captioned “CyberTipline Reporting and Reportability Status.” It encompasses “whether any CyberTipline Report was Transmitted to NCMEC in connection with the Account-Level Enforcement Event.”

•	On April 7, 2026, Plaintiff noticed Anderson’s deposition in the 286 Action for April 28, 2026. On April 10, 2026, Plaintiff re-served the notice with logistical details.

L.	Statutory Imputation and Defamatory Meaning

•	Section 2258A of Title 18 requires an electronic service provider to report to NCMEC’s CyberTipline after obtaining actual knowledge of facts or circumstances from which there is an apparent violation of specified federal child-exploitation statutes. The CyberTipline also receives reports from other sources concerning suspected child exploitation.

•	The statutes enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A include 18 U.S.C. § 2251 (sexual exploitation of children), § 2251A (selling or buying of children), § 2252 (certain activities relating to material involving the sexual exploitation of minors), § 2252A (certain activities relating to material constituting or containing child pornography), and § 2422(b) (coercion and enticement of minors).

•	In the context alleged, a reader of the letter would understand the statement that NCMEC had received two CyberTipline reports “concerning” Plaintiff’s full legal name and identifiers to convey that NCMEC had received two reports associating Plaintiff personally with suspected child-exploitation conduct and that the reported matter could be made available to law enforcement.

•	By linking Plaintiff’s full legal name to two CyberTipline reports, the letter imputes to Plaintiff conduct constituting offenses involving moral turpitude. If the imputation were true, Plaintiff could be indicted and punished for those offenses.

•	The imputation is false. Plaintiff has not engaged in conduct constituting, or reasonably appearing to constitute, a violation of any statute enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.

•	The purpose of the understanding was to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from continuing to attend the 376 Action and the 286 Action as a party, and from testifying freely, fully, and truthfully as a prospective witness in those pending federal proceedings, including on the CyberTipline-reporting question.

•	The intimidation targeted Plaintiff’s continued attendance as a party in the two pending federal actions and his prospective sworn testimony concerning his account, the July 4, 2022 enforcement event, the absence of any law-enforcement contact with him, and his damages.

•	Defendants knew that Plaintiff was pro se. They knew the noticed depositions depended on his personal preparation and examination. They knew the CyberTipline issue was central to the noticed examinations. They knew Plaintiff was a prospective witness concerning his account, the enforcement event, and his damages.

•	The letters bore the letterhead of the federally designated clearinghouse for CyberTipline reporting. They carried the signature of its Corporate Counsel. They called themselves responses to subpoenas before formal service. They associated Plaintiff’s full legal name, alternate name, and email identifier with CyberTipline reports. They omitted the reporting provider, report dates, report numbers, matched identifier, platform, account connection, and disposition. They were keyed to the two federal actions by caption. They issued while the depositions remained imminent and the protective motions remained pending. They were addressed to Plaintiff alone.

•	A reasonable reader would take the letters to communicate this: NCMEC possessed reports generated in connection with apparent violations of federal child-exploitation statutes; those reports associated one or more of Plaintiff’s identifiers with the reported matter; and those reports could be available to law enforcement.

•	Plaintiff understood the letters to mean that federal reporting records connected his identity to suspected child-exploitation conduct and that law enforcement could treat him as a subject of investigation.

•	Defendants intended that fear of investigation, arrest, or prosecution would cause Plaintiff to dismiss or withdraw from the two federal actions. That would deter Plaintiff, as a party, from continuing to attend those proceedings. It would deter Plaintiff, as a prospective witness, from testifying freely, fully, and truthfully. Abandonment of the contemplated CyberTipline discovery and impairment of Plaintiff’s preparation were intended and foreseeable consequences of that deterrence.

On information and belief, Souras approved their wording and authorized or directed their issuance. The publication of each letter constituted the defamation alleged in Counts I and II.

•	The participants understood and intended that the letters would travel through the selected commercial mail channel. They understood and intended that the third-party publication alleged in Counts I and II would occur in carrying out the understanding.

COUNT VI

INSULTING WORDS — VA. CODE § 8.01-45

(Against Defendants Katie Hall, Panayiota Souras, and NCMEC)

•	Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement, Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections, and Sections A, B, C, G, H, I, J, K, L, N, P, S, and T of the Facts, as if fully set forth herein.

•	The words of each letter associated Plaintiff’s full legal name, alternate name, and email identifier with two CyberTipline reports, on NCMEC letterhead, over the signature of NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel, and framed as a response to subpoena process before formal service. Those words, in their usual construction and common acceptation, are insults that tend to violence and breach of the peace. In the context alleged in Section L of the Facts, the words convey the imputation described in that Section.

•	On information and belief, neither report referenced in the letters concerned Plaintiff personally. On information and belief, neither report, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise identified Plaintiff as “Marvelle J. Ballentine.”

She knowingly selected language stating that each letter responded to a subpoena before formal service, when Plaintiff had not waived service or requested an early response. She acted with knowledge or reckless disregard of the falsity of the imputation each letter conveyed.

COMPLAINT

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

1.	On July 4, 2022, Meta Platforms, Inc. invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy against my Facebook account and cut off the contracts I performed through it. I sued them in September 2025. Meta filed a motion to dismiss. Meta did not staple a CyberTipline report to the motion.

2.	When Meta’s co-defendants’ lawyers asserted that a “legitimate violation by Ballentine is consistent with the facts” while repeatedly putting my name beside the words “child sexual exploitation” in their papers, I sued them in February 2026. Defendants filed motions to dismiss. Defendants did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

3.	I sent Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas to NCMEC in April concerning those two cases, and their attorney, Ms. Hall, sent me two letters associating my full legal name, “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” with two CyberTipline reports. I sued them in May 2026 because I have never even used my full legal name to operate any social media account. NCMEC and Hall filed motions to dismiss. NCMEC and Hall did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

4.	I served Meta on July 31, 2026 concerning its role in the drafting, transmission, and delivery of the letters. It filed a motion to dismiss. Once again, it did not staple a CyberTipline report to the motion. Meta substituted the CyberTipline report with a chronicle of my prior lawsuits, their captions, and their procedural history.

5.	I have sworn that I never used my full legal name to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any account on any Meta product or service that I used. The defense may move to dismiss this complaint. Whether or not they staple a CyberTipline report to the motions is to be determined.

6.	That matters because the two letters signed by Hall on behalf of NCMEC stated: “In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its written responses as detailed below. NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.”

7.	So, that leaves the remaining questions up for determination: Where did my legal name come from? How and why did it arrive on those letters? Did either of the two asserted CyberTipline reports, as originally received by NCMEC, actually identify “Marvelle J. Ballentine”? Did Meta submit either report? Why did NCMEC and Hall act before formal service? Why did they not wait the five days until April 27, when one court temporarily stayed discovery, or the nine days until May 1, when discovery in the other action was temporarily stayed? Where did the urgency come from?

8.	I bring six counts: conspiracy under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and Virginia law against all Defendants, for letters sent to frighten me out of my own lawsuits; defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and insulting words against Hall and NCMEC, for what the letters said and to whom. This Complaint adds NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, Panayiota Souras, who, on information and belief, approved the wording of the letters and authorized Hall to send them before formal service. The defamation and insulting-words counts are also asserted against Souras; Count III remains against Hall and NCMEC.

This case is about two letters and the lawyer who wrote them. On April 22, 2026, Katie Hall — Corporate Counsel of the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, the organization this country trusts to track crimes against children — tied my name to "two CyberTipline reports." She chose the words. She signed both letters. She sent them. Each one opened by telling me it was answering a subpoena. No subpoena had been served. Not one. There was no process, no court order, and no obligation of any kind behind the words Hall put on that letterhead.

The CyberTipline exists to catch people who hurt children. Federal law requires companies to report to it. Law enforcement can be given what it holds. Everyone understands what it means when that name appears above a man’s name. That is why those letters landed on me the way they did.

I was not a defendant. I was the plaintiff — one man, without a lawyer, suing Meta Platforms, Inc. and others in the Middle District of Florida. Case No. 6:26-cv-00376-AGM-DCI. Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI. I had asked one question in both: did anyone connected to the July 4, 2022 shutdown of my account send a CyberTipline report about me? I had noticed depositions for April 28, 29, and 30 to ask it under oath. One of those notices told Accenture, in writing, that its witness would have to answer that very question.

On April 21, 2026, every defendant in both cases moved to shut the discovery down and stop the depositions. The letters came the next day. Each one carried the caption and case number of one of my lawsuits. Each one answered the exact question my depositions were set to ask — outside discovery, unsworn, with no one to cross-examine. And each one left out everything a man would need to test it: who reported, when, what number, which identifier, which platform, what came of it. The letters came to me alone. No court was copied. No lawyer was copied.

Consider what was true on April 22. No subpoena had been served. No court had ordered Hall to do anything. I had not asked for an early answer, and I had not waived service. The motions filed the day before were undecided. The ruling dates the movants themselves demanded had not come. The depositions they were trying to stop had not happened. Nothing required Hall to send those letters that day. Nothing required Hall to send them at all.

I had told NCMEC’s Legal Department in writing that subpoenas were coming, and that I would serve them when the notice period ran. A notice is not a subpoena. Mail is not service. Hall is a lawyer who handles subpoenas, and she knows the difference. The brief Hall and NCMEC filed to end the action captioned Ballentine v. National Center for Missing & Exploited Children and Katie Hall, Case No. 1:26-cv-01341-MSN-WBP (E.D. Va.) (the “1341 Action”) states that NCMEC “did not await formal service of the subpoenas.” She did not wait. She answered a subpoena that was never served.

And Hall knew who she was writing to. Before those letters went out, she had either read the pleadings in the 286 Action or been handed what was in them. Those pleadings said, on their face, that I am a survivor of childhood sexual abuse. They said that putting my name next to the language of child exploitation had already hurt me. Hall is the lawyer for the clearinghouse this country built to track crimes against children. She knows what that name does to a man. She sent the letters anyway. Who told her to send them, and what was said before they went out, are answers kept in NCMEC’s files and Meta’s, not mine.

I read the letters on April 28, 2026 — the day my first deposition was supposed to go forward, and did not. I understood what I was reading: that federal records now tied my name to the sexual exploitation of children, and that law enforcement could come for me. I was afraid of being arrested. I was afraid of being searched. I was afraid of being prosecuted. I believed that if I kept litigating, and kept asking about that report, those things would happen to me. My first thought was to dismiss both of my cases. In the days that followed, it took deliberate effort not to.

I bring six counts. Counts I and II are for defamation — per se, and by implication — against Hall and NCMEC, for publishing each letter to third parties, including the employees of the mail service that opened, scanned, and filed them in the ordinary course of business. Count III is against Hall and NCMEC for intentional infliction of emotional distress; Hall did what she did knowing what she knew, and she did it as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel, on NCMEC’s letterhead, from NCMEC’s offices. Count IV is brought under the first clause of 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2), and Count V for common-law conspiracy under Virginia law, against Hall, NCMEC, Meta Platforms, Inc., and the Doe Defendants — against those who agreed the letters would go out, and who prepared, approved, and transmitted them, to frighten me out of attending my own lawsuits and out of testifying freely, fully, and truthfully in them. Count VI is pleaded in the alternative under Virginia Code § 8.01-45, for the insulting words Hall directed to me.
