UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA

ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,

v. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD 1:26-cv-02331

The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;

PANAYIOTA SOURAS, also known as YIOTA G. SOURAS, individually;

NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;

META PLATFORMS, INC.;

and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

FIRST PLAINTIFF’S PROPOSED SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

1.	On July 4, 2022, Meta Platforms, Inc. invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy against my Facebook account and cut off the contracts I performed through it. I sued them in September 2025. Meta filed a motion to dismiss. Meta did not staple a CyberTipline report to the motion.

2.	When Meta’s co-defendants’ lawyers asserted that a “legitimate violation by Ballentine is consistent with the facts” while repeatedly putting my name beside the words “child sexual exploitation” in their papers, I sued them in February 2026. Defendants filed motions to dismiss. Defendants did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

3.	I sent Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas to NCMEC in April concerning those two cases, and their attorney, Ms. Hall, sent me two letters associating my full legal name, “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” with two CyberTipline reports. I sued them in May 2026 because I have never even used my full legal name to operate any social media account. NCMEC and Hall filed motions to dismiss. NCMEC and Hall did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

4.	I served Meta on July 31, 2026 concerning its role in the drafting, transmission, and delivery of the letters. It filed a motion to dismiss. Once again, it did not staple a CyberTipline report to the motion. Meta substituted the CyberTipline report with a chronicle of my prior lawsuits, their captions, and their procedural history.

5.	I have sworn that I never used my full legal name to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any account on any Meta product or service that I used. The defense may move to dismiss this complaint. Whether or not they staple a CyberTipline report to the motions is to be determined.

6.	That matters because the two letters signed by Hall on behalf of NCMEC stated: “In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its written responses as detailed below. NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.”

7.	So, that leaves the remaining questions up for determination: Where did my legal name come from? How and why did it arrive on those letters? Did either of the two asserted CyberTipline reports, as originally received by NCMEC, actually identify “Marvelle J. Ballentine”? Did Meta submit either report? Why did NCMEC and Hall act before formal service? Why did they not wait the five days until April 27, when one court temporarily stayed discovery, or the nine days until May 1, when discovery in the other action was temporarily stayed? Where did the urgency come from?

8.	I bring six counts: conspiracy under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and Virginia law against all Defendants, for letters sent to frighten me out of my own lawsuits; defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and insulting words against Hall and NCMEC, for what the letters said and to whom. This Complaint adds NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, Panayiota Souras, who, on information and belief, approved the wording of the letters and authorized Hall to send them before formal service. The defamation and insulting-words counts are also asserted against Souras; Count III remains against Hall and NCMEC.

This case is about two letters and the lawyer who wrote them. On April 22, 2026, Katie Hall — Corporate Counsel of the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, the organization this country trusts to track crimes against children — tied my name to “two CyberTipline reports.” She chose the words. She signed both letters. She sent them. Each one opened by telling me it was answering a subpoena. No subpoena had been served. Not one. There was no process, court order, or obligation behind the words Hall put on that letterhead.

The CyberTipline exists to catch people who hurt children. Federal law requires companies to report to it. Law enforcement can be given what it holds. Everyone understands what it means when that name appears above a man’s name. That is why those letters landed on me the way they did.

I was not a defendant. I was the plaintiff — one man, without a lawyer, suing Meta Platforms, Inc. and others in the Middle District of Florida. Case No. 6:26-cv-00376-AGM-DCI. Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI. I had asked one question in both: did anyone connected to the July 4, 2022 shutdown of my account send a CyberTipline report about me? I had noticed depositions for April 28, 29, and 30 to ask it under oath. One notice told Accenture, in writing, that its witness would have to answer that question.

On April 21, 2026, every defendant in both cases moved to shut down discovery and stop the depositions. The letters came the next day. Each one carried the caption and case number of one of my lawsuits. Each one answered the exact question my depositions were set to ask — outside discovery, unsworn, with no one to cross-examine. And each one left out everything a man would need to test it: who reported, when, what number, which identifier, which platform, what came of it. The letters came to me alone. No court was copied. No lawyer was copied.

Consider what was true on April 22. No subpoena had been served. No court had ordered Hall to do anything. I had not asked for an early answer or waived service. The motions filed the day before were undecided. The ruling dates the movants demanded had not come. The depositions they were trying to stop had not happened. Nothing required Hall to send those letters that day. Nothing required Hall to send them at all.

And Hall knew who she was writing to. Before those letters went out, she had either read the pleadings in the 286 Action or been handed what was in them. Those pleadings said that I am a survivor of childhood sexual abuse. They said that putting my name next to the language of child exploitation had already hurt me. Hall is the lawyer for the clearinghouse this country built to track crimes against children. She knows what that name does to a man.

She sent the letters anyway. Who told her to send them, and what was said before they went out, are answers kept in NCMEC’s files and Meta’s, not mine.

I read the letters on April 28, 2026 — the day my first deposition was supposed to go forward, and did not. I understood what I was reading: that federal records now tied my name to the sexual exploitation of children, and that law enforcement could come for me. I was afraid of being arrested. I was afraid of being searched. I was afraid of being prosecuted. I believed that if I kept litigating and kept asking about that report, those things would happen to me. My first thought was to dismiss both cases. In the days that followed, it took deliberate effort not to.

I had told NCMEC’s Legal Department in writing that subpoenas were coming and that I would serve them when the notice period ran. A notice is not a subpoena. Mail is not service. Hall is a lawyer who handles subpoenas, and she knows the difference. In the action I later brought over these letters — Ballentine v. National Center for Missing & Exploited Children and Katie Hall, Case No. 1:26-cv-01341-MSN-WBP (E.D. Va.) (the “1341 Action”) — Hall and NCMEC told the Court, in their own filings, that the matter “arises out of two subpoenas sent, but not formally served,” that Hall “was clearly acting in the course and scope of her employment in responding to the subpoenas,” and that “NCMEC responded exactly as instructed in the subpoenas.” By their own account, they did not wait. They answered a subpoena that was never served. In that same action, they moved to shut down discovery when no discovery had been served — telling the Court that what discovery might surface “could give rise to further litigation from Mr. Ballentine.” A response that did nothing but follow instructions has nothing to fear from discovery.

When I moved to bring Meta into that action, Meta had not appeared and was not a party. Hall and NCMEC’s lawyer opposed the motion anyway — not on the ground that adding Meta would burden them, but by arguing Meta’s own defense: that the conspiracy I alleged was “conclusory and imaginary,” and that “there would be no claim asserted as to ... Meta Platforms, Inc.” Counsel for two defendants asked the Court to rule, before Meta appeared, that there was no case against Meta. COUNT V

(Against All Defendants)

300.	Plaintiff incorporates by reference the allegations in the Preliminary Statement, Jurisdiction and Venue, Parties, and Scope of Allegations sections, and Sections A through N O and Sections P Q through R T of the Facts, as if fully set forth herein.

On information and belief, Souras approved their wording and authorized or directed their issuance. The publication of each letter constituted the defamation alleged in Counts I and II.

304.	The participants understood and intended that the letters would be transmitted travel through the selected commercial mail channel channel. They understood and intended that the third-party publication alleged in Counts I and II would occur in carrying out the understanding.

As a direct and proximate result of the combination and the acts in furtherance of it, Plaintiff sustained the damages alleged in Section R S of the Facts and in Counts I and II, including II: presumed damages, humiliation, embarrassment, mental suffering, and injury to reputation. COUNT VI

311.	Hall directed each of the two April 22, 2026 letters to Plaintiff personally personally, at Plaintiff’s mailing address. On information and belief, Souras approved the words of each letter and authorized or directed that they be communicated to Plaintiff.

312.	The words of each letter — associating associated Plaintiff’s full legal name, alternate name, and email identifier with two CyberTipline reports, on NCMEC letterhead, over the signature of NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel, and framed as a response to compulsory legal subpoena process — are, before formal service. Those words, in their usual construction and common acceptance, acceptation, are insults that tend to violence and breach of the peace. On information and belief, Souras approved the words of each letter with knowledge that Plaintiff had supplied the identifiers, that the request sought only a document sufficient to show whether any report existed, and that formal service had not occurred, and acted with knowledge or reckless disregard of the falsity of the imputation each letter conveyed.

NCMEC, acting through Hall Hall, through Souras, and through one or more additional personnel, approved the wording of the letters and authorized their issuance and transmission. NCMEC is liable for the conduct alleged in this Count.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

PLAINTIFF’S RENEWED RULE 56 MOTION FOR PARTIAL SUMMARY JUDGMENT

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56(a) and Local Civil Rule 56 for partial summary judgment on one part of Counts I, II, III, and VI of the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5). In the alternative, Plaintiff requests an order under Rule 56(g). This Motion renews the motion filed at ECF No. 6, which the Court denied without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time. ECF No. 12. A Memorandum in Support under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1), the Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine with Exhibits 3 through 5, Proposed Order A, and Proposed Order B accompany this Motion.

I.	THE DETERMINATION REQUESTED

1.	Plaintiff requests summary judgment on the following part of Counts I, II, III, and VI against Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”): that Defendant Katie Hall acted as NCMEC’s employee and agent, within the course and scope of her employment, when she signed and issued on NCMEC’s behalf the two letters dated April 22, 2026 that appear at ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3 (the “letters”).

2.	The First Amended Complaint sues NCMEC “vicariously for the conduct of Hall committed within the scope of her employment.” ECF No. 5 ¶ 21. Counts I, II, III, and VI each allege that Hall acted within the scope of her employment as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel. Id. ¶¶ 195, 216, 230, 258. The requested determination resolves the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under those counts.

3.	The determination concerns Hall’s relationship with NCMEC. It does not concern any relationship between Hall and any other Defendant. It does not resolve whether Hall’s conduct was tortious, whether any privilege or immunity applies, whether NCMEC authorized or ratified any particular act, whether Hall performed any function described in 18 U.S.C. § 2258D, or any count other than Counts I, II, III, and VI.

II.	THE COURT’S AUTHORIZATION TO RENEW

4.	Plaintiff filed the original motion on August 6, 2026. ECF Nos. 6, 7. The Court denied it on August 12, 2026, “without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time.” ECF No. 12 at 1. The Order identified the filing of the First Amended Complaint and the motion on the same day, and it stated that “Defendants’ answers or other responses to the Original Complaint are not due until August 21, 2026.” Id.

5.	This Motion does not ask the Court to reconsider ECF No. 12. It renews the request on the record that now exists.

III.	THE CHANGED RECORD

6.	NCMEC, Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”), and Hall have each responded to the First Amended Complaint. ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45. Those motions remain pending.

7.	NCMEC’s memorandum in support of its motion states that NCMEC “responded to the subpoenas without awaiting formal service via two substantively-identical letters signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC,” and that Hall “at all times relevant was an employee of NCMEC.” ECF No. 11 at 2, 5 n.2. ECF No. 11 was docketed on August 12, 2026, before ECF No. 12. ECF No. 12 denied the original motion because responses were not yet due; it did not address the merits. Hall’s adoption of ECF No. 11 (ECF No. 45, Sept. 2, 2026) and Plaintiff’s two declarations (ECF Nos. 31, 59-2) came after ECF No. 12.

8.	Hall “adopts and joins in” NCMEC’s motion and memorandum and describes herself in that filing “as an employee of NCMEC.” ECF No. 45 at 1. Hall’s filing came after ECF No. 12.

9.	Plaintiff has filed two declarations under 28 U.S.C. § 1746 concerning the names under which he operated Meta accounts and the reason his legal name appears in the April 9, 2026 materials he transmitted to NCMEC. ECF No. 31 (filed August 24, 2026); ECF No. 59-2 (executed September 7, 2026; filed September 8, 2026). Both came after ECF No. 12.

10.	ECF No. 5 remains the operative pleading, and this Motion rests on it. The declarations are offered as record evidence under Rule 56(c)(1)(A). Their consideration does not depend on adoption of the proposed pleading attached to ECF No. 59, for which leave was denied. ECF No. 84.

11.	The denial of ECF No. 59 is the subject of Plaintiff’s pending objections (ECF Nos. 90, 91, 102). Plaintiff also files concurrently a renewed motion for leave to file a Second Amended Complaint. The proposed pleading retains the claims against Hall and NCMEC to which this Motion’s agency-and-scope request relates. Should leave be granted before determination of this Motion, Plaintiff requests consideration of the corresponding issue under the resulting operative pleading, following any supplemental briefing the Court deems necessary, rather than denial solely because the First Amended Complaint has been superseded.

IV.	THE ALTERNATIVE REQUEST UNDER RULE 56(g)

12.	If the Court does not grant all the relief requested in Part I, Plaintiff requests that the Court consider under Rule 56(g): (a) the agency-and-scope determination described in Part I, if the Court finds that determination not genuinely disputed but declines the form of judgment requested; and (b) the material facts numbered 1 through 17 in Part III of the Memorandum in Support, each considered separately. Plaintiff requests an order stating which of those facts are not genuinely in dispute and treating each such fact as established in this action.

13.	The numbered facts concern: (a) Hall’s employment and the capacity in which the letters issued; (b) the April 9, 2026 transmission and the absence of formal service before issuance; (c) the identifiers listed in Plaintiff’s Schedule A and the identifiers used in the letters; (d) Plaintiff’s account-name history, including that Plaintiff did not use “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to operate any Meta account he used before April 22, 2026, and that he operated the Facebook account involved in Meta’s July 4, 2022 enforcement action under the name “Jay Ballentine”; and (e) what the letters do not identify. The facts in categories (b) through (e) are material to Counts I, II, III, and VI. Not all of them are necessary to the agency-and-scope determination. Plaintiff presents them as alternative relief for that reason.

14.	A dispute concerning one numbered fact does not place any other numbered fact in dispute. Plaintiff requests separate consideration of each.

V.	TREATMENT UNDER RULE 56(e)(2)

15.	Plaintiff requests that, as to any numbered fact that is properly supported by Plaintiff and not properly addressed under Rule 56(c), the Court exercise its discretion under Rule 56(e)(2) and Local Civil Rule 56(B) to consider the fact undisputed for purposes of this Motion. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to treat any fact as established in this action on that basis alone. The Court retains its discretion under Rule 56(e)(1) to permit a party to address a fact, and under Rule 56(e)(4) to issue any other appropriate order.

VI.	WHAT THIS MOTION DOES NOT SEEK

16.	This Motion seeks no determination concerning: the existence, contents, source, or accuracy of any CyberTipline report; the truth or falsity of the letters’ report-existence statement as applied to Plaintiff personally; any agreement among Defendants; any Defendant’s motive or state of mind; damages; the litigation privilege; immunity under 18 U.S.C. § 2258D or 34 U.S.C. § 20505; NCMEC’s direct liability for its own conduct; or any claim against the Doe Defendants. It seeks no liability determination against Meta. It requests no discovery. It does not ask the Court to modify any order concerning scheduling or discovery.

VII.	DEFERRAL AND STATEMENT OF REASONS

17.	If the Court concludes that adjudication of this Motion should await disposition of the pending motions to dismiss or another event, Plaintiff requests that the Court defer ruling to that identified event, whether under Rule 56(d)(1) on any Defendant’s showing or under the Court’s authority to manage its docket, rather than deny the Motion without prejudice. Plaintiff further requests that the Court state on the record the reasons for its ruling, consistent with Rule 56(a).

VIII.	RELIEF REQUESTED

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff requests that the Court:

(1)	grant partial summary judgment, in the form of Proposed Order A, determining that Hall acted as NCMEC’s employee and agent, within the course and scope of her employment, when she signed and issued the two April 22, 2026 letters on NCMEC’s behalf, and that the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under Counts I, II, III, and VI is established;

(2)	in the alternative, if the relief in paragraph (1) is not granted in full, enter an order under Rule 56(g), in the form of Proposed Order B, addressing the agency-and-scope determination and stating which of the material facts numbered 1 through 17 in the Memorandum in Support are not genuinely in dispute, and treating each such fact as established in this action;

(3)	consider undisputed for purposes of this Motion, under Rule 56(e)(2) and Local Civil Rule 56(B) and within the Court’s discretion, each numbered fact that is properly supported by Plaintiff and not properly addressed under Rule 56(c);

(4)	consider each numbered fact separately, so that any showing of a need for discovery concerning one fact is evaluated as to that fact;

(5)	if the Court elects to postpone its ruling, defer ruling to an identified event, whether under Rule 56(d)(1) on any Defendant’s showing or under the Court’s authority to manage its docket, rather than deny the Motion without prejudice;

(6)	state on the record the reasons for its ruling, consistent with Rule 56(a); and

(7)	grant such further relief as is just.

Date: November 1, 2026		                      Respectfully submitted,

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847

Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503

jayballentine@protonmail.com

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S RENEWED RULE 56 MOTION FOR PARTIAL SUMMARY JUDGMENT

I.	NCMEC AND HALL DESCRIBE THE APRIL 22, 2026 LETTERS AS HALL’S WORK FOR NCMEC

NCMEC has told this Court how the two April 22, 2026 letters came to be. “On April 22, 2026, NCMEC responded to the subpoenas without awaiting formal service via two substantively-identical letters signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC.” ECF No. 11 at 2. Hall “adopts and joins in” that memorandum. ECF No. 45 at 1. The letters bear NCMEC’s letterhead. Each carries Hall’s signature above the title “Corporate Counsel.” ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3. In the earlier action over the same letters, NCMEC and Hall, through the counsel who represents both of them here, told this Court that Hall “was clearly acting in the course and scope of her employment in responding to the subpoenas.” ECF No. 7-4 at 7.

Plaintiff renews the request the Court denied on August 12, 2026, “without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time.” ECF No. 12 at 1. The request is narrow. Plaintiff asks the Court to determine under Rule 56(a) that Hall acted as NCMEC’s employee and agent, within the course and scope of her employment, when she signed and issued the two letters on NCMEC’s behalf. That determination resolves the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under Counts I, II, III, and VI. ECF No. 5 ¶ 21. It resolves nothing else.

If the Court does not grant that relief in full, Plaintiff asks the Court to consider, under Rule 56(g), the same determination and seventeen numbered facts. The facts concern Hall’s employment, the April 9, 2026 transmission, the absence of formal service, the wording of the letters, what the letters omit, and the names under which Plaintiff operated Meta accounts. Each rests on a document in the record, a statement of NCMEC or Hall, or Plaintiff’s sworn testimony about his own conduct.

The Motion does not ask what any CyberTipline report contains. It does not ask whether the letters were true, whether any privilege or immunity applies, whether Defendants agreed with one another, or what anyone intended. The submitted issue is the capacity in which Hall acted. The evidence on that issue comes from NCMEC and Hall.

II.	THE RESPONSE POSTURE AND THE EVIDENTIARY RECORD HAVE CHANGED SINCE AUGUST 12, 2026

A.	The August 12 Order.

The Court denied the original motion “without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time.” ECF No. 12 at 1. The Order identified two circumstances. Plaintiff had filed the First Amended Complaint and the motion on the same day. And “Defendants’ answers or other responses to the Original Complaint are not due until August 21, 2026.” Id. The Order found the motion premature on that basis.

B.	What has happened since.

Date

Development

Record

Aug. 6, 2026

Original motion and supporting evidence filed

ECF Nos. 6, 7, 7-1 through 7-9

Aug. 12, 2026

NCMEC moves to dismiss; its memorandum describes Hall’s capacity and states that the letters issued before formal service

ECF Nos. 10, 11

Aug. 12, 2026

Original motion denied without prejudice to renewal

ECF No. 12

Aug. 21, 2026

Meta moves to dismiss

ECF Nos. 21, 22

Aug. 24, 2026

First account-name declaration filed

ECF No. 31

Sept. 2, 2026

Hall moves to dismiss, adopting NCMEC’s motion and memorandum

ECF No. 45

Sept. 8, 2026

Second account-name declaration filed (executed Sept. 7, 2026)

ECF No. 59-2

Oct. 7, 2026

ECF Nos. 15 and 54 denied as premature; ECF No. 59 denied

ECF No. 84

Oct. 22, 2026

Case reassigned to Magistrate Judge Fitzpatrick

ECF No. 96

Oct. 29, 2026

Plaintiff’s scheduling and Rule 26(f) motions denied without prejudice

ECF No. 108

ECF No. 11 was docketed on August 12, 2026, before ECF No. 12. ECF No. 12 denied the original motion because responses were not yet due; it did not address the merits. Hall’s adoption of ECF No. 11 (ECF No. 45, Sept. 2, 2026) and Plaintiff’s two declarations (ECF Nos. 31, 59-2) came after ECF No. 12.

The change since August 12 is not the passage of time. The response posture the Order identified has changed: each appearing Defendant has responded. And the record has expanded. NCMEC’s memorandum states the capacity in which Hall acted and states that NCMEC issued the letters before formal service. ECF No. 11 at 2, 5 n.2. Hall adopted those statements. ECF No. 45 at 1. Plaintiff’s declarations supply testimony, on personal knowledge, about the names he used on Meta’s services and the reason his legal name appears in the April 9 materials. ECF No. 31 ¶¶ 2–7; ECF No. 59-2 ¶¶ 2–10. The letters, the April 9 materials, and the earlier joint filing of NCMEC and Hall were before the Court in August and remain in the record. ECF Nos. 7-4, 7-5, 7-6.

C.	Local Civil Rule 56.

Rule 56(b) permits a motion for summary judgment “at any time until 30 days after the close of all discovery” unless “a different time is set by local rule or the court orders otherwise.” Local Civil Rule 56(A) sets a different time for this District and displaces that default. “The time provisions of Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(b) shall not apply in this District.” The Court’s Order supplies the operative instruction here: renewal “at an appropriate time.” ECF No. 12 at 1. Local Civil Rule 56(C) requires leave of Court for separate motions for summary judgment on separate grounds. This Motion renews the one ground presented in ECF No. 6. Its alternative request under Rule 56(g) concerns the same submission and is not a separate ground.

The timing argument is this. The Court reserved renewal. The parties whose relationship is at issue have since responded and have described that relationship to the Court. The record now includes those descriptions and Plaintiff’s testimony. That is the record on which the submitted component can be assessed. The pending Rule 12 motions test the sufficiency of the pleading; this Motion asks the Court to determine one component on the record.

D.	The Motion rests on the operative pleading and seeks no change to any discovery or scheduling disposition.

IV.	THE GOVERNING STANDARD REQUIRES PLAINTIFF TO ESTABLISH THE SUBMITTED COMPONENT ON THE RECORD

A.	Rule 56(a) and the burden of a plaintiff-movant.

A party may move for summary judgment on “each claim or defense — or the part of each claim or defense — on which summary judgment is sought.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a). The Court “shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Id. A fact is material if it “might affect the outcome of the suit under the governing law.” Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986). A dispute is genuine if “the evidence is such that a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party.” Id. The question is whether the evidence presents a sufficient disagreement to require submission to a jury or is so one-sided that one party must prevail as a matter of law. Id. at 251–52. Credibility determinations, the weighing of evidence, and the drawing of legitimate inferences are jury functions, and the nonmovant’s evidence is believed with justifiable inferences drawn in its favor. Id. at 255.

Plaintiff bears the burden on the component he submits. He must show that the record permits only one conclusion on it: that Hall was NCMEC’s employee performing NCMEC’s business when she signed and issued the letters. The Court assesses the record with the inferences the rule requires in Defendants’ favor. Anderson states the general standard. It did not decide an agency question, and Plaintiff does not cite it for one.

B.	The evidentiary foundations.

Rule 56(c)(1)(A) permits a fact to be supported by citing particular parts of the record, including documents, declarations, and admissions. Rule 56(c)(4) requires a declaration to be made on personal knowledge, to set out facts that would be admissible in evidence, and to show the declarant’s competence. Plaintiff’s facts rest on four foundations, and each does a different job.

First, authentication. Plaintiff’s declarations identify the earlier joint filing of NCMEC and Hall, the letters, and the April 9 materials as true and correct copies obtained from identified sources. ECF No. 7-1 ¶¶ 4–6; Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 2–4. The copies of the letters in the record are reproduced from the exhibits NCMEC and Hall themselves filed in the earlier action. ECF No. 7-1 ¶ 5; Ballentine Decl. ¶ 3. Authentication establishes what a document is. It does not establish the truth of every assertion in the document.

Second, document contents. The letters and the April 9 materials are in the record. ECF Nos. 7-5, 7-6. Their wording is a fact about them.

Third, opposing-party representations. The statements of NCMEC and Hall in ECF Nos. 11 and 45, and in the joint filing reproduced at ECF No. 7-4, are statements of the parties whose relationship is at issue.

Fourth, personal-knowledge testimony. Plaintiff’s declarations state what Plaintiff did. ECF No. 31 ¶¶ 1, 8; ECF No. 59-2 ¶ 1.

C.	Virginia law supplies the substantive test and the effect of its presumption.

Counts I, II, III, and VI arise under Virginia law. Virginia law supplies the test for scope of employment. Where state law supplies the rule of decision, state law governs the effect of a presumption regarding the claim. Fed. R. Evid. 302. The Virginia presumption discussed in Part V therefore carries the effect Virginia gives it. It does not displace the summary-judgment standard, which remains federal.

V.	THE DOCUMENTS AND THE REPRESENTATIONS OF NCMEC AND HALL SUPPORT THE AGENCY-AND-SCOPE DETERMINATION

A.	Virginia law asks whether the employee was performing the employer’s business within the scope of the employment.

“[A]n employer is liable for the tortious act of his employee if the employee was performing his employer’s business and acting within the scope of his employment.” Parker v. Carilion Clinic, 296 Va. 319, 335, 819 S.E.2d 809 (2018) (citation omitted). The inquiry asks whether “the service itself, in which the tortious act was done, was within the ordinary course of [the employer’s] business.” Id. at 336 (citation omitted). The act must have been “within the scope of the duties of the employment and in the execution of the service for which the employee was engaged.” Id. at 338–39 (quotation marks and citation omitted). The employee must have committed the act “while actively engaged in a job-related service.” Id. at 339. Presence at work, use of the employer’s property, and the employer’s time are not enough. Id.

Parker reviewed a demurrer. The court held that the allegations permitted the vicarious-liability claim to proceed. It did not award the plaintiff judgment on the scope of employment. Plaintiff cites Parker for the test it states and for the presumption it describes, not for its result.

B.	The service Hall performed was NCMEC’s response to materials directed to NCMEC’s Legal Department.

The question is what service Hall was performing when she signed and issued the letters. The record describes it. Plaintiff directed his April 9 materials to NCMEC’s Legal Department. Fact 4; ECF No. 7-6 at 2. NCMEC received them. Fact 4; ECF No. 7-4 at 3. NCMEC then “responded.” ECF No. 11 at 2. It responded “via two substantively-identical letters signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC.” Id. The letters speak for NCMEC: “the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) provides its written responses as detailed below.” Fact 3. They issued on NCMEC’s letterhead, over the title “Corporate Counsel.” Fact 2. NCMEC calls them NCMEC’s responses. ECF No. 11 at 3 (“NCMEC responded precisely as requested”); ECF No. 7-4 at 3 (“NCMEC responded exactly as instructed in the subpoenas”). Hall adopts that description. ECF No. 45 at 1. And in the earlier action, NCMEC and Hall described the same conduct as within Hall’s employment. ECF No. 7-4 at 7.

Each of those items describes the same service: the issuance of NCMEC’s legal correspondence, by NCMEC’s in-house counsel, concerning materials directed to NCMEC’s Legal Department. That service was NCMEC’s business. The act at issue did not occur while Hall happened to be at work. The act at issue was the work.

NCMEC’s immunity argument states that “Plaintiff sent subpoenas to NCMEC seeking information it received and maintains pursuant to its statutory charge, and NCMEC responded precisely as requested,” and that “the complained-of activity clearly relates to NCMEC’s clearinghouse role.” ECF No. 11 at 8. NCMEC cannot argue that the letters were performance of its statutory functions and also that Hall acted outside NCMEC’s business.

C.	The employment presumption places the burden of production on NCMEC; it does not relieve Plaintiff of his burden.

Once the employment relationship is established, Virginia law presumes that the employee acted within the scope of employment. The presumption “shifts the burden of production to the employer to present facts sufficient to permit the factfinder to conclude that the employee was not acting within the scope of his employment at the time of his tortious conduct.” Parker, 296 Va. at 333 n.6. The burden of persuasion remains with the plaintiff. Id. at 342. The presumption is rebuttable; it gives way to positive facts to the contrary. Id. It operates at the stages at which the sufficiency of the claim is tested, including summary judgment. Id. at 333 & n.6.

Plaintiff does not rest on the presumption. He rests on the letters and on the statements of NCMEC and Hall about the service Hall performed. The presumption does one thing here. It identifies NCMEC as the party that must come forward with facts of a departure from the employment if NCMEC contends that one occurred. Whether the record then presents a genuine dispute is decided under Rule 56 on the whole record.

D.	NCMEC and Hall have described the conduct as within the scope of Hall’s employment, and those statements are admissible against them.

Statements of a party’s attorney concerning matters within the representation may be admitted against the client. “Generally, statements by an attorney concerning a matter within his employment may be admissible against the retaining client.” United States v. Blood, 806 F.2d 1218, 1221 (4th Cir. 1986). Blood found no admission on its facts, and it did not resolve the distinctions it noted between judicial and evidentiary admissions. Plaintiff relies on it for the general proposition only. Federal Rule of Evidence 801(d)(2) treats as not hearsay a statement offered against an opposing party that was made by a person the party authorized to make a statement on the subject, or by the party’s agent on a matter within the scope of that relationship and while it existed. Fed. R. Evid. 801(d)(2)(C), (D). Counsel’s statements in a signed filing on behalf of a client, concerning the client’s own employee and the client’s own correspondence, fall within those provisions. Rule 56(c)(1)(A) lists “admissions” among the materials that may support a fact.

The earlier joint filing. Plaintiff’s declaration authenticates the filing as the opposition NCMEC and Hall filed at ECF No. 20 in the earlier action. ECF No. 7-1 ¶ 4. The filing concerned the same two letters and the same April 9 materials. ECF No. 7-4 at 2–3. It stated that Hall “is and was an employee of the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, who was clearly acting in the course and scope of her employment in responding to the subpoenas.” Id. at 7. It stated that Hall “was working within the course and scope of her employment, and is entitled to the same defenses as the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.” Id. Counsel signed it for both Defendants. Id. at 9. Those statements were the stated ground for an argument the filing made to the Court. Id. at 7. Plaintiff offers them against NCMEC and Hall, the parties who made them, as evidentiary admissions. He does not contend that they are judicial admissions binding in this action.

The current filings. NCMEC’s memorandum states that the letters were “signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC,” and that Hall “at all times relevant was an employee of NCMEC.” ECF No. 11 at 2, 5 n.2. Those sentences are NCMEC’s own descriptions of its employee and its correspondence. They are not recitations of Plaintiff’s allegations; the memorandum marks its recitations of the First Amended Complaint separately. Compare id. at 2 (“Plaintiff alleges that on April 9, 2026 . . .”), with id. (“On April 22, 2026, NCMEC responded . . .”). Hall adopted the memorandum and described herself “as an employee of NCMEC.” ECF No. 45 at 1. The same counsel signed ECF No. 45 for both Defendants. Id. at 2. Plaintiff does not contend that every factual sentence in a dismissal brief is a binding judicial admission. He contends that these particular sentences are statements of NCMEC and Hall about their own relationship and their own conduct, and that Rule 56(c)(1)(A) and Rule 801(d)(2) permit the Court to consider them.

Hall’s footnote. Hall’s description of herself carries a footnote citing Plaintiff’s allegation that she “served as Corporate Counsel of NCMEC.” ECF No. 45 at 1 n.1. Hall asserted employee status as the ground for her own relief: “because Ms. Hall, as an employee of NCMEC, enjoys qualified statutory immunity under federal law.” Id. at 1 (footnote omitted). A party that asks a court to dismiss a claim because she is an employee has taken the position that she is one. The footnote identifies a source. It does not withdraw the position. Hall also “adopts and joins in” ECF No. 11. Id. That memorandum states independently of any allegation that the letters were “signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC,” ECF No. 11 at 2, and that “she at all times relevant was an employee of NCMEC,” id. at 5 n.2. It refers to “NCMEC or its employee, Defendant Hall.” Id. at 8.

Motive. The First Amended Complaint alleges that Hall acted with knowledge and with actual malice. Alleged intentional wrongdoing does not itself place an employee outside the scope of employment. Parker nevertheless treats the employee’s motive as relevant to the scope inquiry. 296 Va. at 340–41. Plaintiff therefore relies on the evidence that describes the service Hall performed: NCMEC’s own responses, signed by its Corporate Counsel, concerning materials directed to its Legal Department. The First Amended Complaint alleges that NCMEC approved the letters and authorized the use of its name and letterhead. ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 168, 196. Those allegations identify Plaintiff’s theory. They are not summary-judgment evidence, and Plaintiff does not offer them as such.

E.	The determination reaches employment and scope, and nothing else.

The determination establishes that Hall was NCMEC’s employee performing NCMEC’s business when she signed and issued the letters. It establishes nothing else. It does not establish that any tort occurred. It does not establish that the letters were made in a judicial proceeding for purposes of the litigation privilege NCMEC asserts, ECF No. 11 at 5, or that they were not. It does not establish that the letters arose from CyberTipline responsibilities or functions under 18 U.S.C. § 2258D, or that they did not. Scope of employment under Virginia common law and statutory function under § 2258D are different questions. The determination does not establish NCMEC’s direct liability for its own conduct, ECF No. 5 ¶ 21, any requirement for punitive recovery, or any defense. It does not reach any other person’s conduct. Each of those matters remains for later adjudication.

VI.	THE ACCOUNT-NAME AND DOCUMENT-HISTORY FACTS ARE MATERIAL AND WARRANT SEPARATE CONSIDERATION UNDER RULE 56(g)

A.	Plaintiff’s account-name history bears on the identification dispute framed by the pleading and by NCMEC.

The First Amended Complaint alleges that the letters identify Plaintiff by two names and an email address, ECF No. 5 ¶ 70; that the name “Jay Ballentine,” standing alone, is not uniquely identifying, id. ¶ 95; that the letters do not state whether any identifier appeared in any report, id. ¶ 96; and that a reader would understand the letters to associate Plaintiff personally with the reports, id. ¶¶ 100–01. Counts I, II, and VI rest on that association. Id. ¶¶ 187–91, 208–12, 255. NCMEC’s memorandum addresses the same identifiers. It argues that Plaintiff cannot plead falsity because “he does not have access to those reports,” and it describes the possibility that “they, or a person with the same name, or their e-mail address” is linked with a report. ECF No. 11 at 9. That passage identifies three possible referents. It does not establish that the reports concern different people, and it does not establish what NCMEC knows about the referents. It shows that the connection between each identifier and Plaintiff personally is in dispute.

Facts 8 through 12 bear on that dispute. They separate the name Plaintiff used to litigate from the names Plaintiff used on Meta’s services. Plaintiff did not use his legal name to operate any Meta account he used. Facts 8–10. He operated the Facebook account involved in the July 4, 2022 enforcement action under the name “Jay Ballentine.” Fact 11. His legal name appears in the April 9 materials because his federal actions were pending under that name. Fact 12. A fact is material if it might affect the outcome under the governing law. Anderson, 477 U.S. at 248. Which identifiers can be connected to Plaintiff’s own account use bears on the of-and-concerning and falsity elements of Counts I, II, and VI.

The declarations satisfy Rule 56(c)(4). Each is made on personal knowledge. ECF No. 31 ¶¶ 1, 8; ECF No. 59-2 ¶ 1; Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 1, 15. Each states facts about Plaintiff’s own conduct: the names he used, the account he operated, the materials he prepared. Plaintiff is competent to testify to his own conduct.

The facts have limits. Plaintiff’s nonuse of his legal name on Meta’s services does not prove that Meta never learned that name. It does not prove that the name is absent from any provider’s record or from any report. It does not establish the contents of any report or the ultimate falsity of any statement. The Motion asks the Court to establish what Plaintiff did. It does not ask the Court to establish the contents of records Plaintiff has not seen.

B.	The document-history facts establish what was sent and what the letters say.

Facts 4 through 7 and 13 through 17 describe documents. The April 9 materials and the letters are in the record. Plaintiff’s declarations authenticate them. ECF No. 7-1 ¶¶ 5–6; Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 3–4. NCMEC quoted both in its memorandum. ECF No. 11 at 2–3. Fact 5 rests on the statements of NCMEC and Hall.

These facts are material. NCMEC’s litigation-privilege argument describes the letters as a response to a subpoena. ECF No. 11 at 1, 5–7. Facts 4 and 5 establish what Plaintiff transmitted and that no subpoena had been formally served when NCMEC responded. NCMEC’s truth and implication arguments rest on what the letters say and on what Schedule A asked. Id. at 8–11, 13–14. Facts 6, 7, and 13 through 17 establish the identifiers Schedule A listed, the identifiers the letters used, and what the letters do not identify. Plaintiff’s defamation and insulting-words claims rest on the same words and omissions. ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 77, 91–97, 188–91, 255.

The findings establish what the documents say and when they were sent. They do not establish that the letters were prohibited, that no subpoena document existed, that no privilege applies, or that Plaintiff’s materials required the details the letters omit. Those consequences remain for the parties to argue and for the Court to decide.

C.	Establishment would reduce later proof.

If these facts are established, the parties will not need to prove again what the April 9 materials contained, that formal service had not occurred when the letters issued, what the letters state and omit, or which names Plaintiff used on Meta’s services. The findings narrow the identification and falsity disputes. They do not eliminate them.

VII.	THE COURT MAY TREAT PROPERLY SUPPORTED FACTS AS UNDISPUTED WITHIN THE LIMITS OF RULE 56(e)

A.	The sequence under Rule 56(c) and Rule 56(e).

Rule 56(c)(1) requires a party asserting that a fact cannot be or is genuinely disputed to support the assertion by citing particular parts of the record, or by showing that the materials cited do not establish the absence or presence of a genuine dispute, or that an adverse party cannot produce admissible evidence to support the fact. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(1)(A)–(B). Rule 56(c)(2) permits an objection that cited material cannot be presented in a form that would be admissible in evidence. Local Civil Rule 56(B) requires an opposing brief to include a specifically captioned section listing the material facts the opponent contends are genuinely in issue, with citations to the parts of the record relied on. The local rule then provides: “In determining a motion for summary judgment, the Court may assume that facts identified by the moving party in its listing of material facts are admitted, unless such a fact is controverted in the statement of genuine issues filed in opposition to the motion.”

The sequence is this. First, Plaintiff must support each asserted fact. Part III does so. Second, an opposing party may challenge the evidence: its sufficiency to establish the proposition, its admissibility, or its materiality. A legal argument that the cited materials do not establish the proposition is a proper response under Rule 56(c)(1)(B). An objection under Rule 56(c)(2) is a proper response. A showing of immateriality is a proper response. Third, a bare contradiction without record support is not sufficient. Fourth, where a fact is properly supported and not properly addressed, the Court may give an opportunity to address it, consider it undisputed for purposes of the Motion, or issue another appropriate order. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(e)(1), (2), (4). Fifth, any establishment of a fact in the action, beyond this Motion, requires separate consideration under Rule 56(g).

B.	Motion-specific treatment and case-wide treatment are different.

Rule 56(e)(2) permits the Court to consider a fact undisputed “for purposes of the motion.” Local Civil Rule 56(B) permits the same assumption in determining the Motion. Neither establishes a fact for trial. Rule 56(g) reaches further. When the Court does not grant all the relief requested by the motion, it “may enter an order stating any material fact . . . that is not genuinely in dispute and treating the fact as established in the case.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(g). Plaintiff requests the two forms of treatment in that order and keeps them distinct.

A Defendant may accept a fact for purposes of this Motion only. Rule 56(c)(1)(A) recognizes stipulations “made for purposes of the motion only.” Plaintiff’s express request under Rule 56(g) gives notice that each numbered fact is offered for establishment in the action. That notice does not convert a limited acceptance into an unlimited one. A Defendant that accepts a fact for the Motion only may say so in its statement of genuine issues, and the Court may take that limitation into account in deciding whether to establish the fact under Rule 56(g). Plaintiff does not contend that any Defendant’s earlier briefing operates as a response to this Motion. The oppositions to this Motion are where each fact is to be addressed.

VIII.	ANY CLAIMED NEED FOR DISCOVERY SHOULD BE EVALUATED AGAINST THE PARTICULAR DETERMINATION IT AFFECTS

As a general rule, summary judgment is appropriate only after adequate time for discovery. Harrods Ltd. v. Sixty Internet Domain Names, 302 F.3d 214, 244 (4th Cir. 2002). Rule 56(d) supplies the mechanism. A nonmovant that cannot present facts essential to its opposition may show that by affidavit or declaration, “for specified reasons,” and the Court may defer considering the motion, deny it, allow time for discovery, or issue any other appropriate order. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(d). The Fourth Circuit gives such a showing great weight. Harrods, 302 F.3d at 244. The court has also recognized that a nonmovant’s objections may serve as the functional equivalent of an affidavit where they adequately inform the district court of the discovery needed and the nonmovant has not been lax in pursuing it. Id. at 244–45; see Pledger v. Lynch, 5 F.4th 511, 526 (4th Cir. 2021) (applying that principle to the objections of a pro se prisoner). Harrods applied the predecessor of current Rule 56(d). Plaintiff does not ask the Court to hold any Defendant to a form. He asks that any claimed need be stated for the fact it affects.

Harrods identified circumstances in which early summary judgment carries particular risk: where the relevant facts are exclusively in the control of the opposing party, and where the case involves complex factual questions about intent and motive. 302 F.3d at 246–47. The agency-and-scope component should be evaluated against those circumstances. The facts concern Hall’s employment, the capacity in which she acted, and the service she performed when she signed NCMEC’s correspondence. NCMEC and Hall have described those matters themselves, in this action and in the earlier one. The Motion asks the Court to consider those descriptions and the letters. If NCMEC or Hall contends that discovery is needed before the Court can assess the relationship they have already described, that contention should identify what discovery is needed and why.

The document facts rest on the authenticated documents. ECF Nos. 7-5, 7-6; ECF No. 7-1 ¶¶ 5–6. Their wording is before the Court now.

The account-name facts rest on Plaintiff’s testimony about his own conduct. A Defendant may contend that it needs discovery to test that testimony. If so, Rule 56(d) is the vehicle, and the showing should identify the fact affected and the discovery needed. A showing concerning one fact does not reach the others.

Plaintiff requests separate treatment where the facts are separable. The Court may defer ruling to an identified event, whether under Rule 56(d)(1) on any Defendant’s showing or under the Court’s authority to manage its docket, rather than deny the Motion without prejudice. Rule 56(g) permits the Court to establish any material fact not genuinely in dispute. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to establish under Rule 56(g) a fact as to which a Defendant has made a sufficient Rule 56(d) showing. He asks that the showing be matched to the fact it affects, and that the facts it does not affect be decided.

IX.	REQUESTED DISPOSITION

Plaintiff requests the following disposition. First, a determination under Rule 56(a) of the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under Counts I, II, III, and VI, in the form of Proposed Order A. Second, if that relief is not granted in full, consideration under Rule 56(g) of the same determination and of Facts 1 through 17, each separately, in the form of Proposed Order B. Third, within the Court’s discretion under Rule 56(e)(2) and Local Civil Rule 56(B), treatment of any fact properly supported by Plaintiff and not properly addressed under Rule 56(c) as undisputed for purposes of the Motion. Fourth, separate consideration of separable facts where a Defendant shows a need for discovery concerning one of them. Fifth, if the Court elects to postpone its ruling, deferral to an identified event, whether under Rule 56(d)(1) on any Defendant’s showing or under the Court’s authority to manage its docket, rather than denial without prejudice. Sixth, a statement on the record of the reasons for the Court’s ruling, consistent with Rule 56(a).

X.	CONCLUSION

NCMEC and Hall have described the April 22, 2026 letters as Hall’s work for NCMEC. The letters say the same on their face. Plaintiff requests partial summary judgment in the form of Proposed Order A, determining that Hall acted as NCMEC’s employee and agent, within the course and scope of her employment, when she signed and issued the letters on NCMEC’s behalf, and that the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under Counts I, II, III, and VI is established. In the alternative, Plaintiff requests an order under Rule 56(g) in the form of Proposed Order B, with each fact considered separately.

1.	I am the Plaintiff in this action. I make this Declaration based upon my personal knowledge. I am competent to testify to the matters stated herein.

2.	Exhibit 3 is a true and correct copy of the Opposition of Defendants Katie Hall and the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children to Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to File a First Amended Complaint, filed at ECF No. 20 in Ballentine v. The copies in Exhibit 4 are reproduced from ECF No. 5, Exhibits A and B, in the 1341 Action. They are docketed in this action at ECF No. 7-5.

4.	Exhibit 5 consists of true and correct copies of the written materials I transmitted on April 9, 2026 to the Legal Department of the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, providing advance notice of subpoenas I intended to serve. The copies in Exhibit 5 are reproduced from ECF No. 5, Exhibit C, in the 1341 Action. They are docketed in this action at ECF No. 7-6.

5.	On April 9, 2026, I transmitted written materials to the Legal Department of the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, providing advance notice of subpoenas I intended to serve.

6.	Before April 22, 2026, I never used the name “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any account on any product or service owned or operated by Meta Platforms, Inc. that I used.

7.	I never used “Marvelle J. Ballentine” as a username, profile name, display name, account name, or other identity by which I identified myself on Facebook, Instagram, Threads, WhatsApp, Oculus, Meta Quest, or any other Meta product or service that I used.

8.	I did not provide “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to Meta Platforms, Inc. as the name identifying me or any Meta account that I created, maintained, or operated.

9.	On July 4, 2022, Meta Platforms, Inc. invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy against the Facebook account that I operated.

10.	The Facebook account against which Meta invoked that policy was operated by me under the name “Jay Ballentine.”

11.	Meta’s July 4, 2022 enforcement action was not issued against an account operated by me under the name “Marvelle J. Ballentine.”

12.	In connection with my online identity, including my use of Meta products and services, I used the name “Jay Ballentine,” rather than “Marvelle J. Ballentine.”

13.	To the extent “Marvelle J. Ballentine” appeared in the April 9, 2026 correspondence, draft subpoena materials, or other litigation materials that I transmitted to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, I included that name because it is my legal name and the name under which the underlying federal litigation was pending.

14.	I did not include that name because I had used it to identify or operate any Meta account.

15.	The foregoing statements concern my own use of my name, my own operation of Meta products and services, and my own preparation and transmission of the litigation materials referenced above. Each of those matters is within my personal knowledge.

I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the United States of America that the foregoing is true and correct.

       TO PLAINTIFF'S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT

          Defendants the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children and Katie Hall

  (collectively, "NCMEC"), by and through undersigned counsel and pursuant to the Rules and

  Orders of this Honorable Court, hereby respectfully oppose Plaintiff's "Motion for Leave to File

  First Amended and Supplemental Complaint." [Doc. 18] The Motion should be denied, on the

  grounds that the Motion is futile, as Plaintiff's proposed FAC would fail to withstand a motion to

  dismiss as it is predicated entirely on conclusory allegations and factually unsupported non-

  sequiturs. Further, to the extent the proposed FAC fails to state a claim, Plaintiff would have no

  claims to assert against the proposed new defendants. In further support, NCMEC states as

  follows :

  I.      FACTUAL/PROCEDURAL SETTING

          This matter arises out of two subpoenas sent, but not formally served, by the pro se

  Plaintiff, Mr. Marvelle Ballentine to NCMEC, in which subpoenas Plaintiff instructed the

  National Center for Missing & Exploited Children to:

          produce a document sufficient to show whether [NCMEC] received or maintains
          any CyberTipline report, referral, or submission concerning: (1) Marvelle J.

             Ballentine; (2) Jay Ballentine; and/or (3) the account-level identifier
             jaychizza@icloud.com for the period July 2, 2022 through the date of compliance.

  Plaintiff carefully avoids inclusion of those subpoenas in his pleadings, but they are

  highly relevant, as shortly after receiving the letters, Ms. Hall-an employee of the

  National Center for Missing and Exploited Children-wrote two identical responses,

  stating:

             Dear Mr. Ballentine:
             In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for
             Missing & Exploited Children ("NCMEC") provides its written responses as
             detailed below: NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning
             (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level
             identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.

  In other words, NCMEC responded exactly as instructed in the subpoenas. Despite this, and

  despite the fact that Plaintiff chose the language utilized in the subpoenas, Plaintiff has filed the

  present lawsuit, alleging two counts of "Defamation Per Se and Defamation by Implication," and

  seeks compensatory damages of $25,000,000.00, punitive damages, etc.

         NCMEC filed a Motion to Dismiss, which is set for hearing on August 7, 2026. On July

  27, 2026, Plaintiff filed his Motion for Leave to File a First Amended and Supplemental

  Complaint, along with a copy of the proposed First Amended Complaint ["FAC"]. Plaintiff

  appears to seek to drop the National Center for Missing and Exploitd Children as a Defendant,

  join Meta Platforms, Inc. and unidentified "John/Jane Does" as Defendants, to add a claim for a

  violation of 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2), to add a claim for Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress

  as to Defendant Hall, and to allege additional facts as to alleged events occurring after the filing

  of Plaintiff's operative Complaint.

  II.      STANDARD OF REVIEW

           Under Rule 15(a), leave to amend is to be granted freely, "absent bad faith, undue

  prejudice to the opposing party, or futility of amendment." Hardee v. Mun . Jail Va. Beach

  Sheriff's Off, 2025 U.S . Dist. LEXIS 184735, *5 (E.D. Va. 2025) (quoting United States v.

  Pittman, 209 F.3d 314,317 (4th Cir. 2000)); Save Our Sound OBX, Inc. v. NC. DOT, 914 F.3d

  213 , 228 (4th Cir. 2019) (same). A proposed amendment is futile "when it is clearly insufficient

  or frivolous on its face .. . [or[ if the claim it presents would not survive a motion to dismiss."

  Id.; United States ex rel. Wilson v. Kellogg Brown & Root, Inc., 525 F.3d 370,375 (4th Cir.

  2008).

           Under Rule 20, multiple persons may be joined in one action as defendants if:

  "(A) any right to relief is asserted against them jointly, severally, or in the alternative with

  respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or

  occurrences; and (B) any question of law or fact common to all defendants will arise in the

  action." Fed. R. Civ. P. 20(a)(2); Ellis v. Werfel, 86 F.4th 1032, 1035 (4th Cir. 2023).

  III.     ARGUMENT

           A. Amendment Would Be Futile, as the FAC Would Not Survive a Motion to Dismiss.

           First, NCMEC respectfully submits that the FAC suffers from the same defects alleged in

  the pending Motion to Dismiss. Without repeating those arguments verbatim in this matter,

  Plaintiff's claims as to NCMEC are barred by the litigation privilege, NCMEC is statutorily

  immune to Plaintiff's claims, and because Plaintiff has failed to plausibly assert that the

  representations that are allegedly defamatory are false, and Plaintiff's theory of defamation by

  implication would require that the language in question be extended beyond its ordinary and

  common acceptation. Webb v. Virginian-Pilot Media Cos., 287 Va. 84, 89 (2014) (quoting

  Carwile v. Richmond Newspapers, Inc., 196 Va. 1, 9 (1954)). Plaintiff's 41-page proposed FAC

  does not disturb these arguments.

         Additionally, the proposed FAC's additional causes of action appear unlikely to survive a

  Rule 12(b)( 6) motion, as well, and as such are futile . As to proposed Count III-Intentional

  Infliction of Emotional Distress as to Defendant Hall-Plaintiff fails to state a claim upon which

  relief may be granted. In order to succeed on such a claim under Virginia law, a plaintiff must

  show four elements of proof: (1) the conduct was intentional or reckless; (2) the conduct was

  "outrageous or intolerable;" (3) there was a casual connection between the conduct and the

  resulting emotional distress; and (4) the resulting emotional distress was severe. Super Valu, Inc.

  v. Johnson , 276 Va. 356, 370 (2008); Almy v. Grisham , 273 Va. 68 (2007); Young v. Wilson , 2026

  U.S. Dist. LEXIS 147023, *10 (E.D. Va. 2026) (quoting Almy). "[O]nly where the conduct has

  been so outrageous in character, and so extreme in degree, as to go beyond all possible bounds of

  decency, and to be regarded as atrocious, and utterly intolerable in a civilized community" can a

  claim survive. Young, 2026 U.S . Dist. LEXIS at *10 (quoting Russo v. White, 241 Va. 23 , 27

  (1991)). This is an exacting standard-as noted by the Virginia Supreme Court in Russo v.

  White, even if a defendant intended to inflict emotional distress, and acted in a fashion that could

  support an award of punitive damages for another tort, the conduct must be utterly intolerable.

  241 Va. 23 , 27 (1991).

         The proposed FAC falls well short of that standard. Again, this is about Plaintiff sending

  subpoenas to NCMEC, and NCMEC responding without waiting to be formally served. It

  cannot be said that NCMEC responding to those subpoenas, using the exact language specified

  by Plaintiff, is "outrageous," "extreme," goes "beyond all possible bounds of decency," or is

  "utterly intolerable in a civilized community," notwithstanding Plaintiff's conclusory assertions

  to the contrary.

         As to proposed Count IV-"Conspiracy to Deter a Party and Witness, by Intimidation,

  From Attending and Testifying in Courts of the United States--42 U.S.C. § 1985(2)," Plaintiff

  alleges that Defendant Hall and Meta Platforms, Inc. "reached an understanding that Hall would

  issue correspondence asserting the existence of CyberTipline reports associated with one or more

  of Plaintiff's identifiers before service of the intended subpoenas and while motions directed at

  the same discovery remained pending. This allegation rests on the coordinated, case-specific

  sequence pleaded ... below ... " Proposed FAC at~ 118. These allegations are entirely

  conclusory, "upon information and belief," and the numbered proof of the "understanding" is

  flatly nonsensical. For example, Plaintiff seizes on the fact that NCMEC did not wait for formal

  service as proof of the apparent conspiracy. Proposed FAC at~~ 123, 125 . Plaintiff also points to

  the fact that the allegedly-defamatory letters omitted reporting provider, report dates, disposition,

  etc. Id. at~ 126. Again, Plaintiff's subpoenas instructed that the responses were not to include

  "any material beyond what is necessary to show the existence or nonexistence of a

  CyberTipline report, referral, or submission ." It is utterly implausible to build proof of a

  conspiracy upon a subpoena recipient following, to a "t," the instructions in the subpoenas.

  These conclusory and nonsensical allegations-and the tortured inference drawn from them-are

  not entitled to the presumption of truth, and without which, the claim would fail.

         While the existence of this supposed agreement fails, so too does the "purpose of the

  agreement," which is itself a conclusory allegation-that NCMEC responded to the subpoenas

  "to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from continuing to attend [the other lawsuits] ... and from

  testifying freely, fully, and truthfully ... in those pending federal proceedings." Proposed FAC at

  ~ 211.   This proposed Count (as well as proposed Count III) is a "threadbare recital of the

  elements of a cause of action, supported by mere conclusory statements," and cannot state a

  claim upon which relief may be granted. Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009).

           A claim for relief under 42 U.S .C. § 1985(2) requires a plaintiff to "plausibly allege an

  agreement or 'meeting of minds' among the alleged conspirators." Simmons v. Poe, 47 F.3d

  13 70, 13 77 (4th Cir. 1995). Plaintiff's proposed FAC falls well short of that threshold, and

  would not survive a motion to dismiss, as both the existence of, and alleged aim of, the

  conspiracy are entirely predicated on nonsensical conclusory allegations. In the Fourth Circuit,

  "allegations of parallel conduct and a bare assertion of a conspiracy are not enough for a claim to

  proceed" under 42 U.S.C. § 1985 . Thomas v. Salvation Army S. Terr., 841 F.3d 632, 637 (4th Cir.

  2016); A Society Without a Name v. Virginia, 655 F.3d 342, 347 (4th Cir. 2011).

           B. There is No Basis to Include the Proposed New Defendants in this Matter.

           Finally, Plaintiff's proposed FAC seeks to add Meta Platforms, Inc. and six John or Jane

  Doe defendants. For reasons unclear-and despite the fact that Defendant Hall is and was an

  employee of the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, who was clearly acting in

  the course and scope of her employment in responding to the subpoenas-Plaintiff seeks to drop

  the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, add persons who allegedly

  communicated and conspired with Defendant Hall, and add Meta Platforms, Inc. as a defendant

  under the 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) claim.

           As to the exclusion of the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, its

  removal from the lawsuit would have no effect on the pending motion to dismiss, or viability of

  Plaintiff's claims. Defendant Hall was working within the course and scope of her employment,

  and is entitled to the same defenses as the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.

                                                                                                    185




  To the extent Plaintiff believes that singling out Ms. Hall will exert pressure on NCMEC, he is

  mistaken.

         Further, under Rule 20, multiple defendants can be joined in one action only if any right

  to relief is asserted against them "with respect to or arising out of the same transaction,

  occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences, and any question of law or fact common to

  all defendants will arise in the action." Fed. R. Civ. P. 20(a)(2). Absent Plaintiff's conclusory

  and imaginary conspiracy-whereby NCMEC responded to subpoenas, precisely as requested,

  supposedly in order to further a common scheme to intimidate Plaintiff out of testifying-there is

  no transaction, occurrence, or series thereof common to all defendants. (To wit, there would be

  no claim asserted as to John or Jane Does, or Meta Platforms, Inc.)

  IV.    CONCLUSION

         In light of the foregoing, NCMEC respectfully submits that Plaintiffs' Motion for Leave

  to File an Amended Complaint should be denied as futile . The new allegations, and new counts,

  in the proposed FAC are conclusory, lacking factual support, and those counts fail to state a

  claim upon which relief may be granted. Further, the only basis by which there is any common

  transaction, occurrence, or series thereof would be if Plaintiff were to plausibly assert the

  existence of a conspiracy under 42 U.S .C. § 1985(2), which the proposed FAC fails to do . As

  such, NCMEC respectfully requests that Plaintiff's Motion for Leave be denied, and that this

  matter proceed to the hearing set for August 7, 2026 on NCMEC's Motion to Dismiss.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

[PROPOSED] ORDER A — GRANTING PARTIAL SUMMARY JUDGMENT ON THE AGENCY-AND-SCOPE COMPONENT

This matter is before the Court on Plaintiff’s Renewed Rule 56 Motion for Partial Summary Judgment (the “Motion”). The Motion concerns the two letters dated April 22, 2026, signed by Defendant Katie Hall on the letterhead of Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”), that appear in the record at ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3 (the “Letters”). The Court has considered the Motion, the Memorandum in Support, the parties’ submissions, if any, and the record.

The Court finds as follows. The Letters bear NCMEC’s letterhead and Hall’s signature above the title “Corporate Counsel.” ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3. Each Letter states that NCMEC provides its written responses. Id. NCMEC has stated in this action that the Letters were “signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC,” and that Hall “at all times relevant was an employee of NCMEC.” ECF No. 11 at 2, 5 n.2. Hall has adopted that memorandum and has described herself as an employee of NCMEC. ECF No. 45 at 1. In an earlier action concerning the same Letters, NCMEC and Hall, through common counsel, stated that Hall “was clearly acting in the course and scope of her employment in responding to the subpoenas.” ECF No. 7-4 at 7. No party has identified record evidence that Hall acted outside the scope of her employment, or on a motive of her own, when she signed and issued the Letters.

Under Virginia law, an employer is liable for the tortious act of its employee if the employee was performing the employer’s business and acting within the scope of employment, and the inquiry asks whether the service in which the act was done was within the ordinary course of the employer’s business and within the scope of the duties for which the employee was engaged. Parker v. Carilion Clinic, 296 Va. 319, 335–39, 819 S.E.2d 809 (2018). On this record, no reasonable jury could find that Hall was performing other than NCMEC’s business, or acting outside the scope of her employment, when she signed and issued the Letters. There is no genuine dispute as to the material facts stated above, and Plaintiff is entitled to judgment as a matter of law on the part of Counts I, II, III, and VI of the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) identified below. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a). Accordingly, it is hereby

ORDERED that the Motion is GRANTED as to the agency-and-scope component identified in Part I of the Motion, as follows:

1.	Hall was an employee of NCMEC and served as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel when she signed and issued the Letters.

2.	Hall signed and issued the Letters on NCMEC’s behalf, as NCMEC’s agent, within the course and scope of her employment, in the execution of the service for which NCMEC employed her.

3.	The agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under Counts I, II, III, and VI of the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 21, 195, 216, 230, 258) is established. Whether Hall’s conduct in signing and issuing the Letters was tortious, and whether NCMEC is liable for that conduct under any count, remain for later adjudication.

It is FURTHER ORDERED that, if leave to file a Second Amended Complaint has been granted, the determination in paragraphs 1 through 3 above applies to the corresponding claims under the resulting operative pleading.

It is FURTHER ORDERED that this Order does not determine: whether any element of Counts I, II, III, or VI other than the component stated above is established; any defense asserted or available to Hall or NCMEC, including the litigation privilege and any immunity under 18 U.S.C. § 2258D or 34 U.S.C. § 20505; NCMEC’s direct liability for its own conduct; the existence, contents, source, or accuracy of any CyberTipline report; the truth or falsity of any statement in the Letters; the existence of any agreement among Defendants; any Defendant’s motive or state of mind; any claim against Meta Platforms, Inc. or the Doe Defendants; or any question of damages or other remedy. All such matters are reserved.

It is FURTHER ORDERED that this Order does not determine the material facts numbered 1 through 17 in Part III of the Memorandum in Support, except to the extent stated in paragraphs 1 and 2 above.

It is FURTHER ORDERED that this Order is not a final judgment and does not direct the entry of judgment under Rule 54(b).

IT IS SO ORDERED. The Clerk is directed to provide a copy of this Order to Plaintiff at his address of record and to counsel of record.

Alexandria, Virginia

__________, 2026

______________________________

Rossie D. Alston, Jr.

United States District Judge
