UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

[PROPOSED] ORDER B — ESTABLISHING MATERIAL FACTS UNDER FEDERAL RULE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE 56(g)

This matter is before the Court on Plaintiff’s Renewed Rule 56 Motion for Partial Summary Judgment (the “Motion”). The Motion concerns the two letters dated April 22, 2026, signed by Defendant Katie Hall on the letterhead of Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”), that appear in the record at ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3 (the “Letters”). The Court has considered the Motion, the Memorandum in Support, the parties’ submissions, if any, and the record.

The Court has applied the standard of Rule 56(a) to the agency-and-scope component identified in Part I of the Motion. The Court does not grant the Motion’s request for partial summary judgment under Rule 56(a) in the form requested, for the reasons stated by the Court on the record. Because the Court does not grant all the relief requested by the Motion, the Court has considered under Rule 56(g) each material fact listed in Part III of the Memorandum in Support, the parties’ statements of genuine issues, if any, and the opportunity of each affected party to oppose establishment of each fact. The Court finds that the facts stated below are not genuinely in dispute. Accordingly, it is hereby

ORDERED that the following facts are established in this action and shall be treated as established in all further proceedings. Each numbered provision is severable. The Court’s omission of any proposed fact from this Order does not establish any contrary proposition and leaves that matter for later proceedings.

A.	Hall’s employment and the Letters

1.	Katie Hall was an employee of NCMEC and served as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel when she signed and issued the Letters.

2.	Hall signed each of the two Letters. Each Letter is on NCMEC letterhead. The signature block of each Letter identifies Hall as “Corporate Counsel.”

3.	The first sentence of the body of each Letter states: “In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) provides its written responses as detailed below.” The reference line of one Letter identifies the matter as “Marvelle Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al.” The reference line of the other identifies the matter as “Marvelle Ballentine v. Devin S. Anderson, et al.”

B.	The April 9, 2026 materials and formal service

4.	On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff transmitted to NCMEC’s Legal Department a letter giving advance notice of intended subpoenas in two separate matters, together with two signed subpoena forms and a Schedule A for each. The letter stated that each notice was accompanied by a signed copy of the draft subpoena “that will be formally served after the notice period has run.” NCMEC received the materials.

5.	No subpoena had been formally served on NCMEC when NCMEC issued the Letters.

6.	Schedule A to each subpoena form directed production of a document sufficient to show whether NCMEC received or maintains any CyberTipline report, referral, or submission concerning three identifiers. Schedule A listed the identifiers as “(1) Marvelle J. Ballentine,” “(2) Jay Ballentine,” and “(3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com,” and joined them with “and/or.”

7.	Each Letter states that NCMEC has received two CyberTipline reports “concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com.” The three identifiers and the connector “and/or” in that sentence are the identifiers and connector that appear in Schedule A.

C.	Plaintiff’s account-name history

8.	Before April 22, 2026, Plaintiff did not use the name “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any account on any product or service owned or operated by Meta Platforms, Inc. that Plaintiff used.

9.	Before April 22, 2026, Plaintiff did not use “Marvelle J. Ballentine” as a username, profile name, display name, account name, or other identity by which he identified himself on Facebook, Instagram, Threads, WhatsApp, Oculus, Meta Quest, or any other Meta product or service that he used.

10.	Before April 22, 2026, Plaintiff did not provide “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to Meta Platforms, Inc. as the name identifying him for purposes of any Meta account that he created, maintained, or operated, or as the name identifying any such account. This provision concerns the identification of accounts. It does not concern litigation filings or other communications.

11.	Plaintiff operated the Facebook account that was the subject of Meta Platforms, Inc.’s July 4, 2022 enforcement action under the name “Jay Ballentine.”

12.	Plaintiff included “Marvelle J. Ballentine” in the April 9, 2026 correspondence and subpoena materials that he transmitted to NCMEC because it is his legal name and the name under which the underlying federal litigation was pending, and not because he had used that name to identify or operate any Meta account.

D.	What the Letters do not identify

13.	Neither Letter identifies the electronic service provider or other source that submitted either report.

14.	Neither Letter supplies a report number for either report.

15.	Neither Letter supplies a report-specific date for either report. Each Letter refers only to a period “between July 1, 2022 and the present.”

16.	Neither Letter states which of the three listed identifiers matched either report.

17.	Neither Letter identifies any particular Facebook account as the subject of either report.

It is FURTHER ORDERED that, under Rule 56(g), the following fact is established in this action: Hall signed and issued the Letters on NCMEC’s behalf, as NCMEC’s agent, within the course and scope of her employment, in the execution of the service for which NCMEC employed her. This determination concerns the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC’s potential vicarious liability under Counts I, II, III, and VI of the First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 21, 195, 216, 230, 258) and nothing else.

It is FURTHER ORDERED that a statement of NCMEC or Hall considered by the Court in establishing any fact above is not thereby deemed an admission of Meta Platforms, Inc. All questions of liability against Meta Platforms, Inc. are reserved.

It is FURTHER ORDERED that, if leave to file a Second Amended Complaint has been granted, any agency-and-scope determination stated above applies to the corresponding claims under the resulting operative pleading.

It is FURTHER ORDERED that this Order does not determine: whether Hall’s conduct was tortious; any defense asserted or available to any Defendant, including the litigation privilege and any immunity under 18 U.S.C. § 2258D or 34 U.S.C. § 20505; NCMEC’s direct liability for its own conduct; the existence, contents, source, or accuracy of any CyberTipline report; the truth or falsity of any statement in the Letters as applied to Plaintiff personally; the existence of any agreement among Defendants; any Defendant’s motive or state of mind; any claim against the Doe Defendants; or any question of damages or other remedy. All such matters are reserved. This Order is not a final judgment and does not direct the entry of judgment under Rule 54(b).

IT IS SO ORDERED. The Clerk is directed to provide a copy of this Order to Plaintiff at his address of record and to counsel of record.

Alexandria, Virginia

__________, 2026

______________________________

Rossie D. Alston, Jr.

United States District Judge

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

PLAINTIFF’S RULE 54(b) MOTION TO RECONSIDER ECF NO. 108 AS TO ECF NO. 105

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b) for reconsideration of the Order signed and filed October 29, 2026 and entered October 30, 2026 (ECF No. 108), insofar as it denied Plaintiff’s Motion for an Order Directing Completion of the Rule 26(f) Conference and Submission of a Discovery Plan (ECF No. 105). ECF No. 108 also denied Plaintiff’s separate motion for a scheduling order (ECF No. 103). This Motion does not seek reconsideration of that disposition. This Motion is addressed to the Magistrate Judge who entered ECF No. 108. It asks him to revise his own interlocutory order within the authority referred under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). It is not an objection under Rule 72(a). Under Local Civil Rule 7(F), a supporting memorandum, Proposed Order A, and Proposed Order B accompany this Motion.

I.	GROUNDS

1.	ECF No. 105 requested a conference and one report. ECF No. 105 requested an order directing Plaintiff and counsel for each appearing Defendant to complete the conference Rule 26(f) requires by a date certain and to file one written report stating the parties’ agreed proposals and each party’s separately attributed position on the subjects Rule 26(f)(3) requires the discovery plan to address. ECF No. 105 ¶ 11(a)–(c). The report would record any party’s proposal to postpone, phase, or limit discovery. ECF No. 105 ¶¶ 6, 11(b). ECF No. 105 asked that, if the Court postponed the conference, the order identify the scope of the postponement and a definite date or event for renewed consideration. ECF No. 105 ¶ 12.

2.	ECF No. 105 excluded discovery responses and modification of ECF No. 84. ECF No. 105 requested no answers to interrogatories, no production of documents, no sanctions, and no modification of ECF No. 84. ECF No. 105 ¶ 8. It did not renew the requests that ECF No. 84 denied. Id. It asked the Court to decide when the conference would occur, and it left every proposal concerning the sequencing or postponement of substantive discovery to the report. ECF No. 106 at 5.

3.	ECF No. 108 denied the planning request on the attributed discovery-postponement decision. ECF No. 108 identified the request as one for “an order directing the parties to complete a Rule 26(f) conference and file respective discovery plans.” ECF No. 108 at 1. Its case-specific ground is stated in one sentence: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. It denied ECF No. 105 without prejudice. Id. ECF No. 108 may reasonably be read as postponing the parties’ conference and report until the pending motions to dismiss are decided. It does not state whether initial disclosures are postponed. It does not state what step follows the dismissal rulings. Plaintiff asks the Court to reconsider the application of the discovery-postponement decision to the planning request and to state the operative scope of any postponement that remains.

4.	Planning can proceed under an order that does not impose or extend a discovery stay. Rule 26(d)(1) places the conference before discovery. Rule 26(a)(1)(C) runs initial disclosures from the conference “unless a different time is set by stipulation or court order.” Rule 26(d)(2)(B) treats a document request delivered early as served at the first Rule 26(f) conference, and Rule 34(b)(2)(A) provides that a different response time may “be ordered by the court.” The Court’s authority under Rules 16 and 26 over the timing and sequence of discovery permits it to determine that timing and sequence after considering the report. Proposed Order A does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. The timing of substantive discovery, initial disclosures, and responses to requests delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order. Any party requesting postponement, phasing, or modification of discovery or disclosure obligations may state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination. A conference and report on those terms require preparation and participation. Proposed Order A does not itself order discovery responses, document production, depositions, or initial disclosures.

5.	The reconsideration ground. Plaintiff invokes the ground of clear error causing manifest injustice. Carlson v. Boston Sci. Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). Plaintiff asserts no new evidence and no change in law. The asserted error is that ECF No. 108 applied a ground directed to the commencement of discovery to a request that sought no discovery and that itself supplied the vehicle for each Defendant’s proposal to postpone discovery. The asserted consequence is that court-directed planning is deferred for the full pendency of the motions to dismiss, without terms stating what is postponed, whether disclosures are postponed, or what step follows the dismissal rulings. When Plaintiff executed the declaration accompanying ECF No. 105, the parties had not completed the conference and no report existed. ECF No. 107 ¶¶ 10–11.

6.	The alternatives. If the Court declines to find error in the original disposition, Plaintiff asks the Court to consider the narrowed terms in Proposed Order A as a renewed request. ECF No. 108 denied ECF No. 105 without prejudice. Plaintiff does not contend that the characterization of the request as renewed exempts it from the principles that govern reconsideration. If the Court determines that planning remains postponed, Plaintiff requests Proposed Order B, which states the scope of the postponement, identifies the direction on which it rests to the extent the Court relies on one, and establishes the procedure that follows disposition of the pending motions to dismiss.

II.	SCOPE

7.	This Motion does not seek reconsideration of the disposition of ECF No. 103. It does not seek reconsideration of ECF No. 84. It does not renew ECF No. 15 or ECF No. 54. It does not ask the Court to adopt Plaintiff’s discovery proposals, to impose sanctions, or to find that any party acted in bad faith. It does not ask the Court to adjudicate any dismissal or immunity defense. It does not seek relief concerning the designation of the Magistrate Judge. Plaintiff’s pending objections and applications remain presented on their own grounds, and this Motion withdraws and replaces none of them.

III.	LOCAL CIVIL RULE 37(E)

8.	This Motion seeks reconsideration of a case-management ruling. It does not seek an order compelling a disclosure or a response to a discovery request. Local Civil Rule 37(E) reaches motions concerning discovery matters, and Plaintiff does not contend that this Motion is categorically outside that rule. ECF No. 105 § III disclosed Plaintiff’s written efforts to obtain the appearing Defendants’ participation and disclosed that no telephone or in-person consultation concerning that request had occurred. Those efforts appear in ECF No. 107 and Exhibits A through C-2. Plaintiff does not represent that the correspondence satisfies Local Civil Rule 37(E). If the Court determines that Local Civil Rule 37(E) applies to this Motion, Plaintiff requests permission to proceed on the existing record or, in the alternative, an opportunity to complete the consultation the Court requires before the Motion is decided on that ground.

IV.	RELIEF REQUESTED

9.	Plaintiff requests that the Court grant reconsideration of ECF No. 108 insofar as it denied ECF No. 105 and enter Proposed Order A, which:

(a)	modifies ECF No. 108 as to ECF No. 105 only and leaves its disposition of ECF No. 103 unchanged;

(b)	directs Plaintiff and counsel for each appearing Defendant to complete the Rule 26(f) conference within 14 days after entry, by substantive written exchange on the subjects in Rule 26(f)(2)–(3) or by another format the participants agree on or the Court directs;

(c)	directs the parties to file the written report within 14 days after completing the conference and no later than 18 days after entry, stating the parties’ agreed proposals and each party’s separately attributed position on each subject in Rule 26(f)(3), including any proposal to postpone, phase, or limit discovery;

(d)	provides that, if the conference remains incomplete at the reporting deadline, the parties shall file a status report, that a party unable to obtain a joint report shall file its own, and that a status report does not complete the conference, extend the completion deadline, or excuse further participation;

(e)	provides that the order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay; that the timing of substantive discovery, initial disclosures, and responses to requests delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order; that any party requesting postponement, phasing, or modification of discovery or disclosure obligations may state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination; that nothing in the order decides whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed a discovery stay or modifies any other applicable order; and that the Court may determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after consideration of the report; and

(f)	leaves existing preservation duties, the disposition of ECF No. 103, and all pending motions, objections, and applications unchanged.

10.	In the alternative, if the Court determines that planning must remain postponed, Plaintiff requests that the Court enter Proposed Order B, which:

(a)	states that the parties’ Rule 26(f) conference and report are postponed pending disposition of the motions to dismiss at ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45, and states the corresponding treatment of initial disclosures and discovery;

(b)	states the source and scope of any direction of the District Judge on which the postponement rests, to the extent the Court relies on one, or states that the postponement rests on this Court’s own determination under Rule 26(f)(1);

(c)	directs Plaintiff and counsel for the parties remaining in the action to file a status report within 14 days after disposition of the last of those motions, unless a final judgment has ended the action, identifying the remaining claims and parties, any leave to amend and its deadline, proposed dates for the conference, the report, and initial disclosures, and any continuing request for postponement;

(d)	permits any party to request earlier planning as to claims that remain pending after a ruling on fewer than all of those motions; and

(e)	leaves existing preservation duties and all other dispositions and pending applications unchanged.

11.	The 14-day period to complete the conference and the 18-day outer limit for the report are requested terms. The 14-day period to file the report after completing the conference tracks Rule 26(f)(2).

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter Proposed Order A or, in the alternative, Proposed Order B.

Date: November 1, 2026		                      Respectfully submitted,

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847

Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503

jayballentine@protonmail.com

CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE

I certify that on November 1, 2026, I submitted the following documents to the Clerk of Court for filing through the Court’s Electronic Document Submission System (EDSS):

1.	Plaintiff’s Rule 54(b) Motion to Reconsider ECF No. 108 as to ECF No. 105, with its Certificate of Service, Local Civil Rule 83.1(N) Certification, and Generative Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Citation Certification;

2.	Memorandum in Support;

3.	Proposed Order A (Granting Reconsideration of ECF No. 108 Insofar as It Denied ECF No. 105 and Directing Completion of the Rule 26(f) Conference and Submission of a Discovery Plan); and

4.	Proposed Order B (Granting Reconsideration in Part, Stating the Postponement of the Rule 26(f) Conference, and Establishing the Procedure Following Disposition of the Pending Motions to Dismiss).

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S RULE 54(b) MOTION TO RECONSIDER ECF NO. 108 AS TO ECF NO. 105

INTRODUCTION

ECF No. 105 requested participation and reporting, not discovery responses. ECF No. 108 denied that request based on postponement of discovery. The Order states: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2.

Plaintiff asks the Court to reconsider that application under Rule 54(b). The Court can direct the parties’ planning conference and report and determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after considering the report. Rule 26(a)(1)(C) and Rule 34(b)(2)(A) permit the Court to set a different time for the consequences a conference ordinarily triggers. The Court’s authority under Rules 16 and 26 over the timing and sequence of discovery permits it to make that determination after the parties have conferred. Proposed Order A directs the conference and report and does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. The question on reconsideration is whether postponing the planning steps remains warranted on those terms. If the Court concludes that planning remains postponed, Plaintiff asks that the postponement be stated, its source identified to the extent the Court relies on a direction of the District Judge, and the procedure after the dismissal rulings established. That is Proposed Order B.

Three distinctions govern this Memorandum. First, the denial of the conference request and the explanation for it are different things. The dispute concerns the basis and the continuing effect of the denial, not whether a ruling exists. Second, the Court’s authority to postpone planning and its exercise of that authority are different things. Plaintiff challenges the application of the discretion to the request presented, not the existence of the discretion. Third, an error in the original ruling and a reason to modify it now are different things. The narrowed terms in Proposed Order A support modification now. They do not by themselves prove that ECF No. 108 was erroneous when entered.

I.	ECF NO. 105 REQUESTED PLANNING WITHOUT DISCOVERY RESPONSES

ECF No. 105 asked for an order directing the appearing parties to complete the conference Rule 26(f) requires by a date certain and to file one written report. ECF No. 105 ¶ 11(a)–(b). The report would state the parties’ agreed proposals and each party’s separately attributed position on each subject in Rule 26(f)(3), “including any requested sequencing, phasing, or postponement of discovery and any proposed protective or scheduling terms.” ECF No. 105 ¶ 11(b). The order would not require any party to agree with Plaintiff’s proposals. ECF No. 105 ¶ 6. It would permit each party “to state in the report its position on dismissal, immunity, sequencing, phasing, and any requested postponement of discovery.” Id.

ECF No. 105 stated what it did not seek. It did not request adoption of Plaintiff’s discovery proposals, answers to interrogatories, production of documents, sanctions, or modification of ECF No. 84. ECF No. 105 ¶ 8. The supporting memorandum stated the limit of the request: “This Motion asks the Court to decide when the conference will occur. It does not ask the Court to decide any request concerning the sequencing or postponement of substantive discovery; those requests belong in the report, where each party states its position for the Court’s resolution.” ECF No. 106 at 5. The memorandum recognized the Court’s authority: “The Court retains its authority to modify or defer the process under Rule 26(f)(1) and Rule 16.” Id.

ECF No. 105 also requested an alternative. If the Court postponed the conference, Plaintiff asked that the order identify the scope of the postponement and a definite date or event for renewed consideration. ECF No. 105 ¶ 12; ECF No. 106 at 9.

ECF No. 108 identified that request before denying it. The Order lists the forms of relief sought. It describes the second as “an order directing the parties to complete a Rule 26(f) conference and file respective discovery plans.” ECF No. 108 at 1. It describes the fourth as a request that, if any step is postponed, the order state the date or event on which scheduling will next be addressed. Id. It then denies both motions on the discovery-postponement ground, without prejudice. ECF No. 108 at 2. The Court decided the planning request. This Motion contests the basis of that decision and its operative effect.

The determination Plaintiff requests is this: whether the conference and report should remain postponed when the order directing them does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay, permits any party requesting postponement to state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination, and permits the Court to determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after consideration of the report.

II.	THE RECORD SHOWS A DISAGREEMENT ABOUT PLANNING BEFORE THE DISMISSAL DECISIONS

The chronology supplies four facts that bear on reconsideration.

First, the only stated position of any Defendant is that a conference is premature. Counsel for NCMEC and Hall replied on October 28, 2026: “I believe a Rule 26(f) conference is premature at this juncture, as both Meta and my clients have dispositive motions pending which-- if granted in full-- would be fully dispositive of all claims.” ECF No. 107-3 (Ex. C-1). The reply identified no order or other authority postponing the conference, proposed no date, and did not state whether NCMEC or Hall would oppose an order setting a conference deadline. ECF No. 107 ¶ 8. The reply is attributed to counsel for NCMEC and Hall. It did not state that it was sent on behalf of Meta. Id.

Second, Meta had not responded to the October 16 transmission or the October 28 request as of the execution of Plaintiff’s declaration on October 28, 2026. ECF No. 107 ¶ 9. Plaintiff states Meta’s non-response only as of that date.

Third, the October 30, 2026 response date was requested by Plaintiff. It was not set by the Court. ECF No. 107 ¶ 5; ECF No. 105 ¶ 4. Plaintiff did not contend, and does not contend, that any Defendant defaulted on that date. ECF No. 105 ¶ 4.

Fourth, the conference had not been completed as of the execution of the declaration. ECF No. 107 ¶ 10. Plaintiff’s review of the docket through ECF No. 101 located no order expressly postponing the parties’ Rule 26(f) conference. Id. ECF No. 108 was signed on October 29, 2026, the day after ECF No. 105 was filed and before any Defendant filed a response. The docket therefore contains no statement from any Defendant of its position on an order directing planning on the terms of Proposed Order A.

The chronology explains why Plaintiff sought an order. It does not allege misconduct by any party or counsel, and Plaintiff requests no finding of bad faith.

III.	RECONSIDERATION REQUIRES A SUPPORTED ERROR AND A SUPPORTED CONSEQUENCE

Rule 54(b) provides that an order adjudicating fewer than all the claims or the rights of fewer than all the parties “may be revised at any time before the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims and all the parties’ rights and liabilities.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). The Fourth Circuit has held that “[m]otions for reconsideration of interlocutory orders are not subject to the strict standards applicable to motions for reconsideration of a final judgment.” Am. Canoe Ass’n v. Murphy Farms, Inc., 326 F.3d 505, 514 (4th Cir. 2003). A district court “retains the power to reconsider and modify its interlocutory judgments, including partial summary judgments, at any time prior to final judgment when such is warranted.” Id. at 514–15. That power is committed to the court’s discretion, and the law-of-the-case doctrine guides that discretion. Id. at 515. American Canoe addressed an interlocutory standing determination treated as a partial summary judgment. Id. at 514–16. Plaintiff does not contend that its reasoning imposes a heightened duty here.

The discretion has limits. Rule 54(b) allows more flexibility to revise interlocutory orders before final judgment than Rule 59(e) allows after it, but “the discretion Rule 54(b) provides is not limitless.” Carlson v. Boston Sci. Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). The Fourth Circuit treats interlocutory rulings as law of the case and permits revision in three circumstances: “(1) a subsequent trial producing substantially different evidence; (2) a change in applicable law; or (3) clear error causing manifest injustice.” Id. (internal quotation marks and alteration omitted). U.S. Tobacco Cooperative applied the same three circumstances and confirmed that the clear-error ground requires more than disagreement with the ruling. U.S. Tobacco Coop. Inc. v. Big S. Wholesale of Va., LLC, 899 F.3d 236, 256–58 (4th Cir. 2018).

Plaintiff invokes the third circumstance. Plaintiff asserts no new evidence and no change in law. A ruling is not clearly erroneous because a different procedure would have been preferable. Plaintiff bears the burden on this Motion. The Order states that Plaintiff “has not established that he is entitled to the relief he seeks.” ECF No. 108 at 1. Plaintiff accepts that burden. Plaintiff must identify an error in the ruling as entered and a consequence that the error works. Plaintiff addresses each separately. Plaintiff then addresses the narrowed terms that support modification now whether or not the Court finds the original error.

A.	The asserted error: the Order treated the conference and report as the commencement of discovery.

ECF No. 108 rests on the postponement of discovery. Its quoted rationale concerns scheduling orders that “initiate discovery obligations” and the avoidance of “expensive or otherwise burdensome discovery on potentially frivolous claims.” ECF No. 108 at 1–2. Its case-specific ground is the District Judge’s choice “to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2.

ECF No. 105 did not ask the Court to begin discovery. It asked the Court to set the dates for the planning conference and the report. ECF No. 105 ¶ 11(a)–(b). It left every proposal to postpone discovery to the report. ECF No. 105 ¶¶ 6, 11(b); ECF No. 106 at 5. A Defendant that believed no discovery should proceed until the motions were decided could state that position in the report, and the Court would then decide sequencing with each party’s position before it. ECF No. 106 at 5. The request contained the mechanism by which the discovery-postponement decision would be honored.

The Rules separate the conference from discovery. Rule 26(d)(1) places the conference before discovery. Rule 26(a)(1)(C), Rule 26(d)(2)(B), and Rule 34(b)(2)(A) each permit the Court to set a different time for the consequences a conference triggers. The asserted error is that ECF No. 108 applied the discovery-postponement decision as if the conference were the commencement of discovery. The distinction between planning and discovery was presented in ECF No. 105 ¶¶ 6 and 8 and ECF No. 106 at 4–5 and 7–8. Plaintiff does not present it as new. Plaintiff asserts that the Order did not apply it.

ECF No. 108 is an order of this Court. It is not counsel’s assessment of timing, and Plaintiff does not treat it as one. Rule 26(f)(1) permits the Court to order otherwise. Pending dismissal motions do not themselves create an exemption from planning. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 1993 amendment (subdivision (f)). A court may nevertheless direct postponement in the particular action. The question is whether the ground ECF No. 108 states supports postponing planning when the planning order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. On the Order’s own terms, the reason to wait is the burden of discovery. Part V.G addresses that reason as applied to the narrowed procedure.

B.	The asserted consequence: court-directed planning deferred for the pendency of the motions, without implementation terms.

The consequence Plaintiff asserts is limited to what the record supports. When Plaintiff executed the declaration accompanying ECF No. 105, the parties had not completed the conference, and no report containing agreed and competing proposals existed. ECF No. 107 ¶¶ 10–11. The denial defers court-directed planning while three motions to dismiss remain pending. The Order identifies the event that ends the postponement of discovery: resolution of the pending motions to dismiss. ECF No. 108 at 2. It does not state whether the conference and report are postponed with discovery, whether initial disclosures are postponed, what step follows the dismissal rulings, what happens if the rulings issue on different dates, or what happens if a dismissal permits amendment rather than ending the action.

Plaintiff does not assert that evidence has been lost. Plaintiff does not assert an inability to oppose the motions to dismiss. Plaintiff does not assert that the Order prohibits voluntary consultation among the parties. Plaintiff does not assert that procedural uncertainty is, by itself, manifest injustice. The injustice Plaintiff asserts is the postponement of a planning process that the Order’s stated ground did not require to be postponed, for the full pendency of the dismissal motions, if the Court accepts the error stated in Part III.A. If the Court does not accept that error, the implementation terms remain useful, and Proposed Order B supplies them.

C.	The narrowed terms: a reason to modify the Order now.

ECF No. 105 ¶ 11(e)–(f) and ECF No. 106 at 7–9 addressed the relationship between the conference and the Rule 16 schedule and the relationship between the conference and ECF No. 84. They did not make express the terms on the timing of discovery and disclosures that Proposed Order A states. It provides that the order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. It provides that the timing of substantive discovery, initial disclosures, and responses to requests delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order. It provides that nothing in the order decides whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed a discovery stay or modifies any other applicable order. It provides that the Court may determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after consideration of the report. It provides that each Defendant preserves its positions on dismissal, immunity, and the timing of discovery, and states them in the report.

Those terms support modification now. They are not evidence of what ECF No. 105 already requested, and Plaintiff does not present them as such. ECF No. 108 denied ECF No. 105 without prejudice. ECF No. 108 at 2. Plaintiff does not contend that the phrase relaxes the standard for reconsideration. Plaintiff does not read it as an invitation to renew the request before the motions to dismiss are decided. If the Court declines to find error in the original disposition, Plaintiff asks that the Court consider the narrowed terms as a renewed request and decide it on its own merits under Rule 26(f)(1) and Rule 16. Reconsideration remains the principal vehicle. Renewal is a subordinate characterization of the same confined relief.

IV.	RULE 26(f) PERMITS PLANNING WHILE THE COURT CONTROLS DISCOVERY TIMING

A.	The appearing parties share the planning obligation, subject to the Court’s order.

Rule 26(f)(1) provides: “Except in a proceeding exempted from initial disclosure under Rule 26(a)(1)(B) or when the court orders otherwise, the parties must confer as soon as practicable—and in any event at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is to be held or a scheduling order is due under Rule 16(b).” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(1). Rule 26(f)(2) places the obligation jointly on “[t]he attorneys of record and all unrepresented parties that have appeared in the case.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(2). The 1993 Advisory Committee Note states that the obligation “is imposed on all parties that have appeared in the case, including defendants who, because of a pending Rule 12 motion, may not have yet filed an answer in the case.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 1993 amendment (subdivision (f)). Plaintiff relies on the Note for that proposition. Plaintiff does not rely on the Note’s description of deadlines that later amendments replaced.

Two propositions follow. Pending dismissal motions do not themselves exempt a party from planning. The Court may nevertheless postpone planning in a particular action by ordering otherwise. ECF No. 108 is such an order to the extent it postpones the conference. The question on reconsideration is whether that postponement remains warranted when the planning order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay.

B.	The report may present competing proposals, including proposals to defer.

Rule 26(f)(3) requires the discovery plan to state “the parties’ views and proposals” on the timing and form of disclosures; on the subjects and timing of discovery and “whether discovery should be conducted in phases or be limited to or focused on particular issues”; on electronically stored information; on claims of privilege and trial-preparation protection; on changes to the limits on discovery; and on “any other orders that the court should issue under Rule 26(c) or under Rule 16(b) and (c).” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(3)(A)–(F). Rule 26(f)(3)(D), as amended effective December 1, 2025, requires the plan to address “the timing and method for complying with Rule 26(b)(5)(A).” The conference may establish a method for later discovery without requiring immediate production of documents. Plaintiff’s common agenda keys each subject to the provision that requires it. It includes the Rule 26(f)(3)(D) subject. ECF No. 107-1 (Ex. A) § III.

The rule requires good-faith consideration of each subject. It does not require agreement. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(2). The 1993 Note contemplates that the parties may not agree and that the report then indicates their competing proposals. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 1993 amendment (subdivision (f)). A Defendant may propose that no discovery proceed until the motions are decided. That proposal is a view on the subjects Rule 26(f)(3)(B) and (F) identify. The report records it.

Plaintiff does not contend that every planning subject is independent of which claims survive. The scope of preservation, the sources of electronically stored information, and the privilege issues that arise may each depend on the surviving claims. The parties can nevertheless discuss methods and state conditional proposals now, and identify in the report the matters that depend on the dismissal rulings. Proposed Order A requires that engagement. A party may, as to any subject, propose deferral, explain why the subject cannot usefully be resolved before the dismissal rulings, state a conditional proposal, or record a disagreement. Each party must still consider each subject and state its position. A single sentence repeated under every heading is not the participation Rule 26(f)(2) describes.

The 1993 Note also contemplates a report that describes incomplete participation. Id. Plaintiff cannot supply another party’s views. Plaintiff cannot convert an unanswered invitation into that party’s participation. A report describing nonparticipation does not establish that the conference Rule 26(f) requires occurred. Proposed Order A therefore provides for a status report if the conference remains incomplete at the reporting deadline, and provides that a status report does not complete the conference. That provision is a reporting safeguard. It is not an assertion that no other reporting mechanism exists.

C.	Proposed Order A leaves each consequence a conference would otherwise trigger to the Rules and any applicable stipulation or express court order.

Four provisions attach consequences to the Rule 26(f) conference. Proposed Order A addresses each.

Initial disclosures. A party “must make the initial disclosures at or within 14 days after the parties’ Rule 26(f) conference unless a different time is set by stipulation or court order, or unless a party objects during the conference that initial disclosures are not appropriate in this action and states the objection in the proposed discovery plan.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(C). Proposed Order A does not set a different time. The timing of initial disclosures remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order, and any party requesting postponement may state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination. Any objection to disclosures is raised during the conference and stated in the report, as the rule provides.

Discovery sequence. “A party may not seek discovery from any source before the parties have conferred as required by Rule 26(f),” except as the rules, a stipulation, or a court order authorize. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1). The timing of substantive discovery remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order. Proposed Order A does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay, and it does not decide whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed one. It does not restrict informal investigation. It does not displace any order that separately authorizes discovery.

Early document requests. A request under Rule 34 delivered more than 21 days after service “is considered to have been served at the first Rule 26(f) conference.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(2)(B). The responding party must then respond “within 30 days after the parties’ first Rule 26(f) conference,” and “[a] shorter or longer time may be stipulated to under Rule 29 or be ordered by the court.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(A). Local Civil Rule 26(C) prescribes a separate period for serving objections. The record does not establish that any party has delivered a request under Rule 26(d)(2). Proposed Order A addresses the possibility conditionally. It preserves the deemed-service consequence of Rule 26(d)(2)(B), and the time to respond to any such request remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order. It does not declare any request unserved, revive any expired period, or determine any waiver.

Scheduling. Rule 26(f)(1) ties the timing of the conference to the Rule 16(b) schedule. ECF No. 108’s disposition of the scheduling motion, ECF No. 103, is not before the Court on this Motion. Proposed Order A leaves that disposition unchanged. The conference and report it directs are complete in themselves and do not depend on the entry of a scheduling order.

With those provisions, the conference and report require preparation and participation. Proposed Order A does not itself order discovery responses, document production, depositions, or initial disclosures. That is the limited burden the planning order imposes.

D.	Written exchange requires actual engagement.

Rule 26(f)(2) requires the parties to “confer.” The 2000 amendment changed the rule “to require only a ‘conference’ of the parties, rather than a ‘meeting.’” The accompanying Note contemplates other means of conferring, while stating that there are “important benefits to face-to-face discussion,” and the court retains authority to require attendance in person. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 2000 amendment (subdivision (f)); Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(2). The Note does not establish a right to insist on any particular means. Plaintiff does not claim one. Proposed Order A directs substantive written exchange on each subject and permits any other format the participants agree on or the Court directs. Silence does not complete the conference. Transmission of proposals does not complete it. The conference is complete when each participant has stated its position on each subject and the participants have attempted in good faith to agree. ECF No. 107-1 (Ex. A) §§ I, V; ECF No. 106 at 7.

V.	THE ORDER’S DISCOVERY RATIONALE DOES NOT RESOLVE THE MERITS OF THE NARROWED PROCEDURE

Plaintiff addresses the grounds on which the Court or a Defendant may resist the Motion.

A.	The Order’s postponement of planning is the ruling reconsidered, not a ruling denied to exist.

The Order identified the planning request and denied it. ECF No. 108 at 1–2. Plaintiff recognizes that the Order may be read as postponing planning pending the dismissal rulings. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to declare that no ruling on planning exists. Plaintiff asks the Court to reconsider the postponement, on the ground that the reason stated for it concerns the burden of discovery and the narrowed planning order does not itself impose that burden, and in the alternative to state the postponement’s scope and the procedure that follows.

B.	The cost of a report on the narrowed terms is the preparation of positions, not the burden of discovery.

Preparation has a cost. A conference and report require each participant to consider the subjects in Rule 26(f)(3) and state a position. If every claim is dismissed without leave to amend, that work will not be used. The task is limited. The participants are four. Plaintiff’s proposals and agenda already exist. ECF No. 107 ¶¶ 3–4. A Defendant that believes a subject cannot usefully be addressed before the rulings may say so and state a conditional proposal. The report then shows the Court which subjects can be resolved now and which await the rulings. That is the function Rule 26(f)(2) assigns the report. The cost of a report on those terms is the preparation of positions. It is not the cost the Order’s quoted rationale identifies, which is the expense and burden of discovery itself.

C.	The Court can set the timing of each discovery consequence of a conference by order, and Proposed Order A does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay.

A conference triggers discovery consequences absent an order. Rule 26(a)(1)(C) runs disclosures from the conference. Rule 26(d)(1) lifts the bar on seeking discovery once the parties have conferred. Rule 26(d)(2)(B) and Rule 34(b)(2)(A) run the response period for an early-delivered document request from the first conference. Each rule permits the Court to set a different time, and the Court’s authority over the timing and sequence of discovery permits it to determine that timing and sequence after the conference. Proposed Order A does not itself set a different time for any consequence. Any party requesting postponement, phasing, or modification of discovery or disclosure obligations may state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination. Part IV.C states the terms.

D.	The distinction was presented; the narrowed terms were not.

The planning-versus-discovery distinction was argued in ECF No. 105 ¶¶ 6 and 8 and ECF No. 106 at 4–5 and 7–8. Plaintiff does not present it as new evidence. Plaintiff asserts that the Order did not apply it. Plaintiff also presents terms that were not express in ECF No. 105: that the order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay, that the timing of substantive discovery, initial disclosures, and responses to requests delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order, and that nothing in the order decides whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed a discovery stay. Those terms are a reason to modify the Order now. Plaintiff does not present them as proof that the Order was wrong when entered.

E.	The asserted consequence is stated without enlargement, and the alternative relief does not depend on it.

The consequence Plaintiff asserts is stated in Part III.B. It is the postponement of court-directed planning for the pendency of the motions, without stated implementation terms, when the ground stated for the postponement did not require it. Plaintiff asserts nothing more. If the Court finds that showing insufficient, the alternative relief does not depend on it. A statement of the postponement’s scope and the procedure that follows the dismissal rulings is useful on any view of the original ruling, and ECF No. 105 ¶ 12 requested it.

F.	Relief is requested within whichever source of the postponement operated.

ECF No. 108 attributes the postponement of discovery to a choice by the District Judge. ECF No. 108 at 2. It does not identify the order or instruction that records the choice. Local Civil Rule 72 recognizes that matters may be referred to a magistrate judge on a district judge’s instructions, and such an instruction may not appear as a separately entered order. Plaintiff does not contend that the absence of a docketed order establishes that no instruction exists. Plaintiff does not request internal communications or deliberations. Plaintiff requests identification of the operative direction, to the extent the Court relies on one, so that its scope is known to the parties.

Three possibilities exist. First, a direction of the District Judge may encompass the parties’ conference and the report. If so, Proposed Order B is the appropriate form of relief. It states the postponement, identifies the direction and its scope, and sets the procedure that follows the dismissal rulings. Second, a direction may concern substantive discovery and leave planning available. If so, planning is available for the Court’s consideration under Rule 26(f)(1) on the narrowed terms. Availability does not compel a planning order. Plaintiff asks the Court to exercise its own judgment on those terms. Third, the attribution may reflect an inference from the procedural posture of three pending motions to dismiss and no scheduling order. If so, the Court’s own determination under Rule 26(f)(1) governs, and Plaintiff asks the Court to make it on the narrowed terms.

In no case does Plaintiff ask the Magistrate Judge to countermand a direction of the District Judge. The Motion operates within the authority referred under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). Each form of relief requested is consistent with whichever source operated.

G.	The passage the Order quotes concerns the burden of discovery, not an order limited to planning.

ECF No. 108 quotes a decision of another district for the proposition that “Rule 16 Scheduling Orders initiate discovery obligations” and that courts commonly wait for rulings on preliminary motions “to avoid expensive or otherwise burdensome discovery on potentially frivolous claims.” ECF No. 108 at 1–2. Plaintiff addresses that passage as the Order’s stated rationale. Plaintiff does not characterize the holding of the quoted decision, the procedural question it decided, or whether a planning request was before that court. The stated rationale concerns the commencement of discovery and its burden. A planning order that directs a conference and report, and leaves any request for postponement for judicial determination, does not itself initiate discovery obligations. On the Order’s own stated reasoning, the narrowed planning procedure stands outside the reason given for denying ECF No. 105.

VI.	THE PROPOSED ORDERS ADDRESS PLANNING WITHOUT DECIDING DISCOVERY PROPOSALS

A.	Proposed Order A.

Proposed Order A modifies ECF No. 108 as to ECF No. 105 only. The participants are Plaintiff and counsel for NCMEC, Hall, and Meta. The Doe Defendants, unidentified and unserved, are not included. ECF No. 105 ¶ 1. The conference is to be completed within 14 days after entry, by substantive written exchange on the subjects in Rule 26(f)(2)–(3) or by another format the participants agree on or the Court directs. The report is due within 14 days after completion and no later than 18 days after entry. The 14-day period after completion tracks Rule 26(f)(2). The 14-day completion period and the 18-day outer limit are requested terms. To the extent the outer limit requires the report sooner than 14 days after completion, the order shortens the reporting interval under Rule 26(f)(4) and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(1)(b).

The report states agreements as agreements and disagreements as separately attributed positions. Counsel for NCMEC and Hall identifies whether those Defendants adopt a position jointly. ECF No. 107-1 (Ex. A) § V. Plaintiff circulates a proposed report for counsel’s review. The responsibility for the report remains joint under Rule 26(f)(2), and the order adds no interim deadline. If the conference remains incomplete at the reporting deadline, the parties file a status report, or a party unable to obtain a joint report files its own, identifying the participation, the exchanges, and the remaining obstacle. A status report does not complete the conference, extend the completion deadline, or excuse further participation.

Proposed Order A does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. The timing of substantive discovery, initial disclosures, and responses to requests delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order. Any party requesting postponement, phasing, or modification of discovery or disclosure obligations may state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination. Nothing in the order decides whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed a discovery stay or modifies any other applicable order. The Court may determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after consideration of the report. Existing preservation duties remain unchanged, and the order imposes no new preservation obligation. The disposition of ECF No. 103, ECF No. 84, and every other order remain unchanged. Every pending motion, objection, and application remains pending on its own grounds.

B.	Proposed Order B.

Proposed Order B is the alternative if the Court determines that planning must remain postponed. It grants reconsideration only to state and implement the postponement. It denies the request for an immediate conference deadline without prejudice. It states that the parties’ conference and report are postponed pending disposition of ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45. It states that initial disclosures are not due until a date set by further order and that any postponement of discovery is limited to the scope the Court states. It reserves one paragraph for the Court’s statement of the source and scope of any direction of the District Judge on which the postponement rests, or of the Court’s own determination under Rule 26(f)(1). Plaintiff has not drafted that paragraph. Plaintiff cannot state a direction the record does not contain.

Proposed Order B then sets the procedure that follows the dismissal rulings. Within 14 days after disposition of the last of ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45, unless a final judgment has ended the action, Plaintiff and counsel for the parties remaining in the action file a status report identifying the remaining claims and parties, any leave to amend and its deadline, proposed dates for the conference, the report, and initial disclosures, and any continuing request for postponement. A party unable to obtain a joint report files its own. After a ruling on fewer than all three motions, any party may move for earlier planning as to the claims and parties that remain. That motion does not itself impose planning obligations on a party whose motion remains undecided. The filing of a status report does not commence discovery. The phrase “unless a final judgment has ended the action” covers a dismissal with leave to amend, in which the action continues and awaits an amended pleading.

C.	Local Civil Rule 37(E).

The Motion seeks reconsideration of a case-management ruling. It does not seek an order compelling a disclosure or a response to a discovery request. Local Civil Rule 37(E) reaches motions concerning discovery matters, and Plaintiff does not claim a categorical exemption. ECF No. 105 § III disclosed Plaintiff’s written efforts to obtain participation and disclosed that no telephone or in-person consultation concerning that request had occurred. Plaintiff does not represent that the correspondence satisfies the rule. If the Court determines that the rule applies to this Motion, Plaintiff requests permission to proceed on the existing record or, in the alternative, an opportunity to complete the consultation the Court requires before the Motion is decided on that ground.

CONCLUSION

Plaintiff requests that the Court reconsider ECF No. 108 insofar as it denied ECF No. 105 and enter Proposed Order A, directing completion of the Rule 26(f) conference and submission of the report on terms that do not independently impose or extend a discovery stay and that permit any party requesting postponement to state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination. In the alternative, if the Court determines that planning must remain postponed, Plaintiff requests that the Court enter Proposed Order B, stating the scope and source of the postponement and the procedure that follows disposition of the pending motions to dismiss. Plaintiff requests no modification of any other disposition in ECF No. 108.

(Granting Reconsideration of ECF No. 108 Insofar as It Denied ECF No. 105 and Directing Completion of the Rule 26(f) Conference and Submission of a Discovery Plan)

This matter is before the Court on Plaintiff’s Rule 54(b) Motion to Reconsider ECF No. 108 as to ECF No. 105 (the “Motion”). Upon consideration of the Motion, the memorandum in support, any response and reply, and the record, it is hereby

ORDERED as follows:

1.	Disposition. The Motion is GRANTED. The Order entered October 30, 2026 (ECF No. 108) is MODIFIED insofar as it denied Plaintiff’s Motion for an Order Directing Completion of the Rule 26(f) Conference and Submission of a Discovery Plan (ECF No. 105). ECF No. 105 is GRANTED on the terms stated in this Order. The disposition of ECF No. 103 in ECF No. 108 is not modified.

2.	Participants. Plaintiff and counsel of record for Defendants National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”), Katie Hall, and Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) shall participate in the conference required by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(f) as directed in this Order. Defendants John/Jane Does 1–6, who have not been identified or served, are not participants.

3.	Completion of the conference. The participants shall complete the Rule 26(f) conference no later than 14 days after entry of this Order.

4.	Format. The conference shall proceed by substantive written exchange among the participants unless the participants agree on another format or the Court directs one. Nothing in this paragraph precludes the Court from directing attendance in person. Transmission of a proposal, the passage of a response date, silence, or a refusal to participate does not complete the conference.

5.	Content. The participants shall consider each subject identified in Rule 26(f)(2) and each subject Rule 26(f)(3) requires the discovery plan to address, and shall attempt in good faith to agree on a proposed discovery plan. Each participant shall state its position on each subject. A participant may, as to any subject, propose deferral, explain why the subject cannot usefully be resolved before the pending motions to dismiss are decided, state a conditional proposal, or record a disagreement. A participant’s proposal that discovery not proceed until the pending motions to dismiss are decided is a position on the subjects identified in Rule 26(f)(3)(B) and (F) and shall be stated in the report. No participant is required to accept another participant’s proposal.

6.	Report. The participants shall file a written report outlining the proposed discovery plan within 14 days after completing the conference and no later than 18 days after entry of this Order. The report shall state the participants’ agreed proposals and each participant’s separately attributed position on each subject in Rule 26(f)(3), including any proposal to postpone, phase, or limit discovery.

7.	Reporting interval. To the extent paragraph 6 requires the report sooner than 14 days after the conference, the reporting interval under Rule 26(f)(2) and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(1)(b) is shortened to that extent. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(4).

8.	Attribution. The report shall record agreements as agreements and disagreements as separately attributed positions. The report shall not portray any participant’s disagreement, silence, or nonparticipation as assent. Counsel for NCMEC and Hall shall identify whether those Defendants adopt a position jointly or separately.

9.	Preparation of the report. Plaintiff shall circulate a proposed report to counsel for each appearing Defendant for review before the report is filed. The responsibility for the report remains joint under Rule 26(f)(2).

10.	Incomplete conference. If the conference has not been completed by the reporting deadline in paragraph 6, the participants shall file a joint status report by that deadline. A participant unable to obtain a joint status report shall file its own status report by that deadline. Each status report shall identify the participation to date, the exchanges that occurred, and the remaining obstacle to completion.

11.	Effect of a status report. A status report does not complete the conference, extend the completion deadline in paragraph 3, or excuse further participation.

12.	Discovery and disclosures. This Order directs completion of the Rule 26(f) conference and submission of the discovery-plan report. It does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. The timing of substantive discovery, initial disclosures, and responses to requests delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order.

13.	Proposed postponement. Any party requesting postponement, phasing, or modification of discovery or disclosure obligations may state that position and its grounds in the Rule 26(f) report for judicial determination.

14.	Existing orders. Nothing in this Order decides whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed a discovery stay or modifies any other applicable order.

15.	Further direction. The Court may determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after consideration of the report.

16.	Preservation. Existing obligations to preserve discoverable information are not modified by this Order. This Order imposes no additional preservation obligation.

17.	Other matters. Except as this Order expressly provides, ECF No. 108, ECF No. 84, and every other order remain unchanged, and every pending motion, objection, and application remains pending on its own grounds.

Alexandria, Virginia

__________, 2026

______________________________

William E. Fitzpatrick

United States Magistrate Judge

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

PLAINTIFF’S RULE 54(b) MOTION TO RECONSIDER ECF NO. 108 AS TO ECF NO. 103

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b) for reconsideration of the Order signed and filed October 29, 2026 and entered on the docket October 30, 2026 (ECF No. 108), insofar as it denied Plaintiff’s Motion for Entry of a Scheduling Order and, as Necessary, an Initial Pretrial Conference (ECF No. 103). Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick entered ECF No. 108. This Motion asks the Magistrate Judge to reconsider that Order. The ground asserted is clear error causing manifest injustice. Carlson v. Boston Sci. Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). Under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1), a Memorandum in Support accompanies this Motion, with Proposed Order A and Proposed Order B.

I.	GROUNDS

1.	ECF No. 103 requested three forms of relief. First, entry of a scheduling order after the report or consultation Rule 16(b)(1) requires. ECF No. 103 ¶ 9, at 3. Second, if the complete scheduling order should await disposition of a pending matter, a determination whether an initial scheduling conference could proceed now to establish the remaining case-management steps. ECF No. 103 ¶ 10, at 3. Third, if either step was postponed, a statement of the good cause found under Rule 16(b)(2) and the date or event on which scheduling would next be addressed. ECF No. 103 ¶ 11, at 4. ECF No. 103 did not seek immediate interrogatory responses, document production, or depositions. ECF No. 103, Part II, at 3.

2.	The ordinary Rule 16(b)(2) date for the scheduling order was October 13, 2026, subject to a finding of good cause for delay. Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) was served July 31, 2026. ECF No. 3 at 2. NCMEC appeared August 12, 2026. ECF No. 10 at 1. Sixty days after August 12, 2026 was Sunday, October 11, 2026. Monday, October 12, 2026 was a legal holiday. The period ran to Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(1)(C), 6(a)(6)(A), 16(b)(2). The Memorandum sets out the computation.

3.	ECF No. 108 denied ECF No. 103 on the following stated ground: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. ECF No. 108 identified the initial-conference request. ECF No. 108 at 1. It denied that request through the same discovery-postponement rationale applied to the scheduling order. It did not separately explain that application. It contains no express finding under Rule 16(b)(2). Its reasons may be read as an implicit determination that good cause exists to delay the scheduling order. Plaintiff challenges whether those reasons support postponing the initial-conference alternative. ECF No. 108 identifies no order or instruction as the source of the decision it attributes to the District Judge.

4.	A decision to postpone discovery bears on whether the complete scheduling order should be entered now. Judicial consultation at a Rule 16(b) scheduling conference is not itself document production, deposition testimony, or an interrogatory response. Preparatory steps for that conference can affect disclosure and discovery timing. The Court can address those consequences expressly while deciding whether judicial scheduling should proceed. Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(3)(B)(i)–(ii), 16(c)(2)(F). ECF No. 108 applied a rationale directed to discovery to withhold judicial consultation without addressing whether that consultation could proceed while discovery remained deferred. That application is the error asserted.

5.	The source and scope of the decision attributed to the District Judge bear on that application. The District Judge’s entries of record are ECF Nos. 12, 25, 48, 50, and 70. None addresses the Rule 16(b) schedule. Local Civil Rule 72 permits a magistrate judge to act on the instructions of a district judge. The local rule does not itself establish that such an instruction exists in this action or what it says. Plaintiff requests identification of any operative order or instruction to the extent necessary to determine the scheduling obligations in this action and the scope of the authority referred.

6.	Plaintiff requests correction of the disposition or, in the alternative, a stated basis and scope for its continuation and a defined next step. Neither form of relief compels immediate merits discovery. Rule 54(b) permits revision of ECF No. 108 at any time before final judgment. ECF No. 108 was entered Friday, October 30, 2026. This Motion is submitted Sunday, November 1, 2026.

II.	SCOPE

7.	This Motion concerns only the denial of ECF No. 103. It does not seek reconsideration of the denial of ECF No. 105. It does not renew the requests denied in ECF No. 84. It does not seek authorization of interrogatories, document requests, depositions, or any other discovery. It does not seek a determination concerning the successor designation. Plaintiff’s pending applications remain pending on their own terms. None is withdrawn or expanded by this Motion. This Motion does not replace any separate objection required to obtain review of ECF No. 108.

III.	RELIEF REQUESTED

8.	Plaintiff requests that the Court:

(a)	reconsider ECF No. 108 insofar as it denied ECF No. 103, and modify that disposition;

(b)	establish a Rule 16(b) scheduling procedure for this action;

(c)	set a scheduling conference under Rule 16(b)(1)(B) and Local Civil Rule 16(B) on a date certain within 21 days after entry of the order, unless a sufficient Rule 26(f) report filed before that date permits earlier entry of the scheduling order without a conference;

(d)	direct the parties’ preparatory conference and written report on calendar dates fixed by the Court, each falling after entry of the order, with the intervals shortened under Rules 26(f)(1) and 26(f)(4) and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(1) as requested in ECF No. 103 ¶ 9(c), at 3, and provide that a qualifying conference and report already completed satisfy that direction;

(e)	hold the initial conference and establish the remaining case-management steps even if the Court determines that completion of the scheduling order should await disposition of the pending motions to dismiss; and

(f)	in the alternative, if the Court continues to postpone both the scheduling order and the initial conference, identify any operative order or instruction on which the postponement rests and its application to each of those steps; state the Court’s basis for the continued postponement under Rule 16(b)(2); and establish a procedure under which the Court will take the next scheduling step within 14 days after disposition of the last pending motion to dismiss, if the action remains pending, with authority to proceed earlier where an individual disposition permits.

9.	The 21-day, seven-day, three-day, and 14-day periods are requested case-management terms. The rules do not impose them. The alternative request in paragraph 8(f) is not consent to postponement. ECF No. 103 ¶ 12, at 4.

10.	Proposed Order A and Proposed Order B are submitted with this Motion. Plaintiff relies on the existing record.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S RULE 54(b) MOTION TO RECONSIDER ECF NO. 108 AS TO ECF NO. 103

I.	ECF NO. 108 APPLIED A DISCOVERY-POSTPONEMENT RATIONALE TO JUDICIAL SCHEDULING RELIEF

ECF No. 108 denied judicial scheduling relief because the District Judge had chosen to postpone discovery. Plaintiff seeks reconsideration of that rationale as applied to the initial-conference alternative.

ECF No. 108 states its ground in one sentence: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. On that ground, it denied Plaintiff’s Motion for Entry of a Scheduling Order and, as Necessary, an Initial Pretrial Conference (ECF No. 103) without prejudice. ECF No. 108 at 2.

ECF No. 103 requested a scheduling order. ECF No. 103 ¶ 9, at 3. It separately requested that, if the complete scheduling order should await disposition of a pending matter, the Court determine whether an initial scheduling conference could proceed now to establish the remaining case-management steps. ECF No. 103 ¶ 10, at 3. This Memorandum refers to that second request as the initial-conference alternative. ECF No. 108 identified it. ECF No. 108 at 1. It denied the initial-conference request through the same discovery-postponement rationale applied to the scheduling order. It did not separately explain that application.

The ground for reconsideration is clear error causing manifest injustice. Carlson v. Boston Sci. Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). Plaintiff presents no new evidence. Plaintiff relies on no change in law. Plaintiff contends that a rationale directed to the commencement of discovery was applied to withhold judicial consultation without addressing whether that consultation could proceed while discovery remained deferred. The resulting postponement has a stated end event. It has no stated scope and no stated next step.

Plaintiff requests that the Court modify the disposition and set a Rule 16(b) scheduling conference, with preparatory steps on fixed dates. If the Court determines that the complete scheduling order should still await the dismissal rulings, Plaintiff requests the initial conference and the establishment of the remaining case-management steps. In the alternative, Plaintiff requests that the Court identify the basis and scope of the continued postponement and establish the step that follows the dismissal rulings. Proposed Order A and Proposed Order B implement those requests. This Motion does not seek reconsideration of the denial of ECF No. 105.

II.	THE RECORD ESTABLISHES THE REQUESTS, THE DISPOSITION, AND THE ORDINARY SCHEDULING DATE

A.	The chronology.

Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) was one of the first two Defendants served and the first to appear.

Date

Event

Record

ECF No. 3 at 2

August 12, 2026

ECF No. 10 at 1

ECF No. 84 at 2

ECF Nos. 103, 104

ECF No. 108 entered on the docket.

Docket

NCMEC, Meta Platforms, Inc., and Katie Hall have each moved to dismiss. ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45; ECF No. 108 at 1. The docket contains no Rule 16(b) scheduling order. ECF No. 108 denied the request for one. ECF No. 108 at 2.

B.	The ordinary scheduling date was October 13, 2026.

Rule 16(b)(1) applies “[e]xcept in categories of actions exempted by local rule.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(1). Local Civil Rule 16(A) exempts “[p]roceedings upon a defendant’s default and matters involving habeas corpus petitions, other pro se prisoner petitions, bankruptcy proceedings, condemnation cases, forfeitures, and reviews from administrative agencies.” Local Civil Rule 16(A). This action is a civil action by a non-prisoner asserting claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and Virginia law. ECF No. 5. It is in none of those categories. Local Civil Rule 16(B) therefore applies. It directs the Court to schedule an initial pretrial conference “as promptly as possible after a complaint or notice of removal has been filed.” Local Civil Rule 16(B). It permits the Court to enter a scheduling order in addition to, or in lieu of, that conference. It sets the outer time at “not later than sixty (60) days from first appearance or ninety (90) days after service of the complaint.” Local Civil Rule 16(B).

Rule 16(b)(2) sets the same outer time and states the exception: “The judge must issue the scheduling order as soon as practicable, but unless the judge finds good cause for delay, the judge must issue it within the earlier of 90 days after any defendant has been served with the complaint or 60 days after any defendant has appeared.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2). Rule 6(a) governs the computation of “any time period specified in these rules.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a).

Trigger

Computation

Result

Appearance: August 12, 2026. ECF No. 10 at 1.

Exclude August 12. August contributes 19 days (August 13–31). September contributes 30 (49). October contributes 11 (60). Day 60 is Sunday, October 11, 2026. Monday, October 12, 2026 is Columbus Day, a legal holiday. The period runs to the next day that is not a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday. Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(1)(A)–(C), 6(a)(6)(A).

Tuesday, October 13, 2026

Service: July 31, 2026. ECF No. 3 at 2.

Exclude July 31. August contributes 31 days. September contributes 30 (61). October contributes 29 (90). Day 90 is Thursday, October 29, 2026.

Rule 16(b)(2) selects “the earlier.”

The appearance-based date controls.
