The appearance-based date governed absent a finding of good cause for delay. The date passed without a scheduling order.

Plaintiff does not contend that the lapse affected the Court’s jurisdiction, the validity of any later order, or the Court’s authority to find good cause after October 13, 2026. Plaintiff does not contend that the lapse authorized discovery. ECF No. 103 ¶ 7, at 2. From October 13, 2026 forward, Rule 16(b)(2) permits delay on one condition: that “the judge finds good cause for delay.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2).

C.	The requested and denied relief.

ECF No. 103 moved under Rule 16(b)(1)–(3) and Local Civil Rule 16(B). Its scope section stated that it sought initial case management and did not seek enforcement of Plaintiff’s Rule 26(f) proposals, authorization of particular discovery, sanctions, or reconsideration of any prior order. ECF No. 103, Part II, at 3. It did not seek immediate interrogatory responses, document production, or depositions.

Its relief section requested three things. First, a Rule 16(b) scheduling conference within 21 days, or entry of the scheduling order on a sufficient Rule 26(f) report without a conference, with the preparatory intervals shortened under Rules 26(f)(1) and 26(f)(4) and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(1). ECF No. 103 ¶ 9, at 3. Second, if the complete scheduling order should await disposition of a pending matter, a determination whether an initial scheduling conference could proceed now to establish the remaining case-management steps. ECF No. 103 ¶ 10, at 3. Third, if either step was postponed, a statement of the good cause found under Rule 16(b)(2) and the date or event on which scheduling would next be addressed. ECF No. 103 ¶ 11, at 4. The third request was not consent to postponement. ECF No. 103 ¶ 12, at 4. The supporting memorandum set out the Rule 16(b)(2) computation and the two routes to a scheduling order under Rule 16(b)(1). ECF No. 104 at 3–5.

ECF No. 108 addressed ECF Nos. 103 and 105 together. It listed the relief requested, including “an initial pretrial conference.” ECF No. 108 at 1. It stated that Plaintiff “has not established that he is entitled to the relief he seeks.” ECF No. 108 at 1. It noted the three pending motions to dismiss. ECF No. 108 at 1. It quoted a decision of the District of Maryland: “Given that Rule 16 Scheduling Orders initiate discovery obligations, it is standard for courts to wait until any preliminary motions such as motions to dismiss or to remand are resolved to avoid expensive or otherwise burdensome discovery on potentially frivolous claims.” ECF No. 108 at 1–2 (quoting Gurri Rubio v. Mullin, No. 25-CV-2756-ABA, 2026 WL 1194557, at *3 (D. Md. May 1, 2026), appeal dismissed, No. 26-1563 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026) (per curiam) (unpublished)). It then stated that “the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss,” and denied both motions without prejudice. ECF No. 108 at 2.

ECF No. 108 denied the initial-conference request. It did not leave that request undecided. It applied one rationale to each requested step. It identified the event on which the postponement ends: resolution of the pending motions to dismiss. It did not state the scope of the postponement or the step that follows that event.

III.	RECONSIDERATION REQUIRES MORE THAN A PREFERRED SCHEDULING APPROACH

Rule 54(b) provides that an order “that adjudicates fewer than all the claims or the rights and liabilities of fewer than all the parties does not end the action as to any of the claims or parties and may be revised at any time before the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims and all the parties’ rights and liabilities.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). ECF No. 108 denied case-management requests without prejudice. It adjudicated no claim. It is an interlocutory order within Rule 54(b).

The Fourth Circuit recognizes the authority Rule 54(b) describes. “[A] district court retains the power to reconsider and modify its interlocutory judgments, including partial summary judgments, at any time prior to final judgment when such is warranted.” Am. Canoe Ass’n v. Murphy Farms, Inc., 326 F.3d 505, 514–15 (4th Cir. 2003). Motions to reconsider interlocutory orders “are not subject to the strict standards applicable to motions for reconsideration of a final judgment.” Id. at 514.

That authority has limits. A court may revise an interlocutory order in three circumstances: substantially different evidence produced later in the case; a change in the applicable law; or clear error causing manifest injustice. Carlson, 856 F.3d at 325 (citing Am. Canoe, 326 F.3d at 515). Carlson affirmed the denial of reconsideration where the movant relied on deposition testimony that had been available when the original motion was decided. Id. at 325–26. U.S. Tobacco Coop. Inc. v. Big S. Wholesale of Va., LLC, 899 F.3d 236, 256–58 (4th Cir. 2018), applied that framework and emphasized that Rule 54(b) does not supply an unrestricted opportunity to decide the same matter differently.

Plaintiff invokes the third circumstance. Plaintiff presents no new evidence. Plaintiff relies on no change in law. The application Plaintiff challenges concerns requests already presented in ECF No. 103. The specific attribution to the District Judge appears in ECF No. 108. This Motion addresses that attribution and its application to the relief previously requested. The attribution’s first appearance in ECF No. 108 does not create a different reconsideration standard. It identifies what this Motion is about.

Carlson and U.S. Tobacco each addressed revision of a ruling entered by a different judge. ECF No. 108 was entered by the judicial officer now asked to reconsider it. That circumstance removes one concern those decisions address. It does not remove the limits they state.

The relief requested is within the Magistrate Judge’s authority. Rule 16(b)(1) directs that “the district judge—or a magistrate judge when authorized by local rule—must issue a scheduling order.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(1). Local Civil Rule 26(A)(2) authorizes a magistrate judge to conduct the scheduling conference and to issue the scheduling order. Local Civil Rule 26(A)(2).

IV.	THE STATED RATIONALE SHOULD BE RECONSIDERED AS APPLIED TO THE INITIAL-CONFERENCE ALTERNATIVE

A.	Scheduling can proceed while discovery remains regulated.

Three propositions describe the relationship between judicial scheduling and discovery. Plaintiff relies on all three.

First, judicial consultation at a scheduling conference is not itself document production, deposition testimony, or an interrogatory response. Rule 16(b)(1)(B) describes the conference as “consulting with the parties’ attorneys and any unrepresented parties at a scheduling conference.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(1)(B). Rule 16(a) states the purposes a pretrial conference serves, including “establishing early and continuing control so that the case will not be protracted because of lack of management” and “discouraging wasteful pretrial activities.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(a)(2)–(3).

Second, preparatory steps can affect disclosure and discovery timing. Rule 26(f)(1) requires the parties to confer “at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is to be held or a scheduling order is due under Rule 16(b),” except “when the court orders otherwise.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(1). Rule 26(a)(1)(C) sets initial disclosures “at or within 14 days after the parties’ Rule 26(f) conference unless a different time is set by stipulation or court order.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(C). Rule 26(d)(1) restricts discovery before the parties’ conference, subject to exceptions that include a court order. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1). It does not provide that discovery proceeds after the conference regardless of court orders. Setting a scheduling conference calls for a parties’ conference. The parties’ conference carries timing consequences for disclosures and discovery unless the Court orders otherwise. Plaintiff does not contend otherwise.

Third, the Court can address those consequences expressly while deciding whether judicial scheduling should proceed. The scheduling order “may” “modify the timing of disclosures under Rules 26(a) and 26(e)(1)” and “modify the extent of discovery.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(3)(B)(i)–(ii). At any pretrial conference the Court “may consider and take appropriate action on” “controlling and scheduling discovery, including orders affecting disclosures and discovery under Rule 26 and Rules 29 through 37.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(c)(2)(F). Local Civil Rule 16(B) permits the Court to proceed by scheduling order in addition to, or in lieu of, the initial conference. A court that intends to defer discovery until the dismissal rulings can state that in the order that follows the conference, or in a direction entered before it.

A complete scheduling order and an interim case-management direction are different things. The scheduling order “must limit the time to join other parties, amend the pleadings, complete discovery, and file motions.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(3)(A). An interim direction that establishes sequencing and the next step is not a scheduling order unless it contains those limits. Plaintiff requests the complete order where it can be entered. Where it cannot, Plaintiff requests the interim direction. A decision to postpone discovery bears on the first. It bears less directly on the second. ECF No. 108 applied it to both without distinguishing them.

B.	The existing reasons may constitute an implicit good-cause determination.

ECF No. 108 contains no express finding under Rule 16(b)(2). It notes the three pending motions to dismiss. ECF No. 108 at 1. It quotes the practice of awaiting their resolution to avoid burdensome discovery. ECF No. 108 at 1–2. It attributes a discovery-postponement decision to the District Judge. ECF No. 108 at 2. Those reasons may be read as an implicit determination that good cause exists to delay the scheduling order. Plaintiff addresses that reading directly rather than assume that no determination was made.

Plaintiff does not contend that the absence of the words “good cause” is itself error. Rule 52(a)(3) provides that a court “is not required to state findings or conclusions when ruling on a motion under Rule 12 or 56 or, unless these rules provide otherwise, on any other motion.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 52(a)(3). Plaintiff does not contend that each requested step requires its own written finding. Rule 16(b)(2) governs the time to issue the scheduling order. It sets no separate deadline for a preliminary conference. Local Civil Rule 16(B) directs the Court to schedule the initial conference “as promptly as possible” and permits the Court to proceed by order instead.

The question is the reach of the stated reasons. Read as a good-cause determination, those reasons address discovery burden and the complete schedule. Plaintiff acknowledges four points. Pending dismissal motions may supply good cause for delaying a complete schedule. Preparing for a conference consumes the parties’ resources. ECF No. 108 identified resolution of the dismissal motions as the event on which the postponement ends. ECF No. 108 denied the motions without prejudice.

The stated reasons do not address the initial conference separately. They do not state whether the determination extends to judicial consultation held while discovery remains deferred, or why. Plaintiff requests that statement because it would identify the basis and the scope of the postponement. Plaintiff does not request it on the theory that its omission alone invalidates ECF No. 108.

ECF No. 108 stated that Plaintiff “has not established that he is entitled to the relief he seeks.” ECF No. 108 at 1. Plaintiff bears the burden on this Motion. Rule 16(b)(2) nonetheless assigns the scheduling order to the judge: “the judge must issue” it “unless the judge finds good cause for delay.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2). Ordinary scheduling is a judicial responsibility. It does not depend on a party’s motion. The question Plaintiff presents is not whether Plaintiff proved entitlement to a particular timetable. It is whether the reasons stated for delay reach the initial-conference alternative.

C.	The initial conference is the narrower alternative.

ECF No. 103 ¶ 10, at 3, requested the initial conference as a separate step if the complete scheduling order should await a pending matter. ECF No. 104 at 4–5 explained the request. Plaintiff does not assert an unconditional right to that conference. Plaintiff asks the Court to decide the request under the provisions that govern it.

The conference would accomplish four things. It would identify what prevents completion of the schedule. It would establish the sequence of the steps that remain. It would establish the step that follows the dismissal rulings, including after a ruling on fewer than all three motions and after any ruling that grants leave to amend. It would address preservation under Rule 16(b)(3)(B)(iii) and the matters Rule 16(c)(2) identifies, to the extent the Court elects to take them up. None of those steps requires immediate merits discovery. The Court would retain control of every later step. Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(4), 16(c)(2)(F).

The strongest reading of ECF No. 108 is not that scheduling and discovery are the same thing. It is that postponing the linked case-management process avoids work that the dismissal rulings may make unnecessary. ECF No. 108 may be read to rest on that reading. Plaintiff’s response is narrower than a claim of right. The initial conference could establish sequencing and the post-disposition procedure without requiring immediate merits discovery. The conference requires preparation and attendance. If the action remains pending after the dismissal rulings, the Court will require that work then. If the rulings end the action, the work will have been unnecessary. That is the cost the practice quoted in ECF No. 108 addresses. It is a cost of preparation. It is not a cost of discovery. Plaintiff does not contend that the conference is costless. Plaintiff does not contend that its usefulness alone establishes entitlement. Plaintiff asks the Court to reconsider whether a rationale directed to discovery supports withholding that alternative too.

D.	The source and scope of the attributed decision should be identified.

ECF No. 108 states that “the record reflects” the District Judge’s decision. ECF No. 108 at 2. It does not cite the part of the record on which it relies. The District Judge’s entries in this action are listed below.

Entry

Subject

ECF No. 12

Denied ECF No. 6 (partial summary judgment) without prejudice to renewal, as premature.

ECF No. 25

Notice advising Plaintiff of the time to respond to ECF No. 21.

ECF No. 48

Notice advising Plaintiff of the time to respond to ECF No. 45.

ECF No. 50

Directed that ECF No. 10 be decided on the papers.

ECF No. 70

Granted leave to file a sur-reply and deemed it filed.

None of those entries addresses the Rule 16(b) schedule. None expressly postpones it. The one order that addresses discovery timing is ECF No. 84. Magistrate Judge Davis entered it. It stated that “discovery officially begins when the District Judge issues a Scheduling Order and currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case.” ECF No. 84 at 1–2. Plaintiff’s objections to ECF No. 84 are pending. ECF Nos. 89, 90. This Motion does not revisit ECF No. 84.

Local Civil Rule 72 permits a magistrate judge to act on the instructions of a district judge. Local Civil Rule 72. The rule lists that method apart from “an order entered in the action,” so an instruction given that way need not appear on the docket. The local rule establishes the method. It does not establish that an instruction exists in this action, what it says, or how far it extends.

Three possibilities account for the attribution. First, an instruction of the District Judge governing discovery only. Second, an instruction also governing scheduling, or reserving scheduling to the District Judge. Third, a case-management determination by the Magistrate Judge based on the procedural posture of three pending dismissal motions and no scheduling order. Those possibilities can coexist. The absence of a scheduling order alone does not identify the source or terms of the attributed decision.

Plaintiff’s request is limited. Plaintiff requests identification of any operative order or instruction to the extent necessary to determine the scheduling obligations in this action and the scope of the authority referred. Plaintiff does not request internal communications or an account of judicial deliberation. Plaintiff does not ask the Magistrate Judge to depart from any instruction of the District Judge. If an instruction governs discovery only, Plaintiff requests the scheduling determination under Rule 16(b) and Local Civil Rule 16(B). If an instruction also governs scheduling, Plaintiff requests its operative terms as applied to the scheduling order and to the initial conference. If an instruction reserves scheduling to the District Judge, Plaintiff requests that the Order say so, so that the request can be directed accordingly. If the determination is the Magistrate Judge’s own, Plaintiff requests that it be made as to each requested step.

E.	The quotation in ECF No. 108 is addressed as it appears there.

ECF No. 108 quotes Gurri Rubio v. Mullin for the proposition that “it is standard for courts to wait until any preliminary motions such as motions to dismiss or to remand are resolved to avoid expensive or otherwise burdensome discovery on potentially frivolous claims.” ECF No. 108 at 1–2. Plaintiff addresses the quotation as it appears in ECF No. 108. Plaintiff does not characterize that decision beyond its quoted words.

The quotation states a practice and its reason. The reason is avoidance of expensive or burdensome discovery while a dismissal motion is pending. Plaintiff does not dispute the practice as a general matter. The quotation does not address whether a court following the practice may also consult the parties about sequencing before discovery begins. That is the question ECF No. 103 ¶ 10 presented. The quotation’s reference to “potentially frivolous claims” describes the general concern the practice addresses. ECF No. 108 made no finding about Plaintiff’s claims, and Plaintiff reads it as making none.

V.	THE REQUESTED CORRECTION ADDRESSES THE SCHEDULING CONSEQUENCE

A.	The consequence on the record.

Plaintiff does not contend that delay alone is manifest injustice. Plaintiff does not contend that an adverse ruling is. Plaintiff does not contend that the Court has stopped managing the action by giving priority to the dismissal motions. The consequence Plaintiff identifies is procedural, and the record states it.

The action has three pending dismissal motions, no scheduling order, and no initial conference. ECF No. 108 applied a discovery rationale to every form of scheduling relief requested, including the one form that consists of judicial consultation rather than discovery. The resulting postponement ends on resolution of the dismissal motions. Its scope is not stated. The parties cannot determine from ECF No. 108 whether the obligations tied to a scheduling conference are suspended, whether an initial conference is foreclosed until the rulings issue, or what step follows the rulings.

ECF No. 84 supplies context. It denied Plaintiff’s earlier requests because “discovery has not officially begun in this case” and “currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case.” ECF No. 84 at 1–2. ECF No. 103 then requested the scheduling process itself. ECF No. 108 denied that request on a discovery rationale. The record now contains two denials that rest on the absence of the process ECF No. 103 asked the Court to begin. Plaintiff does not contend that ECF No. 84 requires scheduling now. Plaintiff cites it for the consequence of leaving the scheduling process undefined.

The injustice Plaintiff identifies is this: a rationale addressed to discovery was applied to withhold judicial consultation without a determination that the consultation itself should be deferred, and the parties were left without a stated scope for the postponement and without a stated next step. The correction requested is narrow. It asks the Court to decide the initial-conference alternative under the provisions that govern it and to state the scope of any postponement that remains.

B.	The initial conference matters despite the ability to renew.

ECF No. 108 denied the motions without prejudice. Renewal after the dismissal rulings is available. Renewal would present the same request by the same procedure: a motion, briefing, and a ruling. The initial conference would make that step unnecessary. The Court could establish at the conference what follows the rulings, including the procedure if the rulings issue on different dates or grant leave to amend. Rule 16(a)(2) identifies “establishing early and continuing control so that the case will not be protracted because of lack of management” as a purpose of the conference. Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(a)(2). A conference held before the rulings establishes the next step in advance. A motion filed after the rulings asks for it again.

C.	The overlap with ECF No. 105 is accounted for.

ECF No. 103 ¶ 9(c), at 3, requested that the Court shorten the preparatory intervals so that the parties confer before the Court’s conference and file a written report before it. ECF No. 105 requested an order directing the parties to complete their Rule 26(f) conference and submit a discovery plan. The two motions are distinct. The procedural events they concern overlap. A court-set scheduling conference calls for a parties’ conference under Rule 26(f)(1). That parties’ conference is the event ECF No. 105 addressed.

Proposed Order A accounts for that overlap in three ways. It acts on ECF No. 103. It does not reconsider the denial of ECF No. 105. It provides that a qualifying parties’ conference and report completed before its entry satisfy its preparatory direction, so that no party repeats a conference or report already completed. Plaintiff does not claim that Proposed Order A has no effect on the planning process ECF No. 105 addressed. The preparatory direction it contains follows from Rule 26(f)(1) once the Court sets its conference.

D.	The proposed orders.

Proposed Order A modifies ECF No. 108 only as to ECF No. 103. It sets a scheduling conference under Rule 16(b)(1)(B) within 21 days after entry, unless a sufficient Rule 26(f) report permits earlier entry of the scheduling order. It directs the parties’ conference and written report on calendar dates the Court fixes, each after entry, with the intervals shortened under Rules 26(f)(1) and 26(f)(4) and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(1). The report states agreed proposals and each party’s separately attributed position on any matter not agreed, including any position that disclosures or discovery should await the dismissal rulings.

Proposed Order A creates no stay and extends none. Except as it expressly states, it leaves the timing of initial disclosures and of discovery to the Federal Rules, the Local Civil Rules, and the operative orders of the Court. It provides that any additional restriction pending the scheduling conference must be imposed by an express order identifying its scope and the date or event on which it ends. Plaintiff does not request a restriction pending the conference. ECF No. 103 ¶ 7, at 2, stated that expiration of the scheduling deadline did not itself authorize discovery. That statement was not consent to a stay.

After the conference, Proposed Order A provides for one of two things: a scheduling order under Rule 16(b)(3), or an interim case-management order that identifies the step that remains before the complete order can be entered, the basis for deferring completion, the case-management directions established at the conference, and the date or event on which the complete order will be addressed. The interim order is not a scheduling order unless it contains the limits Rule 16(b)(3)(A) requires.

Proposed Order B applies if the Court continues to postpone both the scheduling order and the initial conference. It supplies no finding. It provides for the Court to identify any operative direction of the District Judge being implemented, its application to the scheduling order and to the initial conference, and the Court’s own basis for continuing the postponement. It identifies the postponed steps separately. It provides that, within 14 days after disposition of the last pending motion to dismiss, if the action remains pending, the Court will establish the next scheduling step by entering a scheduling order on a sufficient report, setting a scheduling conference, or directing a procedure that accounts for any leave to amend. It permits that step earlier where an individual disposition allows it. No further motion is required. The 14-day period is a requested term. Plaintiff’s request for Proposed Order B is not consent to postponement. ECF No. 103 ¶ 12, at 4.

VI.	CONCLUSION

Plaintiff requests that the Court: (1) reconsider ECF No. 108 insofar as it denied ECF No. 103, and modify that disposition; (2) enter Proposed Order A, setting the scheduling conference and directing the preparatory steps on fixed dates while leaving the timing of disclosures and discovery to the Court’s determination; (3) if the Court determines that the complete scheduling order should await the dismissal rulings, hold the initial conference and establish the remaining case-management steps; and (4) in the alternative, enter Proposed Order B, identifying the basis and scope of the continued postponement and establishing the step that follows the dismissal rulings. The disposition of ECF No. 105 in ECF No. 108 is outside this Motion and unchanged by the relief requested.

Date: November 1, 2026		                      Respectfully submitted,

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847

Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503

jayballentine@protonmail.com

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

[PROPOSED] ORDER A

This matter is before the Court on Plaintiff’s Rule 54(b) Motion to Reconsider ECF No. 108 as to ECF No. 103 (ECF No. ___). Upon consideration of the Motion, the Memorandum in Support, any response and reply, and the record, it is hereby

ORDERED that the Motion is GRANTED to the extent stated in this Order. The Order signed October 29, 2026 and entered October 30, 2026 (ECF No. 108) is MODIFIED insofar as it denied Plaintiff’s Motion for Entry of a Scheduling Order and, as Necessary, an Initial Pretrial Conference (ECF No. 103). This Order acts on ECF No. 103. It does not reconsider the disposition of ECF No. 105 in ECF No. 108; and it is

FURTHER ORDERED that a scheduling conference under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16(b)(1)(B) and Local Civil Rule 16(B) is set for ______________, 2026, at ______ __.m., before the undersigned, by the means directed by the Court. That date is within twenty-one (21) days after entry of this Order; and it is

FURTHER ORDERED that, under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 26(f)(1), 26(f)(2), and 26(f)(4) and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(1), the intervals for the parties’ conference and written report are shortened as follows. Counsel of record and all unrepresented parties who have appeared shall confer as Rule 26(f) requires on or before ______________, 2026, a date no later than seven (7) days before the scheduling conference. They shall file a written report under Rules 26(f)(2) and 26(f)(3) on or before ______________, 2026, a date no later than three (3) days before the scheduling conference. Each date falls after entry of this Order. The report shall state the parties’ agreed proposals and each party’s separately attributed position on any matter not agreed, including any party’s position that initial disclosures or discovery should be deferred pending disposition of the pending motions to dismiss (ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45); and it is

FURTHER ORDERED that a conference among the parties and a written report completed before entry of this Order that satisfy Rules 26(f)(2) and 26(f)(3) satisfy the preceding paragraph. No party is required to repeat a conference or report already completed. The parties shall file any supplement necessary to address the matters identified in the preceding paragraph on or before the report date set above; and it is

FURTHER ORDERED that, if the report filed under this Order permits entry of the scheduling order without a conference, the Court may enter the scheduling order and vacate the scheduling conference; and it is

FURTHER ORDERED that, except as expressly stated in this Order, the timing of initial disclosures under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(a)(1)(C) and the timing and extent of discovery remain governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, the Local Civil Rules, and the operative orders of this Court. This Order does not create, extend, or lift any restriction on disclosures or discovery. Any additional restriction pending the scheduling conference must be imposed by an express order identifying its scope and the date or event on which it ends; and it is

FURTHER ORDERED that, within seven (7) days after the scheduling conference, or after receipt of a report that permits entry of the scheduling order without a conference, the Court will enter either (a) a scheduling order under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16(b)(3), or (b) an interim case-management order identifying the step that remains before the complete scheduling order can be entered, the basis for deferring its completion, the case-management directions established at the conference, and the date or event on which the complete scheduling order will be addressed. An interim case-management order under clause (b) is not a scheduling order under Rule 16(b)(3) unless it contains the limits that Rule 16(b)(3)(A) requires; and it is

FURTHER ORDERED that, except as expressly stated in this Order, this Order does not modify any other order of the Court and does not resolve any objection or motion pending before the District Judge.

The Clerk’s Office is directed to provide a copy of this Order to pro se Plaintiff at his last known address.

It is SO ORDERED.

Alexandria, Virginia

__________, 2026

______________________________

William E. Fitzpatrick

United States Magistrate Judge

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

PLAINTIFF’S RULE 60(a) MOTION TO CLARIFY OR CORRECT ECF NO. 108

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine moves under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(a) for an order clarifying one passage of the Order signed and filed October 29, 2026 and entered October 30, 2026 (ECF No. 108), and correcting that passage only if an oversight, omission, or unintended ambiguity prevents it from expressing the determination the Court intended when it issued the Order. Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick signed ECF No. 108. This Motion is presented to him. Plaintiff does not request a different determination. Plaintiff requests that the written Order conform to the determination actually made on October 29, 2026. A Memorandum in Support under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) and a Proposed Order accompany this Motion.

I.	THE PASSAGE AND THE REQUESTED CORRECTION

1.	ECF No. 108 denied without prejudice Plaintiff’s Motion for Entry of a Scheduling Order and, as Necessary, an Initial Pretrial Conference (ECF No. 103) and Plaintiff’s Motion for an Order Directing Completion of the Rule 26(f) Conference and Submission of a Discovery Plan (ECF No. 105). ECF No. 108 at 1–2.

2.	ECF No. 108 states: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. The attribution immediately precedes the denial and supplies a stated premise for it.

3.	The passage identifies the District Judge as the officer who made the described choice. The passage does not identify the order, instruction, or other action on which that attribution rests.

4.	The passage describes a choice concerning “any discovery.” Page 1 of ECF No. 108 identifies four requests: entry of a scheduling order; an order directing completion of a Rule 26(f) conference and the filing of discovery plans; an initial pretrial conference; and, for any postponed step, a statement of the date or event on which scheduling will next be addressed. ECF No. 108 at 1. The Order does not state whether the attributed choice was understood to concern substantive discovery only or also the scheduling and planning steps the Order identifies.

II.	GROUNDS

5.	Plaintiff has examined the District Judge’s docketed orders and notices in this action: ECF Nos. 12, 25, 48, 50, and 70. Each addresses a subject other than the timing of discovery, the Rule 26(f) conference, or the Rule 16(b) schedule.

6.	ECF No. 84 addresses discovery timing. It states that “discovery has not officially begun in this case” and that “currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case.” ECF No. 84 at 1–2. Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis signed ECF No. 84.

7.	The documents Plaintiff reviewed do not identify the action described in ECF No. 108. Plaintiff does not treat that absence as proof that no instruction existed. Local Civil Rule 72 recognizes assignment and referral “by an order entered in the action or on the instructions of a district judge.” An instruction need not appear in a separately entered order.

8.	Rule 60(a) permits the Court to correct “a mistake arising from oversight or omission” in an order. The Fourth Circuit reads that phrase to include an inconsistency between the text of an order and the court’s intent when it entered the order, and “an unintended ambiguity that obfuscates the court’s original intent.” Sartin v. McNair Law Firm PA, 756 F.3d 259, 265–66 (4th Cir. 2014). The power is limited by the court’s original intent. Id. at 266. Plaintiff seeks correction only if the wording fails, through a qualifying oversight, omission, or unintended ambiguity, to express that intent.

9.	Plaintiff does not contend that an omitted citation establishes a correctable mistake, or that an intentional inference is a drafting error because it may be disputed. If the passage accurately expresses the original determination, Rule 60(a) requires no textual change, and Plaintiff requests none.

III.	LIMITS

10.	This Motion does not request that the Court grant ECF No. 103 or ECF No. 105, enter a scheduling order, authorize discovery, set new deadlines, make new findings justifying postponement, resolve the successor-designation question presented in ECF Nos. 97–99, or reconsider the substance of the October 29, 2026 disposition.

11.	Plaintiff’s pending submissions concerning ECF Nos. 63, 64, 65, 84, and 96 (ECF Nos. 66, 67, 76, 89, 90, 91, 93, 94, 97, 98, 99) remain pending on their own terms. No request is withdrawn by this Motion.

12.	This Motion does not extend, and does not substitute for compliance with, the period for objections to ECF No. 108 under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 72(a).

IV.	RELIEF REQUESTED

13.	Plaintiff requests a written order that:

(a)	to the extent necessary to address a qualifying omission or unintended ambiguity, clarifies whether the passage quoted in paragraph 2 describes an order or instruction of the District Judge, an inference or determination by the Magistrate Judge, or another identified judicial action, and, for an order or instruction, identifies it by date and docket citation where available or by its operative terms;

(b)	clarifies how the action so identified was understood, when ECF No. 108 issued, to relate to entry of a scheduling order, the initial pretrial conference, the parties’ Rule 26(f) conference, and the discovery-plan report, and whether ECF No. 108 was intended only to deny the requested orders without prejudice or also to recognize or direct postponement of the planning steps requested in ECF No. 105;

(c)	if, and only if, the existing text fails to express the determination actually intended on October 29, 2026, corrects the identified passage by stating the replacement language; and

(d)	leaves the denial without prejudice of ECF Nos. 103 and 105 unchanged through this Motion, creates no new scheduling, discovery, disclosure, or reporting obligation, and resolves no separately filed application.

WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter the accompanying Proposed Order.

Date: November 1, 2026		                      Respectfully submitted,

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

Alexandria, Virginia 22307

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S RULE 60(a) MOTION TO CLARIFY OR CORRECT ECF NO. 108

I.	INTRODUCTION: THE ORDER IDENTIFIES THE ATTRIBUTED DECISION-MAKER BUT NOT THE UNDERLYING ACTION

ECF No. 108 attributes to the District Judge a choice “to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. The Order does not identify the order, instruction, or other action on which that attribution rests. The District Judge’s docketed orders and notices address other subjects. The one earlier docketed order that addresses discovery timing was signed by the previously assigned magistrate judge.

The same passage carries a second question of original meaning. Page 1 of the Order identifies four requests: a scheduling order, a Rule 26(f) conference and discovery plans, an initial pretrial conference, and a statement of the next scheduling event. ECF No. 108 at 1. Page 2 resolves them through a statement about “any discovery.” The Order does not state whether the attributed choice was understood to reach the scheduling and planning steps it identifies, or substantive discovery alone.

Plaintiff requests clarification of the action and scope the Court intended the passage to describe, and correction of the text only if a qualifying oversight, omission, or unintended ambiguity prevents the text from expressing that intent. Plaintiff seeks conformity between the words of the Order and the determination the Court made on October 29, 2026. Plaintiff does not seek a different determination.

II.	RULE 60(a) PERMITS CORRECTION OF EXPRESSION, NOT RECONSIDERATION OF AN INTENTIONAL DETERMINATION

A.	The Rule.

Rule 60(a) provides: “The court may correct a clerical mistake or a mistake arising from oversight or omission whenever one is found in a judgment, order, or other part of the record. The court may do so on motion or on its own, with or without notice.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(a). The Rule applies to an “order.” This Motion invokes subdivision (a) alone. It does not invoke the grounds for relief from a final judgment in subdivision (b).

B.	Sartin.

The Fourth Circuit has fixed the scope of subdivision (a). “Rule 60(a) is not confined just to fixing typographical and other clerical errors.” Sartin v. McNair Law Firm PA, 756 F.3d 259, 265 (4th Cir. 2014). A mistake arising from oversight or omission “occurs when there is an inconsistency between the text of an order or judgment and the district court’s intent when it entered the order or judgment.” Id. at 265–66. The phrase “also includes an unintended ambiguity that obfuscates the court’s original intent.” Id. at 266. The power “is circumscribed by the court’s intent when it issued the order or judgment.” Id. A court may not use the Rule to change its mind about the determination it made. Id. at 265. Original intent “may be ascertained through consideration of contemporaneous documents, such as a memorandum opinion or transcript, and by the presiding judge’s own subsequent statements regarding his intent.” Id. at 266 (internal quotation marks and citation omitted). The Fourth Circuit treated the issuing judge’s subsequent explanation as reliable evidence of that intent and examined whether the contemporaneous record supported it. Id. at 266–67. The Fourth Circuit resolved the validity of an earlier Rule 60(a) clarification order while deciding the causation element of a malpractice appeal. Id. at 263–67.

Two propositions follow. Original intent controls what correction is permitted. The issuing judge’s subsequent statement is evidence of that intent, assessed against the record.

C.	Chavez-Deremer.

The Fourth Circuit has also fixed the boundary. “[A] court is not authorized to use Rule 60(a) to reconsider an issue that has already been decided, or to revisit the court’s decisions already made.” Chavez-Deremer v. Medical Staffing of America, LLC, Nos. 23-2176, 23-2284, slip op. at 69 (4th Cir. July 17, 2025) (published), reported at 147 F.4th 371, 416 (citing Sartin, 756 F.3d at 265). A party may not relabel a substantive ruling as a clerical mistake to obtain further litigation of it. Id., slip op. at 69–70. The movant there sought further litigation of damages determinations the district court had already made. Id. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the denial. Id., slip op. at 70–71.

D.	The threshold applied.

The two decisions state one test. Rule 60(a) asks whether the words of the order express what the issuing court intended when it entered the order. It does not ask whether the court should have intended something else. This Motion asks the first question only.

The threshold carries an acknowledgment. An unexplained attribution is not necessarily an inadvertent one. An omitted citation does not itself establish a correctable mistake. An intentional inference is not a drafting error because it may be disputed. The Court “is not required to state findings or conclusions when ruling on a motion under Rule 12 or 56 or, unless these rules provide otherwise, on any other motion.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 52(a)(3). This Motion does not rest on an entitlement to additional reasons. If the passage accurately expresses the original determination and contains no qualifying oversight, omission, or unintended ambiguity, Rule 60(a) requires no expanded statement, and Plaintiff requests none. The Motion is directed to the possibility that the passage does not express that determination, and to the means Rule 60(a) supplies if it does not.

E.	Presentation to the issuing magistrate judge.

ECF No. 108 disposed of two nondispositive case-management motions. A judge “may designate a magistrate judge to hear and determine any pretrial matter pending before the court,” subject to exceptions not relevant here. 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). Local Civil Rule 72 recognizes referral of such matters by entered order or on the instructions of a district judge. Rule 60(a) applies to an “order.” Correction of the Magistrate Judge’s own nondispositive order to conform it to his intent is presented to the officer whose intent governs. Plaintiff does not reopen the successor-designation question through this Motion. That question is presented in ECF Nos. 97–99 and remains pending there.

III.	THE IDENTIFIED RECORD DOES NOT RESOLVE THE ATTRIBUTION

Sartin identifies contemporaneous documents as one source of original intent. 756 F.3d at 266. The docketed orders and notices in this action that bear on the attribution are these.

Record

Issuing officer

Subject relevant to this application

ECF No. 12 at 1

Judge Alston

Denies Plaintiff’s first partial-summary-judgment motion as premature, “without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time.”

ECF No. 25 at 1; ECF No. 48 at 1

Judge Alston

Provide notice and response opportunities concerning the Meta and Hall dismissal motions.

ECF No. 50 at 1

Judge Alston

Vacates the hearing on NCMEC’s dismissal motion and directs that the motion “will be decided on the papers.”

ECF No. 70 at 1

Judge Alston

Grants leave to file the proposed sur-reply and deems it filed.

ECF No. 82 at 1–2

Judge Davis

Accepts Plaintiff’s motion for leave to file a supplemental memorandum as a reply and directs disclosure of generative-AI use and citation review.

ECF No. 84 at 1–2

Judge Davis

Denies two early-discovery motions as premature, states that “discovery has not officially begun” and that “currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case,” and denies leave to amend.

Two distinctions follow from the table.

First, authorship. ECF No. 84 is the earlier docketed order that addresses discovery timing. Magistrate Judge Davis signed it.

Second, content. ECF No. 84 describes the absence of a scheduling order and states that discovery has not begun. It does not itself expressly identify a district-judge instruction postponing discovery until the dismissal motions are adjudicated. A statement that a scheduling order has not been entered is not the same statement as a description of a judge’s decision not to enter one.

Neither distinction is offered to disturb ECF No. 84. Plaintiff’s objections to ECF No. 84 are pending in ECF Nos. 89 and 90 and proceed on their own grounds. The distinctions serve one purpose here. The reviewed documents do not identify the action ECF No. 108 describes.

The table does not exhaust every possible source of the attribution. Local Civil Rule 72 recognizes referral “on the instructions of a district judge.” An instruction need not appear in a separately entered order. The rule’s text recognizes that method of assignment; it does not establish that a particular discovery-postponement instruction existed or state its terms. Plaintiff does not plead that no instruction existed. Plaintiff pleads that the reviewed record does not identify one and that the passage does not state whether one exists.

IV.	ANY CLARIFICATION OR CORRECTION MUST PRESERVE THE ORIGINAL DETERMINATION

The passage may describe one of three things. The Rule 60(a) consequence differs for each.

A.	An order or instruction of the District Judge.

If the Court intended the passage to describe an order or instruction the District Judge issued, Plaintiff requests identification of that action as it existed when ECF No. 108 issued: by date and docket citation where available, or by its operative terms where it was not separately entered. Plaintiff requests only what is necessary to clarify the published description. Plaintiff does not request chambers correspondence, drafts, internal deliberations, or testimony. If the existing text describes the instruction accurately, no textual correction is warranted, and the clarification identifies the action the Order already names.

B.	An inference or determination by the Magistrate Judge.

The posture on October 29, 2026 was three pending dismissal motions and no scheduling order. If the Court intended the passage to state a conclusion it drew from that posture, rather than a direction communicated by the District Judge, Plaintiff requests that the clarification say so. Plaintiff does not request correction on that ground alone. Where the words express an intentional inference, the words are accurate for Rule 60(a) purposes, and whether the inference is correct is a question for a different procedural vehicle. See Chavez-Deremer, slip op. at 69. Correction is warranted under this heading only if the words “the District Judge has chosen” do not express what the Court meant when it wrote them.

C.	An inadvertent attribution.

If the identification of the District Judge, or the description of the source, resulted from oversight, Rule 60(a) authorizes correction to identify what the Court actually intended. Sartin, 756 F.3d at 266–67 (concluding that the court did not abuse its discretion in using Rule 60(a) to give effect to its original intent to sanction counsel individually, although its sanctions orders named only “Plaintiffs”). Plaintiff proposes no replacement language. A substitute sentence would state a determination the existing record does not establish. The Court must identify its original determination before any replacement text can be settled.

V.	CLARIFICATION SHOULD IDENTIFY THE ORIGINALLY INTENDED REACH OF THE SAME PASSAGE

ECF No. 108 at 1 identifies the four requests before it: “First, Plaintiff requests entry of a scheduling order. Second, Plaintiff requests an order directing the parties to complete a Rule 26(f) conference and file respective discovery plans. Third, Plaintiff requests an initial pretrial conference. Fourth, if any of these steps are postponed, Plaintiff requests that the order state the date or event on which scheduling will next be addressed.” The underlying motions described their own scope. ECF No. 103 sought “initial case management” and disclaimed any contention that passage of the scheduling deadline “authorizes service of discovery.” ECF No. 103 ¶¶ 7–8. ECF No. 105 sought “participation and reporting” and disclaimed any request for “answers to interrogatories, production of documents.” ECF No. 105 ¶ 8.

The passage resolves those requests through a statement concerning “any discovery.” That treatment presents a question about the reach originally intended for the statement. Plaintiff does not characterize the Order as inconsistent with itself. The Order can intentionally deny scheduling and planning relief on the ground that substantive discovery has been deferred. Whether that reasoning suffices is a reconsideration or review question and is not presented here. What is presented is whether the words “any discovery” were intended to describe a decision about substantive discovery alone, or a decision that also reached entry of a scheduling order, the initial pretrial conference, the parties’ Rule 26(f) conference, and the discovery-plan report.

A related question of original operation attaches. Both motions were denied without prejudice. That disposition is not unclear. The question is whether ECF No. 108 was intended only to deny the requested orders, or also to recognize or direct a postponement of the planning steps requested in ECF No. 105. The Order identifies “resolution of the pending motions to dismiss” as the relevant event. ECF No. 108 at 2. The uncertainty concerns which steps the attributed decision was understood to cover before that event occurs.

Plaintiff asks what the Order meant. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to enter a stay, to make a good-cause finding, to decide any present deadline, to establish a resumption procedure, or to rule that planning must proceed. Any clarification describes the Order’s original operation. It does not create a new postponement.

VI.	THE LIMITED CLARIFICATION MATTERS WITHOUT DECIDING THE MERITS

Accurate attribution distinguishes an order that implements a direction of the District Judge from an order that states the Magistrate Judge’s own inference or determination. Accurate scope distinguishes denial of two requested orders from an intended direction concerning the planning steps themselves. Each distinction concerns what the Order is, not whether the Order was right. Plaintiff does not contend that every party’s present obligations turn on this one sentence. Other rules and orders may bear on them. Plaintiff contends only that the sentence should say what the Court meant it to say.

This Motion does not argue that pending dismissal motions cannot support postponement. It does not address the Rule 16(b)(2) date or the sufficiency of good cause. It does not challenge the general proposition the Order quotes from another district court. ECF No. 108 at 1–2. Those matters are reconsideration or review questions and are not presented here. This Motion does not extend, and does not substitute for compliance with, the Rule 72(a) objection period applicable to ECF No. 108.

VII.	CONCLUSION AND RELIEF

Plaintiff requests entry of the accompanying Proposed Order, which (1) to the extent necessary to address a qualifying omission or unintended ambiguity, clarifies whether the passage at ECF No. 108 at 2 describes an order or instruction of the District Judge, an inference or determination by the Magistrate Judge, or another identified judicial action, and identifies any order or instruction by date and docket citation or by its operative terms; (2) clarifies how that action was understood, when ECF No. 108 issued, to relate to the scheduling order, the initial pretrial conference, the Rule 26(f) conference, and the discovery-plan report, and whether ECF No. 108 was intended only to deny the requested orders without prejudice or also to recognize or direct postponement of the planning steps requested in ECF No. 105; (3) corrects the identified passage by stating replacement language only if the existing text fails to express the determination actually intended on October 29, 2026; and (4) leaves the denial without prejudice of ECF Nos. 103 and 105 unchanged, creates no new obligation, and resolves no separately filed application.

The Order attributes a decision to the District Judge and applies it to the requests before the Court. Rule 60(a), as the Fourth Circuit construes it, permits the issuing judge to confirm that the text expresses that determination and to conform the text if it does not. Plaintiff requests that order, with the denial unchanged.

Date: November 1, 2026		                      Respectfully submitted,

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847

Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

PLAINTIFF’S RULE 201 REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine requests under Federal Rule of Evidence 201(c)(2) that the Court take judicial notice of the existence, filing date, signatories, and text of one court record: ECF No. 152 in Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL (N.D. Cal.). A complete copy of ECF No. 152 is attached as Exhibit A. A Memorandum in Support accompanies this Request.

I.	GROUNDS

1.	Federal Rule of Evidence 201(b)(2) permits the Court to notice a fact that “can be accurately and readily determined from sources whose accuracy cannot reasonably be questioned.” Rule 201(c)(2) provides that the Court “must take judicial notice if a party requests it and the court is supplied with the necessary information.” Rule 201(d) provides that the Court “may take judicial notice at any stage of the proceeding.”

2.	Exhibit A is a complete copy of ECF No. 152 as filed in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California. Each of its 25 pages bears that court’s electronic filing header, including “Case 3:26-cv-05939-RFL Document 152 Filed 08/13/26” and a page number. Citations to Exhibit A are to the page numbers in that header.

3.	ECF No. 152 is pleaded in the proposed Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint. ECF No. 59-1 ¶¶ 164–169. It is described in the memorandum supporting that pleading. ECF No. 60 at 9. Leave to file that pleading was denied. ECF No. 84 at 2. Plaintiff’s objections and motions concerning that denial are pending. ECF Nos. 89, 90, 93. Plaintiff’s motion for leave to amend, filed separately, attaches a Proposed Second Amended Complaint that also pleads ECF No. 152. Proposed Second Am. Compl. ¶¶ 180–185.

II.	FACTS TO BE NOTICED

4.	Plaintiff requests notice of the following five facts, and no others.

(a)	Existence and date. A document was filed on August 13, 2026 in Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL (N.D. Cal.), and docketed as ECF No. 152. Ex. A at 1–25 (header).

(b)	Title. ECF No. 152 is titled “Defendants Meta Platforms, Inc., Accenture LLP, Genpact Limited, and TaskUs, Inc.’s Consolidated Motion to Dismiss Plaintiff’s Second Amended Complaint Pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6); Memorandum of Points and Authorities.” Ex. A at 1.

(c)	Signatories. ECF No. 152 is signed “/s/ Michelle L. Visser” for Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP as “Attorneys for Defendants Meta Platforms, Inc. and Genpact Limited,” and is dated August 13, 2026. Ex. A at 3, 24. It is also signed “/s/ Devin S. Anderson” of Kirkland & Ellis LLP as “Attorneys for Defendant Accenture LLP” and “/s/ Kristin C. Christensen” of Ogletree, Deakins, Nash, Smoak & Stewart, P.C. as “Attorneys for Defendants TASKUS, INC.” Ex. A at 25; see also id. at 3 (Anderson signature).

(d)	Text of footnote 3. ECF No. 152 contains a footnote numbered 3. It begins on ECF page 11 of 25 (internal page 3) and ends on ECF page 12 of 25 (internal page 4). Its text reads:

“Beyond the claims raised in this action, Plaintiff has also filed several different actions in other courts raising baseless claims against some combination of the Defendants. These actions include: (1) a defamation action against Meta and counsel for Accenture based on arguments in Accenture’s Motion to Dismiss in Plaintiff’s original N.D. Cal. Action (Ballentine v. Accenture LLP, et al., No. 5:26-cv-472 (M.D. Fla.)), which the district court dismissed based on Plaintiff’s ‘failure to comply with the Standing Order’ regarding the disclosure of the use of artificial intelligence and Plaintiff’s ‘inability to certify compliance with Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure,’ Order, Ballentine v. Accenture LLP, et al., No. 5:26-cv-472 (M.D. Fla. July 24, 2026), Dkt. No. 80; (2) a Florida state court action raising both the civil rights claims raised in this action and Plaintiff’s defamation claims (Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al., No. 5:26-cv-213 (M.D. Fla.), removed from No. 35-2026-CA-000494 (Cir. Ct. Lake Cnty.)); and (3) most recently, a complaint against the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) and its corporate counsel in the Eastern District of Virginia based on allegedly defamatory language in a letter sent by NCMEC to Plaintiff in response to a subpoena (Ballentine v. Katie Hall, et al., No. 1:26-cv-2331 (E.D. Va.)).”

Ex. A at 11–12.

(e)	Reference to this action. Footnote 3 identifies this action by name and case number: “Ballentine v. Katie Hall, et al., No. 1:26-cv-2331 (E.D. Va.).” Ex. A at 12.

III.	LIMITS OF THE REQUEST

5.	Plaintiff does not request notice that any statement in ECF No. 152 is true. Plaintiff does not request notice of any purpose, motive, or state of mind of any signatory. Plaintiff does not request notice that any characterization of this action contained in footnote 3 is accurate. The request is confined to the fact that ECF No. 152 exists, the date it was filed, who signed it, and what it says.

IV.	RELIEF

6.	Plaintiff requests an order taking judicial notice of the five facts stated in Paragraph 4. Plaintiff requests that the noticed facts be available for consideration in connection with ECF Nos. 89, 90, and 93, Plaintiff’s motion for leave to amend, and any other matter in which the Court considers the allegations at ECF No. 59-1 ¶¶ 164–169 or Proposed Second Am. Compl. ¶¶ 180–185. In the alternative, Plaintiff requests an order taking judicial notice of the facts stated in Paragraph 4(a), (b), (c), and (e). A proposed order accompanies this Request.

Date: November 1, 2026		                      Respectfully submitted,

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847

Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503

jayballentine@protonmail.com

1.	Plaintiff’s Rule 201 Request for Judicial Notice, with its Certificate of Service, Local Civil Rule 83.1(N) Certification, and Generative Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Citation Certification;

Counsel of record for Defendants National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, Katie Hall, and Meta Platforms, Inc. are registered users of the Court’s Case Management/Electronic Case Filing (CM/ECF) system. Upon the Clerk’s docketing of the submission, the CM/ECF system will transmit a Notice of Electronic Filing to each of them, and service will be made through that means under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 5(b)(2)(E). EDSS submission is not itself service.

Date: November 1, 2026

Plaintiff, pro se

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S RULE 201 REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE

Plaintiff asks the Court to notice one court record for what it is and what it says. The record is ECF No. 152 in Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL (N.D. Cal.), filed August 13, 2026 and attached as Exhibit A. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to accept any statement in it as true.

I.	RULE 201 REQUIRES NOTICE OF A COURT RECORD WHOSE EXISTENCE AND TEXT ARE NOT SUBJECT TO REASONABLE DISPUTE

Federal Rule of Evidence 201(b)(2) permits the Court to notice a fact that “can be accurately and readily determined from sources whose accuracy cannot reasonably be questioned.” Rule 201(c)(2) provides that the Court “must take judicial notice if a party requests it and the court is supplied with the necessary information.” Rule 201(d) provides that notice may be taken “at any stage of the proceeding.” Plaintiff has requested notice. Exhibit A supplies the information.

The Fourth Circuit has stated that “[t]he most frequent use of judicial notice of ascertainable facts is in noticing the content of court records.” Colonial Penn Ins. Co. v. Coil, 887 F.2d 1236, 1239 (4th Cir. 1989) (quoting 21 C. Wright & K. Graham, Federal Practice and Procedure: Evidence § 5106, at 505 (1977)). The same opinion recognized that “federal courts, in appropriate circumstances, may take notice of proceedings in other courts, both within and without the federal judicial system, if those proceedings have a direct relation to matters at issue.” Id. (quoting St. Louis Baptist Temple, Inc. v. FDIC, 605 F.2d 1169, 1172 (10th Cir. 1979)). Colonial Penn applied those principles on appeal, to state-court guilty pleas entered after the district court’s judgment. Id. at 1239–40. A filing on a federal docket, bearing that court’s electronic filing header on every page, is a court record of the same kind.

Exhibit A is that record. Each of its 25 pages carries the header “Case 3:26-cv-05939-RFL Document 152 Filed 08/13/26.” Its first page states its title. Its signature pages identify its signatories and their clients. Its footnote 3 appears at ECF pages 11–12. The existence, date, signatories, and text of ECF No. 152 can be determined from the face of the document. Those facts are not subject to reasonable dispute.

II.	THE REQUEST IS CONFINED TO EXISTENCE, DATE, AUTHORSHIP, AND TEXT

The Fourth Circuit has stated that whether a fact may be considered under Rule 201 at the pleading stage “depends on the manner in which a court uses this information.” Zak v. Chelsea Therapeutics Int’l, Ltd., 780 F.3d 597, 607 (4th Cir. 2015). This Request fixes that manner in advance. Plaintiff asks the Court to notice that ECF No. 152 was filed on August 13, 2026, that it bears the title stated in Exhibit A, that it was signed by the counsel identified at Exhibit A pages 3, 24, and 25, that footnote 3 reads as quoted in the Request, and that footnote 3 names this action by case number. Request ¶ 4(a)–(e).

Plaintiff does not ask the Court to notice that any statement in footnote 3 is true. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to notice why the footnote was written or what any signatory intended. Request ¶ 5. Notice of what a filing says is different from acceptance of what it asserts. The Request asks for the first and disclaims the second.

III.	THE NOTICED FACTS BEAR ON PENDING MATTERS

ECF No. 152 is pleaded in the proposed Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint. ECF No. 59-1 ¶¶ 164–169. Paragraph 165 quotes the portion of footnote 3 that describes this action. ECF No. 59-1 ¶ 165. The supporting memorandum identifies the filing by court, case number, docket entry, and footnote. ECF No. 60 at 9. Leave to file that pleading was denied. ECF No. 84 at 2. Plaintiff’s objections and motions concerning that denial remain pending. ECF Nos. 89, 90, 93. Plaintiff’s motion for leave to amend, filed separately, attaches a Proposed Second Amended Complaint that also pleads ECF No. 152. Proposed Second Am. Compl. ¶¶ 180–185. The Court’s ability to compare the pleaded quotation with the source record serves the determination of those motions.

Meta and NCMEC have invoked the same mechanism in this action. Meta’s memorandum states that, on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, a court may consider “matters of which the court may take judicial notice.” ECF No. 22 at 8 (citations and internal quotation marks omitted). NCMEC’s memorandum states that this Court “may take judicial notice” of a proposition about subpoena practice. ECF No. 11 at 6. Plaintiff asks for less. Plaintiff asks the Court to notice a court record for its existence, date, signatories, and text.

IV.	CONCLUSION

Rule 201(c)(2) is mandatory where a party requests notice and supplies the necessary information. Plaintiff has done both. The Court should take judicial notice of the five facts stated in Paragraph 4 of the Request. In the alternative, the Court should take judicial notice of the facts stated in Paragraph 4(a), (b), (c), and (e).

Date: November 1, 2026		                      Respectfully submitted,

Marvelle J. Ballentine

Plaintiff, pro se

1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847

Alexandria, Virginia 22307

(407) 794-6503

jayballentine@protonmail.com

15   III.    LEGAL STANDARD
16           To survive a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), a complaint must include “sufficient
17   factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Nayab v.
18   Cap. One Bank (USA), N.A., 942 F.3d 480, 495–96 (9th Cir. 2019) (quoting Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556
19   U.S. 662, 678 (2009)). “The plausibility standard … asks for more than a sheer possibility that a
20   defendant has acted unlawfully.” Id. at 496. Although well-pleaded factual allegations are assumed
21   to be true, “the court is not required to accept as true allegations that are merely conclusory,
22   unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.” Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.,
23   899 F.3d 988, 1008 (9th Cir. 2018) (citation modified). And while pro se pleadings are construed
24   “liberally,” a pro se plaintiff must still allege “factual matter” sufficient “to state a claim to relief
25   that is plausible on its face.” Johnson v. Lucent Techs., Inc., 653 F.3d 1000, 1010–11 (9th Cir.
26   2011) (citation omitted). Where an amended complaint “omits previously-pled material information
27   that harms Plaintiff’s case,” the Court may consider the prior pleadings because the allegations are
28   “appropriately characterized as judicial admissions.” Jackson v. Loews Hotels, Inc., No. ED CV

 6          Plaintiff’s claim fails as a matter of law. First and foremost, Plaintiff’s claim is barred by
 7   Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act because it seeks to hold Defendants liable for a
 8   protected publication decision. Plaintiff cannot circumvent that bar by conspicuously replacing his

10   allegations that Defendants interrupted his ability to perform third-party contracts. Further,
11   Plaintiff’s claim also fails for the independent reason that he does not plead any facts that plausibly
12   support his assertion that Defendants acted because of his race, as Section 1981 requires. And the
13   SAC fails as to each of the Vendor Defendants because it improperly asserts claims against the

17          A.      Plaintiff’s Claims Against Each Defendant Are Barred By Section 230
18          Plaintiff’s SAC fails because it is barred in its entirety by Section 230(c)(1) of the
19   Communications Decency Act (“CDA”), 47 U.S.C. § 230. Section 230(c)(1) states that “[n]o
20   provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of
21   any information provided by another information content provider.” 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1). Section
22   230(e)(3) further states that “[n]o cause of action may be brought and no liability may be imposed
23   under any State or local law that is inconsistent with this section.” 47 U.S.C. § 230(e)(3). The Ninth
24   Circuit has accordingly held that, under Section 230(c)(1), an interactive computer service provider
25   or user cannot be held liable for removing content published on its services by a third party. See
26   Fair Hous. Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommates.com, LLC, 521 F.3d 1157, 1170–71 (9th
27   Cir. 2008) (“[A]ny activity that can be boiled down to deciding whether to exclude material that
28   third parties seek to post online is perforce immune under section 230.”). And where it is apparent

 3   230); Elansari v. Meta, Inc., No. 22-3060, 2024 WL 163080, at *1–2 (3d Cir. Jan. 16, 2024)
 4   (recognizing that Section 230 bars claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 alleging that Meta disabled
 5   accounts for racially discriminatory reasons).
 6           Accordingly, all three requirements of Section 230 are met, and Plaintiff’s claim should be
 7   dismissed in its entirety with prejudice.
 8           B.     Plaintiff Cannot Plead Around Section 230 in His SAC by Omitting Material
 9                  Allegations from the FAC
             The Court should consider Plaintiff’s allegations in the FAC in construing the allegations
10
     in the SAC. In an apparent attempt to creatively plead around the application of Section 230 to bar
11
     his claim, the SAC omits several material allegations necessary to understand Plaintiff’s factual
12
     allegations. In particular, the SAC bases Plaintiff’s entire case on (1) a “Notice” he allegedly
13
     received from Meta on July 4, 2022, which purportedly interrupted his ability to perform third-
14
     party contracts through Facebook; and (2) a Vendor Defendant’s alleged decision to uphold the
15
     Notice on appeal. But the SAC is silent on the content of the alleged Notice, and for obvious
16
     reasons. The FAC clearly alleges that the Notice informed Plaintiff that Meta had disabled his
17
     account for violating Meta’s CSE policy and, when Plaintiff tried to appeal the account
18
     disablement, an unnamed Vendor Defendant upheld it. FAC ¶¶ 54–57. Because claims based on
19
     such account disablement decisions are squarely barred by Section 230, each Defendant moved to
20
     dismiss the FAC in its entirety under Section 230. Plaintiff responded by trying to excise all
21
     references to the account disablement and Meta’s CSE policy from his SAC. But removing
22
     allegations from an amended complaint does not “simply erase those allegations from the case[,]”
23
     and the court “may consider” Plaintiff’s original “allegations as part of its context-specific inquiry
24
     into whether the [SAC] plausibly suggests an entitlement to relief . . . .” In re YogaWorks, Inc. Sec.
25
     Litig., No. CV 18-10696, 2020 WL 2549290, at *3 (C.D. Cal., Apr. 23, 2020) (citation modified);
26
     see also Cole, 2010 WL 532428, at *4 (same).
27
             Similarly, whereas the FAC plainly alleged that Plaintiff “market[ed] his RV repair business
28

                                                                   DEFS’ MOT. TO DISMISS SECOND AM. COMPL.
                                                      10                              NO. 3:26-CV-5939-RFL

Case 3:26-cv-05939-RFL         Document 152         Filed 08/13/26      Page 19 of 25



 1   on Facebook” (FAC ¶ 53), the SAC now omits any reference to content posted by Plaintiff through
 2   his Facebook account, instead referring to the Facebook account only as “the instrument through
 3   which Plaintiff performed [] third-party contracts.” SAC ¶ 30. Again, this omission is a blatant
 4   attempt to evade the application of Section 230, which, as set forth above, applies when the
 5   plaintiff’s claims treat the defendant as the publisher or speaker of content that the defendant itself
 6   did not provide.
 7          As a result of these omissions, the SAC, if considered alone, presents an incomplete and
 8   confusing picture of Plaintiff’s factual allegations and obscures Plaintiff’s allegations that his
 9   Facebook account was disabled and that he advertised his business on his Facebook account.
10   Because the SAC omits key factual allegations necessary to understand Plaintiff’s claims, and does
11   not explain the omissions or contradict those prior allegations, the Court should consider the FAC’s
12   factual allegations to properly evaluate Plaintiff’s allegations and claim in the SAC. See, e.g., J.
13   Edwards Jewelry Distrib., LLC v. Wells Fargo & Co., No. 18-cv-03886, 2019 WL 2329248, at *4
14   (N.D. Cal. May 31, 2019) (holding that the “fact that Plaintiff has now eliminated these allegations
15   and this exhibit from its SAC does not impact the Court’s analysis” because the “‘Court does not
16   ignore the prior allegations in determining the plausibility of current pleadings.’” (quoting
17   Stanislaus Food Prods., Co. v. USS-POSCO Indus., 782 F. Supp. 2d 1059, 1075 (E.D. Cal. 2011))).
18          Plaintiff’s attempt to creatively plead around Section 230 in his SAC by omitting prior
19   allegations about the advertising content posted on his Facebook account and by framing the alleged
20   disablement of his Facebook account simply as the sending of a “Notice” that interrupted his ability
21   to perform contracts and access his account-resident property therefore does not change the
22   outcome. See Lee v. Fin. Recovery Servs., No. 5:24-cv-00861, 2024 WL 5439275, at *2 (C.D. Cal.
23   Nov. 14, 2024) (noting that plaintiff “cannot … avoid dismissal simply by eliminating
24   allegations … especially where she fails to explain why she decided to omit such adverse facts in
25   the amended complaint”). No matter how Plaintiff frames his allegations, at bottom, Plaintiff’s
26   claim is premised on Meta’s alleged decision to disable Plaintiff’s Facebook account and an
27

28

                                                       11                             NO. 3:26-CV-5939-RFL

Case 3:26-cv-05939-RFL         Document 152         Filed 08/13/26      Page 20 of 25



 1   unnamed Vendor Defendant’s decision to uphold that disablement.6 Courts have rejected similar
 2   attempts to “circumvent the CDA’s protections through ‘creative’ pleading.” Kimzey v. Yelp! Inc.,
 3   836 F.3d 1263, 1265–66 (9th Cir. 2016) (affirming dismissal of complaint under Section 230,
 4   rejecting plaintiff’s “artful skirting” of Section 230 based on plaintiff’s “apparent[] hope[] to plead
 5   around the CDA to advance the same basic argument that the statute plainly bars”); see also Barnes,
 6   570 F.3d at 1102 (noting that, for purposes of Section 230 immunity, “what matters is whether the
 7   cause of action inherently requires the court to treat the defendant as the ‘publisher or speaker’ of
 8   content provided by another”).
 9          C.      Plaintiff Fails to State a Claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1981
10          Even beyond the deficiencies described above, Plaintiff’s claim still fails as a matter of law.
11   To state a claim under § 1981, a plaintiff must “allege (1) he is a member of a protected class, (2)
12   he attempted to contract for certain services, and (3) he was denied … the right to make or enforce
13   a contract.” Knight v. Wells Fargo Bank N.A., 459 F. Supp. 3d 1288, 1291 (N.D. Cal. 2019).
14   “Because claims brought under § 1981 are grounded in the Equal Protection Clause of the
15   Fourteenth Amendment, an ‘essential element’ of a valid § 1981 action is that the defendant ‘acted
16   with the intent to discriminate on the basis of race.’” Floyd v. Saber Fitness Hegenberger, LLC,
17   No. 24-cv-01278, 2024 WL 2971669, at *7 (N.D. Cal. June 11, 2024) (emphasis omitted) (quoting
18   McKenzie v. City of Milpitas, 738 F. Supp. 1293, 1301 (N.D. Cal. 1990)). “Thus, to establish a
19   claim under § 1981, the plaintiff must show overt acts by the defendant, ‘coupled with some direct
20   evidence that the defendant’s conduct was motivated by racial animus.’” Id. (citation omitted).
21   “Mere conclusory allegations of intentional discrimination will not suffice.” Gray v. Apple Inc.,
22   No.16-cv-04421, 2017 WL 1709327, at *3 (N.D. Cal. May 3, 2017) (citation omitted).
23          Plaintiff fails to sufficiently plead a § 1981 claim because he does not plead any facts that
24   plausibly support his assertion that Meta disabled his Facebook account or that any of the Vendor
25   Defendants upheld the disablement because of his race. To the contrary, the SAC’s assertion that
     6
26     Even if the Court does not interpret the SAC’s vague allegations of a Notice that interrupted
     Plaintiff’s ability to perform contracts against the backdrop of the SAC, which makes clear Plaintiff
27   is referring to Meta’s disablement of his Facebook account, other allegations in the SAC clarify
     that this is what Plaintiff is referring to. For example, the purported “Comparator” allegations show
28   that underlying conduct involved alleged account suspensions and “return[s] to account access.”
     SAC ¶¶ 61-62.
